articles.title: Ethereum: cómo se ha movido en el mercado este jueves
articles.text:
Ether, comúnmente llamada como ethereum, es la moneda digital #2 en cuanto a términos de capitalización de mercado, por lo que se trata de una de las divisas digitales que más despierta el interés entre los mineros (creadores de las criptodivisas).
Ethereum es una plataforma de blockchain de código abierto que se ejecuta con el uso de su moneda nativa, llamada ether o ETH, por lo que a pesar de que la gente usa estos nombres como sinónimos son cosas distintas.
Ether es un token que se utiliza específicamente en la blockchain ethereum para pagar transacciones. Este token es responsable de impulsar casi todo lo que ocurre en la red, misma que puede ser usada por cualquier persona para crear y ejecutar contratos inteligentes, que son programas de software que se ejecutan de manera autónoma y sin la intervención del usuario.
De acuerdo con el portal de Binance, la moneda digital solana actualmente cuenta con 122.2M de unidades creadas.
La cotización de ethereum para este día a las 14:05 horas (UTC) es de 2010.09 dólares, es decir, que la criptomoneda tuvo un cambio de -2.15 % en el último día.
Por otro lado, registró un cambio de 0.0 % con respecto a su valor hace una hora. En cuanto a su popularidad, se ubica en la posición #2.
Cotización de la criptomoneda Ethereum
Ethereum y su última actualización
Tras varios meses de retraso y con el temor de que ya nunca pasaría, finalmente el 15 de septiembre de 2022 Ethereum llevó a cabo su tan ansiada fusión o actualización al nuevo nivel 2.0 con la promesa de mejorar la experiencia de los usuarios de esta criptomoneda.
“The Merge”, inglés para “La Fusión”, es una transformación en la forma en que Ethereum procesa las transacciones y en cómo se crean nuevos tokens de Ether.
Esta fusión se trata de la combinación de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum con una nueva cadena de bloques separada conocido como proof-of-stake, el cual reduce el consumo de energía de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum en un 99,9 %, según sus propios desarrolladores, lo que la vuelve más “amigable” con el ambiente al tiempo que las transacciones serían más baratas.
Sus defensores creen que la fusión hará que Ethereum resulte favorecido con respecto al máximo rival, Bitcoin, pues podría aumentar su uso.
En el proceso Proof Stake los propietarios de Ether bloquearán cantidades establecidas de sus criptomonedas para verificar nuevos registros en la cadena de bloques, ganando nuevas monedas además de su criptografía “participada”.

articles.title: Connecting AI to the Physical World - EE Times
articles.text:
Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly. Models are becoming more capable, computing platforms more powerful, and tools for building intelligent applications more accessible. As AI moves into robots, industrial machines, vehicles, and drones, however, its progress depends on a practical question: How effectively can these systems obtain information from the physical world?
An intelligent machine needs more than processing power; it needs relevant data about its surroundings, the state of other machines, and the conditions in which it operates. Some information comes from its own sensors.
Other information must arrive from nearby devices, infrastructure, remote systems, or shared computing resources. The usefulness of that information depends on its quality, timing, and availability.
This creates an important opportunity for wireless technology. AI can make use only of information that devices can capture, process, and deliver. When the connection is unreliable, inflexible, or unsuitable for the environment, valuable information may arrive too late, lose essential context, or never reach the systems that need it.
The next stage of physical AI therefore requires progress in the devices and communications systems that connect intelligence to its surroundings. Software-defined radio (SDR) and the software intellectual property that makes it work have an important role to play.
Where standard modems fall short
Standard modems serve many applications well. Specialized systems may need capabilities or control interfaces that a particular modem does not expose. The relevant question is whether the device supports the behavior the application requires within its operating constraints.
A factory robot may need predictable, low-latency communication to coordinate with nearby machines. Inspection cameras may need substantial uplink capacity to send detailed images for analysis. A drone operating beyond terrestrial coverage may need a non-terrestrial link, while a remote sensor must conserve battery power.
Requirements can also change during a mission. A robot may alternate between coordinated movement and image collection. If infrastructure coverage becomes unavailable, an appropriately equipped system may exchange data through nearby devices. Each mode places different demands on capacity, delay, and energy use.
Designing AI processing and communications together helps manage these demands. A device can analyze routine observations locally, send short status updates, and upload detailed recordings when needed. This reduces unnecessary traffic and leaves more capacity for information that must arrive promptly.
Standard modems may support some of these needs, but developers often have limited access to the underlying communications software. If an application requires behavior beyond the modem’s supported features, configuration changes alone may not be enough.
This creates a development gap. AI software can evolve quickly, while adapting the wireless device may require changes to its signal processing, radio hardware, and system design, followed by extensive testing. SDR helps bridge this gap by giving developers more control over communications through software within the capabilities of the hardware.
Making wireless adaptable with SDR
3GPP standards define capabilities for various communications needs, including low-latency services, high data throughput, direct device-to-device (D2D) links, and non-terrestrial connectivity. A product must implement and integrate the relevant capabilities; their inclusion in a standard does not make them available on every platform due to business and use case constraints.
SDR implements key radio functions in programmable processing resources in software running on CPUs, DSPs, vector engines, or GPUs, supported by FPGAs and dedicated ASIC accelerators. Developers can configure and optimize those functions within the capabilities of the hardware and the requirements of the standards.
For example, a robot may need low latency when coordinating movement, more uplink capacity when uploading inspection images, and direct links when exchanging information with nearby robots. Supporting these changing needs requires an integrated software framework that manages the available communications features and resources.
Communications software IP supplies the algorithms, protocol implementation, and hardware integration that make this practical. Standards establish interoperable behavior; implementation choices influence the resources needed to deliver it. Reusable and validated software gives developers a starting point for product engineering and reduces the amount they must build themselves.
Using radio measurements to inform decisions
A programmable radio can also provide information about the conditions in which it operates. Link quality and interference measurements help explain whether a connection can support the application. With suitable hardware, signal processing, and system support, radio signals can also contribute to positioning and sensing.
These functions serve different purposes. Link measurements describe communications conditions; positioning estimates where devices are; sensing may detect movement or changes in the surroundings. Combining them can improve system decisions, but each capability needs its own implementation and validation.
In a network that supports relaying or mesh operation, routing decisions can take account of signal quality, delay, and available capacity. Position and movement information may help anticipate a weakening link. The system can then assess an alternative route before the current connection becomes unusable, where a suitable path exists.
Radio measurements are useful when they lead to an appropriate response. A device might change supported transmission settings, defer a large upload, or report that the requested service cannot be maintained. The response must reflect both the application’s priorities and the options available to the network.
This creates a feedback loop between the physical environment and communications behavior. SDR provides access to relevant measurements and controls; the wider software architecture determines how those inputs affect the application and network.
Connecting AI decisions with communications controls
The next step is to expose this feedback through application interfaces. An AI application can express what information it needs to exchange and its delivery requirements, while the communications software maps those requests to supported controls. This separates application intent from the details of radio implementation.
For example, a robot may request priority for coordination messages or additional capacity for inspection images. The framework can evaluate those requests against current resources, apply supported settings, and report the resulting service. A request for a particular performance level must be checked against what the system can deliver.
Information also flows back to the application. If a link degrades, the robot may reduce its upload rate, process more data locally or reconsider a task that depends on remote information. This makes network conditions part of mission planning rather than an assumption hidden from the application.
Vicinity’s communications software IP and integration expertise provide a foundation for developing these interfaces. The available functions depend on the selected platform and software implementation. Defined controls and tested operating limits help developers connect AI decisions to communications behavior without assuming unrestricted access to every radio function.
Developing both ends of the wireless link
Application interfaces alone cannot resolve every performance constraint. Some requirements depend on coordinated behavior between a terminal and its serving network. Vicinity’s experience across base stations, terminals, and direct D2D communications allows these dependencies to be considered together during system design.
Development begins with the customer’s information requirements and deployment conditions. What must be exchanged, how quickly, and over what coverage area? Which parts of the network can be controlled? The answers guide the choice of processing resources, radio design, and communications features.
Having expertise on both sides of the wireless link is valuable. Improving a terminal can be difficult when its requirements depend on infrastructure behavior that cannot be changed. Similarly, base-station enhancement may have limited value if the connected devices cannot support it. Where a deployment permits control of both ends, coordinated development creates more room to optimize the complete system.
Vicinity combines this system perspective with partners in silicon, baseband, RF, antennas, and core networks. Its work on 5G base stations and terminals, positioning, D2D communications, and non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) spans multiple 3GPP releases. This experience supports the selection and integration of capabilities appropriate to each customer’s product.
From prototype to commercial product
Turning a laboratory prototype into a commercial product requires careful engineering. The device must deliver the required wireless performance within practical limits on power consumption, cost, size, and heat while remaining reliable and easy to maintain.
Meeting these requirements depends on how efficiently the software uses the hardware. Open-source software offers flexibility, but adapting and optimizing it for different platforms can require substantial effort, particularly where processing capacity and power are limited.
Vicinity starts with the customer’s application and practical challenges, then tailors the software and system design around selected hardware platforms. Platform-specific optimization helps achieve the performance and efficiency needed for a viable product. This approach draws on Vicinity’s experience developing and deploying 5G base stations and terminals, including work on positioning, D2D communications, and NTNs across multiple 3GPP releases.
Validation then checks performance under representative operating conditions. Alongside throughput, testing examines latency and its variation, behavior during movement or interference, recovery after interruptions, and operation with multiple devices. Acceptance criteria should follow the application’s needs so that a successful test demonstrates useful performance in the intended setting.
After deployment, regression testing, version control, and careful feature integration support continued development. A receiver improvement may increase processor load, while a scheduling change may affect other traffic. Updates need to be assessed across the system so new capabilities preserve the behavior on which customers already rely.
Differentiations and ownership
This engineering foundation gives customers scope to build products around their own application expertise. They can integrate distinctive features, tailor supported wireless behavior, and develop system designs for particular operating environments. Differentiation comes from how these capabilities serve the customer’s market.
Customers retain ownership of their commercial products and control over their product roadmap. Access to and rights to modify the underlying communications software depend on the agreed licensing arrangement. Making that distinction clear helps align the development model with the customer’s plans for future changes and support.
Vicinity provides the communications IP and engineering support on which customers can build. Reusing that foundation supports a path to manufacturing and deployment at scale while leaving customers room to develop their own features and application value. The architecture and support model must also accommodate the intended product lifetime.
Connecting the next wave of AI
As AI moves further into the physical world, its value increasingly depends on timely information and reliable interaction with the systems around it. Robots, sensors, and autonomous devices need communications that support the conditions in which they operate, from factory floors to remote locations.
SDR helps meet this need by making wireless capabilities adaptable. Developers can tailor connectivity to their applications and evolve it as requirements change. Vicinity provides the communications software IP and platform expertise to turn that flexibility into commercial products.
Vicinity invites hardware partners, device manufacturers, AI developers, researchers, and system integrators to join its ecosystem. Partners can contribute platforms, applications, and deployment knowledge, while Vicinity contributes communications software IP and integration expertise.
A practical collaboration starts with a defined use case and measurable operating requirements. Partners can then select the required capabilities, validate them together, and develop a route to commercial production. This gives new physical AI applications a concrete path from an initial idea to products that can be deployed and supported at scale.

articles.title: I spent 8 days with an Apple HomeView in my kitchen and another on my wall — and they've made me reach for my iPhone less
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Apple's first smart display is a strong start. The HomeView combines a beautiful design, surprisingly powerful sound, thoughtful personalization, and a much smarter Siri into a device that fits naturally into everyday life. It's not perfect — third-party app support is limited, and some Siri requests still take longer than I'd like — but after eight days living with two HomeViews, I've found plenty to love. Most importantly, it's useful when I need it, and happily fades into the background when I don't.
Reasons to buy
- + Modern, thoughtful design with excellent clock faces
- + Excellent sound quality from the tabletop model
- + Personalized experiences and genuinely useful Siri AI
- + Seamless smart-home controls and FaceTime
Reasons to avoid
- - Limited third-party apps
- - Requires an iPhone to set up, with newer models needed for the full experience
- - Siri can be slow to respond to some requests
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Apple HomeView: Two-minute review
Apple's first smart display is a strong start, even if it's a somewhat strange first-generation product. The HomeView gets a lot right, from its distinctly Apple design and excellent audio to its personalized experience and genuinely useful Siri AI capabilities. And after eight days of living with two HomeViews, I really like what Apple has delivered.
First and foremost, though, the HomeView is for folks already invested in the Apple ecosystem. You'll need an iPhone to get the most out of it, and ideally an Apple Intelligence-enabled model to take full advantage of Siri AI and Personal Context. This integration is what makes the HomeView special, letting Siri find information in your messages, control your smart home, and surface personal content without you constantly having to reach for your phone.
The hardware is excellent, with a compact, premium design and a vibrant 7-inch display. I've been using the speaker-mounted 'countertop' HomeView in my kitchen, and the wall-mounted version in my entryway, and both fit naturally into my daily routine. I especially love the Photos clock face, which intelligently cycles through pictures of my dog Rosie, family, and friends.
Audio is another standout. The standard HomeView delivers surprisingly powerful bass, a wide soundstage, and enough volume to fill my kitchen and living room. Music support is so strong that I've actually been occasionally using it as my main speaker.
Siri AI is impressive, too, particularly when tapping into Personal Context, though it's not always the fastest. Simple smart-home requests are generally quick, while more complex tasks can take 10 to 15 seconds. Still, the ability to ask Siri to find a song a friend recommended in my messages and then play it is pretty neat.
There are some limitations, though. There's no App Store at launch, third-party apps are restricted, and video options are limited. While I'd have liked to see more flexibility, I suspect Apple's curated approach is intentional. HomeView feels designed to be a more mindful, ambient device that surfaces information when you need it rather than another screen constantly demanding your attention. That being said, I wouldn’t be shocked if, when WWDC 27 rolls around, a dedicated 'home' OS is announced, and the app experience opens up.
At $299 / £299 / AU$449, the HomeView certainly isn't cheap, but it also doesn't feel like an unfinished first-generation experiment. It's already great for FaceTime calls, quickly checking messages, playing music, controlling smart home devices, and displaying personalized clock faces. These are the kinds of everyday interactions that make it easy to appreciate having the HomeView around, rather than feeling like you're searching for reasons to use it.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Ultimately, the Apple HomeView feels like a natural companion to your iPhone, giving you a reason to leave it in your pocket rather than constantly reaching for it. It's a smart-home controller, digital photo frame, surprisingly capable speaker, and personal assistant rolled into one, but it's also perfectly happy just showing you the time or a favorite photo. It's not perfect, but Apple has delivered a thoughtful, genuinely useful first-generation product that feels like a very strong start, especially if you're already deep in its ecosystem.
- Value score: 4 / 5
Apple HomeView: Design
- Premium, distinctly Apple design with a vibrant 7-inch Liquid Retina display
- Two designs: tabletop and wall-mounted, with the same core features
- Excellent customizable clock faces
The HomeView comes in two distinct styles: standard and wall-mounted. The standard HomeView will likely be the more popular option, and features a square 7-inch Liquid Retina display with soft, rounded corners that sits on an arm extending from a domed, circular base.
It's smaller than you might expect, and pretty cute. It comes in four colors: Starlight, Space Gray, Rose Pink, and Silver. I've been testing Starlight, which looks like an airy gold or more silver depending on how the light hits it. Apple also includes a color-matched USB-C cable and wall adapter, making physical setup straightforward.
The design is distinctly Apple, with a premium aluminum build combining brushed finishes and polished accents, particularly around the hinge connecting the display to the base. At first glance, it's almost like an oversized Apple Watch — perhaps an earlier generation thanks to the fairly thick bezels. There's also a bit of the iconic, potted-plant-like iMac G4 in its DNA, and I quite like that.
The display can tilt up or down, but not left or right. For that, you'll need to manually turn the entire HomeView, though the rubberized bottom, similar to a HomePod or HomePod mini, keeps it firmly planted. And while it’s easy enough to turn it left or right with the display, a swivel mechanism built in here would have made this more seamless.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
I've been testing the standard HomeView in my apartment, where the kitchen flows right into the living space, and I've found a natural home for it on my kitchen island. Thanks to its compact size, I can easily slide it around or turn it to face wherever I am, whether I'm making coffee, cooking dinner, or hopping on a FaceTime call. Center Stage does a good job of keeping me in frame, but it can only follow me so far before I need to turn the display manually. A motorized arm would be pretty dope, and I'm holding out hope for one in a future generation.
The 7-inch Liquid Retina display looks great, with clear text, vibrant photos, and plenty of brightness, though its glossy finish can still catch reflections even when the brightness is cranked up, and I would be surprised if Nano-Texture or a similar coating might be ushered in a future generation.
Apple says it can dim down to just 0.3 nits, the lowest of any display in its lineup, which is likely handy for bedrooms and helps ensure it’s not glowing in the middle of the night or in dimmer conditions. It's excellent for displaying photos, album artwork, or lyrics in Apple Music, and I've never had an issue reading text.
It's also noticeably thicker than an iPad or even Apple's now touch-enabled MacBook Pro, though that's understandable given everything packed inside. Above the display sits a 12-megapixel Ultra Wide camera, while tiny microphone openings are dotted around the frame, including near the camera, along the sides, and on the rear. You won't find any physical buttons or a camera shutter, though, as Apple is betting almost entirely on touch and voice. The only port is USB-C for power.
The base is where much of the audio hardware lives, with dozens of precisely drilled holes around its lower half. There are two full-range drivers built into the display section, while the base houses a downward-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators. I'll dig deeper into sound quality below, but it's surprisingly robust for something this small, with plenty of low-end punch without causing HomeView to vibrate excessively or topple over.
Overall, HomeView feels a good bit more premium than older Echo smart displays or Google's Nest Hub, though it takes a markedly different approach from Amazon's newer Echo Show 8, 11, and forthcoming Echo Show 16. It fits neatly into Apple's broader design ethos, even if the colors, somewhat ironically, don't necessarily match those of the HomePod or HomePod mini.
I've also been testing the second version, which Apple calls HomeView (Wall Mounted). While the standard model is more versatile, there's a lot to like about having Apple's smart display permanently positioned on a wall.
Unboxing is considerably simpler, as you're essentially getting just the display, without the arm or speaker base. On the back is a USB-C port, which is designed to work with compatible mounts, including those from Schneider Electric, which were developed specifically for HomeView.
Importantly, you're not sacrificing the core experience. The wall-mounted version has the same processor, display, cameras, sensors, and software as the tabletop model. The biggest hardware difference is audio, handled by two custom drivers rather than the more elaborate speaker system in the standard HomeView. It's by no means tinny and still offers a surprisingly wide soundstage, but there's less oomph, particularly in the low end.
I suspect most folks opting for the wall-mounted model will want to wire it directly into the wall for the cleanest possible look. But as a renter, I went with Schneider Electric's USB-C wall mount, and it was one of the simplest mounting experiences I've had with a smart home device. Two drilled holes, anchors, screws, and probably less than 15 minutes later, it was on the wall. From there, I connected the lengthy USB-C cable to a power adapter, which you'll need to supply yourself.
I've been using the wall-mounted HomeView in my entryway, and it's a great fit. Walking in to see photos of my pup Rosie, my nieces, or family and friends is a lovely touch, while the customizable Smart Home face turns it into a central control panel. I'll dig into that experience, including some surprisingly useful features, more below.
Ultimately, the standard HomeView likely offers better overall value thanks to its more powerful audio system and flexibility to move between rooms. But the wall-mounted version feels especially well suited to an entryway, kitchen, or another central location where you want information and smart home controls available at a glance. Both feel thoughtfully designed, and Apple has delivered two distinct approaches to what a smart home display can look like.
- Design score: 4 / 5
Apple HomeView: Performance
- Siri AI and Personal Context deliver genuinely useful, personalized experiences
- Excellent sound quality, responsive smart home controls, and impressive FaceTime performance
- Limited third-party apps and streaming options, and complex Siri requests can be slow
I've been living with two HomeViews for eight days, with one serving me well on the entryway wall of my apartment, and the other primarily living in my kitchen. The standard model has also spent some time in my office and even the bedroom, and I've been putting both through their paces.
HomeView is built around your iPhone, and that tight integration is central to the experience. You'll also want an Apple Intelligence-enabled model to get the most out of Siri AI and Personal Context. Thankfully, it all works quite well.
I've used HomeView for everything from music and FaceTime calls to smart home controls, checking messages, and displaying photos. I've even watched some Apple TV, though it's hardly the ideal screen for that.
Setup feels familiar if you've ever paired an Apple Watch or AirPods with an iPhone. Plug HomeView in, wait for it to boot up and say hello, then bring your iPhone nearby. From there, you scan a graphic to pair the devices and follow a few steps, including choosing who you're setting it up for.
HomeView is designed to be communal, sitting in a shared space where multiple people can use it, but also personal when the situation calls for it. It supports up to six registered users, and adding someone starts on HomeView before handing the process over to their iPhone. They'll also need to be part of your Apple Home.
The personalization works particularly well. For instance, while I was viewing my messages, my dad walked into the camera's view, and HomeView immediately stopped showing my personal content until it could recognize me again. It's a clever safeguard, especially for a device that's meant to live in a shared space.
It does mean, though, that some items you’d think would be shared among users are missing. For example, there's no calendar — likely because it might contain confidential items, and Apple wants to make sure those are shown to a registered user. But that does mean the HomeView doesn’t offer a shared calendar like, say a Skylight or an Echo. One solution would be a shared calendar that is shared with each person (up to six) who is registered on the HomeView.
The HomeView runs custom software, not HomeViewOS, that borrows heavily from iOS and watchOS. The app grid, including its tint and customizable widgets, feels like iOS, while customizing the clock faces is more akin to watchOS, complete with complications. It's a bit of a Frankenstein-like approach, but it works.
And speaking of clock faces, they're one of my favorite parts of HomeView. Snoopy is especially delightful, with custom-designed artwork and animations separate from what you'll find on Apple TV. You can even tap Snoopy to trigger an animation, which is an adorable little touch.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The Photos face is equally impressive, and really shows how personal HomeView can feel. You can select people, places, or pets, and HomeView will intelligently surface and cycle through relevant photos. I chose my dog Rosie during setup, and I love seeing different photos of her throughout the day. You can even tap the screen to see when and where a particular photo was taken.
I could easily see HomeView being a great gift for parents or family members for this feature alone, especially since you can use a shared photo album as the source and have new photos appear as they're added. It turns what could have been a pretty ordinary clock face into something much more personal.
There's also the Modular face, which lets you customize the display with widgets and complications, putting useful information and controls front and center. Between that, Photos, and Snoopy, Apple has done an excellent job making the clock faces feel like more than just a way to tell the time.
In terms of responsiveness, HomeView generally feels quite snappy. Apple's A18 chip is under the hood, complete with the Secure Enclave, which plays an important role in the device's privacy protections. Apple handles processing on-device when possible, while more complex requests can be handled through Private Cloud Compute.
You'll still need your iPhone for the more personalized experiences, though, as HomeView draws on the content and apps connected to your device. And that's what enables some of its most impressive tricks.
For instance, I asked Siri which Dave Matthews Band song my friend Benjie wanted me hear. HomeView took a moment to think — probably around 10 to 15 seconds — while displaying updates at the top of the screen as it searched through my messages. It eventually came back with the answer: "Ants Marching."
I then asked Siri to play it, and since I have both Spotify and Nugs connected through my iPhone, it asked which service I wanted to use before starting playback.
It's an impressive interaction, even if Siri takes its time, and I appreciate seeing updates on what it's working on. I could also ask Siri to look at my calendar, find an event in the city, and figure out when I need to leave based on traffic. It's another multi-step request that isn't instantaneous, but it gets me to the answer.
Response times can vary quite a bit, though. When I asked Siri to play Ghosts by Bruce Springsteen, it took about 12 seconds before the song started playing through Apple Music, complete with album artwork on the display. A simpler request, like checking the weather in New York City, took closer to two or three seconds.
Smart home requests, thankfully, are considerably quicker. Asking Siri for the temperature in my apartment, pulling data from both HomeViews, multiple sensors, and my Nest thermostat, takes about two seconds, if not less. I can also quickly turn on my Philips Hue lights or adjust the temperature, and those everyday interactions have worked well.
Of course, you don't have to rely on Siri to control your smart home. The HomeView has a dedicated Home app that's similar to what you'll find on your iPhone or iPad, but it's the Home Modular clock face that really turns it into a smart home control panel, especially when wall-mounted. You can customize it with blocks showing key information, like the temperature or readings from connected sensors, alongside easy touch controls for lights, thermostats, and other smart home devices. Everything is in one place, and I've found it especially useful on the HomeView in my entryway, where I can quickly see what's happening around my apartment or make an adjustment without reaching for my iPhone.
You'll also find automations you've previously created in the Home app, but the HomeView takes things a step further by letting you create new ones simply by asking Siri. These can be single actions or more complex, multi-step routines. For instance, I asked Siri to create an automation that raises the smart blinds in my apartment and turns on the lights every morning at 6am. It handled the request, and just like that, I had a new morning routine without setting it up manually in the Home app.
The broader smart home ecosystem remains somewhat confusing, particularly around compatibility. HomeView works with Apple Home and supports Matter, with Thread connectivity built in, but there's no native Zigbee support. That doesn't rule out Zigbee devices connected through a compatible bridge, though. It's worked well with my existing devices — Philips Hue lights, Google Nest Learning Thermostat 4th Gen, Eve Cam, an Anker Eufy camera, and Ryse Shades — and Apple's own Home Collection is set to arrive in December. Still, it's worth checking which devices will actually integrate before making the jump.
I've also been impressed by the four integrated microphones, which reliably pick up my voice from across the room, even with music playing through a HomeView or the TV on in the background. That's particularly useful in my kitchen, where I can be making coffee or cooking dinner while asking Siri for information, controlling music, or making a FaceTime call without stopping what I'm doing.
FaceTime is another highlight. The 12-megapixel camera delivers good video quality, and Center Stage does a solid job keeping me in frame as I move around the kitchen, though it can only follow me within the camera's field of view.
On the wall-mounted HomeView in my entryway, I've also found myself asking Siri for directions, calendar updates, or simply what I've missed when getting home or starting the day. It's convenient to have that information available in a central location without pulling out my iPhone.
There's also a surprisingly useful Mirror feature, accessible through Control Center, which uses the built-in camera to show a live view of yourself. You can switch between 1x and 2x views, and while it's not something I'd necessarily buy a HomeView for, it's a neat addition for a device mounted near the front door. I've used it for a quick look before heading out.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Of course, the HomeView isn't an iPad, and Apple isn't trying to turn it into one. There's no App Store, and third-party app support is limited. Interestingly, Apple is leaning on CarPlay compatibility to bring select audio and video media apps to the HomeView.
I've been able to use Spotify, Nugs, Apple Music Classical, and SiriusXM, though what's available can change depending on whom HomeView recognizes, since it pulls from that person's profile and connected iPhone.
It's a curated experience, and I think that works well here. I get the sense it's meant to avoiding overwhelming you, or becoming another screen that's constantly demanding your attention. Instead, it's arguably Apple's first truly ambient device, designed to surface information when you need it and fade into the background when you don't. It doesn't even feature notifications except for Home alerts or when a call comes into your iPhone.
It's both touch- and voice-enabled, and Apple's mainstay apps are here, including Music, Podcasts, Safari, FaceTime, Calendar, Messages, Home, Intercom, Weather, Find My, Reminders, Alarms, Timers, World Clock, Audiobooks, Apple TV, and Settings. News is also part of the experience, though the selection is still more limited than what you'd find on an iPhone or iPad.
Although the HomeView has Apple TV built in, don't expect it to replace your television or even an iPad. There are no dedicated apps for YouTube, Disney+, Hulu, Peacock, or Netflix, though you can start a YouTube video on your iPhone and bring it close to your HomeView to hand off playback. And with a seven-inch display, substantial black bars, or a zoomed-in picture that crops the action, it's better suited to casual viewing while doing something else than settling in for a full TV episode or movie.
Audio is another major strength, particularly on the standard HomeView. For something so compact, the sound is seriously impressive, with a wide soundstage, remarkably strong bass, and enough volume to outdo the HomePod mini 2. It easily fills both my kitchen and adjoining living room with rich, robust audio, and I've actually found myself using it as my apartment's main speaker.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
At times, I've also grouped it with the wall-mounted HomeView for music playback across both spaces, and the experience works quite well. The tabletop model definitely has the advantage, though, with fuller sound and considerably more low-end punch. The wall-mounted version still sounds good for its size, but if music is a priority, the standard HomeView is absolutely the one I'd choose.
And while the HomeView is great for controlling my smart home, playing music, following recipes while cooking — especially with multiple pre-set timers — making FaceTime calls, and plenty more, I also appreciate that it doesn't constantly demand my attention. It doesn't make me want to reach for my iPhone, either. Sometimes, I just want to glance over to check the time, see the weather, or enjoy a photo of Rosie, and that's more than enough.
The HomeView is there when I need it and fades into the background when I don't, and I think that's a big part of its appeal.
- Performance score: 4 / 5
Apple HomeView: Specs
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Apple HomeView | Apple HomeView (Wall-Mounted) | 
| Display | 7-inch Liquid Retina display (LED 1088 x 1088) with TrueTone, 500-nits brightness limit. | 7-inch Liquid Retina display (LED 1088 x 1088) with TrueTone, 500-nits brightness limit. | 
| Processor | Apple A18 chip | Apple A18 chip | 
| Camera | 12-megapixel CenterStage Camera | 12-megapixel CenterStage Camera | 
| Connectivity | Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax) with MIMO, Bluetooth 6.0, and Thread | Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax) with MIMO, Bluetooth 6.0, and Thread | 
| Audio | Two custom full-range drivers, dual force-canceling passive radiators, and a single down-firing woofer | Two custom full-range drivers | 
| Sensors | Ambient light sensor, an accelerometer, and a combined temperature and humidity sensor | Ambient light sensor, an accelerometer, and a combined temperature and humidity sensor | 
| Power | 1.5m USB-C to USB-C cable and 30-watt plug included. | Not included. | 
| Size | 5.73 in x 5.38 - 6.82 in x 3.78 - 5.13 in // 145.5 mm x 136.7–173.2 mm x 96.0–130.3 mm | 5.73 in x 5.73 in x 0.39 in // 145.5 mm x 145.5 mm x 9.9 mm | 
| Weight | 952 grams (2.1 pounds) | 286 grams (0.63 pounds) | 
| Price | $299 / £299 / AU$499 | $299 / £299 / AU$499 | 
Apple HomeView: Pricing and Availability
Apple’s HomeView is currently up for preorder at $299 in the US, £299 in the UK, and AU$449 in Australia, and will officially launch — and begin shipping — November 13, 2026. The standard HomeView, which has a base to stand on its own and comes with a wall plug, comes in four colors: Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Gray.
There’s also the HomeView (Wall-Mounted) for the same price, available in Silver or Space Gray. With that, you’ll need to get a separate wall mount made by Schneider Electric, either one that ends with a USB-C port – a good option for renters – or an AC one, which requires proper installation.
Apple HomeView: Should I Buy?
Buy it if…
You've been waiting for Apple's smart display
It's been a long time coming, and the HomeView checks off many of the boxes you'd expect from a smart home hub. From music playback and quick access to Siri AI to smart home controls and a digital photo frame, Apple has delivered a strong first-generation product.
You want a communal screen for everyday tasks
The HomeView is excellent for those quick interactions throughout the day, whether that's checking messages, making a FaceTime call, controlling your lights, or glancing at the weather. And with personalized experiences for up to six users, it feels right at home in a shared space.
Apple HomeView: How I Tested
I spent eight days testing two Apple HomeViews in my apartment, with the standard model primarily living on my kitchen island and the wall-mounted version installed in my entryway. I also moved the standard HomeView into my office and bedroom to see how it worked in different spaces.
I used both devices throughout my daily routine, testing everything from Siri AI and Personal Context to smart home controls, music playback, FaceTime calls, messages, and customizable clock faces. I connected HomeView to my existing smart home devices, including Philips Hue lights, a Nest thermostat, and smart blinds, and tested how well it handled everyday requests and more complex tasks.
I also compared the HomeView to Amazon Echo Show and Google Nest Hub smart displays, along with several speakers, including the original HomePod mini, HomePod mini 2, second-generation HomePod, Sonos Move 2, and Sonos Era 100. I paid particular attention to audio quality, responsiveness, ease of use, and how naturally HomeView fit into my daily routine — including those moments when I wasn't actively interacting with it.
First reviewed November 2026.
Jacob Krol is the US Managing Editor, News for TechRadar. He’s been writing about technology since he was 14 when he started his own tech blog. Since then Jacob has worked for a plethora of publications including CNN Underscored, TheStreet, Parade, Men’s Journal, Mashable, CNET, and CNBC among others.
He specializes in covering companies like Apple, Samsung, and Google and going hands-on with mobile devices, smart home gadgets, TVs, and wearables. In his spare time, you can find Jacob listening to Bruce Springsteen, building a Lego set, or binge-watching the latest from Disney, Marvel, or Star Wars.

articles.title: Dacia tient peut-être son quatrième modèle électrique d’ici 2030 : un SUV à moins de 20 000 € inspiré du Renault Bridger
articles.text:
SUV électrique Dacia à petit prix : pourquoi le Renault Bridger pourrait arriver en Europe
Pour accélérer son électrification à moindre coût, Dacia envisagerait d’adapter le Renault Bridger en Europe, un petit SUV baroudeur initialement conçu pour le marché indien.
Avec des ventes en recul de 10 % depuis le début de l’année, Dacia peine à séduire malgré ses prix bas, impactée par l’offensive des marques chinoises et son retard sur l’électrique. Pour rattraper le coup, la firme roumaine ne dispose pour l’heure que de la nouvelle Spring électrique, en attendant l’arrivée des Sandero et Sandero Stepway en version électrifiée. Mais ce ne serait pas tout : le constructeur étudierait l’importation d’un modèle surprise sur le Vieux Continent, tout droit sorti de la gamme de SUV de Renault en Inde.
Un petit baroudeur né en Inde pour défier les Citroën ë-C3 et Fiat Grande Panda de Stellantis
Selon les informations d’Autocar, cette recrue inattendue serait le Renault Bridger. Dévoilé sous forme de concept en mars dernier, il s’agit d’un petit SUV cubique dans l’esprit du Suzuki Jimny qui dépasse tout juste les 4 mètres de long. Pensé au départ pour l’Inde et l’Amérique latine avec un lancement prévu dès 2027, il n’avait cependant pas vocation à rejoindre nos routes.
Pourtant, François Provost, PDG du groupe Renault, a glissé au Mondial de l’Automobile de Paris que ce véhicule “créé pour l’Inde” pourrait “un jour arriver sur nos marchés également”. En reprenant uniquement sa déclinaison électrique, Dacia s’offrirait un rival direct à des SUV compacts comme les Citroën ë-C3 et Fiat Grande Panda Electric. Deux concurrentes qui avaient d’ailleurs, elles aussi, été conçues d’abord pour les marchés émergents.
Côté tarifs, la marque viserait un prix de départ sous la barre des 20 000 €, pour une autonomie limitée entre 200 et 300 km. De quoi en refroidir plus d’un, qui pourrait voir en la Spring 2 un véhicule suffisant ou plutôt patienter jusqu’aux Sandero électriques en 2028 pour gagner en endurance et en dotation.
Ce Bridger rebadgé compléterait ainsi le plan de Dacia, qui prévoit quatre voitures électriques d’ici 2030 (en plus de sa micro-citadine Hipster). Aux côtés de la Spring et des futures Sandero et Sandero Stepway, il pourrait tout simplement prendre la place de la version électrique du Striker, finalement abandonnée.
Reste à produire ce baroudeur en Europe. En l’assemblant localement, Dacia profiterait des futurs bonus réglementaires européens (catégorie M1E), qui avantagent les petits modèles électriques de moins de 4,20 mètres dans le calcul des émissions de CO2.

articles.title: Exclusive: Menlo IRIS extension gives security teams control over AI use without a new browser - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Exclusive: Menlo IRIS extension gives security teams control over AI use without a new browser
Browser security company Menlo Security Inc. today launched the Menlo IRIS Browser Extension, a new offering that adds its enterprise browser security controls to the browsers employees already use with no need to switch them to separate secure ones.
Delivered as a centrally managed extension, Menlo IRIS is said to give security teams visibility into and control over generative artificial intelligence use, data movement, files and third-party extensions. Installation is claimed to take only hours, as no additional hardware is needed.
Chief Executive Bill Robbins, who took over the top job from co-founder Amir Ben-Efraim in February, said security teams have known for some time that the browser is a blind spot. Many have nonetheless held off on fixing it to avoid replacing an existing security stack, which typically means a big migration project, he added.
“Menlo IRIS removes those obstacles,” Robbins said. “Even a small team can get essential security running quickly on the browsers employees already use.”
To make its case, Menlo pointed to Verizon Communications Inc.’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, released in May, which found regular AI use on corporate devices tripled from 15% to 45% of employees in a single year. Some 67% of people accessing AI services on corporate devices were found to be using noncorporate accounts, with more than 15% of users at the average company also running unauthorized AI browser extensions.
Among the headline capabilities is an audit of third-party browser extensions. Menlo says the audit covers every extension installed across a company, with an enterprise-wide inventory, real-time risk profiling and management controls all included. Few security teams have a count of the extensions their users have installed, according to Menlo. The company also warned that an extension’s risk profile can change at any time without notice.
Data-loss controls cover the clipboard, printing, uploads and downloads, with watermarking, read-only pages, restrictions on developer tools and screenshot deterrence also included. Web filtering steers users toward sanctioned tools, including generative AI services, with limits on what data can be entered into them offered as an alternative to banning the tools outright.
File security is part of the package as well, with inline inspection for data loss prevention violations, viruses and malware. For customers that want it, content disarm and reconstruction can be switched on to strip malicious content from files so they remain usable. Also available as an add-on is HEAT Shield AI for protection against zero-day phishing, social engineering and malvertising at the time of the click.
Deployment is through the Chrome Web Store, Microsoft Intune, Jamf or other device management tools, with support for Chrome, Edge, Safari, Firefox and Chromium-based AI browsers. Since nobody has to switch browsers, security patches from each browser’s vendor are said to keep reaching users as normal.
Most controls are enforced inside the browser session itself, which the company says removes the need for a proxy to route traffic. Menlo IRIS is intended to sit alongside existing network and endpoint tools.
The Menlo IRIS Browser Extension is available now.
Menlo Security has raised $250 million in funding, including a $100 million round in November 2020. Investors in the company include Vista Equity Partners Management, JPMorgan Chase & Co., American Express Ventures and General Catalyst Group Management.

articles.title: Jensen Huang renuncia ao cargo de CEO da Nvidia após escândalos • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Jensen Huang renuncia ao cargo de CEO da Nvidia após escândalos
Cofundador deixa o comando da empresa após denúncias de casos extraconjugais e investigação sobre possível espionagem.
Jensen Huang renunciou ao cargo de CEO da Nvidia nesta quinta-feira (12/11), encerrando uma gestão de mais de três décadas à frente da fabricante de chips. A empresa anunciou que Colette Kress, atual diretora financeira, assumirá o comando interinamente enquanto busca um substituto permanente.
A saída ocorre em meio à repercussão de denúncias sobre relacionamentos extraconjugais do executivo e a uma investigação sobre a possibilidade de ele ter sido alvo de uma operação de espionagem estrangeira.
Aos 63 anos, Huang deixa o comando da empresa que ajudou a fundar em 1993 e que, sob sua liderança, se tornou uma das principais fornecedoras de chips para inteligência artificial do mundo.
Segundo o New York Times, cinco pessoas que trabalharam na fabricante relataram um suposto relacionamento entre Huang e a vice-presidente da área de saúde da Nvidia, Kimberly Powell, que responde diretamente ao CEO.
Powell trabalha na empresa desde 2008 e lidera iniciativas de computação acelerada e inteligência artificial voltadas à área médica. O possível relacionamento contraria as regras internas da companhia, que orientam os funcionários a evitar vínculos pessoais que possam interferir nas decisões profissionais.
No domingo (08/11), Huang reconheceu em uma mensagem aos funcionários que havia sido infiel à esposa e pediu desculpas à família e aos colegas. O pedido ocorreu após reportagens sobre o suposto relacionamento com a ex-executiva da Megaspeed Alice Huang. A empresa é sediada em Singapura e cliente da Nvidia.
Parlamentares dos Estados Unidos convocaram Huang para uma reunião em 18 de novembro, na qual deverá prestar esclarecimentos sobre suspeitas de espionagem industrial.
Segundo a imprensa americana, autoridades dos Estados Unidos investigam possíveis ligações de Alice com o serviço de inteligência da China. As suspeitas, no entanto, ainda não foram comprovadas, e não há confirmação de que informações sigilosas da Nvidia tenham sido compartilhadas.
Em comunicado, a Nvidia anunciou uma investigação para esclarecer se Huang foi alvo de uma operação de inteligência estrangeira e se informações confidenciais foram comprometidas. O conselho declarou ter confiança no CEO e afirmou não haver motivos para acreditar que segredos da empresa ou informações relacionadas à segurança nacional tenham sido expostos.
Acionistas processaram a Nvidia e seu CEO por supostamente omitirem riscos associados ao relacionamento extraconjugal.

articles.title: Verificar el código de Signal era un reto que llevaba años de trabajo de expertos. DeepMind dice que su IA lo ha hecho en un mes
articles.text:
Google DeepMind dice que sus agentes de IA han demostrado matemáticamente que partes clave del código que está detrás del protocolo de cifrado de Signal hacen lo que se supone que deben hacer. El protocolo protege las conversaciones privadas en Signal y Google Messages, y también sustenta el cifrado de WhatsApp, tal y como comparten en Wired. La compañía lo describe como un hito en la seguridad del software, aunque los propios investigadores recalcan que es un paso en un proceso más largo.
Comprobado, el protocolo funciona. La verificación formal significa usar matemáticas, en lugar de pruebas, para demostrar que el software se comporta como se pretende. Se considera la garantía de seguridad más sólida disponible, pero tradicionalmente ha sido lenta y laboriosa. La mayor parte de la verificación de protocolos criptográficos se detiene en la fase de diseño. DeepMind afirma que su sistema ha ido más allá, comprobando la implementación real, que es precisamente donde a menudo se esconden los errores del mundo real.
La compañía dice que es la primera vez que la implementación de un protocolo ampliamente desplegado como este ha sido verificada formalmente por cualquier método, con o sin IA.
Cómo funciona. El sistema se llama AlphaProof Code, un marco que combina varios modelos de IA con expertos humanos. Para ello, investigadores de DeepMind y varios modelos de IA tradujeron los objetivos de seguridad de Signal en especificaciones formales, y expertos humanos revisaron cada una de ellas. Los agentes, impulsados por Gemini Carbon, escribieron las pruebas, generando más de seis millones de líneas de Lean, un lenguaje que permite a un ordenador comprobar las pruebas automáticamente.
Tras ello, los agentes auditaron su propio trabajo y señalaron aproximadamente el 1% de la base de código que necesitaba una segunda revisión por parte de un humano. DeepMind dice que el trabajo llevó cuatro semanas, una tarea que históricamente lleva años a equipos de expertos. Las pruebas cubren propiedades tales como mantener los mensajes protegidos antes y después de que un dispositivo se vea comprometido temporalmente.
¿Detecta realmente errores? El análisis no encontró nuevas vulnerabilidades en las partes de Signal, según comparten desde Wired. Para comprobar si el sistema puede distinguir el buen código del malo, el equipo reintrodujo dos errores reales previamente corregidos en una versión aislada del código de Signal. En ambos casos, dice DeepMind, el sistema produjo una prueba verificada por máquina de que la versión con errores no era segura.
Entre líneas. El proyecto no verificó toda la aplicación móvil de Signal, y Wired señala que DeepMind tenía ventaja gracias a un trabajo previo de verificación formal por parte de la Signal Foundation. Ehren Kret, director de tecnología de Signal, dijo en un comunicado que el trabajo anterior "se centró en porciones más pequeñas del código", mientras que el enfoque de DeepMind "permite una expansión significativa". Añade además que, a medida que crecen las amenazas a la seguridad impulsadas por la IA, la verificación le da a Signal "aún mayor confianza" en sus garantías de privacidad.
Los investigadores también dicen que quieren evitar una configuración en la que la IA escriba tanto los objetivos como las pruebas. "No queremos este tipo de mundo de sensaciones en el que la IA genera los objetivos y la IA genera las pruebas y básicamente toma exámenes que están autoescritos", declaraba a Wired Swarat Chaudhuri, científico investigador de DeepMind. "Hay un término medio". Por ello mismo la parte humana se ha encargado de revisar las especificaciones y las secciones marcadas.
Las preguntas abiertas. Si esto puede escalar, y a qué coste, no está claro. Según Wired, DeepMind ejecutó el análisis de Signal de forma gratuita como un proyecto de investigación, pero no han compartido qué coste tuvo la operación ni si planean un producto de verificación comercial. "Hay un largo trecho por recorrer antes de que podamos escalar esto a todo el software del mundo, y queremos hacerlo", contaba Chaudhuri a Wired.
DeepMind dice que está abriendo el código fuente de sus artefactos de verificación formal para la comunidad, y sugiere que el enfoque podría extenderse eventualmente a sistemas como el firmware de dispositivos médicos y el software de la red eléctrica.

articles.title: Le patron de l’IA mondiale tombe : Jensen Huang quitte Nvidia après une double liaison
articles.text:
Le patron de l’IA mondiale tombe : Jensen Huang quitte Nvidia après une double liaison
Dimanche, il avouait une infidélité et gardait le soutien de son conseil d’administration. Jeudi, il quittait Nvidia. Entre les deux, une seconde liaison révélée par le New York Times, le FBI saisi du dossier selon Donald Trump lui-même, des élus prêts à le convoquer de force et un conseil réuni en urgence mercredi soir pour décider de son sort. L’homme qui a fait de Nvidia la clé de voûte de l’intelligence artificielle mondiale abandonne la direction de l’entreprise qu’il avait fondée en 1993, et jusqu’à son siège d’administrateur.
Jensen Huang a quitté Nvidia jeudi 12 novembre, après trente-trois ans à sa tête. La veille, le New York Times révélait une seconde liaison du dirigeant de 63 ans. D'après cinq personnes ayant travaillé chez Nvidia, il aurait entretenu une relation avec Kimberly Powell, 48 ans, vice-présidente chargée de la santé et l'une des quelque soixante cadres qui lui rendaient directement compte. Tous deux sont mariés.
Trois jours plus tôt, il avouait à ses salariés : "J'ai été infidèle à ma femme", sans nommer personne. Les renseignements américains soupçonnent Alice Huang, une dirigeante de Megaspeed dont il était très proche, d'avoir été recrutée par Pékin pour l'espionner.
	
J'ai été infidèle à ma femme.
Kimberly Powell, la révélation qui a retourné le conseil de Nvidia
Selon le quotidien new-yorkais, le couple aurait été vu en pleine effusion dans un hôtel de San José en mars, en marge de la GTC, la grande conférence annuelle de Nvidia. Joint par téléphone, Jensen Huang a lâché "Je ne pense pas que vous devriez me parler directement", avant de raccrocher.
Nvidia n'a pas souhaité commenter. Kimberly Powell, entrée dans le groupe en 2008, n'a pas répondu non plus. Selon Meg Tirrell, journaliste à CNN, elle a renoncé à son intervention prévue ce jeudi au Milken Future of Health Summit, à Washington.
Le retournement a été brutal. Dimanche, le conseil d'administration affirmait encore sa confiance dans son patron. Mercredi soir, le Wall Street Journal annonçait qu'il préparait son éviction, et les administrateurs se sont réunis en urgence pour trancher, ont confirmé plusieurs médias américains. Les statuts permettaient à une majorité des onze membres du conseil de révoquer le PDG, avec ou sans motif. Le lendemain matin, Nvidia annonçait le départ de son fondateur.
FBI, Congrès, enquête suspendue : l'étau s'était resserré sur Jensen Huang
Lundi, Donald Trump avait confirmé que le FBI s'intéressait à l'affaire, tout en volant au secours de son allié. Le président disait avoir appelé Jensen Huang pour prendre de ses nouvelles. "Il m'a dit : 'Je n'avais aucune idée qu'elle était une espionne', et je le crois vraiment", avait-il raconté.
Une autre révélation alourdissait le dossier. À la fin de l'été 2025, Tim Teter, directeur juridique de Nvidia, a appelé Jeffrey Kessler, le haut responsable du ministère du Commerce chargé des contrôles à l'exportation, rapporte Bloomberg. Il voulait savoir si Washington avait joué un rôle dans les ennuis d'Alice Huang à Singapour, où la police venait de l'interroger et de lui interdire de quitter le pays. Dans les semaines suivantes, les enquêteurs du Commerce ont vu leurs marges de manœuvre fondre : toute demande adressée à Nvidia devait passer par Kessler, et Megaspeed ne devait plus être citée dans leurs échanges extérieurs. Selon le New York Times, le ministère de la Justice a fini par demander au Commerce de suspendre son enquête. Nvidia assure que son juriste ignorait tout de la liaison, et Megaspeed nie toute irrégularité.
L'intéressée, elle, se trouverait désormais à Pékin selon Bloomberg, sans qu'on sache depuis quand. La Chine dément toute activité d'espionnage.
Au Congrès, le délai fixé à Jensen Huang pour accepter une audition à huis clos le 18 novembre expirait mercredi soir. Brian Mast et John Moolenaar, deux des trois présidents de commission signataires, n'avaient reçu aucune réponse dans l'après-midi et préparaient une assignation. Au Sénat, le républicain Kevin Cramer réclamait déjà sa démission. On ignore pour l'heure si les élus maintiennent leur demande d'audition.
Colette Kress prend les commandes de Nvidia par intérim
Nvidia n'avait ni plan de succession public, ni numéro deux chargé des opérations. Le conseil a donc confié l'intérim à Colette Kress, directrice financière depuis 2013, qui conserve ses fonctions, et nommé Harvey C. Jones premier président de son histoire. La recherche d'un successeur permanent est lancée, en interne comme à l'extérieur. Selon Semafor, le nom de Johny Srouji, architecte des puces Apple Silicon, circulait déjà.
L'enjeu dépasse largement Wall Street, où le titre perdait encore près de 10 % avant l'ouverture jeudi. Nvidia conçoit les cartes GeForce des joueurs et les puces sur lesquelles tournent ChatGPT ou Le Chat de Mistral. Jensen Huang en était le visage depuis 1993. Les résultats trimestriels, attendus le 17 novembre, seront présentés sans lui.

articles.title: Microsoft corrigió una falla de Outlook que los atacantes ya explotaban para robar datos de acceso
articles.text:
Microsoft corrigió una vulnerabilidad de Outlook que atacantes ya estaban explotando para obtener datos con los que suplantar a un usuario. El arreglo forma parte de su actualización mensual de seguridad, que según BleepingComputer corrige 1.235 fallas en total.
La falla se identifica como CVE-2026-124194. La empresa la describe como un fallo de suplantación: un atacante envía un archivo de mensaje manipulado y convence a la víctima de abrirlo. Al hacerlo, Outlook se conecta a una ubicación de red controlada por el atacante sin mostrar el aviso habitual de contenido externo.
Esa conexión puede revelar el hash NTLMv2 del usuario, según el aviso de Microsoft que citan SecurityWeek y The Hacker News, medios especializados en ciberseguridad y tecnología. Un hash es un código derivado de la contraseña de Windows: el atacante puede intentar descifrarlo para recuperar la clave o usarlo para iniciar sesión como la víctima en otros sistemas.
Microsoft precisó que el ataque requiere conexión de red y que la víctima abra el archivo. SecurityWeek agregó que la falla no se activa desde el panel de vista previa y que Microsoft la calificó como de gravedad moderada, con 6,5 puntos sobre 10.
Qué productos están afectados y cómo actualizar
Según el registro de la falla, están afectados Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Office LTSC 2021 y Office LTSC 2024. Los datos publicados indican que las versiones corregidas son la 16.0.14334.21048 para Office LTSC 2021 y la 16.0.17932.21140 para Office LTSC 2024.
TechRepublic advirtió que instalar la última actualización de Windows no corrige necesariamente este problema: hace falta la actualización de seguridad de Office o de Microsoft 365 Apps. Malwarebytes, empresa de ciberseguridad, recomienda abrir una aplicación de Office, ir a Archivo > Cuenta y elegir Opciones de actualización > Actualizar ahora.
En equipos de trabajo, esas opciones pueden no aparecer si el área de sistemas administra las actualizaciones de forma central. En ese caso, Malwarebytes aconseja consultar con el equipo de tecnología de la empresa.
Nick Carroll, responsable de respuesta a incidentes de Nightwing, dijo a CSO Online que la puntuación baja no debe llevar a restarle importancia: “no dejes que la puntuación baja te engañe”, afirmó, y pidió aplicar el arreglo de inmediato.
La agencia de ciberseguridad de Estados Unidos confirmó la explotación
La Agencia de Ciberseguridad y Seguridad de Infraestructura de Estados Unidos (CISA) añadió la falla el 10 de noviembre a su catálogo de vulnerabilidades explotadas, que reúne errores cuyo uso en ataques está comprobado. En ese catálogo figura como “desconocido” si se usa en campañas de ransomware, el software que secuestra archivos a cambio de un pago.
CISA dio plazo hasta el 24 de noviembre a las agencias civiles federales para aplicar la corrección. La obligación alcanza solo a esos organismos, pero la agencia recomienda a todas las organizaciones priorizar las vulnerabilidades de su catálogo.
Microsoft no atribuyó los ataques a ningún grupo ni detalló cómo se produjeron, según The Hacker News. El aviso tampoco aclara si el hallazgo ocurrió antes o después de que comenzaran las intrusiones. La empresa acreditó el descubrimiento a un investigador identificado como Nono y a Benoît Sevens, de Anthropic, quien usó Claude.
El total de fallas varía según la información relevada, pero oscila entre 1.093 y 1.259. La diferencia responde a los criterios utilizados para contabilizar las vulnerabilidades, como la inclusión de identificadores de terceros o de fallas que ya habían sido corregidas previamente durante el mes.
Los datos sobre la distribución de las correcciones también varían según el relevamiento: Windows concentra 726 y Office, 174. El número de fallas críticas varía entre 63 y 66. Entre ellas hay varias de ejecución remota de código en Outlook, incluida una que puede activarse con solo seleccionar un correo en el panel de vista previa.

articles.title: Peut-on encore refuser le Linky ? Ce que change l’arrêt européen, et ce que ça vous coûte
articles.text:
Le droit européen ne permet pas d’exiger de garder son vieux compteur électrique. Dans un arrêt rendu le 5 novembre, la Cour de justice de l’Union européenne (CJUE) estime qu’un gestionnaire de réseau « n’est pas tenu de se ranger au souhait d’un client final » qui ne veut pas d’un compteur intelligent. La directive européenne de 2019 sur le marché de l’électricité encourage fortement le déploiement de ces compteurs et donne aux consommateurs le droit d’en demander un, mais pas celui de conserver en toutes circonstances un modèle classique.
Dans une affaire autrichienne, une cliente refusait que le gestionnaire de réseau local remplace son compteur mécanique par un modèle numérique. Elle invoquait la protection de ses données et les ondes électromagnétiques, alors que l’étalonnage de son ancien appareil avait expiré fin 2023. Saisie par le tribunal régional de Sankt Pölten, la CJUE ne tranche pas le litige elle-même, qui reviendra à la justice autrichienne. En revanche, son interprétation du droit européen s’impose aux juridictions de tous les États membres, France comprise.
En France, l’arrêt confirme une obligation déjà en place
Pour les foyers français, la décision change peu de choses en pratique. En effet, le Code de l’énergie confie déjà aux gestionnaires de réseau la pose et le renouvellement des compteurs, et le médiateur national de l’énergie rappelle que les consommateurs ne peuvent pas s’opposer au remplacement. La Cour de cassation avait déjà donné raison à Enedis face à deux clientes réfractaires en avril 2025. L’arrêt européen prive surtout les opposants d’un argument, à savoir celui d’un droit que leur garantirait le droit de l’Union. Le déploiement est d’ailleurs presque achevé et Enedis revendique 38,7 millions de compteurs Linky installés, soit plus de 95 % des foyers qu’il dessert.
Refuser reste possible dans les faits lorsque le compteur se trouve à l’intérieur du logement, puisque le technicien ne peut pas entrer sans l’accord de l’occupant. Toutefois, ce refus a un coût comme nous l’évoquions déjà l’an dernier.
Depuis le 1er août 2026, les foyers non équipés de leur fait paient 6,68 euros HT tous les deux mois, soit 40,08 euros HT par an, même s’ils transmettent leurs relevés. Si aucun index n’a été communiqué depuis plus d’un an, 4,27 euros HT s’ajoutent tous les deux mois, ce qui porte la facture à 65,70 euros HT par an, soit près de 80 euros TTC. À noter que ces frais sont suspendus dès qu’un rendez-vous est demandé pour la pose du compteur, et jusqu’à son installation.
Vos données de consommation restent protégées
L’arrêt répond aussi à l’argument des données personnelles, avancé par de nombreux opposants. La Cour estime que la directive « vie privée et communications électroniques », celle qui encadre notamment les cookies, ne s’applique pas à un réseau électrique, qui sert d’abord à distribuer de l’énergie et non à fournir des services de communication. Les données de consommation restent en revanche couvertes par le RGPD, dont les exigences « doivent nécessairement être respectées », rappelle la Cour.
En France, la CNIL encadre déjà ces données. Par défaut, Enedis ne collecte que la consommation journalière du foyer. Les relevés plus fins, à l’heure ou à la demi-heure, qui peuvent trahir les heures de lever, de coucher ou les absences, ne sont collectés qu’avec l’accord de l’abonné, sauf ponctuellement pour les besoins du réseau. Leur transmission à un fournisseur d’énergie ou à un tiers suppose aussi son consentement, et chacun peut activer ou suspendre ces collectes à tout moment depuis son espace client Enedis.
