articles.title: Ars Live: What drone attacks on data centers mean for modern life in the cloud
articles.text:
Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. This trend represents a new concern for Big Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life.
To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled “Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech” on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts.
Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans.
This year, Jarnecki has written about Iran’s drone and missile strikes on Amazon data centers in the Middle East during the US-Israeli war with Iran, and the broader implications for governments and Big Tech. He has also commented on the impacts of Russia and Ukraine exchanging strikes on each other’s data centers.

articles.title: Notion confirmó que conversaciones con su asistente de IA quedaron expuestas tras un ataque informático
articles.text:
Notion, plataforma de productividad colaborativa, confirmó que conversaciones de usuarios con Notion AI, su asistente de inteligencia artificial, quedaron expuestas tras un ataque informático a Fireworks, la empresa que le proveía infraestructura. La compañía afirma que el incidente alcanzó a menos del 1% de sus espacios de trabajo y que sus propios sistemas no fueron vulnerados.
Según el aviso de seguridad de la aplicación, los datos robados incluyen transcripciones de chats usadas en Insights, una función que permite a los administradores ver cómo su equipo usa la herramienta. La empresa desactivó esa función mientras investiga y dejó de usar Fireworks para ejecutar modelos de código abierto dentro de su producto.
La compañía precisó que, en la gran mayoría de los espacios afectados, las transcripciones son “no atribuibles”: no indican quién escribió el mensaje ni a qué espacio pertenece. Tampoco contienen los resultados de las herramientas que el asistente consulta. Notion aclaró que no hay otra información que vincule cada chat con usuarios o empresas, más allá del texto de la conversación.
Ese texto, sin embargo, es lo que cada persona escribió. Si alguien pegó datos internos, contraseñas o claves de acceso, esa información puede estar en manos de los atacantes. Por eso la plataforma recomienda tratar esos datos “como si hubieran sido expuestos” y cambiar las credenciales que se hayan ingresado en el asistente durante el período del incidente.
Cómo se fue ampliando el alcance
Según la cronología de Notion, el 2 de noviembre Fireworks le avisó de que atacantes habían accedido a un conjunto pequeño de datos. El análisis inicial indicó que eran datos sintéticos de prueba, sin información de clientes. Al día siguiente, Notion se desconectó de Fireworks y borró todos sus datos en esa plataforma.
El 6 de noviembre, Fireworks informó que los atacantes podrían haber accedido a datos de clientes. El 8 de noviembre confirmó el conjunto final de datos afectados, que incluía las transcripciones de Notion AI. El 9 de noviembre, Notion contactó a los clientes afectados. El 11 de noviembre, revocó claves de acceso a su API que encontró dentro de mensajes de usuarios afectados.
La empresa indicó que quien no recibió un aviso no fue identificado como afectado y que por ahora no debe hacer nada. La investigación sigue abierta y mencionaron que escribirán a cualquier cliente que luego identifique como afectado.
Los dueños de los espacios afectados pueden revisar los datos desde la sección de revisión de incidentes de seguridad, según detalló BleepingComputer. Desde ahí pueden compartir con los miembros un enlace para que cada uno descargue sus propias transcripciones.
El ataque a Fireworks, en dos fases
Fireworks, una empresa que permite a otras compañías ejecutar modelos de IA sin montar su propia infraestructura, informó el 9 de octubre de un primer incidente. Tras ese aviso, según su boletín actualizado el 9 de noviembre, descubrió que también se vieron afectados datos de facturación y, en un grupo limitado de cuentas, claves, conjuntos de datos y modelos incompletos.
La empresa dijo que un proveedor de nube que alojaba sus máquinas de desarrollo sufrió un incidente el 23 de octubre. Al día siguiente, un tercero no autorizado usó ese acceso para llegar a esas máquinas y ejecutar una carga de trabajo que afectó a más clientes. Fireworks afirmó que detectó la actividad el mismo día.
La compañía atribuye los hechos a un grupo criminal con motivación económica que busca vender acceso a modelos de lenguaje a redes ilegales, una práctica conocida como LLMjacking.
Fireworks dijo que no detectó impacto en sus servicios de inferencia, es decir, la ejecución de modelos, que por defecto no conservan datos. Notion sostuvo que la firma se había comprometido por contrato a no retener sus datos. El aviso no explica por qué esas transcripciones estaban almacenadas.
Bloomberg Law informó el 9 de noviembre de que Fireworks, respaldada por Nvidia y con más de 10.000 clientes según su sitio web, trabajaba con Notion, Cursor y otros clientes para manejar el incidente. La investigación continúa y, según su boletín, podría revelar más información sobre el alcance del ataque.

articles.title: SoftBank’s billion-dollar loss may have put a cap on AI's natural gas ambitions | TechCrunch
articles.text:
SoftBank might not be the first to invest in a hot trend, but when it does, it goes big.
Witness its $30 billion bet on OpenAI in early 2025 or its announcement in February that its SB Energy subsidiary would spend $33 billion on a 9.2-gigawatt natural gas power plant. If you can’t be first, be biggest, I guess.
That philosophy apparently spilled over into procurement, where orders were also supersized. Starting about two years ago, SoftBank reportedly put down deposits on more than 13 gigawatts of turbines, almost 50% more than it needed.
The decision to over-order undoubtedly helped secure turbines and speed up SoftBank’s projects.
“SB Energy did not have a choice except to overbook turbines in the future if they wanted some turbines right away,” Peter Gardett, CEO of Noreva, told TechCrunch via email.
The energy world was caught off guard by the swiftness and magnitude of AI’s rising power demands. Queues for turbine orders now extend into the early 2030s. As natural gas was shaping up to be a go-to power source for the AI boom, CEO Masayoshi Son bet that by deploying his investment firm’s significant war chest, he could corner a portion of the market. If the AI world wanted power for its data centers, it would have to come to him.
Now that bet appears to have fizzled. SoftBank announced a $7.1 billion quarterly loss on Tuesday, with over half of that stemming from losses related to power-generating equipment. The investor had paid turbine manufacturers nonrefundable deposits to secure orders, and now it considered much of those worthless.
The move was also a costly bit of price discovery, Gardett said. Rather than overpay and potentially still be short of turbines, SoftBank overpaid and over-ordered.
“This charge is just that price discovery finally happening,” Gardett said.
The magnitude of that misplaced bet — over $3 billion — reflects some of the electricity mania that has overtaken the AI world. Faced with years-long waits to connect to the grid, many hyperscalers and developers have turned to natural gas as a sort of energy security blanket, something that is proven and familiar.
As AI data centers spend more time in operation, their operators are getting a better feel for what’s required to keep them operating. Natural gas might seem like a safe bet, but there are still risks, including winter curtailments when supplies dip and demand spikes, Brent Nelson, senior managing director of markets and strategy at Ascend Analytics, told the Equity podcast Wednesday.
In light of that, Nelson said the grid might still be their best bet. Most data centers would be best served by a grid connection, albeit a smaller one than they might normally request. To make up for the shortfall, large batteries are a cost-effective choice, Nelson said. They’d help shave peak loads or ride out requests from the utility to curtail electricity use.
Data center operators might be coming to that same conclusion, leading the natural gas market to develop more slowly than SoftBank expected.
SoftBank’s natural gas-related losses are unlikely to have a domino effect, leading to mass cancellations of gas power plants. AI’s power demand appears to be too large for that. For now, natural gas is riding high, though SoftBank may have found its ceiling.

articles.title: Noctua brings space-grade carbon nanotube thermal pad to AMD AM5 and AM4 processors — promises years of maintenance-free performance for $24.95
articles.text:
Noctua brings space-grade carbon nanotube thermal pad to AMD AM5 and AM4 processors — promises years of maintenance-free performance for $24.95
Designed to last for years.
Austrian cooling outfit Noctua is officially rolling its new NT-CP1 AM5/4 Carbice carbon nanotube thermal pad for AMD AM4 and AM5 processors into the retail market. After announcing its partnership with advanced nanotechnology company Carbice back in June 2026, the premium thermal pad can now be purchased for $24.95 in the US and €24.95 in the European region.
Conventional thermal pastes and most thermal pads gradually lose performance over time due to pump-out, delamination, cracking, and other forms of degradation. However, Noctua says that its new NT-CP1 thermal pad takes a different approach. It makes use of Carbice's vertically-aligned carbon nanotube technology, originally developed for high thermal reliability in aerospace systems. The carbon nanotubes gradually conform to microscopic imperfections of a CPU’s IHS over hundreds to thousands of thermal cycles.
This allows heat transfer performance to improve during the initial activation period rather than gradually deteriorating. The thermal pad can also maintain stable, maintenance-free performance for years once the initial activation phase is complete. Thus, making it a suitable option for users who want consistent thermal performance without having to periodically replace degraded thermal paste.
"Carbice pads offer a unique combination of ultimate performance stability and convenient installation. This makes the NT-CP1 the perfect choice for everyone who’s looking for a thermal pad that’s super easy to apply and never needs to be replaced," said Noctua CEO Roland Mossig in a press note.
Unlike conventional carbon or graphite-based thermal pads, which can be brittle, slippery, and electrically conductive, the NT-CP1 features an aluminum backbone sandwiched between layers of carbon nanotubes. The surface is also protected by a nanoscale polymer coating, which Noctua says makes the pad more robust, easier to handle, and less likely to move during installation. The company recommends a simple peel, press, and peel installation process, while the slightly tacky coating helps keep the pad in place and offers electrical insulation as long as the polymer layer remains intact.
With an ultra-thin 90µm profile and precut 33x33mm size, the thermal pad fits both AM5 and AM4 socket processors. Noctua also highlights its manufacturing process, noting that the pad is produced in the US using recycled aluminum and waste carbon gas to grow the carbon nanotubes. The company claims that its manufacturing process is more energy-efficient compared to conventional graphite and graphene-based pads, while the aluminum structure allows the product to be recycled through standard aluminum recycling channels.

articles.title: Google quiere que olvides las Meta Ray-Ban: sus nuevas gafas con Gemini ya tienen precio y fecha de lanzamiento
articles.text:
Google ya tiene listas sus nuevas gafas inteligentes con Gemini, un dispositivo con el que busca llevar la IA más allá del móvil. A unos meses de su presentación, los primeros modelos desarrollados en colaboración con Gentle Monster, Warby Parker y Samsung ya están listas para reservarse. Las gafas se venderán en versiones de audio y con pantalla e intentarán robarle un pedazo del mercado a las Meta Ray-Ban.
De acuerdo con una publicación en el blog de la compañía, las Intelligent Eyewear están basadas en Android XR y pueden usarse con móviles como el Pixel, Samsung Galaxy o el iPhone. Google ofrecerá dos colecciones: la primera, de la mano de Gentle Monster, incluirá seis modelos en diferentes colores con opciones de lentes transparentes, fotocromáticas o tintadas. La segunda, desarrollada junto a Warby Parker, se enfocará en estilos más clásicos inspirados en algunos de los modelos más populares de la marca.
En términos de funciones, las Intelligent Eyewear utilizan la IA de Gemini para realizar diversas acciones. Los usuarios solo necesitarán invocarla con la frase "Hey Gemini" o tocando una de las patillas. Desde ahí se podrá obtener información contextual sobre lo que se está viendo, pedir recomendaciones en tiempo real y gestionar listas de compra sin sacar el móvil del bolsillo. El asistente puede consultar eventos del calendario y avisarte sobre los pendientes que tienes programados.
Las Intelligent Eyewear cuentan con una cámara ultragran angular de 12 megapíxeles que permite capturar fotos o vídeos con pulsar un botón. De acuerdo con Google, el sistema utiliza estabilización de imagen, procesamiento HDR y grabación de audio espacial para mejorar la calidad del contenido. En caso de que no necesites la cámara o los micrófonos, podrás apagarla por completo y usar el dispositivo como unas gafas comunes.
Las gafas de Google y Samsung plantan cara a Meta y sus Ray-Ban
Una de las cosas que distinguen a las Intelligent Eyewear de las Meta Ray-Ban es la integración a fondo con los servicios de Google. Las gafas pueden conectarse a Google Maps y darte indicaciones paso a paso mediante audio, o usar Google Translate para traducir frases en más de 70 idiomas en tiempo real. Para aquellos que tengan debilidad visual, el dispositivo podrá leer textos pequeños o generar descripciones de audio sobre objetos.
Al igual que vemos con Meta, Google ha apostado por un diseño que pueda pasar desapercibido y sea cómodo para llevarse todo el día. Las Intelligent Eyewear pesan alrededor de 41 gramos y ofrecen hasta nueve horas de autonomía con una sola carga. En caso de que te quedes sin batería, podrás meter las gafas al estuche para recargarlas hasta siete veces.
Otras características incluyen altavoces abiertos para escuchar música, tomar llamadas y escuchar a Gemini. Los usuarios pueden reproducir su lista de reproducción de Spotify, YouTube Music y Apple Music, o escuchar un audiolibro gracias al soporte de Audible.
Google confirmó que sus gafas Intelligent Eyewear estarán disponibles a partir del 10 de diciembre de 2026. El precio para los modelos de Warby Parker es de 395 dólares en adelante, mientras que los de Gentle Monster parten de 449 dólares. Por el momento no hay información sobre un posible lanzamiento en España o América Latina, aunque la tecnológica estaría obligada a hacerlo si quiere competir de frente con Meta.

articles.title: Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS
Agents in multi-agent systems that span organizational boundaries often need to collaborate in a composable, interoperable way, with agents that other organizations build and run. They need a way to discover each other, communicate, and exchange tasks without exposing internals or requiring the same framework on both sides.
The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol addresses this constraint. Without A2A, building composable multi-agent systems across organizational boundaries requires custom integration code for each customer and framework. Independent software vendors (ISVs) can instead build composable, interoperable agents that work with the A2A-compatible frameworks their customers already use.
While we frame this post around the ISV use case, the pattern also applies to organizations that expose agents across boundaries, whether to partners, customers, or internal teams that use different frameworks. As your system grows, you add skills by registering Agent Cards with the orchestrator, without changing the agents already running.
In this post, we walk through a deployed reference architecture on AWS. A LangChain-based enterprise orchestrator communicates with a Strands Agents-based software as a service (SaaS) agent across organizational boundaries using A2A, with the enterprise and the SaaS provider in separate AWS accounts. Neither side depends on the other’s framework or SDK, and the two sides share no secrets. We cover the architecture and implementation patterns, then deploy the system from three Jupyter notebooks and run an end-to-end test.
The A2A protocol is now a Linux Foundation project, and AWS is among the organizations that support it. With A2A, agents can discover each other, negotiate tasks, and collaborate across organizational boundaries through a standardized protocol. The protocol uses existing authentication standards such as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) for cross-boundary security, and is designed to work across A2A-compatible frameworks.
In Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A, we introduced A2A concepts and demonstrated two Strands agents communicating using the protocol on AWS. That post established the foundation with Agent Card discovery, structured task execution, and the A2A server pattern. This post builds on that foundation with cross-framework interoperability, cross-organizational trust boundaries, and OAuth in both directions.
Solution overview
Three agents run in two AWS accounts, one for the enterprise and one for the SaaS provider. The A2A protocol connects them, with OAuth authentication in both directions. Each account has its own Amazon Cognito user pool, so each side authenticates with its own identity provider.
During onboarding, the enterprise and the SaaS provider exchange only public values, such as identity provider URLs, client IDs, scopes, and endpoint URLs. Each side then trusts tokens from the other side’s user pool, and no secrets are shared.
After onboarding, each request follows these steps:
- The enterprise app gets an access token from the enterprise’s Amazon Cognito user pool.
- The app sends a question over HTTPS to the user API in Amazon API Gateway, then polls for the answer.
- Amazon API Gateway forwards the request privately, through a VPC link and an internal Network Load Balancer, to the Enterprise Orchestrator, a LangChain agent.
- When its model decides that the question needs a compliance scan, the orchestrator gets its own token from the enterprise user pool, using a client secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager.
- The orchestrator sends an A2A request to the compliance SaaS agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, using the skill it read from the agent’s Agent Card at startup.
- The compliance agent checks the enterprise context agent’s Agent Card at the callback URL registered at onboarding, then gets a token from the SaaS provider’s own pool.
- The compliance agent calls back to the enterprise context agent for account metadata, finishes its scan, and returns the answer to the orchestrator and then to the app.
On the enterprise side, two agents run on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate. The Enterprise Orchestrator is the entry point for users. LangChain provides the agent framework and tool-calling abstractions, and Amazon Bedrock provides the foundation models (FMs) that power each agent’s reasoning. The orchestrator uses LangChain and Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6). At startup, the orchestrator fetches the SaaS agent’s Agent Card from its well-known URL and creates a LangChain tool for each skill described on the card. The model then decides which tool to call based on the user’s question, so the orchestrator needs no hardcoded routing logic. It sends compliance scan requests over A2A with OAuth bearer tokens and summarizes the results for leadership. Users reach the orchestrator through an Amazon API Gateway HTTPS endpoint that accepts only tokens from the enterprise’s own pool.
The second enterprise agent provides internal context. The Enterprise Context Agent is built with LangChain and Amazon Bedrock (Amazon Nova Lite). It provides internal account metadata such as internal policy rules, data classification, business criticality, and escalation contacts (team on-call rotations). The deployed agent uses the official a2a-sdk (AgentCard, AgentExecutor, and spec-conformant JSON-RPC routes), pinned to a2a-sdk[http-server]==1.2.2. The SaaS agent reaches the context agent through an API Gateway partner API that accepts only the SaaS provider’s callback token.
Both enterprise agents run in private subnets of an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), with no public IP addresses.
On the SaaS provider side, the Compliance SaaS Agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in the SaaS provider’s own AWS account. Built with the Strands Agents SDK, it checks AWS accounts against the enterprise’s own internal policies, such as no public storage in production and encryption at rest for confidential data. In production, the scanning tools would connect to services such as AWS Config, AWS Security Hub, or Amazon GuardDuty. For this demo, the agent uses synthetic data that simulates compliance findings across multiple accounts.
Before it scans, the SaaS agent calls back to the Enterprise Context Agent for enterprise context, such as which accounts are production, which internal policies apply, and who to escalate to. This bidirectional pattern makes the agents true peers instead of a client and a server. The callback goes only to the address the customer registered at onboarding.
The key design decision is to use A2A for all cross-boundary communication. The enterprise has no access to the SaaS agent’s internal tools, system prompt, or model choice. This separation means the ISV can change its internal architecture without changing customer integrations, as long as its Agent Card and A2A interface stay compatible. The SaaS card publishes one curated skill, not its internal tool names.
Amazon Bedrock provides API access to multiple foundation models, so each agent can use the model that fits its workload. In this solution, the orchestrator and SaaS agent use Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 for complex reasoning, while the context agent uses Amazon Nova Lite for metadata lookups. You can choose different models based on your own requirements.
A2A and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) solve different problems in this architecture. MCP connects an agent to its own tools and data sources in a client-server model. A2A connects agents to other agents as peers, where neither side exposes its internals. In production, the SaaS agent could use MCP internally to connect to its compliance scanning tools while exposing itself externally through A2A. The external interface stays the same regardless of how the agent connects to its internal tools.
Prerequisites
The notebooks contain the complete deployment procedure. Before you run them, you need the following:
- Two AWS accounts, one for the enterprise and one for the SaaS provider, in the same AWS Region: us-east-1, us-east-2, or us-west-2. In both accounts, access to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 in Amazon Bedrock, and in the enterprise account, access to Amazon Nova Lite. Before the first run, submit the Anthropic first-time use form in each account, and give the identity you run the notebooks with the AWS Marketplace permissions listed in the Amazon Bedrock model access documentation. Model availability varies by Region. Check the Amazon Bedrock model availability documentation for the current list.
- A Jupyter environment with Python 3.10 or later, either: 
         
  - On your computer: JupyterLab, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) version 2, and an AWS IAM Identity Center profile for each account, set up with aws configure sso. You don’t need Docker: AWS CodeBuild builds the container images.
  - Or an Amazon SageMaker AI notebook instance in each account (ml.t3.medium is enough). See the Guide to getting set up with Amazon SageMaker AI.
- In each account, an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role with permissions to create AWS CloudFormation stacks and the resources in them. Each notebook lists the exact permissions in its Reference section. See the IAM User Guide.
Notebook 3 also runs the end-to-end test described later in this post, so you can verify the deployment.
Running this solution incurs charges for the resources it creates. In the enterprise account, the main always-on resources are a NAT gateway, two AWS Fargate tasks, the internal Network Load Balancer, and two interface VPC endpoints. Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore charge for what you use. Prices vary by AWS Region. See the pricing pages for Amazon VPC, AWS Fargate, Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Elastic Load Balancing. Run the Clean up sections when you finish.
Implement the solution
Deploy the system with three notebooks, run in order with Jupyter, one cell at a time. Notebook 1 (enterprise account, about 3 minutes) creates the enterprise identity and writes an onboarding request. Notebook 2 (SaaS provider account, about 5 minutes) deploys the compliance agent and writes an onboarding response. Notebook 3 (enterprise account, about 20 minutes) deploys the enterprise agents and runs the tests. The onboarding files hold only public values.
- Clone the GitHub repository, and set up two AWS profiles for local runs, or one notebook instance per account with the repository cloned to each.
- Run notebook 1 in the enterprise account.
- Give onboarding-request.json to the SaaS provider.
- Run notebook 2 in the SaaS provider account.
- Give onboarding-response.json back to the enterprise.
- Run notebook 3 in the enterprise account.
- After testing, run notebook 3’s Clean up, then notebook 2’s.
The following sections explain the key implementation patterns behind the deployment. Together, they demonstrate three capabilities:
- Interoperability across frameworks – A LangChain orchestrator calls a Strands agent using A2A, with neither side depending on the other’s SDK.
- Composability across organizational boundaries – An ISV’s compliance agent and an enterprise’s context agent compose into a workflow that neither team built alone.
- Bidirectional collaboration with OAuth – Agents act as peers, calling each other across trust boundaries with token-based authentication.
With A2A, the ISV in this scenario replaces multiple custom integration paths with a single protocol-based interface.
Build the SaaS compliance agent
Build the ISV’s compliance agent with the Strands Agents SDK and deploy it to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. For this demo, the scanning tools return synthetic compliance findings.
The agent exposes three compliance tools using the Strands @tool decorator (listing available accounts, running compliance scans, and retrieving remediation steps), plus a fourth that calls back to the enterprise, covered in the next section. The Agent Card doesn’t list these tools. It publishes one curated skill, so callers’ models see what the product does, not how it’s built. This simplified example shows the scanning tool:
Enable the bidirectional callback
This is where the solution goes beyond typical agent integrations. Most agent-to-agent demos show one-way request and response, where a client agent calls a server agent and waits for the result. That pattern breaks down when the called agent needs information that only the caller has. In production, agents need to be peers that can call each other.
The SaaS compliance agent needs enterprise context. Examples include which accounts are production, which internal policies apply, and who to escalate to. This is information that only the enterprise has.
The SaaS agent calls back over A2A, but only to the callback URL the customer registered at onboarding. It first verifies the customer’s public context card there, then gets a token from the SaaS provider’s own Cognito pool, and sends message/send to the enterprise partner API:
Every failure, from an unverified card to a rejected token, gives the model one message, “Enterprise context unavailable”, and the details stay in the SaaS provider’s logs.
Expose the agent over A2A on AgentCore
The A2AServer class from the Strands SDK handles the A2A protocol, Agent Card generation, and JSON-RPC message handling. The server publishes one curated skill and declares on the card how a caller gets a token:
When deployed to AgentCore, this automatically generates an Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json. The Agent Card is a JSON document that describes the agent’s name, capabilities, and skills. A2A-compatible clients can fetch this card and understand what the agent can do without documentation or SDK integration.
Build the enterprise orchestrator with LangChain
This is the interoperability proof. The enterprise orchestrator uses LangChain, deliberately different from the Strands-based SaaS agent. It uses raw httpx HTTP calls with A2A JSON-RPC and doesn’t depend on the Strands SDK. If the ISV switched from Strands to another A2A-compatible framework, the enterprise orchestrator would keep working without changes, as long as the SaaS agent still speaks A2A and publishes a compatible Agent Card. That is what protocol-level interoperability means in practice.
The orchestrator gets a token from the enterprise’s own Cognito pool and sends the JSON-RPC payload over HTTPS only to the agent URL pinned to the address it fetched the Agent Card from. This abridged code shows the core A2A client:
Discover agents and route requests with the LLM
At startup, the orchestrator fetches Agent Cards from configured ISV URLs. It reads the skill descriptions from each card and creates a LangChain tool for each skill. The orchestrator’s large language model (LLM), Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, then decides which tool to call based on the user’s question. This simplified code shows the pattern:
As a result, when the ISV adds or changes a capability, its Agent Card changes with it, and the orchestrator picks up the new skills the next time it restarts. The two teams don’t need to coordinate the change.
Build the enterprise context agent
The enterprise context agent uses LangChain and Amazon Nova Lite for enterprise metadata lookups, and exposes its capabilities over A2A using the official a2a-sdk. The SDK handles Agent Card serving, JSON-RPC routing, and protocol conformance. Because A2A is JSON-RPC over HTTP, a standard web framework can serve it. The orchestrator shows the client side: it sends A2A requests with plain httpx and no A2A SDK.
The agent also publishes its own Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json, which the SaaS agent checks before it calls back. This is the same discovery mechanism used in the other direction. The A2A specification defines Agent Cards, so they don’t depend on the framework that builds the agent.
Set up cross-boundary OAuth with Amazon Cognito
Agent-to-agent communication across organizational boundaries without authentication isn’t acceptable to most enterprises. Every A2A task request (message/send) in this solution carries a JSON Web Token (JWT). Each side authenticates with a token from its own identity provider, and the receiving side accepts only that provider, one client, and one scope. The only unauthenticated endpoint is the enterprise context agent’s Agent Card, which publishes descriptive metadata so callers can discover the agent.
The solution uses Amazon Cognito as the OAuth provider. The same pattern can use another OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider that issues signed JWT access tokens, after you update the sample’s Cognito-specific checks.
The authentication flow involves four components:
Amazon Cognito: one user pool per account. The enterprise pool issues tokens to the orchestrator and to the enterprise app, and the SaaS pool issues tokens to the SaaS agent for its callback. You can view them in the Amazon Cognito console.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is configured with the enterprise pool’s discovery URL, the orchestrator’s client ID, and one scope. It validates the JWT on every incoming A2A request:
Amazon API Gateway uses JWT authorizers. The partner API accepts only the SaaS provider’s callback token, and the user API accepts only the enterprise app’s token. View the configuration in the Amazon API Gateway console.
AWS Secrets Manager in each account stores that account’s client secret, and an IAM grant and a resource policy that denies every other principal limit each secret to the one workload that uses it. No secret is hardcoded or shared with the other account. You can manage secrets in the AWS Secrets Manager console.
This AWS CloudFormation snippet shows the partner API’s JWT authorizer:
One detail of machine-to-machine authentication is a common source of errors when you wire OAuth between API Gateway and AgentCore. An Amazon Cognito client-credentials access token carries client_id and scope, but no aud claim. When aud is absent, the API Gateway JWT authorizer checks client_id against the audience list. On the AgentCore side, configure allowedClients and leave allowedAudience unset.
Deploy the system with notebooks
The notebooks run the whole deployment from Jupyter. They deploy five AWS CloudFormation stacks, three in the enterprise account and two in the SaaS provider account. The enterprise infrastructure and services stacks are separate because of a chicken-and-egg problem: the ECS services need Docker images, but CloudFormation creates the Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repositories that hold those images. You can monitor the stacks in the AWS CloudFormation console.
The notebooks surface failures early. Each notebook first checks Amazon Bedrock model access with a short test call, before anything is deployed, and each step stops at the first error with clear output. The Clean up sections sit at the bottom of notebooks 2 and 3, after a stop cell, so Run All never reaches them.
Understand Agent Cards and discovery
Agent Cards make discovery possible without agreeing on tool definitions in advance. Without them, the enterprise would need documentation, an SDK, or a meeting with the ISV’s engineering team to understand what the compliance agent can do. With Agent Cards, the enterprise orchestrator fetches a single JSON document. It immediately knows the agent’s name, capabilities, and skills, programmatically, at runtime. This is the card the compliance agent publishes for one customer, abridged:
Each skill’s description becomes a tool docstring, so the orchestrator’s model routes each request to the right agent. The two teams never had to agree on tool definitions or share an SDK. The card also declares how a caller authenticates. The orchestrator checks that declaration rather than following it: it keeps the card only if it names the token endpoint and scope registered at onboarding.
Test end-to-end
Notebook 3 runs one end-to-end test through both accounts. It gets a token for the enterprise app, submits a question, and polls for the result:
The orchestrator discovers the SaaS agent through its Agent Card and routes the request over A2A. The SaaS agent calls back to the enterprise context agent for account metadata (bidirectional A2A), runs compliance scans with its internal tools, combines everything into an enriched report, and sends it back. The response contains data from both agents. This shows that two independently built agents, on different frameworks and different infrastructure, can compose into a workflow that neither produces alone.
The test passes only if the reply has compliance findings, includes an on-call rotation code that only the enterprise context agent knows, and the partner API’s access log shows a 200 from the SaaS callback client. Together they show that the callback worked. Notebook 3 then runs seven trust boundary checks that send a wrong, missing, or forged token to each gate, and every call must be rejected. This is abridged output from a test run (IDs are placeholders):
In that run, the report covered two production accounts and six findings, with the escalation contacts for each account. You can send the same request from any HTTP client, without an A2A SDK.
Production considerations
This demo simplifies several areas for clarity. For production, consider these changes:
- One runtime per customer, or a front door that accepts several customer identity providers, with per-customer callback clients.
- Key-based client authentication (private_key_jwt or mutual TLS) instead of client secrets.
- AWS PrivateLink for private connectivity, and TLS inside the VPC for end-to-end encryption.
- Customer managed AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys for Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon ECR, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.
- VPC Flow Logs and Network Load Balancer access logs. Both API Gateway stages already write access logs.
- A Secrets Manager rotation function for the Cognito client credentials.
- An authenticated onboarding portal or API instead of files.
If calls through API Gateway intermittently return HTTP 503, check that cross-zone load balancing is on for the internal Network Load Balancer. Each ECS service runs a single task that can start in either Availability Zone.
The repository’s README covers the full list in Security controls and Considerations for production.
Security considerations
Deploy this solution only in sandbox accounts with no customer or business data, and delete the stacks after testing. The sample uses synthetic data only, with no personal data. Its compliance agent checks example internal policies. It doesn’t assess or certify compliance with any law, regulation, or standard. The sample includes the following controls. You’re responsible for reviewing and adapting them before you use this pattern in production:
- Transport encryption. Every cross-account call uses HTTPS to Amazon API Gateway or Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and every route except the context agent’s public Agent Card requires a Cognito JWT.
- Guardrails. In this sample, each model call uses an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with prompt-attack and harmful-content filters, and text from the other organization is checked against the same guardrail before a model uses it.
- Least-privilege IAM. Each workload has its own role that names exact ARNs. Only the orchestrator and the compliance agent can read a secret, each only its own.
- Container hardening. ECS containers run with a read-only root filesystem and all Linux capabilities dropped. The base image is pinned by digest.
- Account isolation. The two accounts share no secret, key, or IAM permission. They exchange only public values.
Clean up resources
To avoid ongoing charges, delete all resources when you have finished testing. Run the Clean up section at the bottom of notebook 3, then notebook 2, one cell at a time. The last cell in each section confirms that nothing is left. After cleanup, check the AWS CloudFormation, Amazon ECR, and Amazon Cognito consoles in both accounts, and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console in the SaaS provider account, to confirm that no resources remain.
Conclusion
This post showed how to build a multi-agent system where agents from different organizations, built on different frameworks, collaborate through A2A on AWS.
A LangChain orchestrator on Amazon ECS communicates with a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Neither side needs the other’s framework or SDK. The SaaS agent calls back to the enterprise context agent for account metadata, and each side authenticates with its own identity provider. A new skill from the same ISV requires no changes to the code. Adding a second ISV takes one extension, because the orchestrator holds a single OAuth client today: give it one client and scope per ISV, as the README’s Considerations for production describes. Then run the same onboarding exchange, add its Agent Card URL, and restart the orchestrator.
To get started, clone the GitHub repository and run the three notebooks, in two accounts, with Jupyter on your computer or on Amazon SageMaker AI notebook instances. They handle infrastructure provisioning, agent deployment, and end-to-end testing.
To learn more about the services and protocol in this post, see the following resources:
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide
- Amazon Bedrock User Guide
- Strands Agents SDK documentation
- Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A
If you have questions or feedback, leave them in the comments section.

articles.title: Applications open for Villgro Africa MedTech Innovation Programme - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
The Villgro Africa MedTech Innovation Programme is looking for locally-led, invention-based enterprises developing tech-enabled medical hardware that addresses healthcare needs.
Open to innovators in Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi and Ethiopia with at least a functional proof of concept or prototype, the Villgro Africa MedTech Innovation Programme is seeking startups with diagnostic and patient-monitoring devices; therapeutic equipment; maternal and newborn health technologies; and connected medical devices.
Six selected enterprises will receive tailored technical and venture-building support over 24 months, covering product development and validation; regulatory and quality readiness; manufacturing; market development; and investment readiness.
Applications are open here until November 16.

articles.title: Apple tire un trait sur son forum d’entraide, une institution vieille de près de 28 ans
articles.text:
En octobre 2023, Apple retirait ses spécialistes rémunérés de son forum d’entraide et cessait de répondre aux clients sur X et YouTube. Trois ans plus tard, la firme ferme le forum lui-même, sans préavis. Le bandeau apparu dans la nuit de mardi à mercredi fixe l’échéance au 20 novembre, pour un espace né il y a près de 28 ans.
Un forum verrouillé du jour au lendemain
« La communauté d’assistance AppleCare fermera définitivement le 20 novembre 2026. À compter d’aujourd’hui, le site n’accepte plus de nouvelles publications et reste disponible en lecture seule. » Le bandeau, qui accueille désormais chaque visiteur, redirige vers les pages d’assistance officielles. Au moment de sa découverte, le dernier sujet publié remontait à moins d’une heure, signe d’un site resté actif jusqu’au bout.
Les discussions existantes restent consultables, votes et mentions « Moi aussi » compris, et le bouton de connexion subsiste, quoiqu’il mène désormais à un portail interne réservé aux employés. Apple n’a pas précisé si les archives resteraient lisibles après le 20 novembre ou si elles disparaîtraient avec le site. Le bandeau parle au passage de communauté « AppleCare », un intitulé qui tranche avec la marque publique Apple Support Community.
Mercredi matin, les déclinaisons francophone et germanophone du forum affichaient toujours leurs boutons de publication, sans le moindre bandeau : le périmètre exact de la fermeture reste à préciser.
Une institution née en 1998, abandonnée par étapes
L’espace a ouvert en 1998 sous le nom d’Apple Tech Exchange, avant de devenir Apple Discussions en 2000, puis Apple Support Communities en avril 2011, refonte accompagnée de profils personnalisés et d’un système de réputation. Des clients y dépannaient d’autres clients, du réglage de la batterie d’un iPhone aux problèmes de stockage. Les membres y gravissaient des niveaux à force de réponses utiles, jusqu’à un salon fermé réservé aux plus gradés. Lancé en 2022, le programme Community+ distingue encore chaque année les contributeurs les plus actifs, dont les profils arborent toujours le millésime 2026.
Le 1er octobre 2023, la firme avait pourtant déjà retiré ses propres employés du jeu. Les messages adressés au compte d’assistance sur X, fort d’un million et demi d’abonnés, ne recevaient plus de réponse humaine, le suivi technique des commentaires YouTube s’arrêtait, et le poste de spécialiste rémunéré du forum disparaissait. Les centaines de salariés concernés s’étaient vu proposer une reconversion dans l’assistance téléphonique, présentée à l’époque comme le canal préféré des clients.

articles.title: AI's infrastructure boom is standing on porcelain legs
articles.text:
AI's infrastructure boom is standing on porcelain legs
Why AI agents are straining data infrastructure
AI may look seamless at the surface, but underneath, search and analytics are still pulling in different directions.
There is an image I keep returning to when I think about AI infrastructure – an elephant standing on porcelain legs. The systems being built above the data layer are getting heavier and more ambitious, while the foundations beneath them receive far less attention. Investors and technology companies talk about AI infrastructure constantly, but they usually mean chips, models, and the applications built on top of them.
But AI infrastructure is more than that. Every one of those applications depends on a less fashionable layer underneath – the systems that find, retrieve, and analyze its data.
Co-Founder and CEO of SereneDB.
In many businesses, search and analytics still live in separate systems. One finds relevant information in documents and other unstructured data. The other calculates, compares, and identifies patterns. Pipelines copy and synchronize information between them, while engineers keep the systems working together.
Separating search from analytics was not a foolish design choice. The split became the status quo because it suited the questions, hardware, and users of the time. Now, however, natural-language interfaces and AI agents are exposing the cracks.
A person asks one ordinary question, but the infrastructure may have to turn it into several searches, a retrieval job, and a separate analytical query before it can produce an answer. Did AI create this problem? No. But it has made it much harder to ignore…
One question becomes several jobs
An AI agent can turn one human request into several smaller machine queries before returning an answer. The agent may search for different parts of the request separately, rank the results, and decide whether it has enough evidence to continue. What feels like one action to the user can therefore generate repeated database work.

Some requests only require retrieval. Others ask the system to find evidence and calculate with it. The moment a task needs both, the distinction between search and analytics becomes visible: one system locates the relevant material, while another may be asked to aggregate values or identify a pattern.
Natural language does not respect the way the database industry has divided itself. People do not separate ‘find the relevant documents’ from ‘calculate what they mean’ when they ask a colleague for an answer. Agents do not either. They translate a single intention into whatever sequence of searches and calculations is required.
The extra database activity matters even before we imagine an agent swarm – a group of AI agents working in parallel on parts of a larger task. One apparently simple prompt can already create more database work than the user sees. Every hand-off between systems adds latency, cost, and another place where context can be lost.
Search and analytics grew up apart
AI agents expose these hand-offs because search systems and analytical databases developed separately. Search engines are designed to find relevant information in messy text, logs, and documents, even when the user cannot describe the answer precisely. Analytical databases are built to work with structured data – aggregating large datasets, joining records, calculating averages, and identifying trends.
The separation between search and analytics made sense when businesses mostly asked one system to find information and another to calculate with it. It becomes a problem when a single question needs both.
Search may identify the right set of documents, but another system is often needed to crunch the numbers inside them. Analytical tools can calculate quickly, but they generally work best when the user already knows where the relevant data sits and how it is structured.
To combine search with analytics, businesses build extra copies of data, extraction and transformation pipelines, synchronization jobs, and application code. Vector search can add another specialized system to the chain. Data engineers then spend time maintaining that plumbing, not because the plumbing creates value of its own, but because the underlying jobs remain separated.
Some search and analytical products are already crossing into the other field. Even so, many businesses still run separate systems and maintain the infrastructure that connects them.
Separate systems create costs today
Maintaining separate search and analytics systems means paying for extra copies of data, the pipelines between them, and the engineers who keep everything working. Search indexes need to be refreshed as source data changes. Analytical stores may hold another version of the same information, while vector search can introduce another specialist layer.
The exact architecture varies, but each additional copy consumes storage, every synchronization job needs monitoring, and every hand-off creates another place where data can fall out of date or a query can slow down. Those costs exist before AI agents increase query volumes. Agents make them harder to overlook because one user action may trigger several operations across the same chain of systems.
Open formats change the economics
One way to reduce that duplication is to keep the underlying data in object storage and use open formats so different tools can work with it. In practice, the data might sit in Amazon S3, the object storage service from Amazon Web Services, as Apache Parquet files organized into tables with Apache Iceberg.
This approach separates storage from the databases and servers that process the data. Search and analytics tools can work from the same underlying information instead of requiring a complete copy inside every product. An index and a computing layer are still needed, and some workloads will continue to justify specialized systems, but duplication no longer has to be the default.
Across the industry, search and analytics are beginning to converge as businesses gain more control over where their data lives. When a new workload appears, they can use the same underlying data instead of automatically adding another database, another copy, and another pipeline.
More agents will increase the pressure
Reducing duplicated data and pipelines will become more valuable as businesses give AI agents more work. Vast, concurrent agent swarms are not yet an everyday production reality, but agents are already changing database workloads. One natural-language request can become several underlying database operations, and an agent can repeat that process continuously, without the working hours or pauses that shape human use.
As agents handle more work, query volumes may begin to follow software activity rather than employee headcount. The first signs of that extra demand are unlikely to be a sudden database collapse. They are more likely to appear as queues, slower responses, timeouts, rising infrastructure bills, and greater pressure on the pipelines between systems.
Businesses do not need to assume that swarms are imminent to justify reviewing the data layer. Duplicated infrastructure and operational costs already exist. More agents would increase both.
The status quo is the real competitor
A simpler data layer still has to beat infrastructure that businesses already know and trust. Legacy is often used as an insult, but I mean it more literally – the established status quo. Existing systems became dominant because they solved important problems and, in many cases, continue to solve them well.
Businesses should not rip out working infrastructure simply because AI is fashionable. They should ask more practical questions. How many complete systems hold versions of the same data? How many pipelines exist only to move information between them? How long does it take to answer a question that combines unstructured evidence with numerical analysis? How much specialist time is spent keeping that route operational?
If the answers remain simple and economical, the current architecture may be perfectly adequate. If every new AI feature requires another store, another copy, and another layer of glue, the foundation deserves closer attention.
The elephant is getting heavier, and its legs deserve the same attention as everything being built above them. Changing those foundations, however, will not be easy. There is no fiercer competitor than the status quo.

articles.title: Suspected Chinese spy at center of Jensen Huang affair surfaces in Beijing — Alice Huang last spotted heading to Shanghai after being detained, questioned in Singapore in 2025, allegedly helped China smuggle hundreds of thousands of banned H100 and H200 chips
articles.text:
Suspected Chinese spy at center of Jensen Huang affair surfaces in Beijing — Alice Huang last spotted heading to Shanghai after being detained, questioned in Singapore in 2025, allegedly helped China smuggle hundreds of thousands of banned chips
It's still unclear why Alice Huang is in Beijing.
Alice Huang, the person allegedly involved in an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, has reportedly surfaced in Beijing, marking the first sighting of the Megaspeed executive since the scandal broke out. According to Bloomberg, it’s unclear when the suspected Chinese spy arrived in the capital or why she’s in the area, but she was last spotted leaving Singapore for Shanghai in 2025 after she was detained and questioned during the city-state’s investigation into the $2-billion smuggling case involving Megaspeed.
The Nvidia CEO is now under intense scrutiny after the revelation of his indiscretion with the Megaspeed executive, with Congress threatening to issue a subpoena if he does not respond to their invitation to “a joint, closed-door briefing” with the heads of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence. The FBI is also looking into the relationship between the head of the largest AI hardware company in the world and a person suspected of helping sanctioned Chinese companies secure hundreds of thousands of banned H100 and H200 chips. Overnight, a second bombshell report claims that Jensen Huang was also involved in an extramarital affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell.
Although the Chinese embassy in Washington has denied any links to Alice Huang, calling it nothing but “groundless smears and slanders” against Beijing, there is speculation that she’s under the control of the Ministry of State Security (MSS), which is the primary agency that handles China’s foreign intelligence and counterintelligence operations. The U.S. intelligence community suggests that she may be passing on information to the MSS, but it remains unclear if she was specifically tasked by Chinese intelligence to target Jensen Huang or if they were only leveraging her relationship with the Nvidia chief to get insights into the U.S. AI industry.
A deeper investigation into Alice Huang, known by her Chinese name as Huang Le, revealed that she supposedly worked in media before jumping into banking and finance. The Wall Street Journal reports that it’s unclear when she met her husband, Kang Wei, but the couple ran a private equity and investment management firm called Shanghai Hexi in 2016. This allowed the couple to invest in companies across industries, including gaming, pharmaceuticals, and, eventually, data centers and cloud computing.
The couple is known for riding trends and isn’t a stranger to scandals. Their firm, Shanghai Hexi, invested in gaming companies in the 2010s, especially when mobile gaming started to boom across the world, while Chinese regulators fined Kang and the company in 2018 for disclosure failures and other violations while it was in the midst of a takeover battle for a corporation. Kang’s moves in the gaming industry are what allowed him to meet Jensen Huang, which eventually led to a close relationship between the couple and the Nvidia chief. Sources told the WSJ that Kang apparently accepted Alice and Jensen’s extra-marital relationship, even sometimes jokingly telling people that she was Jensen’s “personal assistant.”
It seems that the couple is used to leveraging their relationships to gain business advantage, and with investments in AI data centers expected to hit $32 trillion by 2050, Alice Huang’s “close” relationship with Jensen Huang put Shanghai Hexi in an excellent position to take advantage of the trend through Megaspeed and make big money. And with U.S. sanctions making it harder for competitors to acquire Nvidia chips, it appears that their access has turned into a gold mine for the company. But whether Alice Huang acted solely out of business interest with the supposed procurement of Nvidia chips or was leveraged by Chinese authorities to import these chips, the fact remains that $7.5 billion worth of banned chips reportedly made their way into China despite Washington’s efforts.

articles.title: Vi la NFL en el Bernabéu y llegué a una conclusión: el fútbol americano se ha convertido en un 'videojuego' lleno de datos
articles.text:
El pasado domingo, tuve la oportunidad de disfrutar en vivo y en directo del NFL Madrid Game, que ha celebrado este año su segunda edición. El partido de fútbol americano entre los Cincinnati Bengals y los Atlanta Falcons se disputó en un Bernabéu vestido de gala para la ocasión (plagado de controles de seguridad, por cierto) y acabó con un 34-17 a favor de los Bengals.
Pero el resultado, para mí, fue lo de menos. Era mi primera vez en un partido de la NFL y, como en Xataka nos gusta buscar el lado tech de cualquier evento, acudí al estadio acompañada del equipo de AWS (Amazon Web Services). ¿Por qué AWS? Pues porque es el socio tecnológico de la NFL desde hace más de una década.
Con AWS, la NFL ha pasado de medir estadísticas básicas a analizar cada movimiento en el campo en tiempo real y traducirlo en lo que ellos denominan 'Next Gen Stats' (NGS), unas métricas avanzadas que ayudan a los espectadores a entender el juego, a los equipos a planificar estrategias y a los jugadores a prevenir lesiones.
La irrupción de los chips en el terreno de juego. Durante más de un siglo, el fútbol americano solo se medía por resultados, como las yardas ganadas, los touchdowns o los placajes, pero esos datos no mostraban todo lo que ocurría realmente en el campo. Y ahí es donde aparece AWS, que se alió con la NFL en 2015.
A raíz de ese acuerdo, se empezaron a colocar pequeños chips de rastreo (RFID) en las hombreras de los jugadores, dentro del balón y en los marcadores, además de instalar más de 20 antenas en cada estadio. Así nació 'Next Gen Stats' (NGS), que registraban la posición exacta (con precisión de centímetros) de los jugadores 10 veces por segundo y del balón 25 veces por segundo.
La explosión de los datos. Al principio, los datos obtenidos por los chips solo servían para medir cosas sencillas, como la velocidad máxima de un jugador o cuánto tardaba el quarterback en lanzar el balón. Pero en 2018, la NFL amplió su alianza con AWS y entró en juego el aprendizaje automático (machine learning).
A partir de ahí, la NFL y AWS convirtieron todos esos datos de seguimiento de jugadores en una plataforma de datos en tiempo real que hoy en día puede reconocer patrones, generar estadísticas avanzadas y ofrecer una visión mucho más amplia de lo que ocurre en el campo.
Más de 200 estadísticas por jugada. Uno de los mejores ejemplos de esas estadísticas avanzadas es la métrica de 'probabilidad de pase completado' (Catch Probability). En ella, un algoritmo analiza en tiempo real factores como la presión sobre el pasador, la distancia del lanzamiento o la cercanía del defensor al receptor para calcular el porcentaje de dificultad del pase y mostrarlo en la retransmisión del partido.
Para hacernos una idea de la evolución, en la última década, Next Gen Stats ha pasado de medir únicamente la velocidad a ofrecer más de 40 modelos estadísticos, como Pressure Probability (probabilidad de presión) o Tackle Probability (probabilidad de placaje), que permiten generar más de 200 estadísticas distintas por jugada.
La revolución en la retransmisión del fútbol americano. Actualmente, 75 modelos de inteligencia artificial procesan millones de datos por partido en menos de un segundo. Con toda esa información, las retransmisiones de televisión muestran a los aficionados gráficos y estadísticas avanzadas al instante que ayudan a entender la dificultad de cada jugada. Y eso es algo que, personalmente, agradecí bastante durante el partido de los Bengals y los Falcons.
Además de ser útil para las retransmisiones, los entrenadores usan toda esa información para, por ejemplo, evaluar fichajes, diseñar estrategias y preparar los partidos. Y la NFL también combina los datos con simulaciones basadas en IA para analizar los impactos y el esfuerzo físico que sufren los jugadores, y reducir así el riesgo de lesión. Ellos lo llaman 'NFL Digital Athlete'.
Una misión imposible que ya no es imposible. Otro de los aspectos que más me llamó la atención es la dificultad que entraña elaborar el calendario de la NFL. Según AWS, es uno de los retos computacionales más complejos del deporte profesional porque, para distribuir 272 partidos en 18 semanas, la NFL debe tener en cuenta más de 26.000 factores: desplazamientos, disponibilidad de estadios, rivalidades de división, partidos en horario de máxima audiencia, criterios de competición...
Dicho así, no suena exagerado, pero cada temporada, más de 4.000 instancias de Amazon EC2 ejecutan unas 1.000 permutaciones al día que permiten a la NFL analizar más de 100.000 calendarios posibles de entre unos mil billones de combinaciones. Casi nada.
