articles.title: How eHealth Africa is using tech to close immunisation gaps
articles.text:
Getting a vaccine to a child starts long before anyone loads a cold box. It starts with knowing the child’s community exists.
About 2.1 million Nigerian children, representing 24% of the country’s estimated 8.7 million under-one population, had not received a single routine vaccine dose, according to the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF). The 2023 estimate made Nigeria the country with the highest number of zero-dose children globally.
Some live in remote settlements cut off from health facilities by difficult terrain and long distances. Others live in conflict-affected communities or settlements missing from the maps and population estimates used to plan campaigns. Without reliable information about where people live and how to reach them, health authorities risk excluding them from vaccination campaigns.
For more than a decade, eHealth Africa, a non-profit developing data-driven solutions for health systems, has supported Nigeria’s immunisation programmes through geospatial settlement mapping, digital campaign planning with PlanFeld and vaccine delivery tracking. In the first half of 2026 alone, vaccination campaigns supported by the organisation reached more than 23 million children across over 205,000 settlements in Nigeria, according to its 2026 Mid-Year Report. But these tools will only endure if Nigerian institutions can fund, operate and maintain them.
Finding communities the health system cannot see
Before digital tools became part of immunisation planning, programmes relied on traditional leadership structures to identify and reach communities. Abubakar Shehu, who leads eHealth Africa’s Disease Prevention and Monitoring interventions, says networks linked paramount rulers to smaller communities through subordinate leaders, extending to individual settlements.
“No matter how small a community is in northern Nigeria, they have a leader, and that leader is as important to us as somebody within the traditional system,” Shehu says.
In a 2021 publication, UNICEF said Nigeria’s immunisation programme relied on multiple paper-based registries to record maternal and child health information. Delays in getting those records to decision-makers, alongside manual data collection and analysis, contributed to children missing campaigns, particularly in hard-to-reach, conflict-affected and urban-poor communities.
For eHealth Africa, one response was to improve settlement mapping. “We’ve gone from hand-drawn maps to GIS maps. So it has helped us to be able to correctly identify the settlements and the missed communities in the field,” Nnenna Ohaeri, project manager at eHealth Africa who was involved in developing its digital microplanning programme, said.
The organisation’s geospatial work collects information about settlements, including their locations, habitation status, accessibility, community leadership and public amenities such as schools, markets, churches and mosques.
But knowing where a settlement is does not always mean the local government responsible for it can reach it easily. Shehu describes communities that fall within one local government area but are more accessible from another because a river separates them from the first. In such cases, vaccination teams from the neighbouring local government can reach the settlement, while the relevant records are transferred to the local government responsible for it.
“Having the technological details of the locations where the people are residing is different, and also accessing the community is different,” Shehu said.
Geospatial tracking also helps eHealth Africa identify settlements vaccination teams have missed. Shehu said the organisation began using the technology to track vaccination teams after administrative reports showed 100% coverage even as outbreaks continued.
“When we started using it in Nigeria, we discovered that the actual geographical coverage is far lower than what has been reported by the administrative data,” he said.
Knowing where communities are and how to reach them is only the first step. Health authorities must also translate that information into vaccination plans, schedules and team assignments.
Turning settlement data into vaccination plans
To address planning challenges, eHealth Africa developed PlanFeld, a digital tool that generates microplans and daily implementation plans for vaccination teams.
Conventional microplanning could take four to five days per local government area, sometimes stretching to 10. It also required money for refreshments and hired personnel, Shehu said. With a limited health workforce, he argued, taking health workers away from their duties for days to plan campaigns was inefficient.
“We were able to reduce the turnaround time of the microplanning from maybe five days in some instances, even up to 10 days, to between five and 10 minutes,” Shehu said.
PlanFeld generates daily implementation plans alongside the broader microplan, removing the need for health workers to return to ward level to prepare assignments. It stores settlement information in one repository and allocates workloads to teams, helping prevent omissions of sub-settlements under manual planning, Shehu said.
Ohaeri said PlanFeld had also reduced the funds allocated to microplanning, creating savings for government. “We have reduced the number of funds that are usually allocated for that process. So we have been able to have some cost savings for the government,” she said.
The plans depend on reliable data. Shehu said eHealth Africa and other polio eradication partners validate settlement information every two months with community leaders, local government officials and programme partners. This is especially important in northern Nigeria, where insecurity can change whether settlements are inhabited between campaigns. The updated information feeds into PlanFeld.
eHealth Africa tested the tool’s team-allocation approach in Kebbi State, which had repeatedly complained that it lacked enough teams to immunise the number of children it needed to. After observing three campaign rounds, the organisation introduced the digital microplan in the fourth.
The exercise found Kebbi needed only seven additional teams, less than 5% of its existing total. The bigger problem was the uneven distribution of teams across local governments.
“There are some local governments that have several teams that are beyond what they needed, and there are some that have fewer than they needed,” Shehu explained. “We were able to do rationalisation within the state, and that significantly reduced the number of settlements that were being missed during the implementation.”
Shehu said the proportion of settlements planned for vaccination but missed during implementation fell from more than 20% in an observed campaign to around 6% in a subsequent round using the digital microplan.
Once vaccination teams have their assignments, the next challenge is getting vaccines to the facilities they serve.
Getting vaccines to the last mile
eHealth Africa said it supports a push model of vaccine delivery, collecting vaccine commodities from state central medical stores and transporting them to health facilities. The organisation uses geospatial technology to plan delivery routes, helping officers reach facilities while managing time and logistics costs.
“Logistics is always difficult to handle, but if you have a system in place to support the delivery model that you are using, it tends to make it easier,” Shehu said.
eHealth Africa’s Logistics Management Information System (LoMIS) supports deliveries by giving health authorities visibility into vaccine movements and facility stock levels. State and local government immunisation officers can track vaccines in transit, identify facilities needing replenishment and redistribute excess stock to facilities facing shortages.
“From the comfort of the office of the state control officer, you’ll have visibility in terms of the location of every vaccine,” Shehu said.
Delays in receiving facility-level data can slow state decisions about where vaccines are needed.
“If your data is coming to the state level late, it will delay decision-making. And when you delay decision-making, the program tends to suffer,” Shehu said.
Vaccine shortages can also undermine demand. Shehu said caregivers turned away because a facility has run out of stock often do not return.
“Despite all the effort being put into the demand side, if vaccines are not available at the facility, caregivers who bring their children for immunisation may be asked to return another day. In most cases, they will not come back,” Shehu said.
The programme also handles reverse logistics: eHealth Africa collects vaccine waste from health facilities and transports it to a central point for incineration, Shehu said.
When vehicles cannot reach a facility, a representative may meet a delivery officer at an accessible central location to collect vaccines, Shehu said.
In Sokoto State, eHealth Africa’s 2026 mid-year report said the number of health facilities served through its Vaccine Direct Delivery intervention increased from 351 to 407. The programme also delivered approximately 3.41 million vaccine antigens in the state during the first half of 2026 to support immunisation services in underserved communities.
In Borno State, eHealth Africa said it uses Indigo Vaccine Carriers to support immunisation in communities affected by insecurity. The carriers maintain vaccines at +2°C to +8°C for up to five days without ice or electricity. Since 2021, the organisation says Indigo systems have immunised more than 496,000 children.
“Facilities using Indigo have cut transport costs by 50%, moved from two sessions a week to daily services, and are reaching almost twice as many children compared to ice-pack carriers,” Tahir Buhari, senior research manager at eHealth Africa, said.
Keeping vaccines potent at health facilities
Getting vaccines to health centres is only part of the challenge; keeping them potent is another, particularly with Nigeria’s unreliable electricity supply.
“If you expose some of the vaccines and they freeze, they are damaged. If you expose them to temperatures above eight degrees Celsius, they are damaged. So what that means is you have to have a constant way of powering your refrigerators to keep your vaccines potent,” Shehu said.
With support from UNICEF, eHealth Africa said it has installed solar power systems at primary healthcare centres through its Renewable Energy for Primary Healthcare (RE4PHC) programme. Shehu said the intervention improved service delivery at solarised facilities, particularly in maternal and newborn healthcare, with an increase in the number of deliveries conducted at some primary healthcare centres.
The organisation also remotely monitors the systems to detect faults and send technicians to affected facilities. “So it’s a smart system that is beyond just providing electricity,” Shehu said.
According to eHealth Africa’s 2026 mid-year report, the organisation had solarised 238 primary healthcare centres across 12 states. In the first half of 2026, 226 remotely monitored facilities generated 277,800 kWh of electricity, avoiding an estimated ₦166 million in fuel costs.
Building systems that can outlast projects
Immunisation systems depend not only on technology but also on people to operate them, resources to maintain them and funding to keep them running. Shehu identified limited technical capacity, high upfront costs and donor dependence as major sustainability challenges.
“There are some systems that work in advanced countries, but if you bring them into the Nigerian context or an African context, we don’t have the capacity to manage them at the initial stage,” he said.
He said sustainability must be considered before deployment, with government and intended users involved from the design stage, particularly given the cost of introducing technologies and maintaining them after donor funding ends.
“If you want sustainability in all your interventions, the first thing you need to do is consider human-centred design, designing with the government as well as the beneficiaries,” he said.
Technology partners must also consider what governments would spend to develop, deploy and operate systems after external support ends, Shehu said.
“Why most of the technology innovations are failing is because we focus more on designing and implementing them, but we don’t take into consideration how much it will cost for the government to continue running that intervention after our exit,” he said.
Ohaeri stressed the need for domestic funding to sustain these programmes. Under the 2001 Abuja Declaration, African governments committed to allocating at least 15% of their annual budgets to healthcare, but Nigeria has yet to meet that target, she said.
“With the Abuja Declaration of 2001, we agreed on a 15% investment, but I don’t think that Nigeria has ever gone beyond 5%,” she said.
She added that governments must also build the capacity of local health workers to continue using these tools and improving healthcare delivery without relying on donor or international partner support.
This infrastructure could also support maternal, newborn and child health, disease surveillance, emergency preparedness, and sexual and reproductive health services, Shehu said.
Governments would need to coordinate digital health investments, establish common data standards and make platforms interoperable to avoid disconnected systems, he said.
“Ultimately, Africa does not simply need more digital health platforms. We need connected, sustainable and people-centred systems that translate reliable data into better decisions, stronger service delivery and equitable access to healthcare,” he said.

articles.title: From prototype to production: Engineering agents with Agent DLC | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
From prototype to production: Engineering agents with Agent DLC
Over the past year, AI agents have moved from exploration into engineering. Enterprise teams are shipping large language model (LLM) systems that call tools, orchestrate APIs, and answer questions over internal knowledge.
A successful demo can show what an agent is capable of. Before release, the team needs to answer a further question: “Is this agent ready for production?” The person responsible for that decision needs evidence that the agent meets the agreed requirements.
To make that decision consistently, teams need a repeatable, affordable way to assess the agent’s current behavior and whether the latest change has improved it.
In traditional software development, teams answer these questions with unit tests, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), and passing builds. Those mechanisms are necessary but not sufficient for agents, for three reasons, each requiring additional checks. This post explains these three properties and presents a measured case where an aggregate metric hides a coverage problem. It then introduces the Agent Development Lifecycle (Agent DLC): one lifecycle, two loops, and a single explicit standard for judging every change.
A note on terminology: Throughout this post, gold standard means one specific artifact: the bundle of verifiable criteria, their thresholds, and the approved examples they are checked against. Business owners approve this standard as the basis for acceptance decisions.
1. Three properties of agents that require additional engineering practices
Conventional software testing and CI/CD still apply to agents, but three properties require additional checks. First, agents are non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different outputs and execution paths. Second, changes to prompts, tool descriptions, retrieval settings, or memory configuration can alter behavior in ways that a text review alone can’t reveal. Third, model endpoints, knowledge bases, and external APIs can change independently of the repository and affect agent behavior. Table 1 summarizes the engineering practices needed to address each property.
Table 1. What each property invalidates, and what it requires instead.
| Property | The conventional answer | Why it falls short | What Agent DLC requires | 
| Non-determinism | One assertion per case in CI | Measures a single sample of a distribution. Passes and fails for reasons unrelated to your change | Run each example k times. Judge on pass rate and failure distribution | 
| Prompts are source code | Review the diff, approve the change | Behavior can’t be read off the text of a prompt | Every prompt, tool, retrieval, and memory change is versioned with an evaluation attached, and the lineage is kept | 
| Dependencies move on their own | Pin versions, validate on upgrade | Doesn’t fire because nothing in your repository changed | Re-run the standard on a schedule and alert on deviations from the baseline | 
2. A measured example: High retrieval precision can hide missing information
The following example shows how the choice of metrics affects diagnosis.
We built a reference implementation to exercise the method end to end: an internal policy assistant answering HR policy questions over a document knowledge base. We chose a narrow, well-scoped domain to make the evaluation and diagnosis straightforward to follow. The following results were measured on this reference implementation. It isn’t a customer outcome and it isn’t a benchmark result.
The accompanying AWS Samples repository includes infrastructure deployment, the HR agent, custom evaluators, and scripts for baseline evaluation and prompt-change re-evaluation (09-run-eval.sh and 10-optimize-prompt.sh). It also includes optional checks for judge repeatability, model comparison, cost, and latency. The scripts reproduce the workflow. Scores can vary across runs and repository versions.
Three golden questions, five measures each:
- Groundedness: Decompose the answer into claims and check each against the retrieved sources.
- Chunk-level source precision: Is each retrieved chunk, as a whole, necessary for this question?
- Fact-level source precision: Decompose each chunk into individual facts and check whether each fact is necessary.
- Retrieval coverage: For each sub-question, does any retrieved chunk answer it?
- Response precision: Of the claims in the answer, how many are necessary?
Table 2. First evaluation round. Measured on the reference implementation. Not a customer outcome.
| Question | Groundedness | Chunk-level precision | Fact-level precision | Retrieval coverage | Verdict | 
| Performance review | 0.83 | 1.00 | 0.59 | 1.00 | Pass | 
| Benefits enrollment | 0.90 | 1.00 | 0.53 | 1.00 | Pass | 
| Sick-leave certificate | 0.39 | 1.00 | 0.09 | 0.00 | Fail | 
Chunk-level precision is 1.00 for all three questions. A release gate based only on this metric would accept all three answers.
Fact-level precision tells a different story: 0.59, 0.53, 0.09. For the third question, roughly nine out of ten facts in the retrieved material are irrelevant to what was asked. Chunk-level precision only asks whether a passage is on topic. It doesn’t measure how much of the passage is relevant.
Then we changed exactly one thing: the system prompt. We added three constraints: ground strictly in retrieved content, ignore irrelevant retrieved content, and keep answers focused. The agent, the knowledge base, the evaluators, and the questions were untouched, so the before-and-after differs by one variable.
Table 3. After a prompt-only change. One change, two opposite outcomes.
|  | Performance review, before | Performance review, after | Sick leave, before | Sick leave, after | 
| Groundedness | 0.83 | 0.87 | 0.39 (fail) | 0.31 (still fail) | 
| Fact-level precision | 0.59 | 0.85 | 0.09 | 0.04 | 
| Response precision | 0.58 | 0.73 | 0.33 | — | 
The first question improved substantially. The third got worse.
The evaluation suggested where to investigate before we made the change. Look at the third row of Table 2 again: chunk-level precision 1.00, fact-level precision 0.09, retrieval coverage 0.00. Together, these scores suggested a knowledge-coverage problem: the retrieved material was nominally on topic but didn’t answer the question. Telling the model to “ground strictly in retrieved content” couldn’t supply the missing information.
We checked that diagnosis against the source documents used in the experiment. The corpus lacked a dedicated sick-leave policy document, although the leave-management policy contained brief references to sick leave. The next step was to address policy coverage and then check retrieval, rather than keep changing the prompt.
In this case, the source material lacks the information needed to answer the question, so prompt changes alone can’t resolve the failure.
In this example, evaluation helped identify what needed investigation before further changes.
Another result shows why groundedness needs to be checked alongside other criteria. The benefits-enrollment answer passed with groundedness 0.90, and it contained this sentence: “I also noticed from your profile that your preferred contact method is Social Media.” No such profile exists.
The policy document lists contact preference as an option inside a process step. The public, crowd-sourced, noisy FAQ corpus contains a pair answering that question with “social media”. The model combined a policy option with an unrelated FAQ answer and presented it as a fact about the user. The high groundedness score didn’t catch this false personal claim. Passing a quality threshold doesn’t establish that responsibility constraints have been met.
These scores can vary between runs, and a borderline Pass can become a Fail. Interpret score differences alongside repeated runs and the underlying evidence. Section 5 discusses how to check evaluator reliability.
This small reference-implementation example illustrates how evaluation can guide diagnosis. It doesn’t establish a general improvement rate or validate a production release.
3. Agent DLC: One lifecycle, two loops
Agent DLC connects six activities around one explicit gold standard: Define, Build, Evaluate, Release, Observe, and Feed Back.
Evaluation-driven development has been described in earlier work, including Xia et al.’s Evaluation-Driven Development of LLM Agents: A Process Model and Reference Architecture. Agent DLC applies this approach to delivery through six activities with explicit acceptance conditions, release authority, and evidence requirements.
The acceptance-first approach also appears in Fotor’s published AWS customer case study. The team defined scalability, cost, isolation, and architectural flexibility criteria before migrating to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, then validated changes against operating data. The case reports workflow overhead falling from minutes to seconds, excluding model inference, and support for thousands of concurrent active sessions. It documents Agent DLC-guided architecture delivery. Quality evaluation is identified as the next step.
Define translates business objectives into criteria, thresholds, and approved examples. Build designs the prompts, tools, context, memory, and runtime mechanisms that must satisfy them. Evaluate produces the evidence that says whether a candidate version does. When it does, the version goes to a controlled release. Observe watches it in production. Feed Back returns what production teaches to Define.
Figure 1 shows how each activity uses or updates the standard, making its role in development and release explicit.
Inside that outer loop runs a faster inner loop: score → inspect the path → change one thing → re-evaluate. It operates on one candidate version and answers two questions: where to change, and whether the change helped.
The two loops do different jobs, and the difference matters. The inner loop improves the agent against a fixed standard. The outer loop lets the standard change. Finding during development that the agent recommends products without checking inventory is an inner-loop problem. Suppose production users ask the agent to look things up on behalf of a family member, but no criterion covers this case. This requires the outer loop: define the authorization boundary and add examples. Then use the inner loop to meet the updated standard.
Confusing the two can lead teams to try to fix a missing criterion with a prompt change. Teams might also widen the standard during an improvement cycle, leaving them unable to tell which change moved the score.
Both loops build reusable assets: business criteria, approved examples, evaluators, and the record of how past failures were handled. These assets outlive the model and the framework. When you change models, evaluate the replacement against the same criteria and examples.
The next four sections explain how to define good so it can be checked (section 4) and improve the agent against that standard (section 5). They then cover updating the standard through production feedback (section 6) and designing the architecture to provide evaluation evidence (section 7).
4. Define good: Five dimensions, three tiers
Start with a business outcome defined by its owner. For a recommendation agent, this might be: “Recommend suitable products to returning customers while protecting their information.” Translate that requirement into verifiable criteria across five dimensions.
Table 4. Consider all five dimensions when defining criteria.
| Dimension | Key question | Areas of focus | 
| Domain understanding | Does it actually understand your business? | Terminology, aliases, multi-hop relationships, internal enterprise knowledge | 
| Quality | Is it correct, complete, and consistent throughout? | Correctness, completeness, consistency, support for citations | 
| Responsibility | Are permissions, boundaries, compliance, and auditability addressed? | Unauthorized access, information disclosure, compliance hard constraints, traceability | 
| Cost | What does each run cost, and does it stay economical at scale? | Token consumption, evaluator cost, redundant steps | 
| Performance | Is it fast, stable, and able to carry the load? | Latency, throughput, stability, availability | 
For each criterion, specify how it’s verified and who approves it. “It must be accurate” is a goal. “Every factual claim must be traceable to a retrieved source” is verifiable. Business experts should approve examples that make the expected behavior concrete.
Table 5. Criteria fall into three tiers. The tier, not the dimension, decides whether a criterion blocks a release.
| Tier | Blocks release? | How it’s expressed | Example | 
| Hard constraint | Yes | Boolean, evaluated per run | Disclosing another customer’s information | 
| Release gate | Until it’s met | Pass-rate threshold over k runs | At least 95% of cited clauses traceable to a source | 
| Monitoring only | No | Tracked and reviewed, promoted later | Tone appropriateness, until its evaluator is calibrated | 
Assign each criterion its own tier and, where applicable, threshold. Never let a high score elsewhere offset a hard-constraint violation.
In the recommendation example, recommendation quality is a release gate under Quality, while protecting another customer’s information is a hard constraint under Responsibility. One business requirement produces criteria in different dimensions and tiers. Assess each against its own acceptance condition.
These criteria also determine what evidence the system must expose. The next section uses that evidence to improve the agent and decide whether to release it. Section 7 explains how evidence requirements shape the architecture.
5. The inner loop: Evaluate, diagnose, and improve
Score. Match the evaluator to the criterion. Use code for unambiguous rules, runtime telemetry for cost and latency, and load tests and operating data for capacity and availability. Use model-based judges for criteria requiring judgment, calibrated against human-reviewed examples. Include authorization and cross-user isolation tests alongside checks for prohibited fields when evaluating information protection. Run each example k times to assess variable behavior.
For model-based judges, repeat evaluations to measure scoring variability and compare their judgments with human-reviewed examples. Small score gains need supporting evidence before they count as improvements.
Inspect the path. Locate a failure at three levels: session, trajectory, and step. If a recommendation exposes a phone number, follow the affected session to response composition and inspect where profile fields entered the draft. The cause might be upstream of the visible symptom, as section 2 showed.
Change one thing, then re-evaluate. Correct the identified cause and repeat evaluation against the unchanged standard under the same conditions. Verify that disclosure stopped and recommendation quality still meets its gate.
Assess release readiness separately for each task type, or intent. Release only those that meet their criteria, with any fallback for an unreleased intent also meeting the agreed release conditions.
Table 6. Release decisions by dimension, tier, and intent.
| State of the grid | Decision | 
| Any hard constraint failed | Don’t release. | 
| All hard constraints pass, but one or more release gates missed | Don’t release the affected intent unless a limited rollout was approved in advance with explicit safeguards and stop criteria. Otherwise, route it to a human. | 
| All hard constraints pass, and all release gates met | Full release. | 
A limited rollout needs acceptance conditions, safeguards, and stop criteria agreed before evaluation. It can’t override a hard constraint or lower a threshold after a failed result.
Before release, include blocked and refused requests in the evaluation, checking whether each was handled as expected. Record the criteria, thresholds, evaluator versions, and release decision so the team can trace why a version was approved.
Passing these checks supports release within the tested scope. Production monitoring then checks whether the agent continues to meet the standard as usage and dependencies change.
6. The outer loop: Keep the data flowing
Record execution traces from the first test request so failures can be diagnosed in development and production. Sample and evaluate production interactions to identify failures, then review them with the business owner to confirm the expected behavior. Add cases covered by existing criteria to the regression set. When a case reveals a missing requirement, update the standard and use the inner loop to meet it.
Run evaluations regularly to catch behavior changes caused by external dependencies. When the standard changes, compare results under both versions to distinguish agent regression from broader test coverage. Link each result to its standard, test set, evaluator, and agent version.
7. Design the architecture to support evaluation
The evaluation and feedback loops need evidence that the architecture must provide. Work backward from each criterion to the system behavior and records needed to verify it.
For example, to distinguish a tool-selection error from an execution failure, define the tool’s purpose, accepted inputs, outputs, and error conditions. Expose the actual inputs, results, and errors in traces so evaluators can locate the failure.
Acceptance criteria therefore shape both evaluation and architecture. With those foundations in place, start with one business task and establish a baseline.
8. Getting started on AWS
Choose one clearly scoped business task and aim to establish an initial evaluation baseline within a week.
- Days 1–2. Have the business owner and engineers agree on acceptance criteria, tiers, and thresholds. Prepare 20–30 golden examples covering common requests and important edge cases, with expected behavior approved by the business owner.
- Days 3–5. Implement the evaluators described in section 5 and run the golden set repeatedly. Publish the baseline, including failures and the evidence needed to investigate them.
- Week 2. Change one thing and re-evaluate under the same conditions. Record the release decision and its supporting evidence.
After reviewing the baseline, integrate evaluation into the release process and run it regularly to detect drift. Assign an owner to review production failures and feed confirmed cases back into the standard.
On AWS, use models available through Amazon Bedrock to build the agent. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, assesses agent behavior with built-in evaluators and supports custom evaluators for business-specific criteria. AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, provides execution visibility, complemented by Amazon CloudWatch for runtime monitoring and diagnostics. AgentCore runtime, Gateway, Identity, and Memory support execution, tool integration, identity management, and memory management.

articles.title: Logitech offers 7,000 employees a paid day off to play GTA 6
articles.text:
The takeaway: Ahead of next week's GTA 6 launch, Logitech has announced a novel initiative called Logi Game Day, giving all of its employees one paid day off to play video games. While the move is unusual for a tech company that isn't a game developer or publisher, game studios and publishers are known to host company-wide launch parties and gaming sessions as part of major launch-day events.
Logitech explained that the program applies to all 7,000 full-time employees and interns globally, who can take the time off to play any video game of their choice, not just GTA 6. The company also clarified that the day can be used anytime between now and November 2027, and doesn't have to coincide with the launch of GTA 6.
In a statement, Logitech CEO Hanneke Faber said the Logi Game Day initiative is intended to challenge the perception that gaming is unproductive. "It's time to retire the stereotype that gaming is a waste of time," she said, adding that as a company that designs both enterprise and gaming products, Logitech believes that "engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other."
The initiative follows Logitech's Ctrl Tomorrow study, in which 81% of gamers agreed that "gaming builds real-world confidence, reduces anxiety, and correlates with stronger day-to-day work performance."
A separate Logitech study of enterprise IT decision-makers (ITDMs) found that 98.8% of respondents believe gaming skills translate directly to workplace capabilities, such as problem-solving and performing under pressure.
Faber said she plans to join the Logi Game Day festivities on November 19, when the company will host a gaming event at its San Jose office, with workspaces converted into gaming lounges to celebrate the much-awaited launch of GTA 6. The event will also be streamed online for fans.
The data cited by Logitech contrasts with some estimates suggesting the US economy could lose up to $1 billion in productivity on November 19 as 1.5 million workers call in sick to play GTA 6. However, the figures have been disputed by Victor Matheson, an economist at the College of the Holy Cross, who argues that any short-term loss will be made up for in the long term.
GTA VI will launch on November 19, 2026 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series consoles, with a PC version rumored to arrive sometime next year.
The game is available for pre-order starting at $80 for the standard edition and $100 for the "ultimate" edition. Rockstar is also selling a whopping $400 Collector's Edition, but that box is merchandise only and doesn't include the game.

articles.title: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen, finally replacing 3.8 Flash
articles.text:
Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen. These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen’s purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google’s ecosystem use.
With Google’s recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company’s products.
Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it’s 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces “fabricated claims” by more than 5x, according to Google’s analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash’s score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon.

articles.title: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before Congress | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said on Thursday, according to reports from Bloomberg and NBC News.
Huang, who stepped down as CEO following reports of an alleged affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, agreed to testify Wednesday after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.
Huang has agreed to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving, which falls later this month.
The development comes after House Republicans Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford sent Huang a letter on November 4 requesting that he appear before their committees. Moolenaar chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, Mast chairs the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and Crawford chairs the House Intelligence Committee.
“Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.”
The testimony will take place behind closed doors, though Mast said he expects the briefing to be recorded on video and transcribed.

articles.title: La Unión Europea propuso que los usuarios puedan apagar el desplazamiento infinito y la reproducción automática
articles.text:
La Comisión Europea presentó el 11 de noviembre la Ley de Equidad Digital, una propuesta que obligaría a redes sociales, plataformas de video y videojuegos a ofrecer una herramienta para apagar las funciones pensadas para enganchar: el desplazamiento infinito, la reproducción automática y las notificaciones sin relación con la actividad del usuario.
El texto, que todavía debe pasar por el Parlamento Europeo y el Consejo de la Unión Europea, reemplazaría la directiva de 2005 sobre prácticas comerciales desleales por un reglamento de aplicación directa. Según The Next Web, eso sustituiría 27 regímenes nacionales por una sola norma, válida para cualquier empresa que venda a consumidores europeos, esté donde esté.
El artículo sobre diseño adictivo enumera cuatro funciones que el usuario podrá desactivar, una por una o todas juntas: la reproducción automática sin pausas efectivas, las notificaciones ajenas a su actividad, los premios o castigos según la frecuencia de uso y los mensajes insistentes con que un chatbot simula una relación personal.
La obligación es ofrecer el interruptor, no prohibir esas funciones. Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal, asesora de políticas de la organización de derechos digitales EDRi, cuestionó ese punto ante EUobserver: “¿Por qué reconocer tan explícitamente el problema del diseño adictivo sin introducir obligaciones más fuertes para prevenirlo?”.
Videojuegos: cajas de premios y monedas virtuales
Los videojuegos son el sector con más restricciones. Las cajas de recompensas pagas, que entregan un objeto al azar, tendrían que mostrar la probabilidad de obtener cada premio. Quedarían prohibidas para menores de 18 años, y los adultos también podrían desactivarlas.
Las monedas virtuales deberán indicar cuánto equivalen en dinero real. Si el producto está dirigido a menores o la empresa sabe con razonable certeza que los usa, esas monedas estarían desactivadas por defecto hasta que un padre o tutor las autorice. Los mecanismos para pagar y avanzar más rápido también quedarían vedados a menores, según el borrador de la Comisión.
Para las redes sociales, las plataformas de video y los chatbots de compañía, el proyecto remite a otra norma en preparación, la ley europea de protección de menores en línea, que ya prohibiría esas funciones a los menores. La Ley de Equidad Digital se aplicaría a los adultos y a los servicios que esa otra norma no alcance.
Influencers, suscripciones y multas de hasta el 6%
Los influencers deberían marcar cada publicación comercial con las palabras “publicidad” o “colaboración comercial”, y no podrían presentarla como una opinión personal. Las marcas y agencias que los contratan tendrían que asegurar por contrato que cumplen la norma. Tampoco podrían promocionar productos peligrosos ni cuya publicidad esté prohibida.
Agustín Reyna, director general de la organización de consumidores BEUC, dijo que los usuarios esperan consejos genuinos de los influencers y no que les vendan “en silencio” una crema o una prenda de moda.
Sobre las suscripciones, The Next Web, que cita el adelanto de Euronews, informó que las pruebas gratuitas no podrían convertirse en pagas sin aceptación expresa, que las renovaciones llegarían con aviso previo y que cancelar debería ser posible en línea en pocos pasos, con derecho a hablar con una persona.
El mismo medio añade que una revisión paralela de las normas de cooperación en consumo permitiría a la Comisión investigar por sí misma las infracciones transfronterizas graves, con multas de hasta 6% de la facturación mundial de la empresa.
La Comisión estima que las medidas reducirían en 88.400 millones de euros el perjuicio financiero de los consumidores entre 2025 y 2035, según el resumen de DigWatch. The Next Web agrega que el costo anual para las empresas rondaría los 678 millones de euros.
El antecedente que justifica la propuesta es un estudio de 2022 de la Comisión: el 97% de los sitios y aplicaciones más populares usaba diseños engañosos, que orientan al usuario hacia la opción más rentable para la empresa, según informó EUobserver.
La propuesta pasa ahora al Parlamento Europeo y al Consejo, donde deberá negociarse antes de convertirse en ley. The Next Web anticipa años de negociación.

articles.title: 'Star Wars: Una nueva esperanza' vuelve a los cines por su 50 aniversario: ya hay fecha de estreno
articles.text:
El 2027 va a ser un año grande para Star Wars. Y es que la legendaria franquicia galáctica ucmplirá 50 años. una fecha señalada desde ahce tiempo en el calendario de todos los fans porque se esperan todo tipo de celebraciones. Ahora, se ha confirmado lo que todos esperaban. La primera película de la saga, Star Wars: Una nueva esperanza, vuelve a los cines.
Tal y como ha informado Disney, Lucasfilm estrenará una versión restaurada de La guerra de las galaxias (1977) en miles de salas de cine de todo el mundo. La fecha del reestreno de Star Wars: Una nueva esperanza en cines será el 19 de febrero de 2027. Además, se sabe que la película estará disponible en IMAX 70 mm en mercados seleccionados. Los formatos de proyección en España pendientes de confirmación.
Además del estreno en cines, la compañía ha anunciado un reestreno extra en algunos lugares de Estados Unidos. Y es que Cosm presentará una versión en Shared Reality de la película (en la versión de 2019) en espacios inmersivos de Atlanta, Dallas, Detroit y Los Ángeles a partir de marzo de 2027. Junto a todo ello, se ha presentado un espectacular póster para conmemorar una cita tan especial como es el regreso a los cines de una de las películas más importantes de todos los tiempos.
2027: el 50 aniversario de Star Wars
Lo cierto es que el histórico reestreno en cines de la película original de 1977 no es la única sorpresa que Disney ha anunciado para el 50 aniversario de Star Wars. Antes de la llegada a los cines de Una nueva esperanza, la compañía estrenará la esperada segunda temporada de Ahsoka el 20 de enero en Disney+. Protagonizada de nuevo por Rosario Dawson como la querida Jedi, la serie se ambienta tras la caída del Imperio y el ascenso de la Nueva República, en la que Ahsoka se enfrenta a lo que significa ser una Jedi mientras la galaxia encara a un terrible adversario, el Gran Almirante Thrawn.
Ya en abril, la saga galáctica volverá a vestirse de gala. Del 1 al 4 de abril se celebrará en Los Ángeles la Star Wars Celebration. Este evento será una vez más la máxima experiencia para los fans de Star Wars. En ella se celebrarán paneles para hablar sobre el presente y el futuro de la saga en todas sus vertientes. A su vez, contará con cientos de expositores, merchandising exclusivo e invitados especiales.
En esas mismas fechas, los días 2 y 3 de abril, Lucasfilm, Disney Concerts, AMP Worldwide y Live Nation Hewitt Silva darán vida al legado musical de Star Wars con Star Wars in Concert: The Skywalker Saga en el Hollywood Bowl. este fue el lugar que acogió el primer concierto oficial de Star Wars en noviembre de 1977. Presentadas por Anthony Daniels, el intérprete de C-3PO, estas actuaciones especiales de las icónicas bandas sonoras de John Williams incluirán escenas y música de las nueve películas de la saga Skywalker.
Y ya en mayo, Lucasfilm prepara todavía más celebraciones. El 4 de mayo (May the 4th) se estrenará en Disney+ The Hero Awakens, un nuevo documental inédito de Lucasfilm del aclamado cineasta R.J. Cutler. En él se narrará cómo se hizo Star Wars y se ofrecerá a los fans una mirada única a la película a través de material de archivo y grabaciones de audio captadas durante su rodaje en 1977 y en torno a él.
Y el 28 de mayo llega a los cines de todo el mundo la esperadísima Star Wars: Starfighter. Dirigida por Shawn Levy y protagonizada por Ryan Gosling, la próxima película de la saga transcurre en una era totalmente nueva de Star Wars y presentará personajes y escenarios nunca vistos. Cuando un cínico y solitario aventurero se enfrenta a su pasado, se ve arrastrado a una peligrosa aventura por toda la galaxia que lo llevará a encontrarse cara a cara con su destino.
Por otro lado, Star Wars se ha asociado con un montón de marcas y empresas como Hasbro, Grupo LEGO, Adidas, Mars o Aston Martin para presentar colecciones especiales creadas para conmemorar este 50º aniversario. Por si fuera poco, según promete la compañía "Disney y Lucasfilm revelarán próximamente más colaboraciones intergeneracionales a finales de este año y a lo largo de 2027, con grandes marcas globales y anuncios para todas las generaciones de fans."

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after alleged affairs
articles.text:
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s president and CEO following revelations of affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.
In a release published by Nvidia, the company confirmed that current executive vice president and CFO, Colette Kress, will serve as interim CEO until a permanent successor to Huang can be named. Kress will also continue to serve as CFO during this time.
“Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” Nvidia said.
The company’s shares have been in free fall since the news of Huang’s affairs broke, and his departure will likely spur further declines. As of writing, Nvidia’s stock was down nearly 13 per cent on Thursday.
Huang’s affair raised concerns among U.S. national intelligence leaders, leading to an FBI investigation. Further, U.S. lawmakers demanded Huang testify about the allegations, especially given Huang’s efforts to lobby U.S. President Donald Trump to ease restrictions on AI chip sales to China.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the spying allegations “pure fabrication” and claimed the reports were an effort to destabilize U.S.-China relations.
On Nov. 11, the New York Times reported on Huang’s second alleged affair, this time with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare.
Nvidia has played a significant role in the AI industry, with its chips powering much of the technology. Huang’s affairs and departure will likely spur increased scrutiny of Nvidia and its dealings, which have been at the centre of a circular cycle where the company invested in AI companies that would then use the money to buy Nvidia’s chips.
Header image credit: Shutterstock

articles.title: 'We like transparency, but we also like control': Software vendors need to make their tools more accessible without dumbing them down, and Adobe thinks it's got the winning formula
articles.text:
'We like transparency, but we also like control': Software vendors need to make their tools more accessible without dumbing them down, and Adobe thinks it's got the winning formula
Software vendors are under immense pressure to deliver to all ends of the spectrum
Software is evolving – new doors are opening up to give users access to vendors' tools without necessarily having to interact with the conventional software at all, but Adobe still believes traditional software interfaces still have a future.
We've spent the last couple of decades building a habit of opening a specific app to complete our desired task, but as expectations have grown, so has application complexity – Adobe's software has long been associated with creative professionals, but its apps have often been daunting for more casual users.
From the outside, Adobe looks to be one of the earlier companies actively exploring this shift with a clear willingness to open itself up to agentic AI and MCP. But while the company is heading in a direction of conversational interfaces, it's not leaving its traditional software routes behind.
Do creative pros still need the full app experience?
Speaking exclusively to TechRadar Pro at Adobe Max, Senior Product Director for Adobe Agentic Zorana Gee explained that while emerging AI tools is making the company's tools more accessible to more users, creators will still need different levels of control depending on what they're trying to achieve.
"I think it depends on who you talk to," Gee said when asked whether software is becoming less of a UI-centric destination and more of an invisible layer. "We see people who are still really wanting knobs and controls to change things."
But at the other end of the spectrum, other users might not have the time or expertise to learn complicated applications, so describing what they need and making less advanced changes might suffice.
Adobe wants its tools to meet you wherever you're working
During a separate fireside chat with the media, Product Marketing VP Deepa Subramaniam explained how the company is increasingly separating its capabilities from the interfaces traditionally used to access them. For many users now, the first point of entry has become their chosen chatbot or AI agents.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
From there, users can choose to move into one of the Creative Cloud apps, where Adobe's own Creative Agent can help bridge some of the learning gaps typically involved by offering a more conversational interface.
But rather than forcing users to adopt Adobe's own AI assistant, the company is ready to open the doors and allow new ways of working, like AI agents, to be the point of interaction with its tools.
"We're breaking down silos and walls in terms of domain expertise and domain opportunities, and that's happening all the way to the core of how we build products," Gee added.
For Adobe, that represents a significant change from the traditional software model, but it's already a familiar conversation that we're having away from software. Countless studies have already pointed toward companies having to redefine a new way of working rather than plastering AI on top of existing processes, and Adobe's readiness to reconsider its longstanding software strategy is an extension of this.
Software isn't becoming less relevant
The prospect of controlling apps through natural language is becoming more of a reality, and barriers to entry are already being broken, but Gee was cautious about suggesting that those will totally replace traditional software.
"Being more descriptive and being able to articulate verbally the things that you want is definitely a reality," she said, stressing that the transition from traditional input to conversational won't stop at 100% – it'll likely stop much sooner, at a point where both types of input can coexist.
"Will it be 100%? I think it's unlikely or maybe it's a slow progression."
"Words are hard, communication is hard," she said, and that's an important distinction for pros. For example, a photographer adjusting a particular aspect of an image might want to make a precise fine-tune change that a text prompt could misinterpret or overestimate.
Gee also admitted that Adobe is still working out how far its integrations and evolutions should go, and that it's navigating these changes through experimentation together with a community of customers who are helping to shape tools based on what really works.
Is Adobe using Firefly as the front for its evolving software strategy?
Adobe's flagship apps are highly capable, but that's led to the steep learning curve often associated with apps like Photoshop and Premiere. Firefly serves as a different starting point, shoehorning some of the most in-demand tools and controls across many of the Creative Cloud apps into an AI-first interface.
Even pros at the top of their game may struggle to work across disciplines – Gee gave an example of a highly-skilled Photoshop user wanting (and struggling) to use motion graphic tools in After Effects.
All in all, Gee sees AI-assisted design as both "lowering the floor and raising the ceiling at the same time."
But finding a simple way to integrate AI can be complex – I wanted to know how users can make the best model choice when they're faced with so many options. Firefly supports multiple models from different vendors (the company just announced a deeper collaboration with Google to make Gemini Omni, Veo and Nano Banana more widely available in its apps), but expecting every end user to understand the pros and cons of each and make a selection defeats the purpose of adding AI in the first place.
It's another area where Adobe's desire to add precision, control and simplicity in one hit is clear. "The agent will always help if they understand the intent," Gee said, but if users have a preference, they can still opt for one that suits their budget or output needs.
"We like transparency, but we also like control," Gee added.
Where does this leave the software industry?
It's clear that AI's enabling Adobe to accommodate a wider range of users, including many who will have previously been turned about by the complexity of its advanced tools.
And that's probably the essence of it – software vendors are having to become less prescriptive about how people interact with their tools, while AI creates new entry points for new demographics of users.
In some ways, it feels like the Firefly environment is being used as an experiment for the company to determine, together with its users, what the next chapter of software looks like.
But while AI agents become increasingly capable of navigating software on our behalves, and vendors start putting these tools closer to our agents, it doesn't mean we're set to see the end of software. For Adobe, it's about a future where opening an app is a choice rather than a necessity, and the next challenge lies in making its tools accessible through as many doors as possible without compromising on the depth and precision that made them what they are in the first place.

articles.title: Rethinking Memory For AI Inference
articles.text:
Processing data closer to memory could reduce power and boost performance, but software, thermal, and architectural challenges remain.
Key Takeaways:
The shift from AI training in data centers to AI inferencing at the edge will require a fundamental rethinking of where and how data is processed and stored, how it is prioritized, and what needs to be traded off in terms of power and performance to stay within a limited power budget.
At the center of these efforts is a recognition that the explosion of data — especially in physical AI where data is being live-streamed from sensors — requires much of that data to be processed as close to memory as possible. This has been a topic of discussion since the inception of the Internet of Things, but it really began gaining traction with AI due to the flood of data and concerns about the amount of power required to move and process it. In battery-electric vehicles and drones, for example, the less energy spent on processing data, the greater the range per charge and the more energy that can be allocated to critical and not-so-critical functions.
The challenge is understanding what data needs to be kept, what can be discarded, and what needs to be acted upon. Those are very different priorities. Making those choices requires advanced processing, and the quickest path to results using the least amount of energy is to minimize the distance data needs to travel between processing and memory.
“The realities of these LLMs getting into physical devices are causing everyone to rethink how they architect their memory,” said Frank Ferro, group director for product management at Cadence. “Even with conventional memory — without even talking about processing in memory — how do I partition these models to maximize the performance both of the overall processor and memory subsystem?”
Solving those issues will require several new approaches, such as processing near memory (PNM) and processing in memory (PIM), as well as improvements across multiple technologies and approaches. Compilers and operating systems will need to catch up, and standards will need to be established.
“AI in the data center and all these large language models have been the focus of everyone’s attention for the last couple of years, and now these models have been trained and pushed out into the field, into the edge of the network and physical AI,” Ferro said. “The reality is you have limited compute power and limited memory.”
AI inferencing at the edge presents different challenges than training AI models in AI data centers.
“Training almost always involves highly variable memory access patterns, and mostly involves the use of interpreted code — for example, Python to PyTorch — which necessitates the complexities of coherence across layers of memory,” said Steve Roddy, chief marketing officer at Quadric. “Once inference begins, the use model changes dramatically. Whether you are looking at big LLMs running in a data center, or models running locally, such as smaller LLMs or VLAs (vision-language-action) in cars, the model is known before you run it. That means the data access patterns are known ahead of time. This is where ahead-of-time compilation can start to take great advantage of the various at-memory, processing-in-memory, or in-memory-compute (IMC) options. The system knows exactly where, when, and how the compute is going to occur. There is no need for one element of a compute solution to guess if something manipulated the data while it was in another memory subsystem, because the entire system orchestration was planned out hours, days, or weeks before, when the AI inference model was compiled.”
Certain stages of the AI inference pipeline benefit from near-memory solutions more than others.
“Pushing the compute into the DRAM or near the DRAM has interesting implications,” said Sharad Chole, chief scientist and co-founder of Expedera. “You’re moving your communication pattern — my activation goes to memory, rather than my memory goes to activation — and that changes how much communication you need to do. These sort of solutions are okay for low-batch decode. For example, if you have batch one and you are trying to do decode and you are not reading all the weights, as soon as we move to large-batch decode, which is cost-optimized, or prefill, which is large-batch execution, the activation communication becomes the challenging part. These are the two ways to think about it. In the end, you have to break your execution into parts that are either storage-sensitive, in terms of how much data you need to store, or bandwidth-sensitive, or batching-sensitive.”
Either way, bringing compute closer to data can reduce the time and the energy spent moving it, and processing in the same memory package (custom HBM), or on the same memory die (LPDDR6-PIM), provides two fundamental advantages. “One of them is performance,” said Kos Gitchev, product marketing director at Cadence. “If we’re looking at a CPU or a core sitting inside the SoC, and every time you need to do an operation you’ve got to go out to memory, there’s a transaction that says, ‘Okay, get me some data from the memory that’s going to hit a cache somewhere in the SoC.’ That will eventually go to memory. It will come back to the cache and eventually come back to the processor. This operation really takes some time.”
So while chip architects can get compute running quickly on an SoC, the SoC has to wait for data to arrive. “Processing in memory to a large degree addresses this,” said Gitchev. “Now you can say, ‘I have this chunk of memory data in the memory, go do something with it, and I’m just going to go read the results. I’m going to skip this whole step of reading it, compute again, and putting it back. I’m just going to do a read, and that’s all I need.'”
| Term | Domain | What it means | Where the math happens | Data form | Examples | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CIM (compute-in-memory) / IMC (in-memory computing) | Hardware | The memory array itself performs the computation | Inside the bit cells and bitlines | Often analog (currents/charges summed on bitlines); digital variants also exist | Analog multiply-accumulate on SRAM or ReRAM bitlines | 
| IMC (in-memory computing) | Enterprise software | Databases or analytics run on data held in RAM rather than on disk | Conventional CPUs | Digital | SAP HANA. Not the meaning used in this article | 
| PIM (processing-in-memory) | Hardware | Logic placed on the same DRAM die as a standard memory array | Digital logic beside the banks | Digital, read out of the array | LPDDR6-PIM (JEDEC standard nearing completion) | 
| PNM (processing-near-memory) | Hardware | Logic placed in the memory package but on a separate die | Digital logic on the base/logic die | Digital, read out of the array | Compute on custom HBM4/HBM4E base dies (roadmap) | 
Fig. 1: Compute-in-memory vs. processing-in/near-memory — where the math happens and what each term means. Note that CIM and IMC are used interchangeably in hardware to describe architectures that perform computational tasks directly within the memory array, but IMC also has a separate software meaning. Source: Semiconductor Engineering
Reducing data movement
Ultimately, the entire system needs to be optimized to make this scheme work.
“The framing has shifted from, ‘We need more memory,’ to, ‘We need fabric that keeps memory fed without starving other traffic,'” said Nandan Nayampally, chief commercial officer at Baya Systems. “More recently it’s, ‘How to architect around scarcity itself.'”
Others agree. “AI systems are increasingly limited by the ability to move data efficiently between compute, memory, accelerators, chiplets, and dies,” said Andy Nightingale, vice president of product management and marketing, at Arteris. “This makes the interconnect and memory architecture as important as the memory device itself. This reinforces the need for scalable NoC, chiplet, cache coherence, and system mapping technologies that help customers optimize data movement before silicon.”
Interconnects, caching schemes, and packaging all play increasingly significant roles at the edge, but choosing the right combination while also keeping costs down is a challenge. So while new versions of high-bandwidth memory are enabling more processing in the base die of a multi-die stack, an LPDDR6-PIM that places slices of compute alongside the DRAM banks may be more attractive, depending on the cost.
“Near-memory computing is still using an external channel interface,” said Hoshik Kim, senior vice president and fellow at SK hynix.[1] “But by putting processing units near memory data, we can actually get rid of or remove a lot of data movement and have higher energy efficiency. Also, we can offload the compute function from the CPU or GPU, so that we can have better utilization of the host CPU or GPU.”
Typical use cases involve memory controllers inside the base die. “We are integrating some useful near-memory processing units to offload simple MAC operations,” said Kim. “Because, if you think about inference workload operations, most function computation is a simple MAC operation. So we could put MAC operations inside the base die to expand for and then work with the GPU for a more complex, compute-intensive operation.”
Multi-year process
Some of the necessary technologies are available today. Others will take years to develop, or improve enough to the point where they can make a difference.
“We are looking at in-memory applications in three to five years, maybe around 2030,” said Vishal Chandrasekar, director of product management at Ayar Labs. “You want to be able to connect up many GPUs so that you are able to have different GPUs access the memory of others. People are trying to ramp up the amount of memory per GPU, but you’re limited by packet size and HBM bandwidths and the like. Compute in memory is one path, which makes it so the base die of your memory now has compute capabilities of some kind.”
Still, that technology is not quite ready for commercialization. “It’s a little aggressive to say that we’re already seeing it out in the market,” said Cadence’s Ferro. “There might be some very specific embedded applications that are using a type of processing in memory, but as a broad usage, it’s still pretty early.”
Processing-in-memory solutions are slowly moving from research to commercialization. For example, Samsung announced the architecture and performance benchmarks for its LPDDR6-PIM chip aimed at low-power, mobile on-device AI applications.
“LPDDR-PIM is the one that has got the most attention within JEDEC,” said Randy White, memory solutions program manager at Keysight. “There is active development and discussion around LPDDR-PIM, but there are challenges for both the hardware and software. From a hardware standpoint, you’re mixing logic process with DRAM process, and they’re optimized for different metrics, so that innovation itself makes the manufacturing process more complex and expensive. You have to be very selective and make sure you know your application can sustain the added cost of that.” Applications for LPDDR6-PIM will range from fixed-node edge servers optimized for performance to mobile phones and tablets optimized for efficiency.
Trickier than hardware?
The software challenges may be even more difficult. “How do you manage workload skew and load balancing?” White noted. “Let’s say you take a checkerboard-style memory array or core, and every 10 columns or so of memory, you stick a vertical slice of logic silicon. If you were to take that PIM die, put it under a microscope, you’d see a checkerboard with slices repeated every certain number of rows. That by itself has some timing constraints. While you’re accessing one row, you have to wait for calculation to an instruction to be complete on the compute engine. So it’s not just a matter of fetching data and balancing timings between different bank accesses. Now you have memory access coupled with waiting for compute data. The whole point is that I don’t have to move data as much. I’m moving data between adjacent cells, and that’s great. From a hardware standpoint, you get lower power, etc. But for the engineer who’s writing the BIOS, who has to create the scheduler for synchronizing, that has just exploded in terms of complexity.”
PIM architectures need to be considered in terms of the impact on the rest of the system. “The hardware has to be designed and optimized so you have the right number of compute coefficients and things like that,” said White. “Then the memory has to be segregated in a way that you don’t have too fine resolution, so you have the right coarse and fine trade-offs in terms of separation.”
Fig. 2: What must be solved for near-data computing to achieve its potential. Source: SK hynix/DAC
Additionally, memory programming models are still in flux, particularly with the rise of non-traditional memory systems such as PIM, CIM, CXL-attached tiered memory, and heterogeneous memory architectures.
“I don’t think the industry will settle on a single programming model and coherence implementation,” said Steven Woo, fellow and distinguished inventor at Rambus. “Over the last 40 years, different programming models, coherence protocols, and consistency models have been implemented that provide different trade-offs to systems designers and application developers. The diversity of architectures and coherence implementations is driving the need for more high-performance libraries to be developed that allow programmers to call common functions that are implemented in ways that are optimized for different systems. High-performance libraries maintain a level of abstraction that improves program portability and performance scalability without burdening the programmer with understanding all details of the underlying hardware.”
Compiler and memory controller considerations
Software innovations are needed to support new memory architectures.
“The question is no longer whether a PIM is viable or makes sense,” said SK hynix’s Kim. “It’s a reality. The problem is how to make a software compiler framework and system software. All of the ecosystem needs to follow up.”
Cadence’s Gitchev agreed. “The real challenge is that currently the systems are designed so that the compilers, operating system, and everything works with a processor core or an accelerator sitting inside your SoC, and everything is designed for this processor to do all the work,” he said. “That’s the infrastructure. Now, essentially, you can offload some of that processor work and say, ‘I need to do this operation, and I don’t really need the processor to do it.’ There’s a whole infrastructure behind that to be able to do that. There’s a software aspect. The operating system and the processor need to understand, ‘These operations I can send to memory, they’ll do it, and I’ll just get the results, but these operations I still have to do locally because the memory I have may not be able to do it, or my system is not as efficient.'”
There’s also the need for standardization inside the chip. “How do you connect these things together?” said Gitchev. “Today we don’t really have a good way to say, ‘Go and do this operation in memory,’ as far as the type of transactions that move from the processor to the SoC fabric to memory. This infrastructure is not there. We need the hardware and protocol to be able to tell memory to go do this stuff, and then we need the software and the operating system to support the system to be able to do this and decide what’s efficient.”
This comes down to two streams of data. “I’ve got a stream of data that’s storing and reading and writing,” explained Ferro. “Then I’ve got a stream of data that’s compute, and that’s not native to the way operating systems and processors are built. You now need cooperation with the processor companies, the interface between the processor and the fabric, the system, and then of course the operating system. All those pieces need to get adjusted. It may or may not be a big adjustment, but without standardization, everyone’s system is going to be highly customized.”
Home agents and memory controllers
Near-memory and in-memory architectures introduce distinct pressures to traffic management and system coherence.
“In traditional hardware coherent systems, home agents are responsible for tracking where shared data is being used throughout the system and making sure processing elements have correct copies of the data,” explained Rambus’ Woo. “Hardware coherency eliminates the need for programmers to manage the updating of data across processing elements, simplifying programming. Synchronization primitives like locks and barriers, and software coherence give applications an additional level of control over how and when data is updated. Together, these hardware and software mechanisms enable efficient algorithms to be designed that maintain a level of hardware abstraction that hides the details of the underlying hardware, easing the task of programming and managing the way data is updated to maintain coherence in systems.”
That means software engineers increasingly need to understand the hardware, and vice versa.
“Achieving good, scalable performance as problem sizes grow and the number of processing elements increases is becoming more difficult,” said Woo. “While home agents remove the burden of managing coherence from the programmer, the messages sent by home agents to maintain coherence can become performance bottlenecks. Programmers increasingly need to understand the underlying structure and functions of the hardware to achieve good performance. Algorithms are often modified to shard data in ways that maximize the independence of tasks and minimize the amount of coherence traffic traveling in the system. In some systems, utilizing no hardware coherence mechanisms results in the best performance, but complicates the task of programming.”
The memory controller faces a twofold challenge. “One part is the memory subsystem, which consists of a PHY and a controller,” said Cadence’s Gitchev. “The controller itself is where these commands need to actually do the work. But now you have a different set of commands. Before that, you fundamentally had two different commands — read data, write data, and that’s about it. The control is a lot more complicated than that, but at a high level, that’s what it does. It reads data and writes data in the most efficient way possible. Now a different challenge is coming in where we need a different set of commands and rules to say, ‘Hey, now can you go take this data and multiply it, and take this data inside the memory and divide it, or do an operation.’ It’s not a significant challenge for a controller to do that. We add more commands, and we’ll figure out how that works, and try to make it efficient.”
The second challenge is harder. “The processor needs to be able to send those commands,” said Gitchev. “It needs to prepare a memory inside the memory subsystem to say, ‘If I’m going to multiply this data by that data, do I have the right data in the right place? Do I have the results in the right place? This operation is complete.’ The controller manages some of that, but it also has to have very close collaboration with the overall system.”
Thermal, physics, and CIM
Processing near memory can help reduce data traffic, but it could amplify existing physics problems, such as thermal issues.
“The memory shortage is partially due to current state-of-the-art design and use of available memory,” said Satish Radhakrishnan, head of global field applications and solutions at Vinci. “Innovative design can help reduce demand per unit and improve utilization. The most viable solutions to increasing memory utilization — including higher HBM stacks, custom HBM, near-memory, in-memory compute, and chiplet-based disaggregation — all share one property. They trade a bandwidth problem for a physics problem. Stacking memory closer to compute concentrates heat in exactly the places it’s hardest to remove. Heterogeneous material stacks and micron-scale interconnects create thermo-mechanical stress and warpage behavior that doesn’t respect the boundaries between die, package, and board. Heat doesn’t stop at the chip, and neither do the constraints that come with it.”
For this reason, memory companies tend to announce new thermal technology with their new architectures. For example, SK hynix announced an integrated HBM (iHBM) solution that embeds integrated cooling elements (ICEs) within the HBM package. Micron’s recent roadmap included vertical HBM (vHBM) with thermally aware design and a heat spreader over the PHY. Samsung is tackling heat issues with a range of solutions, including hybrid copper bonding (HCB) and a heat path block (HPB), which it plans to include in HBM5. [2]
SK hynix’s Kim proposed in-memory compute to reduce heat in the HBM base die. “If you put DRAM on top of logic, DRAM is very sensitive to temperature,” he said. “Logic is very prone to hot spots. Basically, the hot spots happen at the bottom of memory. Thermal can be a real challenge, and you need to resolve these issues. In-memory computing can be an answer. It has extremely low power consumption, so you can probably put in-memory computing at the base die or the bottom of memory.”
In practice, IMC/CIM could work with custom HBM4 or HBM4E because the base die is built on a foundry logic process. SRAM is the native memory, meaning that SRAM CIM macros can be built there. CIM does multiply-accumulate inside the SRAM array, so weights aren’t repeatedly moved between memory and a separate MAC unit. Data movement is where most of the energy goes, which is why SRAM CIM macros report far better energy efficiency, in operations per watt, than conventional digital accelerators. Less energy per operation means lower power density, so fewer hot spots under the DRAM.
Conclusion
Software support remains the missing link between near-memory hardware and its promise for AI. For compilers and AI frameworks, processing-near-memory and in-memory architectures are emerging targets that could let developers offload mathematical operators directly to the memory subsystem, but the software needed to support that shift is still catching up.
The available compute — and the limits on it — differ by architecture. LPDDR6-PIM is limited to MAC units or simple ALUs suited to matrix-vector multiplication and element-wise math. A custom HBM4/HBM4E logic-process base die can add other memory-control functions. But that flexibility comes with a thermal ceiling — how much compute fits depends on the heat it adds beneath the DRAM.
“We have spent a lot of time over the last two years talking about custom HBM and how to use that base layer,” noted Cadence’s Ferro.
AI is driving the push to bring compute closer to memory, but proximity alone will not deliver the gains. Broader adoption depends on matching workloads to the hardware, managing heat, and giving compilers and operating systems the tools to decide what to offload. Moving the compute is only part of the solution; making the system use it efficiently is the next test.

Related Reading
How Will The Custom HBM Business Work?
There is no one-size-fits-all — yet.
