articles.title: Five ways Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia could damage the AI industry | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s confession that he had an affair (and reports of another one with a direct report) that led the board to oust him on Thursday isn’t just your run-of-the-mill salacious billionaire CEO sex scandal.
In this case, one of his lovers is suspected by the U.S. government of being a spy for China. She’s also an executive of a Singapore-based neocloud that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China.
These affairs show undeniably poor judgment by Huang and, I’d argue, unchecked hubris on many levels. Such choices are not only a betrayal of his wife of 40 years, they’re also a liability for his company. Sleeping with any Nvidia partner is bad enough, but he also chose one in a tinderbox of a geopolitical situation. Even if Alice Huang’s company wasn’t suspected of helping Chinese firms evade chip restrictions (and he was somehow unaware of this), it was still exploiting a legal loophole by renting powerful AI infrastructure to Chinese companies.
It’s those potential national consequences that may land him in a hellscape of ongoing public humiliation. Republican committee chairs are already summoning him to testify in closed-door sessions about the security ramifications.
Will Democrats, who are set to take over key committees when the new Congress convenes in January, also haul him in to testify on the Hill? No one knows yet, but Huang has flaunted his close relationship with President Trump. Remember when Trump called him while he was onstage at the All-In Summit in September? Nvidia also donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom, a deeply unpopular project with American voters. Several Democratic lawmakers have already vowed to investigate the money behind it.
In other words, he is a billionaire close to Trump. He was — until Thursday — the face of AI and data centers (also a deeply unpopular political topic with voters), and he has publicly admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Even though he’s no longer CEO, that seems too juicy a target for Democrats to ignore.
Beyond whatever may be coming, Huang’s influence has been lost right when he was using it to push the tech industry in a number of directions. These areas have now lost their biggest champion.
Open-weight AI models as competitors to closed-source labs
Huang has been the biggest, loudest advocate for open-weight AI models in the tech industry and among government policymakers. Nvidia not only offers its own open-weight models, it also offers a lot of other open source tech for agents, AI security, and more. It has even agreed to acquire the biggest site that hosts them, Hugging Face, for $12.9 billion. (That deal is supposed to close in the first half of next year, pending regulatory approval.)
In July, when Anthropic and OpenAI were reportedly urging the Trump administration to ban Chinese open-weight models, Huang organized a letter of support for open-weight models generally (if not Chinese models specifically), signed by hundreds of tech companies.
Open-weight models give enterprises choice in the market and reduce costs. Without Huang, the next biggest advocate for them is perhaps Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, but he’s not out there organizing the industry to speak up.
Pushing the AI industry to clean up its security
Both OpenAI and Anthropic revealed incident after incident this year as their AI agents hacked into others’ networks or performed other misdeeds. Huang loudly proclaimed the AI industry still didn’t need regulation and would deal with safety itself.
As the industry mulled over what they should do (auditors? a FINRA-like board?), Huang rallied the tech industry again. Nvidia got over 100 companies to sign on to his Open Agent Safety Platform, a largely open source effort to solve the epidemic of misbehaving AI agents.
Naturally, this effort hasn’t instantly solved the problem, and now the top spokesperson for self-regulation via technology solutions is out of his position of influence.
Arguing AI is a tool, not a life form
Huang has also been among the loudest voices insisting that AI is an engineered system that creates products, and so can be controlled like any other engineered system. This viewpoint counters the AI doomers and even the big AI labs themselves, which sometimes position their models as on the verge of consciousness (Anthropic) or as alien minds (OpenAI).
While Huang deals with the fallout of his actions, the loudest voice of this counter-narrative is, for the foreseeable future, silenced.
A new Nvidia-powered AI PC industry
Huang also just convinced a long list of PC makers to buy into his long-time dream of providing CPUs (the main processor chips) for them. In this age, when most Americans have not experienced AI beyond a chatbot, he orchestrated a new line of high-end AI PCs geared for running agents locally.
These new PCs are due out this holiday season, and they may sell well for their intended targets: creators, developers, and others already savvy with agents. But now that Huang has become a meme for cheating on his wife with an alleged spy, he’s perhaps not the best choice to help market these devices as a cool alternative to the Mac mini.
Financial engineering to fund data centers
Huang demolished his reputation right as bond underwriters (lenders) and bond buyers are pretty much over AI build-out-related debt. Of roughly $80 billion in data center bonds issued this year, nearly half were rated high-risk “junk,” Forbes reports.
Undeterred, Huang has been coming up with ways to continue financing the boom and keep his company’s revenues growing. Certainly, he’s authorized a mind-boggling number of so-called circular deals, where Nvidia buys stakes in companies to fund their expansion so they can buy chips. By some accounts, the company had committed to $750 billion in such deals as of July, Bloomberg reported. In August, Nvidia got even bolder, agreeing to backstop $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio, CNBC reported.
Huang also convinced a whole new set of financiers to pony up. In August, he announced that deep-pocketed PE firms Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR had committed up to $500 billion for data center build outs. He promised them that the data centers’ Nvidia GPUs could be used as collateral because Nvidia was guaranteeing the chips would retain value.
Huang sold a vision of Nvidia as “investable infrastructure” with a long resale cycle, like airplanes. Then he made the rounds with the financial press, as he often did, to pitch his vision. Now, however, Wall Street is concerned that Nvidia’s stock will crash and take their portfolios, and possibly the economy, with it.
Nvidia has lost its top salesperson and the AI industry has lost its top hype man. Even if Huang somehow comes back into the public eye to champion AI again, every interview and meeting will be about his sex life, choices, and national security — not his vision for the industry.
We’ll have to wait and see how Nvidia navigates the scandal Huang heaped onto it, but now that the company is finally in its post “founder mode” era, and hunting for a new CEO, it’s doubtful it has the cache to push the industry the way Huang was.

articles.title: Ascenso y caída de Jensen Huang: de llevar a NVIDIA a la cima a renunciar entre infidelidades y una presunta espía
articles.text:
La renuncia de Jensen Huang como presidente, CEO y miembro del Consejo de Administración de NVIDIA ha sacudido al mundo entero. La principal cara visible de una de las empresas más importantes del mundo acaba de irse por la puerta trasera, tras más de tres décadas conduciéndola. Esto, por dos grandes escándalos de relaciones extramatrimoniales: uno con una supuesta espía china; el otro, con una empleada de la compañía.
Como ya hemos mencionado, hasta hace pocas semanas era imposible pensar en NVIDIA sin Jensen Huang como CEO. El empresario no solo fue cofundador, sino que la lideró desde el primer día para convertirla en una de las empresas más importantes del mundo. En ese camino logró posicionarla en primera instancia como la referencia más importante del mundo gaming, gracias a su línea de tarjetas gráficas.
Con el tiempo, la apuesta paralela por el hardware especializado para IA pagó con creces, pues la explosión de los modelos generativos convirtió a NVIDIA en la empresa más importante del mundo, no solo del sector tecnológico. Huang fue el principal responsable de tamaño éxito, aunque su coqueteo con el poder tal vez haya sido lo que terminó marcando su caída.
Jensen Huang y NVIDIA: de un restaurante a una mole de 5 billones de dólares
Jensen Huang nació en Taiwán el 17 de febrero de 1963 y se mudó a Estados Unidos cuando todavía era un niño. Se graduó de la universidad como ingeniero electrónico e inició su carrera en el mundo de la tecnología en la década de 1980, primero en AMD y luego en LSI Logic.
En 1992, se produjo el punto de quiebre tanto para Jensen Huang como para el mundo tecnológico tal y como lo conocemos en la actualidad. Reunidos en Denny's, un restaurante de comida rápida, Huang y dos ingenieros de Sun Microsystems llamados Curis Priem y Chris Malachowsky tomaron la decisión de iniciar su propia empresa de tarjetas gráficas. Así nació NVIDIA, cuya fundación oficial se produjo en abril de 1993.
Con solo 30 años, Jensen Huang se convirtió en el CEO de NVIDIA y se encargó de llevar las riendas de la empresa hasta hoy. Así las cosas, el empresario fungió como consejero delegado de la compañía durante más de 33 años ininterrumpidos, abandonando su cargo tras un doble escándalo por infidelidades y un posible caso de espionaje.
El correr de los años le permitió a NVIDIA convertirse en la referencia máxima del hardware para ordenadores enfocados en gaming. Las GPU de la empresa se posicionaron como la opción más buscada debido a sus capacidades y rendimiento, logrando exposición mundial de la mano de amplios acuerdos con múltiples socios fabricantes.
NVIDIA salió a bolsa en 1999 y se mantuvo durante varios años como una tecnológica interesante, pero que los inversores miraban mayormente de reojo. Recién a partir de 2013 comenzó a mostrar números de crecimiento interanual más consistentes, aunque su explosión máxima se dio desde finales de 2022 gracias a la IA.
En paralelo con su apuesta por las tarjetas gráficas para gaming, Jensen Huang impulsó el abordaje del segmento dedicado a la infraestructura para empresas. Puntualmente, al desarrollo de chips avanzados para servidores de inteligencia artificial. Esto le permitió dar un salto bestial tras la popularización de los modelos y las aplicaciones generativas, que se inició con el debut de ChatGPT.
Hasta principios de noviembre de 2022, la capitalización bursátil de NVIDIA rondaba unos nada despreciables 350.000 millones de dólares. Pero la entrada en escena de OpenAI, Anthropic y un sinfín de otras startups de IA generativa llevó al gigante verde a un ascenso meteórico. En junio de 2023, superó 1 billón de dólares de valor de mercado, y en abril de 2024 pasó la barrera de los 2 billones. Apenas unos pocos meses después, en julio, ya valía 3 billones de dólares. La historia se mantuvo bajo la misma tónica en 2025, cuando los por entonces dirigidos por Jensen Huang se convirtieron en los primeros de la historia en superar los 5 billones de dólares de marketcap.
Desde entonces, solo Apple ha logrado superar esa barrera. El pico de capitalización bursátil de NVIDIA llegó a comienzos de octubre de este año, cuando marcó más de 5,6 billones de dólares. Claro que el panorama ha cambiado drásticamente en los últimos días, pues los escándalos de Jensen Huang han impactado sobre la acción de la empresa, borrando varios cientos de miles de millones de dólares.
De hecho, en los minutos posteriores a conocerse la renuncia de Jensen Huang, la acción de NVIDIA cayó hasta un 15 %. Esto llevó a que la empresa quedara por debajo de los 4 billones de dólares, siendo temporalmente tercera detrás de Apple y Microsoft. Al momento de redacción de este artículo, logró reponerse parcialmente para volver a ser segunda en capitalización bursátil.
El coqueteo con el poder, la caída y el futuro
El éxito de NVIDIA de la mano del boom de la IA generativa convirtió a Jensen Huang en una de las figuras más poderosas de Silicon Valley, con llegada directa a la Casa Blanca. Así, el empresario cultivó una relación muy cercana con Donald Trump tras el inicio del segundo mandato del republicano. De hecho, en la más reciente cena entre el presidente de EE. UU. y los principales referentes del sector tecnológico, Huang se sentó a la derecha del mandatario.
Jensen Huang era la personificación del too big to fail ("demasiado grande para fracasar"), pero la cosa cambió solo en un puñado de semanas. A finales de octubre, The New York Times publicó que el CEO de NVIDIA tenía una "relación cercana" con una presunta espía china. Alice Huang, ejecutiva de Megaspeed, una empresa con sede en Singapur dedicada a los centros de datos para IA, estaba bajo sospecha de Estados Unidos de colaborar con la inteligencia del gigante asiático. Incluso se reportó que Trump conocía sobre el asunto pero que evitó involucrarse.
NVIDIA negó de inmediato que el vínculo entre ambos tuviese algo raro, aunque el tono del discurso cambió poco después. El domingo pasado, con una pesquisa del FBI ya en marcha, la compañía anunció que también haría una investigación interna que contaba con el aval de Jensen Huang. En simultáneo, el CEO de la compañía reconoció haber mantenido una relación extramatrimonial con la sospechada de ser una espía.
El panorama no era prometedor, pero nada hacía pensar que el futuro de Jensen Huang al frente de NVIDIA pendiera de un hilo. De hecho, se ha reportado que la mayoría de los integrantes de la junta directiva de la firma eran muy cercanos a él. También, que durante los últimos 10 años el ejecutivo se negó a discutir sobre un posible plan de sucesión.
El vuelco definitivo se dio ayer, 11 de noviembre, cuando un nuevo reporte echó luz a una segunda aventura extramarital de Huang. El jefe del gigante verde mantuvo una relación a escondidas con una empleada de NVIDIA, lo que representaría una violación a las políticas de la compañía respecto de los vínculos entre ejecutivos y subordinados. Esto disparó titulares sobre un Consejo de Administración que analizaba destituir a la principal cara visible de la empresa.
Esta mañana, Jensen Huang finalmente renunció a la conducción de NVIDIA tras 33 años. Colette Kress, jefa de finanzas y vicepresidenta ejecutiva de la compañía, será la CEO interina hasta que se designe un reemplazo permanente. Huang se fue por la puerta trasera, sin un comentario de despedida, 4 días después de pedir disculpas públicas a su esposa por una infidelidad.
Por estas horas hay demasiadas especulaciones sobre el futuro de la firma californiana. Kress se ha comprometido a "seguir construyendo sobre la base extraordinaria que Jensen ha forjado a lo largo de los últimos 33 años". Es lógico pensar que NVIDIA no dejará de ser la principal referente del mundo del hardware para IA, las GPU avanzadas y los chips superpotentes como RTX Spark de la noche a la mañana. No obstante, son lógicas las dudas sobre quién podría tomar las riendas de una compañía hecha a imagen y semejanza de su líder saliente.
No todos en el mundo tecnológico han salido a patear a Jensen Huang mientras yace en el piso. Elon Musk dijo que sería "un honor" contratarlo, mientras que Tim Sweeney manifestó que despedirlo como CEO sería de "un nivel de idiotez" similar al de cuando Apple echó a Steve Jobs. Consumada la renuncia, el jefe de Epic Games expresó que era un "día triste para NVIDIA, los desarrolladores, Estados Unidos y toda la humanidad".

articles.title: Apple TV 4K: Siri AI and a mic are welcome additions
articles.text:
Among my Apple ecosystem, the device I use the most is my iPhone (currently the Duo), but my second most-used product from the Cupertino tech giant is my Apple TV. So, when the new Apple TV 4K was revealed, I was pretty ecstatic. I don’t even need an Apple TV; my TV is smart, but I’ve always liked using the Apple TV remote and seeing how it’s all organized.
Siri AI is here
This new Apple TV 4K is one of the most exciting yet, with a microphone directly on the streaming box. What does a microphone on the Apple TV get you? Siri, and in my case, Siri AI. While AI could potentially one day lead us to our inevitable end, Siri AI on a set-top box is pretty nice. However, it’s worth mentioning that the Apple TV always had Siri, but you needed the remote to activate the assistant. With the new Apple TV, you can activate the AI just by saying “Hey Siri.”
And because I’m using it with Siri AI, the assistant has access to broad world knowledge, allowing the Apple TV to answer questions about anything, alongside personal context, which works with your handset to answer personal queries.
Most importantly, you can use Siri on the Apple TV to ring your remote, which has already saved me countless minutes in searching for the remote. Yes, the Siri Remote now has a little speaker so that you can ring it when you can’t find it. You can also use Find My for Precision Finding on the remote, which is one of the most useful features ever.
Personalized experience
After setting up Siri AI and ‘Personal Content,’ I was able to get Siri to talk about shows and movies that my partner sent me. And even just asking Siri, “What are some shows that have been recommended to me?” and it listed different shows that I’ve talked about in my texts.
I could ask Siri AI to recommend shows with LGBTQ characters, and it’ll list various series that it considers popular. If you’re already watching something, you’ll see Siri answer in the top right corner, but if you’re not, Siri AI will take over the whole TV and populate a page with thumbnails about the different options.
Honestly, I’ve really liked this. I’m always looking for the next show to watch, and I like that I can ask Apple TV for recommendations. Because it’s Siri AI, you can keep talking to the assistant without having to say the command phrase again. I also have a horrible memory, so I like that it can recall shows from my text messages, and because of broad world knowledge, you can ask something like “what’s the name of that funny vampire show?” and you’ll get a list of comedic vampire shows; surprisingly, there’s more than you’d guess. You can follow up with “put on What We Do in the Shadows,” and the Apple TV will direct you to the series.
And to keep things private, no one can just ask Siri about the messages you’ve received because Siri can recognize each user’s voice. For instance, when my partner asked Siri what shows were recommended via text, Apple couldn’t populate the answer because it didn’t recognize him.
Probably, the worst part of the Siri AI experience is that after you invoke the AI, the text bubble doesn’t just go away. I need to press the back button, or tell Siri to go away. Another negative, though, is that if you have too many devices, Siri can activate the wrong device, which can be a bit annoying.
You can also use Siri AI to view and control smart home accessories, but I don’t have anything to test this out. And if you have four HomePods (including the 2023 HomePod or the 2026 HomePod mini), you can set up surround sound. Unfortunately, I didn’t get the chance to try this out either.
Faster, stronger, smoother
The Apple TV 4K is powered by the A19 chip and offers up to 50 per cent faster CPU performance and 2x faster GPU performance. This is the same chip that powers the iPhone 17, and you can tell how responsive the Apple TV 4K is compared to its predecessor. Navigation is faster, and animations are quick; I really like how smooth the experience is. Especially with Siri AI, it pulls up information incredibly fast too, or tells you it can’t find that answer.
The Apple TV 4K also obviously offers 4K output, high dynamic range (HDR) and supports Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos. Of course, this isn’t new to the Apple TV 4K, and I’ve had an experience with the previous set-top box. Other features include controlling your Apple TV with ‘Remote Control’ on your iPhone or Apple Watch. Private listening with your earbuds is still available as soon as you pull out your earbuds.
You don’t need this Apple TV 4K; I don’t need it either, especially considering its $429. However, I like the experience, especially being able to find the remote simply with my voice. I also never dreamed of the day that I’d use AI on the Apple TV, but when I forget the name of a show I wanted to watch or am looking for my next series, the assistant has come in clutch.
It’s worth mentioning Siri AI is still in beta, and you’ll need to change your language to U.S. English to try out the experience. If you’re seeing the same ol’ Siri on your iPhone, it’s likely because you haven’t made this change yet. And you’ll need to make sure you’re updated to iOS 27.2.
The new Apple TV 4K is available Friday, November 13, for $429. Alongside the Apple TV 4K, Apple’s new HomeView is also out on Friday.

articles.title: Google reworks TPU silicon into specialized systems for agents and security
articles.text:
Google adds two new specialized chips for AI agents and security to 8th-gen TPU lineup — TPU 8i Max puts two chips on one package for long-context work, TPU 8tx swaps Arm hosts for AMD EPYC
Google has yet to share specs, prices or ship dates for either new system.
Google's eighth-generation TPU family has now expanded further. Back in April, the company announced TPU 8t for training AI models and TPU 8i for general-purpose inference workloads. Google has now introduced TPU 8tx, built on the same silicon as the previously announced 8t, for confidential, hardware-isolated inference aimed at regulated enterprises and governments, and TPU 8i Max, which combines two 8i chips on one package for long-context agentic work.
TPU 8tx swaps the Arm-based Axion hosts of the 8t and 8i for a 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU, adopting a Boardfly network, and the 8i Max doubles the compute, SRAM, and HBM bandwidth of the original 8i. The original split, the TPU 8t and 8i, made natural sense. The 8t targets large-scale training, while the 8i leans toward low-latency inference and reasoning. TPUs have become a fast-growing business, with the company claiming nearly 100 customers, including Meta’s recent move to TPUs. The more modular approach is flexible and can deliver specialized systems “in a matter of months rather than years,” helping that popularity along.
| Google’s eighth-generation TPU systems |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Header Cell - Column 0 | TPU 8t | TPU 8i | TPU 8tx | TPU 8i Max | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Built for | Large-scale pre-training | Sampling, serving and reasoning | Secure, confidential inference; small-scale training | Long-context agent work | 
| Silicon | TPU 8t | TPU 8i | Same silicon as TPU 8t | Two TPU 8i chips on one package | 
| Host CPU | Arm Axion | Arm Axion | 5th Gen AMD EPYC | Not stated | 
| Network | 3D torus | Boardfly | Boardfly | Not stated | 
| Peak FP4 PFLOPS | 12.6 | 10.1 | Not stated | About 20.2 (derived) | 
| HBM bandwidth (GB/s) | 6,528 | 8,601 | Not stated | About 17,202 (derived) | 
| HBM capacity (GB) | 216 | 288 | Not stated | Not stated | 
| On-chip SRAM (MB) | 128 | 384 | Not stated | 768 (derived) | 
| Availability | Coming soon | Coming soon | Coming soon | Coming soon | 
For the new parts, the TPU 8i Max isn't innovative on the surface, as it’s just two TPU 8i chips combined into a single package. The result is twice the theoretical compute, but more importantly, it fits twice the silicon within the “existing rack footprint,” and Google claims more compute per square foot and per watt.
Doubling both SRAM and HBM bandwidth helps keep things scaling, which would put the 8i Max at about 20.2 FP4 PFLOPS, 768 MB SRAM, and about 17.2 TB/s HBM bandwidth. This compares to Nvidia’s Rubin R200 GPU at a rated 50 FP4 PFLOPS for inference and 22 TB/s of HBM4 per socket, or AMD’s MI455X with 40 FP4 PFLOPS. The compute gap is closing.
The memory bandwidth doubling is also potentially one way around moving to HBM4. The memory wall, as Google calls it, or the bandwidth bottleneck, is a real concern “when dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase.” Larger context windows — with larger models targeting 1 million tokens — mean larger KV caches, partly held in SRAM, and each new token has to read that cache back from memory, which is where the extra HBM bandwidth helps. It’s a different route from Nvidia’s LPX: more bandwidth in one package, rather than a second chip type for decoding and a storage tier for context.
Google also provides useful software for agents to get the most out of its hardware. TPU Sync is an open-source “model-state layer for TPU clusters” that moves KV caches off the chip’s HBM, “automatically tiering massive KV caches off the chip in milliseconds” down to host DRAM and, experimentally, shared storage. Google says this can cut KV transfer latency by “more than 90%,” with time-to-first-token gains that vary by workload. The company has also announced the Agent Compute Engine, a Google Cloud service that pauses idle agent sessions and moves their working memory aside until they’re needed again, another memory-saving effort.
Google credits its vLLM-TorchTPU stack with “state-of-the-art price-performance marks” on InferenceX and AgentX, which test realistic agentic coding and long-context work. However, the only published third-party numbers so far are for the last-generation Ironwood TPU. In SemiAnalysis’s InferenceX tests in September, running Qwen3.5 397B in FP8, Ironwood delivered 50.4% more tokens per dollar than Nvidia’s B200 and 96.0% more than the B300 at 20 tokens per second per user. One issue with that, however, is that Ironwood lacks native FP4, although newer November results show its FP8 beating Nvidia’s FP4 GB300 NVL72 on the same model, at 1.67 times the performance per dollar. There is also no eighth-gen result yet to compare how the new generation differs.
In contrast to the 8i Max, which is designed for long-context work, the new TPU 8tx, “built on the same silicon as TPU 8t,” is “optimized for secure and confidential inference” as well as small-scale training. The security is built into the hardware with isolation to prevent snooping on sensitive data, including model weights. Normally, data has to be unlocked in memory during processing, which is the step this isolation is meant to cover.
This chip is intended for areas where security and confidentiality are high priorities, which means regulated enterprises and governments, particularly those who are using frontier or proprietary models. In that case, the operators may want to “fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents,” without having to move sensitive data between clusters. Agents and security meet here for “secure agent execution.” Back in April, the Pentagon and Google reportedly held discussions for TPU usage in classified settings, although the 8tx chip is not specifically named.
Google’s Private AI Compute, its “hardened TPU platform” with protections “comparable to a typical TEE,” per its September technical brief, already runs confidential serving on TPUs. The 8tx appears to be that capability turned into a product for customers. Alternatives include Nvidia’s NVL72, with one security domain across 72 Rubin GPUs, 36 Vera CPUs, and the interconnects, and Intel’s TDX, which is adding trusted I/O to cover data moving to accelerators.
The TPU 8tx hosts are based on 5th Gen AMD EPYC boards, instead of the Axion hosts on the 8t, which replaced x86 in April. There's one Axion for every two TPUs on the 8i, compared with one Xeon per four on Ironwood. Google gives no reason for the change, but its Confidential VM configuration list has both AMD and Intel series chips, with no Arm-based ones listed. Private AI Compute uses “an AMD-based hardware Trusted Execution Environment” for its CPU workloads, suggesting Google swapped something it already runs on its confidential stack.
The 8tx also adopts the 8i’s Boardfly network over the 8t’s torus, which Google claims can deliver “up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t” with almost no performance penalty, although it’s not clear what measure Google is using. The alternative torus network suits training, since chips mostly swap data with neighbors in a predictable manner, but inference on large mixture-of-experts and reasoning models can send smaller messages between distant chips, with every hop adding delay. With Boardfly, it’s at most seven hops against 16 at 1,024 chips.
What is lacking is a full specifications table, the amount of HBM capacity, pod sizes, an availability date, pricing, and customers for either system. Details on attestation, that is, the ability for the customer to verify confidentiality, are also missing for 8tx. The 8tx and 8i Max are currently listed, along with the 8i and 8t, as “coming soon” on Google’s Cloud TPU page.
Delivering two new TPU systems nearly seven months after April’s pair shows Google wants to turn out specialized systems much more quickly than has been the case in the past. Now, it just needs to prove them, through benchmarks and an availability date when the hardware is actually in customers’ hands.
Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: Apple HomeView looks like a smart hub, but fills a different niche
articles.text:
Apple’s HomeView is the company’s newest line of products that are sort of in competition with the likes of Google’s Nest Hub and Amazon’s Echo Hub.
However, the HomeView is quite different from those other devices—it fills a specific niche that just isn’t for me, at least not yet.
Location matters
I live with roommates, and so I decided to keep the HomeView in my bedroom. It’s also literally the only room in the house that didn’t already have smart speakers, and I didn’t want to go through the process of setting up my roommates on the smart hub. I’d have to invite them all to my “Home,” and it wasn’t worth it.
So, I kept the HomeView in my room and added my partner to my Apple Home account, so he could use it when he was over. I should mention, I didn’t need to actually add my roommates to the HomeView, they could use it in ‘Guest’ mode, but setting that up was too much hassle.
So the HomeView is in my room, on the night table beside my bed. The HomeView’s placement is quite important because, unlike a Nest Hub or an Echo Hub, your HomeView is meant to be touched. You swipe down from the top to invoke Siri or swipe up from the bottom to pull up your home page, which looks a lot like your iPhone with widgets and apps. I can access my calendar, messages, music, Apple TV, even some book apps. So it’s been good to have it beside my bed so I can check my messages or tomorrow’s weather while my phone’s on the wireless charger.
And profiles are important for the HomeView because it can dramatically change the experience. My partner and I needed to set up face and voice recognition and connect it with our Apple accounts, which allows it to show a personalized experience based on who’s interacting with the device.
Personalization includes showing my calendar, my text messages and my dashboard. If my partner looks at it, it’ll pull up his profile instead. And if he unlocks his profile and I try to look at his messages, it’ll stop it from happening and require his face or smartphone to allow it. Further, if a room is too dark, you’ll need to unlock the HomeView with your phone.
Siri AI
We’ve mostly used the HomeView to ask Siri queries, play music, and share what we’re watching. Awkwardly, the feature we use most, Siri, gets interrupted by the many devices in my room. I also have the Apple TV 4K, and my iPhone, so sometimes when I try to invoke the HomeView, my devices get confused. Eventually, I turned off the microphone on the HomeView because most of the time I was speaking to the Apple TV.
Still, as I mentioned, it’s pretty easy to activate Siri with the HomeView by swiping down on the screen. Probably what I use it for the most is to set alarms for the morning. I’m typically already in bed, so reaching over to activate the HomeView is pretty easy. Otherwise, I would use it for Siri AI’s broad world knowledge, but I ended up mostly using my Apple TV for this.
Besides using it for Siri, I really liked using the Handoff feature that lets you continue what you were doing on your phone on the HomeView with a simple touch. So if I’m watching a YouTube video or surfing the net on my iPhone, I’ll just tap the HomeView, and it’ll quickly transfer over.
When I’m using the iPhone 18 Pro, it’s nice to switch to the larger display; I’ll be watching a video and tap the HomeView and finish it there. Also, when I want to show my partner something, it’s easy to just tap the HomeView, and we’re both surfing Safari or showing each other what we’re listening to. It’s incredibly easy, and the animation is so smooth. The feature is enjoyable and something that the other ‘Hub’ devices can’t do.
Playing some tunes
The HomeView is great for music. The HomeView features two custom full-range drivers with a down-firing woofer, and two force-cancelling radiators are built into the base. The HomeView is loud, easily filling my bedroom, and when I tried it in the living room, it worked great — but my HomePod (2nd gen) provides a better listening experience.
The bass is great too, and the listening experience is incredibly rich and crisp. And Dolby Atmos offers a multidimensional music experience. My partner is a huge pop music girly with AirPods in his ears 24/7, but now he loves sharing what he’s listening to by tapping his phone to the HomeView. It shows animated album art too, and you can easily pop up the lyrics with a tap.
The HomeView is definitely more than what I use it for. I think the HomeView would work better for me in my kitchen, living on the counter, where I don’t also have an Apple TV and iMac. Plus, a HomeView in the kitchen would be great for cooking, which offers an ingredient experience with the list of items you need, measurements, and step-by-step instructions.
The HomeView would also be more useful if I had more home products, like smart lights or a smart thermostat. Unfortunately, my house isn’t smart enough for the HomeView.
Maybe a little too late?
It feels like Apple is playing catch-up this year; its first touchscreen laptop, first folding phone, and first hub-like device. And while the PROLED MacBook and the Duo both fit in well OK in this tech world, the HomeView feels a little late.
And despite the HomeView looking like the Nest Hub, it feels like it’s trying to carve its own niche, and is sort of like Google’s Pixel Tablet, though you can’t just grab it and walk away. I think that might have been a more useful device for me, like an iPad that could attach to a charging hub and speaker with MagSafe.
The HomeView isn’t bad, but I think I would prefer that alternative. But I’m looking to move on my own next year, and maybe I’ll have more of a smart home and a kitchen that I can put the HomeView in. But until then, I’ll be jamming out in my room, setting reminders, checking my messages and asking Siri questions with the HomeView.
The HomeView comes out on November 13 and costs $429. It’s available for pre-order now.

articles.title: Leclerc casse le prix de Mafia: The Old Country sur PS5
articles.text:
Si vous ne savez pas dans quoi vous lancer avant GTA 6, E.Leclerc vous propose un détour par la Sicile avec Mafia : The Old Country pour 17,05 €. La livraison en magasin est offerte, avec une arrivée prévue entre le 13 et le 16 novembre.
Bienvenue en Sicile, la famille vous attend
Mafia: The Old Country emmène la saga là où tout a commencé, dans la Sicile du début des années 1900, plusieurs décennies avant le premier épisode. Le chant des cigales et le soleil de plomb remplacent les lampadaires d’Empire Bay, et on troque les grosses berlines contre un cheval ou une voiture d’époque qu’on démarre à la manivelle.
On y suit Enzo Favara, un ancien mineur des mines de soufre qui va gravir les échelons jusqu’à devenir l’un des hommes de main les plus fidèles de la famille Torrisi. L’histoire tourne autour de l’amour, de la mort et de l’honneur, dans un monde où la trahison n’est jamais loin. Elle ne révolutionne pas le genre, mais elle repose sur un casting que notre test juge « impeccable ».
Hangar 13 avait promis une expérience contenue, centrée sur la narration, et c’est exactement ce que livre le jeu. Pas d’immense monde ouvert rempli de quêtes, mais une aventure linéaire d’une dizaine d’heures, qui se dévore comme une série Netflix. La réalisation suit. Le jeu est très joli, les éclairages sont soignés, et les transitions entre cinématiques et phases de jeu se font sans coupure.
Un conseil pour en profiter pleinement, lancez la partie en version sicilienne sous-titrée en français. L’immersion y gagne énormément.
Une offre qu’on ne peut pas refuser ?
Le jeu était sorti à 49,99 €. Au moment de notre test, à l’été 2025, Leclerc le vendait encore 33,62 €. À 17,05 €, son prix a donc été divisé par deux. En comparaison, il est actuellement proposé à 24,99 € sur la Fnac et à 36,16 € sur Amazon.
Évidemment, tout dépend de ce que vous attendez. Le gameplay n’est pas vraiment le point fort du jeu. L’infiltration est basique, l’IA peu inspirée, et les duels au couteau finissent vite par lasser. Si vous voulez un défi ou un bac à sable à la GTA, passez votre chemin. En revanche, si vous cherchez une bonne histoire de gangsters à savourer comme un film, dans un décor qu’on voit rarement en jeu vidéo, ce prix fait de Mafia: The Old Country un très bon candidat pour vos soirées d’hiver et encore plus à moins de 20 euros.
Dernier point, l’offre se retire uniquement en Click & Collect (gratuit), dans les magasins Leclerc qui participent, jusqu’au 3 janvier 2027. Vérifiez la disponibilité près de chez vous sur la fiche produit avant de vous déplacer. L’extension Man of Honor, sortie à l’été 2026, n’est pas comprise dans l’offre.

articles.title: Anthropic-IPO: Banken drängen auf höheren Startpreis der Aktie
articles.text:
Anthropic hat am Dienstag die Roadshow für den Börsengang gestartet. Dabei wollen die begleitenden Banken offenbar einen besseren Startpreis für die Aktie durchsetzen und die Bewertung auf 1,5 Billionen Dollar oder mehr erhöhen, wie die „Financial Times“ unter Berufung auf Insider berichtet.
Laut aktualisiertem Börsenprospekt peilt Anthropic eine Gesamtbewertung von über einer Billion Dollar an. Zunächst sollen rund 825 Millionen Aktien für einen Preis von 70 bis 78 Dollar angeboten werden. Strategische Investoren wie Alphabet, Nvidia oder Microsoft können für weitere 26 Milliarden Dollar besondere stimmrechtslose Aktien zum IPO-Preis kaufen. Insgesamt könnte Anthropic so bis zu 90,4 Milliarden Dollar einnehmen.
Damit würde die Bewertung des KI-Unternehmens inklusive Mitarbeiteroptionen und reservierten Aktien auf bis zu 1,4 Billionen Dollar steigen. Das ist deutlich mehr als die 965 Milliarden Dollar, mit denen Anthropic bei der letzten Finanzierungsrunde von Investoren bewertet wurde, aber auch deutlich weniger, als Investoren noch im Sommer erhofft hatten. Damals stand eine Bewertung von bis zu zwei Billionen Dollar im Raum.
Banken wollen höheren Startpreis
Die Banken streben laut dem Bericht einen Aktienpreis von rund 83 Dollar an. Zu welchem Preis die Aktie in den Handel startet, entscheidet sich voraussichtlich am 18. November. Einen Tag später könnte Anthropic an der Nasdaq unter dem Kürzel „ANT“ an die Börse gehen. Bis zu 20 Prozent der angebotenen Papiere sollen dann an Privatanleger gehen. Auch in Deutschland werden Anleger Anthropic-Aktien zeichnen können.
Trotz der hohen Bewertung wird Anthropic damit den Mega-IPO von SpaceX im Juni dieses Jahres nicht überflügeln. Das Raumfahrtunternehmen von Elon Musk nahm bei seinem Börsengang 75 Milliarden Dollar bei einer Bewertung von rund 1,75 Billionen Dollar ein.
In den vergangenen Jahren ist der Umsatz bei Anthropic rasant gewachsen: 2023 setzte Anthropic noch 41 Millionen Dollar um, 2025 waren es knapp 4,6 Milliarden. In den ersten neun Monaten 2026 stieg der Umsatz auf 33,2 Milliarden Dollar. Die Run Rate, also der aufs Jahr hochgerechnete aktuelle Umsatz, lag Ende Oktober bei 81 Milliarden Dollar. Allerdings warnt Anthropic selbst im Börsenprospekt davor, dass sich das Tempo des Wachstums so nicht halten lässt.
Was Analysten erwarten
Die Analysten von Goldman Sachs rechnen für 2030 mit rund 685 Milliarden Dollar Umsatz, wovon 586 Milliarden allein aus dem Geschäft mit Unternehmenskunden kommen sollen. Das entspräche mehr als dem Achtfachen der aktuellen Run Rate. Diese optimistische Einschätzung stammt allerdings von der Bank, die den IPO federführend begleitet, also am Verkauf der Aktien entsprechend mitverdient.
Die Analysten von Morningstar rechnen dagegen im Basisszenario mit einem Wachstum von 47 Prozent pro Jahr für die Jahre 2027 bis 2031, wenn das KI-Unternehmen noch mehr Unternehmenskunden gewinnen und bestehende Kunden an sich binden kann.
Im optimistischen Szenario gehen sie von einer Wachstumsrate von mehr als 60 Prozent über einen Zeitraum von fünf Jahren aus, wenn es Anthropic gelingt, erhebliche Marktanteile zu gewinnen und an Konkurrenten wie OpenAI vorbeizuziehen. In diesem Fall könnte die Aktie um über 150 Prozent auf bis zu 188 Dollar steigen, mehr als doppelt so hoch wie im Basisszenario.
Finanzprofessor Aswath Damodaran von der New York University hält eine Bewertung von 1,5 Billionen Dollar für möglich, falls der Umsatz bis 2036 auf eine Billion Dollar wächst. Im schlechtesten Fall könnte Anthropic allerdings auch erst in zehn Jahren 200 Milliarden Dollar Umsatz erreichen, während hohe Rechenkosten die Marge auf zehn Prozent drücken.
Knappe und teure Rechenkapazitäten könnten eine Wachstumsbremse für Anthropic werden. Laut Börsenprospekt hat sich das KI-Unternehmen Rechenleistung und Infrastruktur für rund 895 Milliarden Dollar vertraglich gesichert, und im dritten Quartal machte das Unternehmen auch wegen kurzfristig zugekaufter Kapazitäten wieder einen operativen Verlust.
Damodaran sieht außerdem „Warnsignale“ in der ungewöhnlichen Führungsstruktur von Anthropic. Das KI-Startup ist als Public Benefit Corporation (PBC) strukturiert und damit nicht nur dem Profit, sondern auch dem Gemeinwohl verpflichtet. Ein unabhängiges Gremium, der sogenannte Long-Term Benefit Trust, darf Vorstandsmitglieder ernennen und abberufen. Außerdem haben sich die Gründer um die Geschwister Dario und Daniela Amodei über Sonderaktien 50,1 Prozent der Stimmrechte gesichert.
Tech-Werte erholen sich, Nvidia bricht ein
Anleger hatten in der vergangenen Woche pessimistisch auf KI-Unternehmen geblickt. Tech-Aktien verloren nach dem überraschend deutlichen Sieg der Demokraten bei den US-Midterms zeitweise zweistellig, da sich der Ausbau von Rechenzentren aufgrund einer strengen Regulierung nun verlangsamen könnte.
Angesichts des Anthropic-IPO steigt die Laune bei Tech-Werten nun aber wieder. Ausnahme ist Nvidia: Die Aktie brach am Mittwoch nachbörslich um mehr als acht Prozent ein, nachdem Berichte aufkamen, der Verwaltungsrat erwäge wegen der Affärenvorwürfe die Ablösung von CEO Jensen Huang.

articles.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO following reports of two extramarital affairs
articles.text:
Ripple effect: In what was looking like an increasingly inevitable outcome, Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of Nvidia. It comes after reports that Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, followed by a more recent revelation of a second affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell. Colette Kress, the company's current executive vice president and chief financial officer, will take over as interim CEO.
"Nvidia Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately," the company said in a statement. "Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of Nvidia, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer.
Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates."
The billionaire CEO's troubles began when reports emerged that Huang had been involved with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed International. US intelligence officials believe she was working for China's Ministry of State Security, tasked with gathering information about American AI technology and potentially influencing Nvidia's boss to push for fewer restrictions on advanced chip exports to China.
Also read: Without Jensen Huang, is it game over for GeForce?
Huang admitted to the extramarital affair on November 8, apologizing to his wife, family, and colleagues. Nvidia's board launched an independent investigation into whether any company secrets or national security interests had been compromised, although it said there was no evidence this had happened.
Things quickly went from bad to worse. Nvidia's shares fell almost 5% following the admission, wiping around $190 billion off its market value in a single day. A class-action lawsuit was also filed against Huang and the company, accusing them of misleading investors by concealing the relationship.
Nvidia shares have now plunged to around $158 following Huang's resignation, their lowest level since July 2025. Nvidia's market value has crashed by $2 trillion since the stock's peak in early October. It's starting to look like the AI bubble could burst sooner than many expected.
Then came another revelation, one that seemingly sealed Huang's fate. On November 11, reports emerged of a second affair, this time with Powell, who reports directly to Huang. The relationship raised questions about potential violations of Nvidia's code of conduct and claims that the board was set to oust Huang.
Despite expressing confidence in Huang just three days earlier, Nvidia's board reportedly met on Wednesday to discuss removing him. His resignation ends his 33-year reign as the company's only CEO. Huang co-founded Nvidia in April 1993 alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem.
Huang is known for having a close relationship with President Donald Trump, having joined his technology advisory council earlier this year. The Nvidia boss has repeatedly praised Trump's policies and successfully pushed the administration to loosen restrictions on AI chip exports to China. Trump even awarded Huang the National Medal of Science in October.
The president defended Huang after the affair allegations emerged, calling him an "honorable guy" who had done an "amazing job" for the country. Trump later said Huang had assured him he knew nothing about Alice Huang's alleged espionage activities, a claim the president said he believed.
Huang also accompanied Trump on a trip to China, and in August, he took a call from the president while discussing AI safety and regulation on stage at the All-In Summit, putting Trump on speakerphone for the audience to hear.
Speaking after her appointment as interim CEO, Kress said, "Nvidia's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years. We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders." There has been no statement from Huang.

articles.title: Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash
articles.text:
CHICAGO—Families joined protests in seven cities nationwide on Wednesday, rallying against what they see as Google’s bid to entrench its AI models in schools, turn kids of all ages into Gemini guinea pigs, and hook them on AI.
The backlash follows a Google statement last week, confirming that there will be no way for students to use Google Search without AI. While Google claimed it was giving schools “more choice, not less”—by turning off Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook by default—it would not provide an option that allowed Search without AI. For students, the only way to avoid interacting with AI was to remember to add “-ai” to every query, parents worried.
In Chicago, many families showed up to protest Google, despite cold, rainy weather. Waving signs, dozens of protesters marched up to Google’s downtown office as workers seemed to be leaving for the day, shouting chants like “Hey Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini” and “Hey, Google, leave our kids alone!”
Ashley Belanger
Ashley Belanger
Ashley Belanger
Ashley Belanger
ILFPS executive director Cassie Creswell rallied the crowd.
Ashley Belanger
ILFPS executive director Cassie Creswell rallied the crowd.
Ashley Belanger
Ashley Belanger
ILFPS executive director Cassie Creswell rallied the crowd.
Ashley Belanger
Called to action by a nonprofit grassroots advocacy group, the Illinois Families for Public Schools (ILFPS), some parents and students had previously won a major AI fight. In August, the group pressured Chicago Public Schools (CPS) to pull out of a Gemini pilot that would have roped in all high school students districtwide—without consulting parents. And now, ILFPS is demanding a moratorium on AI until risks to students are better understood and CPS can draft a policy to protect students from potential learning setbacks or more harmful outcomes from engaging Google’s AI bots. If the group wins, it will join cities like Los Angeles and New York City in cautiously banning AI in schools.
Lawsuit: Gemini was student’s “suicide coach”
Most alarming to parents, Google now faces a lawsuit from a 13-year-old student in Durham, North Carolina named “Emma Doe.” As Emma has alleged, she was a happy, well-adjusted, straight-A student when she started using Gemini on her school-issued Chromebook. Emma’s parents had no idea she was using Gemini, as the lawsuit alleged that Google “deliberately” kept them in the dark while driving Emma into so-called “AI psychosis.” Over time, normal school-related interactions with the chatbot led to more intense chats, and ultimately the chatbot allegedly coached Emma to plan her own suicide and funeral. The school warned her parents and averted the danger after an internal system flagged a chat labeled “Funeral,” but Emma’s story stoked fears of parents joining protests not just in Durham, but also in Boston; Boulder, Colorado; Chicago; Los Angeles; New York City; and Portland, Oregon.
Emma’s lawsuit accuses Google of exploiting its dominant position in education technology and “sneaking” Gemini into Chromebooks, while falsely marketing them as safe.
“As a direct consequence of Google’s choices, Emma was baited by its defectively designed products into repeated, unmonitored, sycophantic AI chatbot interactions on her school Chromebook without her parents ever knowing. And, but for a fortunate turn of events, Google’s AI may well have manipulated Emma into taking her own life,” the lawsuit alleged. “Google must be held to account for treating the lives of children as disposable in service of its bottom line.”
Google only publicly addresses learning harms
Google has promised to “continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure we are giving schools more choice, more controls, and improved Search for learning.” However, Google’s statements so far attempting to address parents’ concerns focus exclusively on documented harms to learning. On that front, Google claims that it’s solving the problem of AI eroding students’ critical thinking skills by launching yet another pilot for students. In this pilot, students using AI Mode and AI Overviews will be offered a “step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork,” Google said.
Cassie Creswell, executive director of ILFPS, told Ars that she’s been an advocate monitoring edtech issues for more than a decade. And even she was blindsided by Google’s AI moves.
“I am aware of AI Overviews when you search, which have a whole slew of problems, but I did not know that you really actually just have an interface where you can interact with Gemini in the chatbot way on everyone’s Chromebook still in Chicago public schools,” Creswell said. “And that’s so disturbing.”
She acknowledged that kids encounter AI on their phones and shared that her daughter said her friends like using ChatGPT better than Gemini. But she said that the fact that some kids use AI on personal devices doesn’t mean that schools should be encouraging adoption at young ages when kids’ brains are still developing, and risks remain largely unknown.
“There’s all kinds of dangerous things out in the world, but we don’t have our school district handing it to kids at their desk,” Creswell said.
No one knows how Google uses student data
Meanwhile, schools seem to be part of the transparency problem.
Creswell said that currently, the Chicago school district “is telling us their official line is that kids don’t have access to generative AI tools and that we don’t need a district-level policy on generative AI because they have guidebooks.” However, she’s reviewed Google’s CPS contracts, and they suggest that kids are interacting with generative AI and frontier models. The ongoing confusion has led parents to demand “a real policy” that the CPS “board votes on and that has the input of teachers, parents, students, and experts who are not being funded by the tech industry.”
Creswell told Ars that parents are particularly upset that Google is not transparent about how it processes and uses student data. She’s exhaustively researched Google contracts through Freedom of Information Act requests and told Ars that dozens of agreements she reviewed offer no indication of how CPS partners like Google—as well as Anthropic and OpenAI—are handling student data. Although she understands that “it’s probably just an honest statement of fact” that Google has built AI inextricably into Search, parents have a right to know how their children’s data is ingested into Google’s models, she said.
“Any sort of transparency on what is actually happening in terms of the data that they collect and what they do with it, that is absolutely missing,” Creswell said. And “it’s very unclear what data is being saved.”
To Creswell and other advocates, it seems likely that kids’ data is collected no matter what, since “even if you do ‘-AI,’ and you don’t get a text summary, your search data and what’s being returned is all basically inside the generative AI model.” Although Illinois law only allows commercial use of de-identified data, parents think Google should clearly explain what steps it takes to ensure data can’t be recombined to re-identify kids.
Parents: No AI training on school kids’ data
Ars reached out to Google to see if the company could clarify if Creswell’s read is accurate or if there’s any meaningful distinction between adding “-AI” to an individual query versus building a button that would automatically add “-AI” to every query. Google did not clarify, instead emphasizing that schools will control whether students can access the Gemini app, Gemini Notebook, and Search, with options to toggle each off individually, but no option to use Search without AI.
Emma Doe’s lawsuit alleged that Google has taken advantage of a dominant position it has held in schools since 2007 to push AI on kids and seize their data without meaningfully protecting them from the worst potential harms of its chatbot’s sycophantic design. In Chicago, CPS signed a contract with Google in 2020, “long before Gemini was rolled out,” Creswell found. Over the next two extensions of that contract, no updates were introduced to protect students’ privacy as AI advanced.
To Creswell, it remained “totally unclear” in contracts how Google’s processing of student data may have changed, beyond updates to the privacy policy for Google Workspace for Education.
Currently, that policy specifies that “we receive customer data through the Core Services and process it according to the school’s (the customer’s) instructions. This customer data includes anything submitted, stored, sent, or received through Core Services by you or your school.” Google collects that data on that activity, as well as account information “like name, email address and password” and location information, the policy said.
The policy didn’t discuss Gemini but noted that data from using core services helps maintain services, improve personalization, and increase security. And “the data we collect in the Additional Services is used across our services to deliver, maintain, and improve our services; develop new services; provide personalized services; measure performance; communicate with you; and protect Google, our users, and the public.”
To parents, the policy provides no reassurance that their kids’ data isn’t part of Google’s plan to dominate the AI industry.
“We should not have any child data being collected in a school setting being used for commercial purposes,” Creswell said.
“What about the future of our minds?”
Parents’ privacy concerns go beyond Google, Creswell noted. But since Google has “captured so much of the education space and so much of the education experience,” parents are focusing their energy on interrogating those AI systems in schools early on.
In Chicago, a recently re-elected CPS school board member, Karen Zaccor, is pushing for an AI moratorium in schools after talking with city and community colleges about an allegedly noticeable decline in reading, math, and writing skills from students graduating from CPS schools. In Emma’s case, Google allegedly suppressed chat logs, and the school withheld safety logs, frustrating parents who already viewed AI as more harmful than beneficial in education.

At the Google protest Wednesday, parents waved signs that threatened to eject Google from schools, with slogans like “No Google + No AI = Win/Win.” Many kids used favorite cartoon characters from shows like Beavis and Butthead and South Park to slam Google’s seemingly cynical approach to introducing AI in schools. One young girl wearing pink rain boots held up a cardboard sign, declaring in colorful markers, “I like to read!!”
At its peak, about 60 people stood outside Google’s downtown Chicago office, enduring the rain and listening to teachers and students who oppose reckless AI adoption.
One particularly moving speech came from a CPS student, Reese Mackey, who spoke for students. She challenged Google to more carefully weigh the long-term harms of aggressively pushing AI onto students by claiming they’ll be left behind and struggle to find jobs without AI skills. Creswell told Ars the opposite seems true, as Emma Doe’s lawsuit pointed to research branding Gemini as “the most dangerous marketed for use by youth” and “confirming the existence of AI-induced psychosis.”
“What about the future of our youth?” Mackey said. “What about the future of our minds?”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

articles.title: Beyond Bandwidth: AI Inference Is Reshaping The Memory Wall
articles.text:
Longer contexts, higher concurrency, multimodal models, and AI agents will continue changing where memory pressure appears.
AI infrastructure has spent the past several years in a race for compute. More accelerators, larger heterogeneous clusters, and higher peak performance have enabled increasingly capable models. As AI moves into large-scale deployment, infrastructure must support more users, larger models, longer context windows, and more complex applications. Performance still matters, but so do latency, power, utilization, predictability, and cost per inference.
The challenge extends beyond bandwidth. AI systems must balance memory capacity, bandwidth, latency, power, data movement, utilization, and cost. Improving one dimension can create pressure elsewhere. The key-value (KV) cache illustrates this trade-off. KV cache reduces repeated computation during generative AI inference, but requires the system to retain and repeatedly access growing amounts of data. As context lengths and concurrent requests increase, the trade-off becomes more significant.
The result is not simply another memory bottleneck. It is a coordination problem across compute, memory, interconnect, and software. Adding capacity or bandwidth helps only if the system can place, move, and retrieve data without allowing latency, congestion, power, or complexity to erase the benefit.
The memory wall predates AI. Processor performance historically has improved faster than the ability of memory systems to supply processors with data. AI magnifies that problem. Increasing arithmetic throughput delivers limited benefit if accelerators spend more time waiting for data.
But bandwidth is only part of the constraint. AI systems also need sufficient capacity for models, intermediate data, application context, and inference state. Latency affects responsiveness. Power constrains how much data can be moved economically. Packaging and physical connectivity limit how much high-performance memory can be placed near compute.
These requirements frequently conflict. High-bandwidth memory close to an accelerator can deliver tremendous bandwidth, but its capacity, power, and cost are constrained. Larger-capacity memory may be more economical but may not provide the same bandwidth or latency. Moving data among tiers can expand effective capacity, but consumes bandwidth, power, and time.
The memory wall is therefore becoming a multidimensional system constraint.
Fig. 1: AI scaling turns the memory wall into a system-level trade-off among bandwidth, capacity, latency, power, cost, and utilization.
A system may have substantial aggregate memory, but not all of that capacity is equally useful. Data in a lower tier may technically be available, yet still be too distant, congested, or costly to move within the application’s service-level objective (SLO).
The practical limit is not installed capacity alone. It is usable capacity within the workload’s latency, bandwidth, and power envelope.
Training large models requires enormous compute resources and memory bandwidth, but it is fundamentally a process of building or updating a model. Inference is dynamic and ongoing. Every prompt, generated token, agent action, and application interaction consumes infrastructure resources.
Inference also is not one workload. A conversational assistant may emphasize latency. An enterprise AI assistant may process substantial proprietary context while supporting many users. AI agents may retain information across multiple steps. Consumer services may prioritize throughput and cost per token. Batch inference may emphasize utilization.
Each creates a different balance among bandwidth, capacity, latency, power, and cost. The architecture must follow the workload.
During transformer inference, attention mechanisms generate key and value representations for tokens in a sequence. Retaining those representations allows subsequent decoding steps to reuse prior states rather than recomputing them for earlier tokens. That improves inference efficiency, but reduces repeated computation while increasing pressure on memory capacity and data movement.
Longer context windows increase the KV-cache footprint of each sequence. Higher concurrency multiplies that requirement across simultaneous requests. An optimization intended to reduce compute demand therefore creates more data that must be retained and accessed.
Fig. 2: Reducing repeated computation improves efficiency, but longer contexts and greater concurrency increase the data that must be retained, moved, and managed.
KV state also has a lifecycle. It is created during prefill, repeatedly accessed during decode, and may be retained for reuse. Depending on the serving architecture, it may be moved, replicated, compressed, or evicted. Each phase places different demands on bandwidth, capacity, latency, and control.
KV cache is therefore a data-lifecycle problem, not only a memory allocation. Moving KV state to a lower-cost tier is beneficial only when the higher-tier capacity it frees, or the recomputation it avoids, outweighs transfer latency, bandwidth consumption, energy, and the risk of missing an SLO. In other words, every movement of data must earn its cost.
A latency-sensitive assistant may benefit from keeping frequently accessed data close to the accelerator. A long-context enterprise application may emphasize capacity. AI agents may require longer-lived state and more frequent reuse. Large-scale consumer inference may prioritize throughput, utilization, and cost per token.
Frequently accessed data may justify residing near compute. Other data may tolerate additional latency for greater capacity or lower cost, or move among tiers as access patterns change. The objective is not to eliminate the memory hierarchy. It is to coordinate that hierarchy efficiently.
Bandwidth remains critical, but optimizing exclusively for bandwidth ignores other constraints. Capacity determines how much model and inference state can remain accessible. Latency affects response time. Power determines whether increasing data movement is sustainable. Utilization indicates whether expensive compute resources are working or waiting for data.
High aggregate throughput can hide unacceptable time to first token, inter-token latency, or tail latency during congestion. A more meaningful measure may be tokens per watt or dollar while meeting latency targets. Headline bandwidth alone does not solve the memory wall.
The relevant question is: Which combination of compute, memory, interconnect, and software delivers predictable performance within the available power and cost envelope?
High-bandwidth memory can supply data quickly near accelerators. Larger-capacity tiers can complement it where capacity matters more than maximum bandwidth. Expansion and pooling can provide capacity beyond the memory next to an accelerator. Software can place, reuse, compress, move, or discard KV state according to workload requirements.
But every additional tier introduces more decisions. A useful architecture must address four questions:
Moving data to a larger-capacity tier may increase effective capacity but add latency. Replicating state may avoid recomputation but consume bandwidth and capacity elsewhere. Pooling may improve utilization, but only if contention and quality of service remain controlled. The advantage comes not from maximizing one memory specification or adding another tier. It comes from coordinating the hierarchy as a system.
Higher-bandwidth memory, greater capacity, faster interconnects, compression, and smarter cache management can relieve constraints, but not eliminate the challenge. As one bottleneck improves, applications and models use the additional resources. Longer contexts, higher concurrency, multimodal models, and increasingly sophisticated AI agents will continue changing where memory pressure appears. Hardware-software co-design is therefore critical because every layer influences data movement.
The next phase of AI infrastructure scaling will not be defined by compute alone or solved simply by adding memory. The harder task is coordinating where inference data resides, when it moves, and whether moving it is more efficient than recomputing it. The memory wall is becoming something broader: a test of how effectively the system converts distributed memory resources into predictable AI performance.

articles.title: Mira el tráiler del remake de 'El secreto de Thomas Crown', la nueva película de Michael B. Jordan como director después de ganar el Oscar
articles.text:
Michael B. Jordan ya está de vuelta. El actor regresa a los cines después de levantar su primer Premio Oscar el año pasado por su papel doble en Los Pecadores. Y esta vez lo hace con un proyecto muy especial. Se trata de El secreto de Thomas Crown, que acaba de lanzar su nuevo tráiler. El filme será el segundo remake de la mítica película de 1968 con Steve McQueen. El anterior, la icónica versión de 1999 con Pierce Brosnan.
Además de dirigir, Michael B. Jordan también produce y protagoniza El secreto de Thomas Crown. La cinta promete ser un thriller de robos de guante blanco visualmente deslumbrante, sensual y conmovedor, donde según indica el Amazon MGM Studios. "el hombre más peligroso es aquel al que nadie está observando".
Por el momento, la sinopsis oficial se mantiene en secreto, pero el tráiler de El secreto de Thomas Crown confirma que volverá a ser una auténtica cacería, un juego del ratón y el gato. Y es que, en la película original, el protagonista es un verdadero galán que se dedica al robo de obras de arte. En su aventura se cruza con una detective que le seguirá muy de cerca la pista a la vez que ambos empiezan a sentir una peligrosa atracción mutua.
Mira el tráiler de El secreto de Thomas Crown
Junto a Michael B. Jordan, el reparto de El secreto de Thomas Crown lo componen Kenneth Branagh, Adria Arjona, Lily Gladstone, Danai Gurira y Pilou Asbæk, entre otros. "Es un bebé mío que llevaba mucho tiempo queriendo hacer, así que estoy muy ilusionado, declaró Jordan hace unos meses en una entrevista a Deadline.
Creo que tampoco va a ser exactamente lo que la gente espera. Cuando reimaginas algo, no se trata de un remake. No es un reboot. Es una reinterpretación, y estoy muy ilusionado con ello porque me importa mucho esta película y su título", añadió.
El secreto de Thomas Crown se estrena en cines el 5 de marzo de 2027.

articles.title: Techie uses voltage glitching hack to turn $2,500 Nvidia 8GB cryptomining GPU into a full-fat $20,000 A100 with 80GB of VRAM — hack carefully blows onboard fuses to unlock entire VRAM and shader modules
articles.text:
Techie uses voltage glitching hack to turn $2,500 Nvidia 8GB cryptomining GPU into a full-fat $20,000 A100 with 80GB of VRAM — hack carefully blows onboard fuses to unlock entire VRAM and shader modules
The most dangerous thing in the world is a bored engineer with a screwdriver. If you see a soldering iron, run for the hills.
Enterprising techies looking to build their own local AI cluster have far more interesting options than buying DGX Sparks or Apple Mac Studios. Used data center GPUs are everywhere, and a server rack's garbage is an enthusiast's treasure. This option has become even more popular with CMPunlocker, a soft-mod for Nvidia CMP-170HX cards that unlocks abilities well beyond stock. Now, a techie has taken it a step further, blasting through the remaining limitations with voltage glitching and creating a card faster than the actual $20,000 Nvidia A100 GPU with 80GB of VRAM... but from an $2,500 8GB CMP-170HX mining card.
The volt-mod was done by Kate (GitHub link here), who got her starting point from a paper that described how one could exploit GA100 cards' microcode. She turned her attention to the normally protected onboard fuse controller. Although it's rarely discussed, a "fuse box" has been integral in most any CPU and GPU for a while — though it's normally used once at the factory to break physical connections in chips to parts that have tested poorly, thus disabling them so they can be sold as a lower-end model.
If you're wondering how people are getting 80-40GB of VRAM out of 8-10GB, the explanation is simple: the GA100 silicon actually includes all the corresponding HBM2e VRAM dies within; but they get disabled at the factory like the shader modules. The smaller version is more desirable, as it's based on the variant of GA100 with 80GB of HBM2e within, while the 10GB cards spawn from the 40GB GA100.
The Nvidia cards in question have quite an elaborate eFuse controller (16,384 in a 512 x 32 array) — which can be read to obtain the card's current configuration. Most every part of the card has related fuses: VRAM sections, individual shader modules, PCIe 4.0 and NVLink, and even video codec hardware. However, as Kate succinctly put it: Nvidia's design is insecure, as popping fuses can grant access to more features, not fewer.
Under normal conditions, these fuses can't be popped, or "written to," by the user — but a geek armed with a soldering iron isn't a normal user. Kate had GPT-6 Astra design a simple circuit board based on an $8 STM32G4 microcontroller to tap into the power signals on the card's PCB.
The voltage regulators (VRMs) on the card "speak" PWMVID, an Nvidia standard, and Kate's board intercepted the PWM signals sent into the VRM controller, forcing it to produce voltage glitches on the line feeding the GPU, where the fuse controller lies.
Remember when we said the fuse controller was read-only? With the voltage glitches, many fuse-status reads in a tight loop, and she managed to set the controller to a state in which its security bit flags allowed writes through. From that point, it was "easy" to reconfigure her card. She was careful to force-disable any shader modules previously marked as defective, because these are physical fuses — there's no "undo" button.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
She applied the mod to her cards and, after testing with multiple workloads, found that nine had the full 80 GB of VRAM working, and one card "only" had 64 GB usable. Most interestingly, unlocking all the shader modules (SM) nets her FP16 FMA performance 20% beyond a regular A100 card. She thinks this is due to the chips often having 120 or more usable SMs — over the 108 on the spec sheet. The GA100 die starts with 128 SMs to account for defects, which is normal in chip manufacturing.
The CMPUnlocker soft mod is required for enabling the "new" features on the drivers, but it doesn't unlock the card's full potential: the VRAM upper limit is 40-64GB (depending on the variant), many shader modules remain locked, and PCIe bandwidth only goes to 2.0. Additionally, there's no ECC, NVLink, or multi-instance GPU support, all of which are critical in a server setup and are also used for product segmentation.
Kate's volt-mod does away with all of these limits, and her best test card is happily working at PCIe 4.0 speed with the full feature set. She didn't test the video encoder bits, but it's unlikely anybody using these cards cares much for that.
As for the cost, a CMP-170HX 8GB is currently hovering around $3,000, and the 10GB variant costs around $2,500. A full-fat Nvidia A100 80GB in a PCIe configuration can reach $20,000 or more. The SXM server-module versions are cheaper, but they require infrastructure around them. Note that these prices will likely vary significantly, especially as people become increasingly aware of the mods.
Kate says she's publishing her research now because another person independently found the same issue. She has informed Nvidia of the vulnerability, though there's not much the company can do for existing cards already on the market.
