He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Struggling marijuana farms pivoting to becoming AI data center sites to escape falling weed revenue — existing water and power infrastructure makes cultivation sites ideal for decentralized ‘mini data center nodes’
articles.text:
Struggling marijuana farms pivot to becoming AI data center sites to escape falling weed revenue — existing water and power infrastructure makes cultivation sites ideal for decentralized ‘mini data center nodes’
Let's get high... on AI.
The AI data center boom is bringing hope to struggling cannabis farmers as they face increased competition, costs, and taxes amid reduced demand for marijuana. According to Arizona Public Media, the cannabis industry is in decline, with sales peaking in 2024 and oversupply driving prices down. And now, several growers are considering selling their cultivation facilities or converting them into “mini data center nodes.” These facilities already have many of the ingredients needed for AI data centers, such as the increasingly hard-to-get supply of electricity and water infrastructure.
"For some reason, there's a lot more cannabis grown in Arizona than Arizonans use. And so, a lot of folks are getting out of that business, like myself, at least on the cultivation side. But these facilities can potentially be repurposed to be mini data center nodes," Moe Asnani, the former owner of two Tucson D2 Dispensaries, told the public broadcaster. He also added, "The whole idea is if you create these smaller nodes where people control their own data, where they're not at the mercy of other people's updates and things like that — that's kind of where the idea came in, because I believe in decentralization."
Cannabis farming is both power- and water-intensive. Forbes looked at a 32,850-square-foot cannabis facility in Kalamazoo, Michigan, which is currently wired for 1.5 megawatts, which can be expanded to 2.5 megawatts in under a year and 15 megawatts in the long term. It's also provisioned for fiber internet and equipped with a state-of-the-art HVAC system for climate control, which should make it a tempting property for anyone wanting to put up a small data center — something that even OpenAI and Anthropic are interested in as massive hyperscale sites face opposition from the community.
This concept is dubbed "adaptive reuse," with Tucson City Council member Paul Cunningham saying that it’s a more palatable alternative to massive, purpose-built sites sitting on the outskirts of town. "Data centers are dirty words, and everybody knows that. And no one wants to build a brand-new data center anywhere," the politician said. "But if we have buildings that were using that amount of water and that amount of energy already in their previous function and [it] can be done without being invasive, I'm OK with exploring that option."
There is massive demand for data centers, but it’s not a guaranteed payoff for struggling cash-strapped growers looking to unload their unprofitable properties. Niki Krear, vice president of acquisitions of real estate investment trust New Lake Capital Partners, said that there’s a sweet spot between connectivity, costs, and regulation that data center operators look for in a site.
"It’s a combination of finding affordable power, dense fiber networks, and favorable tax policies," Krear told MJBizDaily. Even though many cultivation facilities already boast higher-than-average power capacity for lighting and climate control, data centers often demand twice to thrice more, with upgrades possibly taking up to five years.
Data center operators looking for smaller sites may also have to contend with NIMBY — not in my backyard — fights from neighbors. Additionally, there may be zoning restrictions, moratoriums, and regulatory hurdles, and the lack of economies of scale could end up costing operators more.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
This is particularly important as AI chips are expected to increase in power and efficiency in the next five years. As these new AI GPUs become available, data centers will need to sell their existing equipment and buy new hardware to remain competitive. Because suppliers usually offer favorable pricing for larger orders, upgrading these smaller sites will likely end up being more expensive on a per-unit basis. That said, growing opposition toward large new projects could make these former cannabis farms suitable alternatives for operators desperate to get more compute online quickly, provided they check all (or most of) the boxes they need.

articles.title: Intersport retire 500 € au Nakamura Crossover V LTD, son VTC électrique à cadre ouvert
articles.text:
À mi-chemin entre le vélo de ville et le VTT, les VTC électriques ont l’avantage de s’adapter à presque tous les terrains. Ils permettent de se déplacer au quotidien sur le bitume, tout en s’aventurant sur les chemins le week-end, sans trop sacrifier le confort. Le Nakamura Crossover V LTD coche justement ces cases, et profite en ce moment d’une remise de 500 € chez Intersport.
Ce modèle de la marque maison d’Intersport s’affichait à 1 899,99 €. Pendant le Black friday, il est aujourd’hui proposé à 1 399,99 €, soit une remise immédiate de 500 €.
C’est quoi, ce Nakamura Crossover V LTD ?
Un VTC, ou vélo tout chemin, se place entre le vélo de ville et le VTT. Le Crossover V LTD suit cette logique. Son cadre en aluminium est ouvert, avec un enjambement bas : on monte dessus sans passer la jambe par-dessus la selle, ce qui peut s’avérer pratique si on porte une grosse veste. À l’avant, une fourche suspendue offre 120 mm de débattement. Les pneus renforcés de 40 mm de large sont prévus pour le bitume comme pour les chemins de terre.
L’assistance vient d’un moteur central Naka E-Power Mid de 70 Nm, placé au niveau du pédalier. Cette position abaisse le centre de gravité et équilibre le vélo, contrairement aux moteurs logés dans le moyeu d’une roue. Un capteur mesure l’effort du cycliste pour doser l’aide, avec quatre niveaux d’assistance et un mode boost. La batterie de 460 Wh est intégrée au cadre. Intersport annonce jusqu’à 100 km d’autonomie dans des conditions optimales, et 3h30 pour une recharge.
L’équipement est complet pour un usage quotidien. Le vélo a une transmission Shimano Acera à 8 vitesses, des freins à disque hydrauliques Shimano MT200, un porte-bagages, des garde-boue, une béquille et un éclairage LED alimenté par la batterie. Un écran couleur TFT, connecté en Bluetooth, affiche les informations de trajet et le niveau d’assistance. LE VAE pèse en revanche 24,3 kg : il roule très bien, mais le monter au troisième étage sans ascenseur risque d’être sportif.
À ce prix, le Crossover V LTD est-il une bonne affaire ?
Les 500 € de remise représentent plus d’un quart du prix initial. À 1 399,99 €, le Nakamura Crossover V LTD devient particulièrement intéressant face aux autres VAE de cette gamme de prix. Là où beaucoup se contentent d’un moteur placé dans la roue arrière, il propose un moteur central de 70 Nm, des freins à disque hydrauliques et une fourche suspendue. Un équipement plutôt généreux pour un vélo capable de vous accompagner aussi bien dans vos trajets quotidiens que lors de sorties sur les chemins le week-end (c’est la période des champignons !).
Black Friday 2026 : tout ce qu’il faut savoir
Depuis une dizaine d’années, le Black Friday s’est infiltré dans le calendrier commercial des grandes marques et enseignes françaises. Avec l’expérience, on peut vous dire que cet événement fait partie des meilleurs moments pour faire de bonnes affaires.
Les dates du Black Friday
Bien qu’il porte encore le nom du vendredi noir, le Black Friday s’étend désormais sur un mois chez de nombreux revendeurs. Un format moins typique qui lui retire un peu son petit côté FOMO. On dirait presque les soldes, finalement. Mais c’est aussi moins le rush, ce qui est une bonne chose pour ceux qui veulent faire des achats plus raisonnés. Globalement, on peut résumer ce Black Friday en quatre temps forts :
- Début novembre : les avant-premières Black Friday.
- Autour du 20 novembre, selon les enseignes : la Black Week commence généralement plusieurs jours avant le jour J.
- 27 novembre : la date du Black Friday, même si les offres commencent généralement avant et se prolongent le week-end des 28 et 29 novembre.
- 30 novembre : le Cyber Monday.

Que faut-il acheter pendant le Black Friday ?
Globalement, tous les rayons profitent des remises, mais il ne faut pas pour autant se jeter sur les premiers prix bradés. N’oubliez pas que pour les enseignes, ce moment est aussi l’occasion de déstocker de vieux produits, dont les plus remisés frôlent parfois l’obsolescence.
Qu’il s’agisse d’un téléviseur, d’un smartphone, d’un casque sans fil ou d’un aspirateur balai, on ne peut que vous conseiller de suivre nos guides d’achat dédiés pour savoir quels modèles valent le coup en 2026.
Pour les produits phares comme les AirPods, la PS5, la Switch 2, un iPhone ou un Samsung Galaxy, sachez que nos tests sont là pour vous aider à savoir s’ils méritent votre argent.

articles.title: Windows : deux failles BitLocker permettent de lire les fichiers protégés
articles.text:
Parmi les 1 235 failles corrigées par le Patch Tuesday de novembre, deux vulnérabilités concernent BitLocker. Intégré à Windows, cet outil chiffre le contenu du disque dur. C’est lui qui protège vos données si votre ordinateur portable est perdu ou volé. Concrètement, il rend les fichiers illisibles pour une personne qui ne possède pas la clé de déchiffrement. Sur de nombreux PC, le chiffrement est activé par défaut.
À lire aussi : Windows 11 permet enfin de personnaliser le menu du clic droit
Deux failles qui mettent en danger
La première faille permet tout simplement de contourner le chiffrement de l’appareil. Selon Microsoft, un attaquant peut accéder à toutes les données chiffrées stockées sur le disque. Pour exploiter la défaillance, le pirate doit simplement disposer d’un compte utilisateur sur l’ordinateur. Il n’y a pas besoin de privilèges particuliers.
La seconde brèche est liée à une erreur de gestion de la mémoire. Elle permet de contourner le Secure Boot, le démarrage sécurisé de Windows, une protection qui empêche normalement le lancement de logiciels malveillants. D’après Microsoft, l’attaque ne nécessite ni compte ni intervention de la victime.
Dans les deux cas, le pirate doit d’abord obtenir un accès physique à l’ordinateur. Il n’est pas possible d’exploiter les failles à distance, depuis Internet, ce qui limite le champ des attaques. C’est néanmoins un problème pour les individus qui perdent leur ordinateur ou qui se le font voler. Les deux brèches sont classées « importantes », le niveau juste en dessous de « critique », même si leur exploitation n’a pas été jugée « probable ».
Bonne nouvelle, Microsoft précise que ces deux failles n’ont pas été rendues publiques avant le déploiement du Patch Tuesday. Elles n’ont donc pas été exploitées par des pirates. Les vulnérabilités touchent Windows 10, Windows 11 et plusieurs versions de Windows Server. Ce n’est pas la première fois que BitLocker est touché par une faille cette année. D’autres failles du même type ont déjà été corrigées le mois dernier, lors du Patch Tuesday record déployé par Microsoft.
Pour vous protéger d’éventuelles attaques indiscrètes, installez sans tarder la mise à jour de sécurité de novembre sur votre ordinateur. Ouvrez les Paramètres de Windows, puis allez dans Windows Update, puis cliquez sur « Rechercher des mises à jour ». Redémarrez ensuite l’ordinateur pour finaliser l’installation.

articles.title: Apache HTTP Server patches critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaw
articles.text:
A critical vulnerability in the HTTP/2 module of Apache HTTP Server could be exploited by an unauthenticated attacker to obtain remote code execution (RCE).
The Apache Software Foundation has fixed the issue, now tracked as CVE-2026-119618, but a significant number of servers are vulnerable and reachable over the public internet.
Discovered by Anthropic’s OSS Scanner and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research teams, the vulnerability is a race condition in the mod_http2 module that can corrupt heap memory.
An attacker successfully exploiting it could run code with the web server process’s privileges in HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, and standalone mod_h2 version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42.
Apache describes the problem as “Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server's mod_http2 in assign_headers() can lead to RCE.”
Apache HTTP Server is a free and open-source software that handles requests from web browsers and serves pages, images, and other website content. It is a widely used tool estimated to back roughly one out of five websites.
According to telemetry data from cloud security company Wiz, 64% of the cloud environments have vulnerable resources, and roughly half of them have publicly exposed instances.
However, the numbers do not account for server configuration, which requires HTTP/2 to be enabled (default is off).
Researchers at cybersecurity company watchTowr confirmed this condition and recommend technicians to "patch now or drop h2 until you can."
"Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption," Wiz researchers say.
"This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process."
Wiz assesses the severity of the vulnerability to be critical, although no official score is available. The company says that it is currently unaware of any public exploits or attacks targeting the flaw, but this could change soon.
The latest version of Apache HTTP Server also addresses two additional flaws, CVE-2026-106023 - a null pointer dereference in ‘mod_md,’ and CVE-2026-109163 - a low-severity data overwrite flaw in ‘mod_vhost_alias.’

articles.title: Beyond the first transaction: Building inclusive digital payments for Bharat
articles.text:
Beyond the first transaction: Building inclusive digital payments for Bharat
At TechSparks 2026, Sagar Kumar of PayU discussed how payment systems can improve accessibility, build user trust, and bring more consumers and small businesses into the digital economy.
For digital payments to work for Bharat, getting someone to make their first transaction is only the beginning. The bigger challenge is making sure they feel confident enough to return, whether they are shopping online in their preferred language, making a payment independently, or running a small business.
At TechSparks 2026, Sagar Kumar, Vice President of Engineering at PayU, joined Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director – Strategic Content & Video at YourStory, for a fireside chat on the engineering behind inclusive digital payments.
Balancing speed with reliability
Having worked at early-stage startups and on systems handling millions of transactions, Kumar explained how engineering priorities change as businesses scale.
In the early stages, startup teams focus on speed, launching products quickly and learning as they go. But architecture remains important. Loosely coupled systems make it easier to add new business verticals without rebuilding everything from scratch.
At scale, speed is still important, but there is less room for error. Feature flags, incremental rollouts and A/B testing allow teams to introduce changes gradually, test them with specific customer groups and limit the impact of potential problems.
“Speed is the constant. It's just that the room for error will be smaller when you grow to a larger scale ecosystem, and in that process, you have to build enough safety nets,” he said.
Building for the next 100 payments
With UPI now familiar to many users in smaller cities and towns, Kumar believes the next step is to make online payments as intuitive as offline transactions.
PayU’s checkout pages default to a scan-and-pay option, offering an experience similar to what customers are used to at physical stores. The company has also launched Checkout for Bharat, which allows users to view checkout pages in multiple languages, making it easier for those who are less comfortable with English to complete payments.
But a simpler interface is only part of the solution.
For a first-time online shopper, seeing money debited from their account followed by a payment failure message can quickly undermine confidence. Kumar explained that payment systems need safeguards such as idempotency checks, which ensure that repeating the same request does not change the outcome after the first successful attempt.
These checks help prevent duplicate debits. Clear communication about failed transactions and automatic reversals are also important so customers do not have to initiate refund requests themselves.
“The next level of inclusivity, in my opinion, is not to bring a first-time user online to make payments, but to gain the confidence so that he makes another 100 payments. We engineer our systems to achieve that kind of a goal,” Kumar said.
Making accessibility part of engineering
In August, PayU launched an RBI-compliant checkout page designed to help blind and visually impaired users make payments independently.
The features include screen-reader voiceovers that identify important information such as payment amounts, merchant details, and transaction status. The company also made changes to button sizes, text layouts, and other visual elements.
PayU tested the checkout experience with blind and visually impaired users, who were able to complete payments independently rather than rely on someone else.
The company has also made accessibility part of its software development lifecycle, treating it as a consideration alongside functionality and performance when developing new features.
Kumar pointed out that these improvements can benefit other users too. High-contrast displays, for example, make it easier for delivery partners to view payment pages in bright sunlight. Clearly labelled interface elements can also help AI agents navigate checkout pages.
Keeping transactions running at scale
PayU processes close to 20 million transactions on an average day. At that volume, even a 0.1% failure rate could mean 20,000 unsuccessful payments.
Kumar explained that the challenge of operating at this scale comes from the number of systems involved. A single transaction can depend on merchants, issuing and acquiring banks, payment networks, aggregators, and multiple gateways. A slowdown or disruption in any one of these systems can affect the payment.
PayU uses intelligent routing to manage this complexity. Its systems monitor gateway success rates across several parameters, while machine-learning (ML) models help determine the best route for each transaction.
The algorithms also send a portion of transaction traffic through alternative routes to test their performance. This gives the system a real-time view of how different gateways are functioning.
If a gateway's performance deteriorates, transactions can be redirected to another option. Kumar said PayU has patented this routing algorithm.
The aim is to manage these complexities in the background so merchants and customers can complete transactions without having to deal with them.
Turning payments into business opportunities
Kumar also discussed how payment data can create opportunities beyond transactions.
UPI payments generate transaction histories that can help businesses understand customer payment behavior and support financial underwriting for specific credit needs.
PayU’s LazyPay addresses buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) use cases, while its merchant lending product helps small and medium businesses manage cash-flow requirements, including purchasing goods at more favourable prices. Repayments can be collected through daily settlements.
The company has also launched Agent HQ, which helps small businesses automate operational tasks such as following up with customers who abandon their websites, reconciling payments and initiating refunds.
By reducing the time founders spend on these activities, such tools can allow them to focus on growing their businesses.
For Kumar, the benefits extend beyond individual merchants. As small businesses grow, the wider digital payments ecosystem stands to gain too.

articles.title: Ecovacs X12S OmniCyclone : le robot laveur à rouleau perd 500 € pour le Black Friday
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 - L'aspirateur robot laveur Ecovacs Deebot X12S OmniCyclone est à 799 € (-38 %)
Rouleau laveur de 27 cm, prétraitement des taches et lavage à 75 °C : l'aspirateur robot Ecovacs X12S OmniCyclone Care kit passe à 799 € chez Amazon, soit 500 € de moins.
Vendu et expédié par Amazon, ce robot affiche 799 € contre 1 299 € pour le prix conseillé, soit une remise de 38 % dans le cadre des offres pré-Black Friday d'Amazon. Il n'était pas descendu sous 1 299 € au cours des 30 derniers jours.
Un rouleau laveur autonettoyant
Le X12S lave les sols avec le rouleau OZMO Roller 3.0 de 27 cm, qui exerce une pression de 4 000 Pa et tourne à 260 tours par minute en se nettoyant en continu. Le système FocusJet pulvérise de l'eau et du détergent sur les taches avant le passage du rouleau.
Côté aspiration, Ecovacs annonce une puissance 60 % supérieure à la génération précédente, avec un système anti-enchevêtrement ZeroTangle 4.0 et une brosse latérale qui s'étend pour atteindre les bords.
Une station qui lave à 75 °C
La station lave le rouleau à l'eau chaude à 75 °C grâce à une pompe à 32 jets, puis évacue l'eau sale. Une recharge rapide restaure 13 % de batterie en trois minutes pendant le nettoyage du rouleau, utile dans les grands logements.
Pour éviter les obstacles, le robot s'appuie sur le système AIVI 3D 4.0. Il est noté 4,3/5 sur Amazon, sur un petit nombre d'avis.

articles.title: ¿Cómo funciona el mercado de criptomonedas y cuál es su valor este jueves 12 de noviembre?
articles.text:
Las criptomonedas son un activo digital innovador que han experimentado un crecimiento monumental en los últimos tiempos debido a varios elementos que contribuyen a ello, entre ellos que algunos gobiernos hayan decidido darles una oportunidad como moneda de curso legal; no obstante, también han sufrido descalabros que han puesto en duda su viabilidad, como el más reciente episodio conocido como el "criptoinvierno".
Pese a este panorama, cada vez más personas han empezado a adquirir criptomonedas para poder invertir en algo "seguro" y "fiable" tanto a corto como a largo plazo, a pesar de los niveles extremos de inestabilidad que sufre constantemente.
Sin embargo, invertir o comprar en criptodivisas es más fácil de lo que parece. Hay que recordar que se trata de monedas virtuales, por lo que serán controladas en carteras o monederos que comparten esa particularidad, pues a diferencia del dinero corriente, no tienen un soporte físico.
El precio de las criptomonedas hoy
Esta es la cotización de las criptodivisas más destacadas en este momento.
El Bitcoin, cotiza a 73.460,01 dólares, lo que implicó un cambio de -0,682% en las últimas horas.
La segunda criptomoneda más popular del mercado, Ethereum, ha mostrado un movimiento de -0,485% en las últimas 24 horas, por lo que su valor se ubica en 2.045,9 dólares.
En el caso de TetherUs, su precio es de 1 dólares, por lo que en el último día tuvo un movimiento de -0%.
Por su parte, BNB, tiene un valor de 672,38 dólares, con un cambio de -1,06%, en cambio el Litecoin cotizó a 49.634 dólares, tras una variación de -2.059579.
Finalmente, el Dogecoin, una de las monedas virtuales que fue impulsada por Elon Musk, tiene un valor de 0,07 dólares tras presentar un cambio de -1,51% en las últimas 24 horas.
Qué pasa con las criptodivisas
Luego de que en las primeras semanas de mayo del 2022 se viviera el "criptocrash" o "criptoinvierno" que dejaron al descubierto la enorme volatilidad de estas monedas digitales, ha llegado un nuevo periodo de relativa estabilidad.
Bitcoin, ethereum y BNB han mostrado variaciones "controladas", puesto que no se han disparado los precios como en semanas previas. Por ejemplo, a inicios de agosto, las mencionadas anteriormente tuvieron un cambio menor del 2%.
Por otra parte, algo que esta llamando la atención en el mundo de las criptomonedas es que China está ablandando sus restricciones y podría comenzar a permitir su uso. Específicamente sería Hong Kong en donde este cambio se haría presente.
Sumado a ello, la plataforma de transacciones digitales PayPal anunció su propia stablecoin llamada PayPal USD (PYUSD), que cuenta por el respaldo de depósitos en dólares, bonos del Tesoro de Estados Unidos a corto plazo y activos equivalentes.
La compañía ha afirmado en su declaración que permitirá la transferencia de fondos a monederos digitales de terceros y proporcionará detalles sobre cómo integrar su servicio en exchanges centralizados y descentralizados, con el objetivo de ser utilizado en Finanzas Descentralizadas (DeFi, por sus siglas en inglés). Por lo tanto, es muy probable que se utilice ampliamente en la industria Web3.
Criptomonedas en Latinoamérica
Criptomonedas en México: el Banco de México (Banxico) ha determinado que ninguna de las instituciones que participan en el sistema financiero nacional podrá hacer uso o deberá permitir operaciones de ninguna clase a través de este medio de pago.
En territorio mexicano el empresario Ricardo Salinas Pliego, uno de los más ricos del país, ha mostrado interés en las criptomonedas y ha asegurado que varios de sus negocios aceptarán bitcoin en el futuro, incluido su banco; hasta el momento una de sus tiendas más populares ya lo hace.
Criptomonedas en Perú: el Banco Central de Reserva del Perú (BCR) ha dejado en claro que su misión no es ser el primero ni el segundo banco central que regule el uso de las criptomonedas, ello debido a la inestabilidad que las caracteriza. Sin embargo, hace días el presidente del (BCR) aseguró que el BCR trabajaba en un proyecto de moneda digital propia.
Criptomonedas en Colombia: en la nación sudamericana hay más de 500 sitios donde es permitido pagar con criptodivisas. Colombia ocupa el puesto 14 entre 26 países de adopción de criptomonedas, según el informe de Finder.
Criptomonedas en Centroamérica: en el gobierno de El Salvador, el bitcoin, que en septiembre de 2021 se convirtió en moneda de curso legal, ha perdido oficialmente este estatus en este enero del 2025 tras una reforma aprobada por la Asamblea Legislativa del país. Según informó la prensa local, la modificación de la Ley Bitcoin fue impulsada por el gobierno del presidente Nayib Bukele y respaldada por la mayoría oficialista en el órgano legislativo. Este cambio marca el fin de una política que había colocado al país centroamericano en el centro del debate global sobre las criptomonedas.
¿Cómo crear una criptomoneda?
Al momento de crear una criptomoneda es importante primero determinar qué se desea tener: una moneda o un token. La primera usa su propia blockchain, mientras que la segunda se basa en una red preexistente.
De acuerdo con el sitio de Binance, para crear una criptomoneda se necesita de un gran equipo de desarrolladores y expertos; mientras que para el token sí se requieren conocimientos técnicos pero es posible crearlo en minutos a través del uso de otras blockchains como Ethereum o BNB, que son las más populares.
Los costos de creación, el tiempo requerido y el uso de fuerza de trabajo dependerá de si se opta por hacer una moneda virtual o un token. En éste último caso también se puede usar un código establecido para crear tokens o pagar para usar un servicio de creación de monedas.
Es importante saber que antes de crear una criptomoneda se debe considerar su utilidad y estado legal.
En el caso de elegir crear una criptomoneda, entonces se debe elegir una blockchain, posteriormente se debe hacer un plan acorde al funcionamiento y la funcionalidad de la blockchain para diseñar los nodos y la interfaz.

articles.title: Marcelo, exjugador del Real Madrid: “Pasé 16 años en Madrid, compré inmuebles e hice inversiones. Hoy por hoy, no tengo de qué preocuparme”
articles.text:
Marcelo Vieira contó su situación económica tras dejar el fútbol profesional. Explicó que tenía inmuebles e inversiones y que a su familia le iba bastante bien. “Vivo muy bien, no te voy a mentir”, dijo en la entrevista que mantuvo con David Broncano en La Revuelta.
Con estas palabras dejó claro cómo veía su situación financiera en el momento. Sin embargo, no es posible saber el total de su patrimonio. No se sabe qué beneficios genera cada uno de los negocios en los que está involucrado. Además, ante la pregunta sobre cuánto dinero tiene, no especificó un monto. Sí indicó que tiene propiedades y que está implicado en el mundo futbolístico brasileño.
Uno de estos casos es el edificio de varios pisos que compró en 2023 en la plaza de la República Argentina, en el barrio madrileño de El Viso. Se trata de una operación que hizo a través de la compañía Belluly por 3,7 millones de euros.
En el registro de constitución de Belluly aparece como administrador único. La finalidad de la compañía es la promoción inmobiliaria. También fue nombrado administrador único de otra empresa llamada Borsen Trade. En este caso, en su asiento consta que su actividad es la explotación comercial de derechos de imagen de deportistas.
El Viso es un barrio de alto precio. De hecho, en septiembre de 2026, el precio medio del metro cuadrado de las viviendas en venta era de 9.402 euros (según Idílico Realty). Sin embargo, esto no quiere decir que el edificio de Marcelo tenga ese precio. No sabemos cuál es su rentabilidad.
Los negocios de fútbol requieren distinguir participaciones y control
En 2022 también anunció que iba a abrir una barbería en Río de Janeiro. Por otro lado, también participó en un proyecto brasileño de futbolistas. Se trata del Azuriz Futebol Clube. En él estaban centrados en el proceso de formación y venta de jugadores a otra entidad.
Por otro lado, también hay constancia de su inversión en el América de Natal. Invirtió a través de la sociedad inversora del club. Sin embargo, no fue el único accionista. No podemos decir que sea el propietario único del equipo ni que controle toda la gestión.
El proceso de formación de futbolistas puede llevar a generar ingresos (por traspaso), pero no es posible afirmar que controle todo el proceso (de Brasil a Europa). Además, tampoco es seguro que los jugadores que tiene un club acaben en alguno de los proyectos en los que ha estado implicado.

articles.title: CEOs drängen zum KI-Einsatz – und ernten "Work-Slop" von Mitarbeitenden
articles.text:
CEOs drängen zum KI-Einsatz – und ernten „Work-Slop“ von Mitarbeitenden
KI ist in vielen Bereichen der Arbeitswelt nicht mehr wegzudenken. Es gibt zahlreiche Unternehmen, die den Einsatz von KI explizit gefördert haben, um die Produktivität im Konzern zu erhöhen.
Doch dieser gutgemeinte Gedanke kann auch nach hinten losgehen. Unternehmen, die den Einsatz von KI zunächst gefördert haben, stellen nun Regeln gegen sogenannten „Work-Slop“ auf: also KI-generierte Nachrichten und Dokumente, die die Posteingänge überfluten.
Chefin an Mitarbeitende: „Hört bitte auf, wie Roboter mit mir zu sprechen“
Eine solche Unternehmensleiterin ist Michelle Volberg. Als CEO des auf den Tech-Sektor spezialisierten Personalvermittlungsunternehmens Twill stattete sie ihr zehnköpfiges Team mit einer Unternehmenslizenz für den KI-Chatbot Claude aus. Mittlerweile hat sie aber genug davon, dass ihre Mitarbeiter:innen roboterhaft mit ihr kommunizieren. Sie schickte eine E-Mail mit einer klaren Botschaft an ihr Team: „Hört bitte auf, wie Roboter mit mir zu sprechen.“
Volberg berichtete gegenüber Business Insider, dass die Slack-Nachrichten und E-Mails ihrer Mitarbeiter:innen plötzlich wirkten wie die Vorschläge ahnungsloser externer Berater:innen. Perfekte Zeichensetzung, fehlender Kontext zum Kunden und gelegentliche „Halluzinationen“ der KI.
KI-Slop am Arbeitsplatz kann auch kontraproduktiv sein
Wie verbreitet ist „Work-Slop“ mittlerweile? Laut einer aktuellen Umfrage des Stanford Social Media Lab und von Betterup Labs gaben 53 Prozent der befragten Büroangestellten an, bereits „Work-Slop“ verschickt zu haben. Der Anteil derjenigen, die solche Inhalte erhielten, sank zwar leicht von 40 auf 38 Prozent, doch die Betroffenen schätzten, dass sie monatlich drei bis vier Stunden damit verbringen, das zu korrigieren.
KI-Slop am Arbeitsplatz ist nicht nur nervig, sondern kann auch kontraproduktiv sein. Sobald Menschen den Eindruck gewinnen, dass sie nur noch mit KI-generiertem „Müll“ (Slop) konfrontiert werden – egal ob Kolleg:innen oder Kund:innen –, hören sie in vielen Fällen auf, weiter zuzuhören.
Für die interne Kommunikation ist die eigene Stimme gefragt
Volbergs neue Richtlinie in ihrem Unternehmen ist simpel: KI darf genutzt werden, um Ideen zu entwickeln oder auszuarbeiten – für die interne Kommunikation ist jedoch die eigene Stimme gefragt. „Wenn du es nicht auch persönlich, per E-Mail oder in Slack so sagen würdest, dann verschicke es auch nicht“, betonte sie.
Wer sich nicht an solche Vorgaben hält, kann durchaus Probleme bekommen. Medienberichten zufolge ist es bereits zu Entlassungen von Mitarbeiter:innen gekommen, die trotz einer ausdrücklichen Warnung weiterhin KI für Aufgaben einsetzten, bei denen dies untersagt war.

Egypt’s remittances hit a record $38.2 billion
Egyptians living abroad are sending home more dollars than ever, and their country has plenty of reasons to be grateful.
According to the Central Bank of Egypt (CBE), remittances reached a record $38.2 billion in the first nine months of 2026. Between July and September alone, Egyptians sent home $13 billion, up 20.4% from the same period last year.
Explain like I’m new here: Remittances are money people working abroad send home, usually to support their families. For Egypt, they’re also an important source of foreign currency, helping the country pay for imports and meet international obligations.
Catch up: In March 2024, Egypt allowed its currency to trade more freely. Before then, Egyptians abroad could get better exchange rates outside official banking channels. Closing that gap helped bring more transfers into banks, where the dollars could support the wider economy.
Here’s the interesting part: The rebound has held up despite renewed currency pressure and concerns that workers in Gulf countries might cut transfers amid regional conflict.
But there’s a catch: Egypt’s remittances reached $47.3 billion in the financial year ending June 2026. Yet, its merchandise trade deficit widened to $64.8 billion, while its current account deficit reached $22.5 billion.
Zoom out: Egyptians abroad are helping keep dollars flowing into the country. But until Egypt earns more from exports, its economy will remain heavily dependent on remittances.

connectivity
Ghana wants 70% 5G coverage by March 2027
Ghana wants 70% of its population within reach of a 5G network by March 2027. It’s an ambitious target, especially for a country that recently abandoned its original rollout plan.
Samuel Nartey George, Ghana’s communications minister, announced the target at an International Telecommunication Union (ITU) conference in Qatar.
Explain like I’m new here: Ghana initially placed its 5G ambitions in the hands of Next Gen InfraCo, a shared telecoms infrastructure company. The company received exclusive rights to build a wholesale 5G network for ten years, with mobile operators expected to rent capacity rather than build competing networks.
But the arrangement struggled to gain traction. By May 2026, Next Gen InfraCo reportedly had just 49 sites, while major mobile operators had yet to sign up to use its network.
In July, Ghana’s National Communications Authority (NCA) ended the company’s exclusivity, opening 5G spectrum licencing to competing operators. By October, MTN Ghana and Telecel received 5G permits.
Why it matters: Ghana is betting that competition will speed up network deployment. Operators can now pursue their own 5G infrastructure instead of waiting for a single provider.
The government is also completing 2,016 rural telecommunications sites and upgrading older networks to support faster connectivity.
Zoom out: More towers won’t automatically mean more 5G users. Affordable smartphones, data prices, and actual demand still matter. Ghana has changed who gets to build its networks. Whether more Ghanaians can afford to use them is another question.
Cybersecurity
Kenya launches cybersecurity centre amid growing cyber threats
Kenya has launched the SecureKE Sovereign Security Operations Centre (SOC) about 65 kilometres southeast of Nairobi. The Konza Technopolis Development Authority (KoTDA), the government agency responsible for developing the country’s flagship technology and innovation city, established the centre through a partnership with SecureKE, a Kenyan cybersecurity company. The centre will provide government institutions and private organisations with access to cybersecurity services.
Explain like I’m new here: Kenya has a national cybersecurity response system called the National Kenya Computer Incident Response Team–Coordination Centre (KE-CIRT/CC). It coordinates incident responses, issues threat alerts, and works with local and international organisations to tackle cyber threats. SecureKE is designed to give institutions a shared operational service for monitoring their own digital systems and responding to suspicious activity.
Why Kenya is doing this:INTERPOL’s 2025 Africa Cyberthreat Assessment found that cybercrime accounts for more than 30% of reported crime in both West and East Africa. It also found that 90% of African countries surveyed needed significant improvements in law enforcement or prosecution capacity. Kenya detected 4.56 billion cyber threat events in late 2025, while reported banking cyber-fraud losses reached KES1.9 billion ($14.6 million), which shows the scale of activity security teams must contend with. As the country puts more public services and business activity online, the goal is to ensure security grows alongside connectivity.
Telecoms
Telkom challenges South Africa’s ownership rules locking out operators like Starlink
Starlink has spent months knocking on South Africa’s regulatory door, hoping to launch its satellite internet service in the country. It may have found an unlikely ally in Telkom, one of South Africa’s biggest telecoms operators, which is questioning some of the rules keeping it outside.
What happened? Telkom has challenged South Africa’s ownership requirements for telecoms licences in a submission to the Independent Communications Authority of South Africa (ICASA), the country’s telecom regulator. The company, in which the South African government holds a 40.5% stake, said the rules are too rigid and overlook other ways companies can support economic empowerment, such as skills development, local supplier investment and infrastructure funding.
Explain like I’m new here: South Africa’s Electronic Communications Act requires individual telecoms licence holders to have at least 30% ownership by historically disadvantaged groups. This has been a stumbling block for Starlink, which has resisted giving up a 30% stake to local investors.
Communications Minister Solly Malatsi proposed Equity Equivalent Investment Programmes (EEIPs) that would let foreign companies contribute through investments in local suppliers, skills development, infrastructure and digital inclusion instead of selling shares. However, the proposal attracted pushback, with Malatsi being accused of trying to circumvent the law to accommodate Starlink. ICASA opposed Malatsi’s proposal in May, but one wonders whether those critics will have the same objections now that a major local operator is also questioning the rules.
It’s more than Starlink for Telkom: The company argues that rigid ownership requirements could make it harder for telecoms operators to attract foreign capital and expand infrastructure. Allowing alternative empowerment mechanisms could give companies more flexibility to invest in skills and network infrastructure without changing their ownership structure.
If the rules also create uncertainty for established local operators, the question is whether South Africa can attract the foreign investment needed to expand its digital infrastructure without watering down its economic empowerment goals.

articles.title: Chicago schools tell Google they'd rather lose Search than be forced to accept AI
articles.text:
Ripple effect: Not long after Google announced its definitely-not-petulant response to schools banning its AI services by threatening to remove its search engine completely, Chicago Public Schools has said it will simply use a different search solution. Google's actions have also led to protests against the company, with demonstrators chanting the catchy slogan, "Hey Google, nice try. We don't want your Gemini."
At the start of November, Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager for education, said K-12 schools will soon have to accept the company's AI services to retain student access to its search engine. The reason, he claimed, was that Search and AI are now deeply integrated services. Instead of the usual results, students will see a message from their school stating that the services are not available.
A lot of people didn't take this well, claiming Google was essentially blackmailing schools into using a service they didn't want. Chalkbeat Chicago reports that it led to protests in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and in Chicago, where the city's school district recently blocked student access to generative AI tools such as Gemini.
Chicago Public Schools (CPS) has yet to respond to Google's announcement, but a CPS spokesperson said in a statement that the district was "actively exploring all options to independently suppress" the AI Overviews that appears at the top of Google searches. The spokesperson added that if CPS cannot provide students access to Google's search engine without its AI feature, the district will "look to other search solutions."
It's not just CPS that's unhappy about Google's behavior. About 30 protesters, including parents, educators, and students, demonstrated outside Google's office in Chicago's West Loop.
"We are owed lessons and feedback from the people CPS hired, people who are passionate and dedicated to making learning fun," said Reese Mackey, a junior at Kenwood Academy High School. "Not by a bot whose only job is to be a yes man and compile random sources from the internet for a nonsensical answer."
A Google spokesperson said the company was working to improve Search for classroom use, including testing its "Guided Learning" feature, which uses AI to guide students through problems one step at a time instead of simply giving them answers.
Chicago is far from alone in pushing back. In October, Frederick County's school board voted 6 – 1 to restrict student AI use from pre-K through 12th grade, just weeks after allowing older students to try Gemini with teacher permission. Board members raised concerns about the lack of warning to parents and teachers' inability to disable the tool on student devices. Exceptions remain for lessons about AI and accommodations for students with disabilities.
New York City also introduced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI from preschool through eighth grade for the 2026 – 2027 school year. High school use is limited to approved tools in supervised pilot or career-readiness programs, while Los Angeles has temporarily blocked generative AI tools on student devices across all grades.
Google faces an uphill battle to convince schools that using AI is the way forward for students, but threatening to remove search from those who say no is hardly going to help convince them otherwise.

articles.title: Google Open-Sources TPU Sync for KV Cache and Weight Transfer on TPUs
articles.text:
Google Cloud has open-sourced TPU Sync, a native C++ library that moves KV cache blocks and model weights between TPU HBM, host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network. GCP also announced the TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max systems, the project targets two workloads where accelerators often wait on data: long-context and disaggregated LLM serving, and reinforcement learning loops that push updated weights from trainers to rollout samplers.
For prefill/decode disaggregation, Google says median KV transfer latency for Qwen3 235B fell from several seconds to about 230 ms, with average TTFT reductions of 60% for that model and 90% for a 480B model at low concurrency. For prefix caching, it reports up to 90% lower average TTFT on 64K-context workloads.
Developers get Python wheels for JAX and PyTorch, with KV cache manager, KV store, and weight synchronizer APIs. TPU Sync acts as the KV connector for vLLM-TorchTPU through vLLM's KVConnector interface, as the disaggregation and hierarchical-cache backend for SGLang-TorchTPU, and pairs with llm-d 1.0 on GKE for prefix-cache-aware routing. The RL weight-sync module for Pathways and multi-controller JAX is experimental. The GitHub repository, which absorbed the earlier TPU Raiden codebase, warns that APIs are changing rapidly and that only development builds are on PyPI, and recommends pinning to its last-known-good commit. It is validated on TPU v7x and v6e, and the PyTorch wheel requires a matching torch_tpu build that is not on a public index.
On GPUs, similar problems are handled by NVIDIA Dynamo and its NIXL transfer library, LMCache, which offloads KV cache to CPU memory, disk, or remote stores, Mooncake, the KVCache-centric serving architecture behind Moonshot AI's Kimi, and vLLM's own disaggregated prefill connectors. TPU Sync differs mainly in being tied to PJRT and TPU tile layouts, and in covering RL weight transfer in the same library.
Early reactions focused on data movement rather than the new chips, with developer Anand Butani sharing:
TPU sync cutting kv transfer latency 90% matters more to me than the chip names, long-context serving mostly dies on moving cache between nodes.
Another developer posting under the pseudonym @lgoodbookd ran rough numbers on why bandwidth alone does not solve the problem:
8i Max doubles HBM bandwidth to ~17.2TB/s, yet one 64K session on a 235B MoE still eats ~12.6GB of KV cache. That's why open-sourcing TPU Sync (host-DRAM KV tiering, ~223GB/s per v7x host) may matter as much as the new package. Bandwidth helps; capacity is still the wall.
TPU Sync is available under the Apache 2.0 license, and its repository includes architecture documentation, C++ and Python APIs, and examples for single-host and multi-host disaggregated serving and host KV offloading. Until a stable release is cut, the JAX and PyTorch packages are published only as development builds, while the storage tier and RL weight synchronization remain experimental

articles.title: Netflix releases new trailer for Ray Gunn
articles.text:
We caught the first trailer for the upcoming Netflix animated film Ray Gunn in September and were charmed by director Brad Bird’s blend of a Jetsons-like future with classic 1930s noir detective thrillers. Bird has described it as a mashup of The Maltese Falcon and Buck Rogers, and the latest trailer definitely gives off that energy.
As previously reported, Bird has directed some of our all-time favorite animated films: The Iron Giant (1999), The Incredibles (2004), and Ratatouille (2007), with the latter two snagging well-deserved Oscar wins. He’s been kicking around the idea for Ray Gunn for the last 30 years, working on his many other film projects while the Ray Gunn script—co-written by Matthew Robbins, who also co-wrote 1987’s Batteries Not Included with Bird—“stayed in a filing cabinet at Warner Brothers,” the director said earlier this year.
The film’s inspiration came when Bird heard the opening of the B-52s’ “Planet Claire” (a personal favorite that also provides the soundtrack to the new trailer) and initially thought it was a cover of Henry Mancini’s theme music from the classic TV show Peter Gunn. Bird is a longtime fan of film noir and hard-boiled detectives, and he came up with the idea of a futuristic detective named Ray Gunn (a play on “raygun,” of course). “It’s film noir and a hard-boiled detective story, but it’s got a lot more comedy and a lot more action than the average film noir,” said Bird.

articles.title: I wanted to love this Garmin Forerunner rival, the Suunto Race 3S — I just didn’t love the price
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Suunto Race 3s makes for a much more compelling purchase than its predecessors thanks to a bevy of small but welcome updates — although some might feel it's too little, too late when compared to the likes of Garmin, Coros, Apple and Samsung, especially at this price. There’s competency here, but little to make it stand out.
Reasons to buy
- + Accurate heart rate tracking
- + Good battery life
- + Still a good-looking smartwatch
Reasons to avoid
- - The price has gone way up
- - No NFC payments
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Suunto Race 3S: One-minute review
Suunto has been pretty great over the last few years at delivering mid-to-premium smartwatch options, but if there was one miss, it was the Suunto Race series.
As we pointed out in 2024, the Suunto Race S felt premium in terms of its design despite being cheaper than many of its rivals, but the heart rate tracking left a lot to be desired. It was followed by a Race 2, with no smaller ‘2s’ model.
With Suunto announcing a new model, the Race 3S, though, we expected big things. What we got, however, was almost the inverse of the Race and Race 2: The price is up (way up), and while there are some neat improvements ranging from “nice to have” to catching up with rivals, its fitness tracking is, thankfully, much better.
And at this price, it really needed to be. Whereas its predecessor launched at $449, this model is $150 more. In a market that’s already crowded with excellent budget and mid-range smartwatches and fitness trackers, it feels a little like Suunto has overshot its category somewhat.
Suunto Race 3S: Specifications
| Component | Suunto Race 3S | 
| Price | $599 / £435 / AU$999 | 
| Weight | 56g | 
| Case/bezel | Titanium | 
| Display | 1.32-inch AMOLED display | 
| GPS | Dual-band GPS | 
| Battery life | Up to 12 days | 
| Connection | Bluetooth | 
| Water resistant? | 50m | 
Suunto Race 3S: Price and availability
- Starts at $599 / £435 / AUS$999
- Much pricier than the prior Race S model
- Available in three color options
Available in three colors of Titanium, the Suunto Race 3S will set you back considerably more than its predecessors, somewhat undoing the charm of the last model.
It’s not the most expensive smartwatch around, but that puts it close to Garmin’s Forerunner 570 and a whole $200 more than an Apple Watch Series 12.
My review unit is the pink-hued ‘Orchid’ colorway, but there’s also a black version (handily called ‘Black’), as well as a grayish ‘Feather’.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
- Value score: 2/5
Suunto Race 3S: Design
- Display is nice and easy to read
- Digital crown and button combo is easy to learn
- Titanium and sapphire crystal
If you were wondering where the extra budget has gone in the Suunto Race 3S, then it’d be fair to say some of it has been lavished on the exterior.
The watch comes with a titanium bezel like the Garmin Fenix 9, with a very slight lip over the AMOLED display. Will it survive a sharp rock on your next trail run? I’m not at liberty to hurl it in the name of science, but the Sapphire Crystal glass will definitely protect against just about anything else.
On the underside, you’ll find a reworked heart sensor (more on that later), and I’m pleased to see the Race 3S continue with the more traditional “pin” design for installing the straps. They’re the usual polymer fare here, but the colored strips are a nice touch that give it a little more personality.
On the side, you’ll find two navigation buttons and a digital crown, while you can prod at the screen with your digits, too. All in all, navigating is really easy to pick up, so if this is your first smartwatch, there’s a good chance you can hit the ground, well, running.
- Design Score: 4/5
Suunto Race 3S: Features
- A step up from its predecessor in almost every aspect
- Tougher, faster, and larger storage
We’ll get to performance shortly, but much of what Suunto has put in the Race 3S feels like natural extensions from the prior model, and helps it keep pace (pun intended) with its rivals — if not actually outstripping them.
The processor is faster, but it’s not as if you’re running third-party apps that can really push it to its limits (Suunto doesn’t support them), and the whole thing has dropped 4g in weight to be a little more comfortable (although I’m unsure you’d notice it much).
There’s one thing that I can’t get my head around, though, and that’s the storage capacity being increased. Despite Suunto’s onboard maps being relatively small in size and the ever-climbing price of computing components, including storage, Suunto has doubled the 32GB onboard storage to 64GB.
I’m not complaining (if you’re the type to put music on your watch, you’ll no doubt appreciate it), but I wonder if the whole package may have been a little cheaper with a smaller storage SKU. It’s also worth noting that there are no streaming services here; it’s all offline MP3s.
There are also no NFC contactless payments, which is a shame.
- Features Score: 4/5
Suunto Race 3S: Performance
- 12 days of battery life
- Accurate heart rate readings
- AI coaching subscription feature
The Suunto Race 3 comes into its own with its heart rate tracking this time around, and it’s a huge step beyond anything else from the Race range.
Throughout testing, I found the new optical heart rate sensor to be in near lockstep with my Apple Watch Series 11. Suunto puts this down to more sensors, and if you're worried about that affecting battery life, then there’s good news on that, too.
Despite the brighter display (which is very welcome in sunlight, or what’s left of it in good ol’ Blighty), you’ll still get around 12 days of general usage in smartwatch mode. Naturally, the more you’re using it to track your exercise routines or prodding at the screen, that’ll decrease, but you’re still getting around 35 hours (in my testing) with the always-on display active and multi-band GPS tracking.
New this time around is an AI coaching subscription feature (just like, well, every other wearable apart from Apple and Samsung now), with Suunto getting on board the trend with machine learning and chatbot-style Q&A. In essence, it means you can pull out your phone and ask it to put together a summary of your week’s training, highlight the difference month on month of your fitness, or ask questions about your recovery rate.
This stands separate from the existing Suunto Coach, and will essentially allow you to interrogate your data using natural language support and build fresh fitness plans on demand, like the Google Health Coach
As with a lot of what’s on offer here, it’s good to see Suunto closing the gap to its rivals, but I’m more curious about its MCP, which will allow the likes of Claude or Cursor to access your health data.
- Performance Score: 4/5
Scorecard
| Category | Comment | Score | 
| Value | Struggles to justify the price hike | 2/5 | 
| Design | Looks and feels great | 4/5 | 
| Features | More storage will no doubt make some happy, but no NFC | 4/5 | 
| Performance | Excellent heart rate tracking and solid GPS | 4/5 | 
Should I buy?
Buy it if:
You want excellent heart rate tracking
The Suunto Race 3S is great at heart rate tracking, with impressive accuracy in our testing.
You’re looking to upgrade your older Race model
The increased screen brightness, smaller footprint, and additional software features.
Don’t buy it if:
You’re on a budget
The Suunto Race 3S is considerably pricier than some of its rivals, so you’ll need to weigh up how much the impressive heart rate tracking is worth to you.
Also consider
Garmin Forerunner 970
A top-tier expensive running watch from Garmin.
Read our full Garmin Forerunner 970 review
Coros Pace 4
A cheaper but still excellent running watch from Coros
Read our full Coros Pace 4 review
How we tested the Suunto Race 3S
I’ve been testing the Suunto Race 3S while walking, swimming, and in the gym. I tested it across a more rural area, and in central London on my way to the office.
And, as ever, I had my Apple Watch Series 11 on the opposite wrist to monitor any differences in heart rate tracking and GPS positioning between them.
First reviewed: November 2026
Lloyd Coombes is a freelance tech and fitness writer for TechRadar. He's an expert in all things Apple as well as Computer and Gaming tech, with previous works published on TopTenReviews, Space.com, and Live Science. You'll find him regularly testing the latest MacBook or iPhone, but he spends most of his time writing about video games at Dexerto.

articles.title: Trump floats Apple chairman Tim Cook as Jensen Huang's successor | TechCrunch
articles.text:
In the wake of the industry-shaking news of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation on Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump is floating the idea that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should take over the position.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote that “only one man” could take Huang’s place: Tim Cook of Apple.
“A Legend replaces a Legend!” he wrote.
Cook stepped down as Apple’s CEO on September 1, 2026, after 15 years running the company, but he’s still very much involved with Apple. While John Ternus took over as Apple’s CEO, Cook transitioned into the role of executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors, which sees him continuing to engage with global policymakers and manage international relationships, including Apple’s relations with China.
Trump is not the only one to suggest Cook as a replacement for Huang. Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, Senior Associate Dean for Leadership Studies at Yale School of Management, who studies CEO leadership and corporate governance, penned an op-ed in Time on Wednesday, suggesting Cook should be among the potential candidates. He wrote that Cook has “an unparalleled track record of succeeding a bigger-than-life founder,” in reference to Cook taking over from Apple founder Steve Jobs.
Whether or not Trump agrees with this opinion, or is simply blasting off an idea that hopped into his mind, is anyone’s guess.
“Tim Nvidia,” however, doesn’t quite have the same ring as “Tim Apple” does.

articles.title: Conexus Venture Capital raises additional $5 million for Fund II | BetaKit
articles.text:
Regina’s Conexus Venture Capital (CVC) has raised more for its latest fundraising round than originally planned, adding another $5 million to its Fund II after reopening to investors earlier this year.
The news: CVC announced the additional fundraise on Nov. 12, bringing the total closing dollar figure to $35 million. CVC, which initially closed investment to Fund II in November of 2025, cited strong participation demand from investors and early portfolio momentum as key to its decision to re-open the fund.
From the source: “We are grateful to our investors for their continued confidence in our team, our thesis, our fund, and, most importantly, our founders,” Jordan McFarlen, CVC’s managing director, said in a press release. “Reopening the fund due to increased demand is an excellent signal. We’re excited to put the capital to work.”
The context: As the venture capital (VC) branch of Conexus Credit Union, CVC typically invests in early-stage tech companies, an area of Canadian VC that has seen significant declines in recent years. CVC’s Fund I ranked among the top performers in its size category in 2019. Fund II has grown its portfolio by 10 companies as of press time, including investments into fellow Regina startup Offstreet, Saskatoon’s Alto Technologies, Judi.ai, and Cyder, among others.
CVC hasn’t disclosed who contributed to the initial or follow-on raises for Fund II, but the firm’s parent credit union is the anchor limited partner, putting $15 million into the pot. In an interview with Regina’s Leader-Post, McFarlen said investment came from both repeat participants and new financiers.
Final thought: The Canadian VC landscape has been shrinking in the past half-decade, with the Canadian Venture Capital Association (CVCA) reporting that spending fell from nearly $15 billion in 2021 to $8 billion in 2025. Early-stage investment has, in particular, been impacted by that drawback of private dollars. However, 2026 has seen two high-profile deals in Western Canada that delivered significant returns to early-stage investors, including PurposeMed’s acquisition by Grindr and CoolIT Systems sale to Ecolab. CVC’s reopening of Fund II amid increased investor demand may indicate changing tradewinds when it comes to the perceived risk around early-stage investment.

articles.title: Canadian tech gifts driven by nostalgia, physical ownership: survey
articles.text:
Canadians are leaning into the nostalgia factor for tech holiday gifts, driven by a growing desire to own physical products, according to a new survey.
Named the Holiday Tech Gifting Report, the study was done by Best Buy and Angus Reid. It surveyed 1,500 Canadian adults between Oct. 16-20, 2026, who were members of the Angus Reid Forum.
Starting things off, the study shared that four in ten (40 per cent) of Canadians are likely to buy a tech gift because of the nostalgia factor. To make it specific, Best Buy notes that Millennials (53 per cent) are the most likely generation to do so, while Boomers (22 per cent) are almost half as likely to do so. Millennials are also the most likely to say that it reminds them of a certain time in their life (20 per cent), almost double that of Boomers (11 per cent).
The survey also noted that if Canadians could bring back one piece of tech, the iPod (15 per cent) was the highest voted, with the physical keyboard-sporting BlackBerry, Nintendo 64, or Super Nintendo all following behind. In terms of age groups, Gen Z favoured the iPod (22 per cent), while Millennials chose the Nintendo 64/Super Nintendo (24 per cent). Boomers on the other hand, were most likely to pick VCR/VHS tapes (17 per cent).
Why the rise in nostalgia? Well, according to the survey, one in three Canadians say their main reason for being drawn to old tech is a preference for owning physical products — with nearly one in four (23 per cent) having bought music, movies, or games within the last year. Interestingly, Millennials (32 per cent) and Gen Z (30 per cent) were more than twice as likely to have purchased physical media within the last year.
The survey also said that 46 per cent of Canadians are considering a tech product as a holiday gift this year. These people also said that what matters most is that the recipient will use it regularly and that it reflects their interests (both at 46 per cent), that it is a good value (36 per cent), and that it lasts for years (30 per cent).
Of course, the survey notes that Boomers (24 per cent) were more than twice as likely as Gen Z (9 per cent) to say that ease of setup matters most.

articles.title: Deadpool y Lobezno (Wolverine), confirmados oficialmente en 'Avengers: Doomsday': así se ha revelado su cameo secreto
articles.text:
Lo que durante mucho tiempo ha sido un secreto a voces parece que ya es oficial. Ryan Reynolds y Hugh Jackman, los actores de Deadpool y Lobezno (Wolverine) estarán en Avengers: Doomsday. Ambos intérpretes regresan a Marvel para la próxima película de los Vengadores, que se estrena en diciembre y que se ha convertido en uno de los lanzamientos más esperados del año.
En realidad, Marvel había tratado de mantener en secreto su participación en la película. Incluso se ha jugado al despiste llevando al propio Ryan Reynolds solamente como público a convenciones en las que se presentaba el proyecto. Pero ahora, se ha revelado definitivamente que sí son parte de la historia de Avengers: Doomsday. Lo curioso es que no ha sido cosa de Marvel ni de los intérpretes.
Resulta que el Sindicato de Guionistas (WGA) ha actualizado los créditos de Avengers: Doomsday bajo el concepto "Additional Literary Material". Esto se utiliza cuando se quiere acreditar a personas que han trabajado en un guion pero en un porcentaje demasiado pequeño como para ser considerados guionistas del filme. Y resulta que entre los nombres incluidos en este nuevo listado están los de Ryan Reynolds y Hugh Jackman.
Por tanto, ya está confirmado que ambos han participado en el guion de la película. Y, evidentemente, ha tenido que ser para sus propios personajes. Es decir, que gracias a esta nueva información ya sabemos que Deadpool y Lobezno (Wolverine) tendrán al menos un cameo en Avengers: Doomsday.
Más guionsitas para Avengers: Doomsday
En realidad, Ryan Reynolds y Hugh Jackman no son los únicos añadidos por el WGA. Con el mismo concepto de "Additional Literary Material" están Eric Pearson (Thunderbolts*), Chris McKenna y Erik Sommers (Spider-Man: Brand New Day), Jeff Loveness (Ant-Man y La Avispa), Andrew Lanham y Destin Daniel Cretton (Shang-Chi y la leyenda de los Diez Anillos).
Pearson es un habitual de Marvel al que la compañía le suele encargar que ayude a que un guion encaje dentro de la gran narrativa del UCM. Ya ha colaborado en películas como Los 4 Fantásticos: Primeros pasos o Viuda Negra. En cuanto a Loveness, fue quien debía escribir originalmente Avengers 5, titulada por aquel entonces La dinastía de Kang.
Uno de los nombres más destacados de la lista es el de Cretton, que acaba de dirigir Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Pero aunque esto podría anticipar el regreso del arácnido, la presencia de Lanham, guionista de Shang-Chi y la leyenda de los Diez Anillos, da a entender que lo más probable es que ambos hayan trabajado codo con codo en el arco narrativo del propio Shang-Chi.
Avengers: Doomsday se estrena en cines el 18 de diciembre.

articles.title: A third of UK businesses on Google Maps have no working website — and many of those that do are struggling to keep them up to date
articles.text:
A third of UK businesses on Google Maps have no working website — and many of those that do are struggling to keep them up to date
UK businesses admit their Google listing sends customers to a dead end
- Digital Royalty study finds 33% of 6,266 owner-claimed Google listings across 12 UK towns and cities had no working website
- Health and beauty fared worst at 53%, and large cities interestingly did worse than small towns
- Follow-up data shows 18.9% of working sites with a readable footer year still display 2024 or earlier
Roughly a third of UK businesses that have claimed their Google listing are sending would-be customers somewhere other than a website they control, and a fair share of the sites that do load look as though nobody has touched them in a while.
The findings come from a recent census of Google Business Profile listings published by Digital Royalty, which checked 8,426 open listings across 12 UK towns and cities and 12 everyday business types, from plumbers and electricians to hair salons and accountants.
Of the 6,266 listings their owners had claimed, 2,095, or 33%, had no working website.
Claimed, verified, and going nowhere?
The inactive group covers four situations: no website on the listing at all, a link only to a social profile, a link only to a page on someone else's platform such as a booking or food-ordering app, and a site that is dead or parked.
Including unclaimed listings, the figure rises to 44%, though that also includes stale and spam entries that nobody maintains.
Health and beauty was the worst-performing group by some distance, with 53% of its 1,074 claimed listings lacking a working site, led by hair salons (54%) and beauty salons (53%).
Much of that traffic goes to Instagram profiles and booking apps instead: 12% of all health and beauty listings pointed only to a social or booking page, compared with 1%-5% in the other groups.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Trades came next at 35%, with plumbers (41%) and electricians (38%) showing up as the worst offenders, followed by hospitality (29%), retail (26%), and professional services (19%), where real estate agencies (17%) and accountants (21%) were the most likely to have a working site.
Somewhat surprisingly, bigger places fared worse. Large cities posted a 37% rate, compared with 25% in small towns, with Birmingham the highest of the 12 places at 42%. Each region is represented by a single place, however, so region and town size are tangled together, and Digital Royalty itself cautions against reading the results as a regional ranking.
Then there are the sites that used to work: Of the 5,533 listings showing a website link, 495 (8.9%), or roughly one in 11, led to a dead or parked site, while another 353 (6.4%) pointed only to a social or third-party page. Among sites that did load, 5.3% did not load over HTTPS, and 3.3% lacked a mobile viewport tag.
Digital Royalty concluded that "the bigger gap is the missing site, not a poor one," though HTTPS and a viewport tag are low bars that most modern website builders clear by default, so passing them says little about whether what is on the page is still accurate.
For scale, the government's latest business population estimates, published on November 5 2026, counted 5.59 million private sector businesses in the UK at the start of 2026. Of these, 5.54 million are small businesses with fewer than 50 employees, but only 1.47 million have any employees at all. The other 4.1 million are run by their owners alone, making them effectively single-person businesses.
The census was not designed to be scaled up, so any national figure carries significant caveats. If the one-in-three rate holds across the UK's 1.47 million employers, that would mean roughly 490,000 businesses whose Google listing leads nowhere they control.
Applying the same rate to all 5.54 million small businesses would produce about 1.85 million, but doing that could stretch the data available to us too far, since many one-person operations never set up a Google listing in the first place.
The government's own UK Business Data Survey, published in June and based on responses from 4,450 businesses between October 2025 and January 2026, offers a useful cross-check. It found that 78% of UK businesses say they have a website, up from 68% in 2023 to 2024, with ownership ranging from 92% among small businesses to 84% among micro businesses and 76% among sole traders. Applied to the 5.59 million total, the 22% without one works out to roughly 1.2 million businesses.
A footer that gives it away
To gauge whether working sites are being kept current, Digital Royalty shared follow-up data with TechRadar Pro, noting that on November 5 2026, the company fetched the homepage of each of the 4,592 sites it had counted as working and looked for a copyright year it could read.
Of the 1,944 sites that displayed one, 1,437 (74%) showed 2026 and 140 (7%) showed 2025. The remaining 367, or 18.9%, showed 2024 or earlier, and 114 (5.9%) still displayed 2019 or earlier. Hospitality had the highest share of stale footers at 21.6%, closely followed by professional services (21.2%), health and beauty (20.9%), and trades (19.1%). Retail was the clear outlier at 8.8%.
In all fairness, a copyright year is a blunt instrument; Many website builders and WordPress themes automatically generate the current year, so a 2026 footer does not prove that anyone has updated the page, and a stale footer can sit beneath perfectly current opening hours. The most it reliably shows is that nobody has edited the bottom of the page in a while.
The sample also thins out: Only 42% of the working sites displayed a readable year: 1,354 had no year at all, and 1,294 returned no page to read on the second pass. That gap in data could also interestingly reflect bot protection, since the original census counted sites that blocked its checks as working, pages that only render with JavaScript, or sites that stopped working in the month between the two checks (Digital Royalty's original census and its communication with TechRadar Pro).
At the same time, it is important to note that a dead or parked domain is not just lost business, either. A parked page can mean an owner still holds a name and never built anything on it, but it can also mean the name lapsed and has since changed hands, in which case the Google listing keeps sending customers to whoever bought it.
There is a thriving market for exactly that. Infoblox Threat Intel counted roughly 65,000 expired domains re-registered every day in the first half of 2026, close to a fifth of all new registrations, and estimated, by extrapolation, that one operation had spent more than $7 million acquiring expired names for their inherited traffic.
As Renée Burton, vice president of Infoblox Threat Intel, put it, expired domains can offer "a shortcut to both trust and traffic." The census does not say how many of its 495 dead or parked sites have changed owners.
The UK Business Data Survey linked above also hints at why sites drift: When asked who manages their website, 29% of businesses said they use a mix of in-house and external help; 27% do it entirely in-house; 24% rely entirely on an external developer or platform; and 17% manage it in-house through a platform provider.
Sole traders were the most likely to go it alone. The report's authors suggest the variation by size and sector may reflect "differences in how businesses engage with and maintain their online presence once established."
A site run entirely by someone else stays current only as long as that relationship does, and a domain renews only as long as the card on file keeps working. For owners, the first check costs nothing: open the website field on your Google Business Profile and tap it on a phone, as a customer would.
Turning on domain auto-renewal closes off the lapsed-domain risk, and for anyone starting from scratch or moving off an abandoned site, our guides to the best small business website builders and best web hosting are a reasonable place to begin.
For a third of the claimed listings in this sample, though, the problem is not a slow or dated website; It is that there is no website at the end of the link.
