articles.title: Author Q+A: finprim is a Case for One Financial Validation Library in TypeScript
articles.text:
finprim, which is an MIT-licensed TypeScript library that puts IBAN, BIC, card, sort code, VAT, routing number and loan calculations behind one API, has published its fifth release, 0.1.4. The repository has 81 stars.
InfoQ asked author Oluwatosin Adelaja what pushed him to build it, and where he wants it to stop.
InfoQ: What pushed you to build finprim?
Adelaja: Honestly, it came from doing the same work too many times. At Sprint Technology Solutions we had several products, and each one ended up with its own copy of the same financial validation, sort code checks in one place, IBAN formatting in another, card validation somewhere else, all written slightly differently by whoever got there first.
The moment it really landed for me was on a payout flow. We had account and sort code validation on the web side, and then the mobile app needed the same thing. Rather than share it, the validation got rewritten for mobile, and the two copies drifted. One of them was a little stricter than the other, so a bank detail that the web form accepted would get rejected on mobile, and we had people re-entering details that were actually fine. It took longer than it should have to track down, because nobody thinks to check whether two "identical" validators are actually identical. The fix was easy once we found it, but the real problem was that there were two of them at all.
I hit the same shape of thing again later building a daily pay feature for NHS workers, where the same rules needed to hold on web and on mobile. That is when I stopped treating it as a one-off chore and started thinking it should just be one library, written once and tested once, that any product could pull in and trust.
InfoQ: What was missing that justified a unified library rather than assembling existing single-purpose packages?
Adelaja: You can absolutely wire together a pile of single-purpose packages, and plenty of teams do. The problem is what you are left maintaining. Each package has its own API shape, its own types, its own idea of what a valid result looks like, and often its own dependencies. So you end up writing a layer of glue code just to make them agree with each other, and that glue becomes its own thing to test and keep working.
finprim's bet is that financial validation is coherent enough to live behind one consistent API. The same shape of input, the same shape of result, and the same typing approach across IBAN, sort code, card, VAT, all of it. And zero runtime dependencies, so there is no tree of other people's packages to audit or keep patched. For something sitting in the path of a payment, I wanted fewer moving parts, not more.
InfoQ: What concrete class of bugs do branded types prevent, and why not rely on plain runtime validation?
Adelaja: The bug class is the one where a string that was never validated gets used as if it had been. To the compiler, a validated IBAN and a random string are both just a string, so nothing stops you passing the wrong one into a function that assumes the value is good. It compiles fine, and then it fails at runtime, which in this domain means it fails in the middle of a live transaction.
Branded types close that gap. A validated IBAN comes back as its own distinct type, not a plain string, so if you try to use an unchecked value where a validated one is required, the compiler rejects it before the code ever runs. The runtime validation still happens, that does not go away. The branding just guarantees it actually happened and that nobody quietly skipped it on some code path. It moves a whole class of "we forgot to validate this one route" mistakes from production back to compile time.
InfoQ: For something handling payment data, how do you think about trust, what can you guarantee, and where do you draw the line?
Adelaja: The honest answer starts with being clear about what finprim is and is not. It validates and formats financial data. It does not store anything, it does not send anything over the network, and it does not process payments. No database, no telemetry, no outbound calls.
So the guarantees I can actually make are narrow and specific. It checks values against published standards, IBAN structure, checksum rules, card network ranges, and tells you whether they are well formed, deterministically, without logging the sensitive values it is handling. That last part is deliberate. You do not want account numbers or card numbers turning up in logs, so the library does not put them there.
Where I draw the line matters just as much. finprim does not tell you a payment is safe to make, it is not a compliance tool, and it is not a replacement for the checks your payment provider runs. It confirms the data is shaped correctly before it goes anywhere. Treating a validation library as more than that would be the real mistake.
InfoQ: How do you source and maintain the correctness of 80+ IBAN formats, VAT quirks and card ranges, and how is it tested?
Adelaja: The rules come from the published standards rather than from me guessing. IBAN is checked against the ISO 13616 country formats, card numbers use Luhn plus the published network ranges, VAT uses the documented per-country formats, and so on. Where there is an authoritative spec, that is the source of truth.
On testing, each validator runs against known-good and known-bad values taken from those reference sources, so the tests check behaviour against the standard, not just against themselves. Overall coverage is around 91% of lines and 88% of statements. The core validation modules are the most heavily covered, the IBAN, card, VAT, routing, BIC and sort code logic sits around 94% of lines with full function coverage, and the thinner coverage is in the optional React bindings rather than the validation itself. I would rather be straight about that split than quote one headline number, because the part that actually handles financial data is the part that is tested hardest.
Keeping it correct over time is mostly manual, I update the formats as the standards change, and this is one place the outside contributors have genuinely helped, because people using it in different countries spot edge cases I would never hit on my own.
InfoQ: SEPA and ACH generation is a big jump from validation into transaction generation. Where do you want finprim to end up?
Adelaja: That is a fair thing to push on, because generation is a genuinely different job from validation, and I do not want to pretend otherwise. Validating an IBAN is self-contained. Producing a SEPA credit transfer file or an ACH batch means taking on formatting rules, sequencing and a lot more responsibility for getting something exactly right that is going to be submitted to a bank.
Where I want finprim to sit is as a validation and formatting toolkit first. I am deliberately cautious about the generation side. If it does move into producing standard file formats, I would want that to be safe, well-tested generation of documented formats, not finprim turning into a transaction engine or a payments platform. I would rather it did one layer really well than spread itself thin doing a half version of what a payment provider already gives you.
Narrower tools exist, such as ibankit for IBAN and BIC alone, and on DEV a commenter called the Dinero.js approach solid while warning that teams get burned when a library's precision assumptions diverge from the processor's.
Adelaja is a senior full stack engineer. All five releases have stayed within 0.1.x, so upgrading has meant patch releases rather than code changes, and there is no dedicated migration guide, so the README and release notes are the reference.

articles.title: Whoop just launched a social network | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Whoop, the maker of screen-less fitness bands, is launching a social network on Thursday that lets its members follow friends and family and share their health data.
The network, called Whoop Humans, will be rolled out in the Whoop app to members at every membership tier at no extra cost. Members can follow anyone on Whoop and choose what to share, from sleep and recovery to workouts and achievements. Followers can react and comment; members can also attach photos and commentary to their data. It’s all opt-in, CEO Will Ahmed tells us.
Whoop already has a social feature, Teams, which a little more than half its customers use, according to the company. But Teams is built around groups and leaderboards, and everyone in a group sees everyone else’s information. Humans is meant to be more intimate. Members decide who follows them and who sees what, so a trainer can track a set of clients without the clients seeing one another’s data, for example.
I found myself questioning how much a spouse wants to know about the other’s sleep score when Ahmed mentioned this particular scenario, so I asked him how else beta members used these newer social features. He said the company learned that people were more engaged when someone reported a low recovery score than a nearly perfect one, suggesting that the new feature may be particularly helpful for understanding when someone is struggling and might need attention.
Indeed, the bigger story here is where Whoop continues to be headed, which is into medical wellness. Like its most direct rival, Oura, the company is pushing faster and more aggressively into the wellness opportunity that an aging population presents.
Whoop had already added FDA-cleared ECG and atrial fibrillation detection, blood pressure insights, blood testing, and medical-record uploads. Asked if older customers are gravitating to Whoop, Ahmed said, without offering specifics, that Whoop has seen “huge growth” among people over 60 over the past 18 months. He also said his was among the first companies accepted into a Medicare program that reimburses qualifying wearables that can show they improve health outcomes, and that it now has Medicare members.
He added that he expects families to be big users of Humans. (You can imagine adult children checking in on aging parents.)
But the company’s efforts to be thought of as the “brand for personal health” raises questions, naturally, about privacy. Ahmed said members choose which metrics to share, can remove followers, and can switch on “stealth mode” to go dark for a few days without changing their settings. Activities marked sensitive aren’t shared by default, and Ahmed said health alerts and medical information aren’t shared at all. Members can also report any comment or photo that they deem disturbing, and the company said reported content is reviewed.
As for minors, Whoop’s minimum age is 13 for all members (higher in some countries), meaning customers of that age can share their data subject to consents and privacy settings. Asked whether a parent could follow a teenager’s data, he didn’t answer directly and pointed to the privacy controls.
Ahmed also said Whoop doesn’t sell member data. “Our product is not you; it’s the membership,” he said, adding that the company doesn’t license data to third parties.
He was candid about dealmaking. Asked about Oura’s announcement this week that it will pay $625 million for Counsel Health, a service offering on-demand physicians, Ahmed said he expects “more consolidation” among AI-focused, clinician-focused, and wearable companies, and that Whoop is always on the prowl. Its deep relationship with members, he said, puts it “in a position to be an acquirer.”
He was more guarded about the company’s own finances, declining to share revenue or say whether Whoop is profitable. He did say that the company now has about 1,200 employees, membership on its software platform has increased more than 70% a year for three years running, and that it expects to have nearly 4 million members by year-end.
As for an IPO (the company raised a very big round earlier this year), he said only that Whoop “will certainly IPO in the future.” He also wouldn’t comment on Oura, which shelved its own IPO of up to $2.2 billion in September citing market uncertainty.
In the meantime, Whoop is widening its reach. The company announced that its devices will be sold through Ulta stores beginning next March (around 500 locations of the beauty retailer to start, and a target to retail in more than a thousand stores eventually). Indeed, Ahmed said Whoop’s female audience has more than doubled from last year.
As for competition, in addition to Google’s new Fitbit Air band, Whoop may soon have to contend with Apple, which is reportedly developing a Whoop-style band. But Ahmed mostly shrugged off those concerns, suggesting that building a product doesn’t guarantee success. Instead, he said, Whoop’s job is to stay true to the “aspiring” people it serves.

articles.title: Foto brasileira da Chapada dos Veadeiros sob a Via Láctea vence prêmio mundial
articles.text:
Uma fotografia da Chapada dos Veadeiros, em Goiás (GO), conquistou reconhecimento internacional ao vencer o Grande Prêmio Global do 17º Greenstorm Photography Festival. Intitulada “Pandora”, a imagem foi registrada pelo fotógrafo brasiliense Marcio Cabral e mostra a Via Láctea alinhada a um morro, com dezenas de chuveirinhos do Cerrado iluminados em primeiro plano.
A fotografia concorreu com trabalhos de outros 116 países e foi escolhida entre mais de 14 mil imagens inscritas nesta edição do festival, que teve como tema “Belas Pastagens e Campos”.
A cerimônia oficial de premiação aconteceu no final de agosto, durante a 17ª sessão da Conferência das Partes (COP17) da Convenção das Nações Unidas para o Combate à Desertificação (UNCCD), na Mongólia. O prêmio concedido ao fotógrafo foi de R$ 55 mil.
Para Cabral, a conquista também representa oportunidade de chamar a atenção para a preservação do Cerrado. “O Cerrado enfrenta pressão imensa de desmatamento, perda de biodiversidade, e aí ver essa espécie do chuveirinho, que é uma espécie emblemática da Chapada dos Veadeiros, ser reconhecida globalmente na cúpula da ONU, traz visibilidade internacional para a urgência de preservar nosso bioma”, afirmou, em entrevista ao g1.
A organização do festival também destacou a importância da imagem para a conservação ambiental. Segundo os responsáveis pela premiação, a fotografia representa a conexão entre a humanidade e a natureza e reforça a necessidade de proteger os ecossistemas do planeta.
Leia mais:
- Teoria sugere que universo é mais antigo e dispensa matéria escura
- Asteroide misterioso acelera no espaço e desafia explicações científicas
- Meteorito marciano de mais de 4,1 bilhões de anos pode mostrar detalhes primitivos de Marte
Como a fotografia da Via Láctea foi feita?
- O registro foi feito em 2023, no Jardim de Maytreia, ponto turístico de Alto Paraíso de Goiás. Para conseguir o enquadramento, Marcio precisou calcular previamente a posição da Via Láctea e esperar por condições climáticas específicas;
- A captura aconteceu por volta das 22h, quando o céu estava sem nuvens e não havia vento. As flores também receberam iluminação especial, produzida com uma lanterna óptica, que permitiu destacar as plantas sem interferir no brilho das estrelas;
- “Pandora” é resultado da combinação de nove fotografias de longa exposição feitas no mesmo local e posteriormente unidas em um computador;
- O fotógrafo explicou que o planejamento envolveu reunir várias condições pouco comuns ao mesmo tempo: o alinhamento da Via Láctea, céu limpo, ausência de vento para evitar que as flores se movessem durante as exposições e uma florada especialmente intensa dos chuveirinhos;
- A última condição é importante porque as plantas não florescem com a mesma intensidade todos os anos. Por isso, conseguir registrar o cenário desejado dependeu também de acertar o período da floração.
Fotografia já recebeu outros prêmios internacionais
O reconhecimento do Greenstorm Photography Festival é mais uma conquista para “Pandora”. A imagem já venceu o Oasis Photo Contest, na Itália, e o The Nature Photography Contest, na Espanha, além de receber premiações na Inglaterra e destaque na revista científica Nature.
Segundo Marcio Cabral, a fotografia também foi a única obra de um brasileiro selecionada para integrar um livro especial da National Geographic. A publicação reúne 200 das melhores fotografias de todos os tempos da instituição.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Coraltalk wants universities to stop chasing AI cheaters and start measuring learning | BetaKit
articles.text:
“Show your work” is an instruction known to just about anyone who has gone to school.
With generative AI now capable of producing entire assignments, universities have good reason to revisit that old classroom principle. Asking students to explain their reasoning can help instructors establish what they’ve actually learned, but in a large university class, that’s easier said than done.
Suppose a university professor wanted to sit down with each of their 75 students and ask them a few questions about their latest assignment. If they were to dedicate 15 minutes per student, the exercise would take close to 20 hours, before accounting for preparation, scheduling, or grading. Melissa Morgan, co-founder and CEO of Toronto-based EdTech startup Coraltalk, believes technology could make these kinds of assessments achievable on a much larger scale.
“A detector estimates whether text may have been produced by AI,” Morgan said. “It cannot tell a professor whether the student understands the argument, could explain a decision, or would know what to do if the facts changed.”
Coraltalk is using conversational AI to bring oral examinations into the digital age. Instructors provide the platform with course materials, assignments, and grading criteria, which the software uses to question students about their work. As students respond, the AI asks follow-up questions to probe their understanding.
A new take on an old-school approach
Consider a business student who has submitted a class assignment recommending that a company expand into a new market. Coraltalk’s platform would ask the student to explain their recommendation and identify its underlying assumptions before introducing a new constraint to see how they respond.
Once the assessment is complete, instructors can review the conversation in video form, as well as the transcript and feedback aligned with their rubric. Importantly, the instructor retains the final say over grades. Coraltalk’s role is to handle the labour-intensive part of the assessment and make individualized questioning practical for professors who would otherwise have to conduct dozens of interviews themselves.
Smita Bakshi, an investor in Coraltalk, said she took oral exams known as “vivas” during her university days. “That was possible with a class of 50, but is not possible today without the use of a technology like Coraltalk,” Bakshi said.
There are obvious technical complications that come with putting an AI system in charge of questioning students, particularly when the same technology has a well-documented tendency to hallucinate or misinterpret information. Oral exams can also disadvantage students whose language proficiency, confidence, or communication style affects their ability to answer questions aloud.
Coraltalk co-founder and CTO Adhikansh Mittal said developing the platform presented several technical challenges. One was latency, since conversations need to flow naturally between students and the AI system. Another was ensuring the privacy and security of student voice recordings and assessment data, which meant accounting for institutional requirements early in the platform’s development.
Mittal said it was also important to ensure questions draw on an instructor’s course materials, and that faculty can review results and make their own assessments.
“Those safeguards reduce risk, although no AI system can eliminate bias or hallucinations entirely, so ongoing evaluation and human oversight remain essential,” Mittal added.
Finding traction in the classroom
Coraltalk was founded in 2025 but has already found a receptive audience. The company says it has reached users in more than 60 countries without spending money on paid marketing.
Educators associated with institutions including York University and James Madison University are among those who have engaged with the platform. The company has also raised $768,000 CAD ($570,000 USD) in funding, and this year won the Higher Ed Shark Tank competition at New York’s EdTech Week.
Morgan attributed much of the early interest to professors recommending Coraltalk to colleagues, often out of frustration with the limitations of conventional assignments.
“They did not want another tool that accused students of cheating,” Morgan said. “They wanted something practical that worked with the courses they already teach.”
David Kwok is familiar with this need. Alongside his position as Director of Entrepreneurship and Innovation at York University’s YSpace, he teaches at the Schulich School of Business, where AI is changing the way students approach their coursework.
“While AI is a powerful tool, we need to ensure students continue developing the critical thinking, problem-solving, and communication skills essential to their future careers,” Kwok said, adding that he sees promise in Coraltalk’s focus on students’ ability to explain and apply their knowledge, skills that will remain relevant long after graduation.
International by necessity
Building Coraltalk has required the founders to work across several countries, and not entirely by choice. Morgan is Canadian, while Mittal is based in New Delhi, India. When Mittal was unable to obtain a visa to visit Canada, the duo began looking for other places where they could develop the company. Their travels have taken them to Vietnam, Indonesia, Malta, and Mexico.
“It has made us resourceful and given us an international perspective, although I wish it were easier for Canadian startups to collaborate in person with exceptional global talent,” Morgan added.
Coraltalk participated in various YSpace programs, including the ELLA Women Accelerator, a program supporting women-led businesses. Through YSpace, the startup gained access to experienced entrepreneurs and support with fundraising and partnerships.
Marlina Ramchandran, ELLA Entrepreneurship Manager at YSpace, said Morgan’s ability to overcome obstacles is characteristic of the adaptability YSpace wants to cultivate among entrepreneurs in the program.
“From shifting primary markets due to visa restrictions to building a business in a completely new language, she has consistently adapted, overcome every barrier, and emerged stronger,” Ramchandran said.
Back to the business of learning
Coraltalk is now looking at how its technology might be incorporated into existing education platforms. The company has developed an integration with Canvas, a widely used learning management system, and is pursuing a broader strategy to embed its technology in third-party platforms.
“Schools and learning platforms already have workflows they rely on,” Mittal said. “An API can bring conversational assessment into those products without asking everyone to adopt a separate system.”
The startup’s longer-term ambitions include applications beyond higher education, including hospitality training, where employees could practice handling difficult customer interactions, and professional development programs focused on communication and decision-making skills. Language education is another potential market the company is watching.
In a 2025 survey by the York University Faculty Association, 60 percent of respondents reported spending more time dealing with academic integrity issues than they had five years earlier. With generative AI further complicating the assessment process, Morgan believes universities need a better way to establish what students actually understand.
“AI is changing what students can produce, and that makes human skills like reasoning, communication, judgment, and adaptability even more important,” Morgan said. “My hope is that we build a future where students are invited to demonstrate those skills, teachers have meaningful evidence of learning, and using AI does not automatically turn every learner into a suspect.”
PRESENTED BY
YSpace is building a stronger Canadian tech ecosystem by fostering a community of innovators, entrepreneurs, and change makers with dedicated programs for women (ELLA) and Black (BEA) entrepreneurs, and sector-specific initiatives like SmartTO for automotive and mobility-related ventures. articles.title: Tout savoir sur UVEX, le télescope spatial de la NASA qui va traquer les plus violentes explosions de l’Univers
articles.text:
Fusions d’étoiles à neutrons, supernovas… Certains cataclysmes cosmiques échappent à Hubble, trop lent à pivoter pour les saisir à temps. Mais la NASA vient de confirmer UVEX, le télescope ultraviolet qui les observera juste après leur apparition.
Fin août, le télescope Nancy Grace Roman a pris son envol avec la mission de percer les mystères de la matière noire. Mais dans la foulée, le Swift, l’observatoire qui scrutait les sursauts gamma, a poursuivi sa chute pour venir s’abîmer dans l’atmosphère début novembre. Quant au vénérable Hubble, la NASA vient de lancer un appel au secteur privé pour tenter de lui offrir une seconde vie car il se dirige, lui aussi, vers sa destruction. Mais pas de panique : l’agence spatiale prépare la relève.
Cartographie du ciel
Car c’est désormais officiel : UVEX, pour UltraViolet EXplorer, n’est plus un simple projet. La NASA vient de lui faire passer avec succès la revue « KDP-C », un examen technique et budgétaire qui scelle l’engagement définitif de l’agence. Elle promet ainsi un lancement d’ici à janvier 2031, pour un coût total de 590 millions de dollars.
Le télescope a été retenu en 2024 via le programme Explorers, le plus ancien de la NASA, qui a envoyé plus de 90 missions dans l’espace depuis Explorer 1 en 1958. Fiona Harrison, professeure de physique au prestigieux Caltech, en est la responsable scientifique, et va collaborer avec l’université de Californie à Berkeley, le Jet Propulsion Laboratory de la NASA, Northrop Grumman et Space Dynamics Laboratory pour le mener à bien. De quoi concrétiser « un audacieux bond en avant », estime Ray Jayawardhana, président de Caltech.
Sa mission de fond va ainsi consister à dresser les premières cartes profondes de l’ensemble du ciel en ultraviolet, une lumière invisible à l’œil nu. Il y parviendra grâce à des capteurs CMOS conçus par Caltech, qui lui offriront un bond de sensibilité inégalé dans ce domaine.
Ses cartes viendront compléter celles de SPHEREx, qui observe en infrarouge, du télescope terrestre Vera C. Rubin, qui scrute l’hémisphère Sud en lumière visible, et du Nancy Grace Roman, tout juste lancé. Ensemble, ils dessineront une carte de l’Univers sur une large part du spectre lumineux.
Tous les événements qu’UVEX va scruter
Mais surtout, UVEX va se spécialiser dans l’observation des étoiles à neutrons, ces cadavres d’étoiles si denses qu’ils concentrent une à deux fois la masse du Soleil dans une boule d’une vingtaine de kilomètres. Quand deux d’entre elles se percutent, elles créent un environnement d’une violence extrême.
Ces fusions sont aujourd’hui détectées grâce aux ondes gravitationnelles. Les scientifiques observent ensuite leurs conséquences en lumière, des rayons gamma aux ondes radio. UVEX ajoutera l’ultraviolet, et pourra pivoter pour regarder l’événement très peu de temps après qu’il s’est produit.
Le télescope s’intéressera aussi aux supernovas, qui marquent la mort des étoiles massives et la naissance d’étoiles à neutrons et de trous noirs. Celles-ci se produisent lorsqu’une étoile massive n’a plus de carburant pour sa fusion nucléaire et ne peut plus résister à sa propre gravité : son cœur s’effondre et ses couches externes sont projetées vers l’extérieur.
Il devrait également nous renseigner sur les étoiles bleues dont les couches externes d’hydrogène ont été arrachées par une étoile compagnon. Car elles offrent aux chercheurs une occasion unique d’étudier l’intérieur des étoiles, habituellement masqué. Enfin, UVEX pourra repérer des millions de petites galaxies proches et faibles, remplies de jeunes étoiles qui émettent une vive lumière ultraviolette.
Elles se trouvent bien plus près de la Voie lactée que celles observées aujourd’hui par le télescope James-Webb. « Chaque fois que l’on regarde le ciel dans une nouvelle longueur d’onde, on apprend quelque chose de nouveau et d’inattendu », précise Kareem El-Badry, professeur associé d’astronomie à Caltech. De quoi nous aider à percer un peu plus les mystères du cosmos.
KDP‑C (Key Decision Point‑C) est une étape formelle du processus de gestion de projets de la NASA qui valide l’engagement de l’agence sur une mission. Elle sert à figer une architecture technique jugée mûre et un budget/planning réalistes, après examen des risques et des marges. Une fois KDP‑C franchi, le projet passe en phase de développement avec des objectifs, coûts et jalons de référence (baseline) beaucoup plus difficiles à modifier. Ce jalon conditionne aussi la contractualisation industrielle et l’enchaînement vers l’intégration et les tests.
L’ultraviolet (UV) met en évidence des phénomènes énergétiques et des populations d’étoiles jeunes et chaudes, souvent moins visibles en lumière optique ou en infrarouge. Observer en UV depuis l’espace est crucial, car l’atmosphère terrestre absorbe une grande partie de ces longueurs d’onde. Une « cartographie profonde » signifie imager très large (tout le ciel) tout en étant sensible à des sources très faibles, ce qui permet des catalogues massifs et homogènes. Ces cartes servent ensuite de référence pour comparer les objets à travers plusieurs bandes (UV, visible, IR) et mieux contraindre leur température, leur activité et leur évolution.
Dans un télescope, la sensibilité dépend notamment de l’efficacité quantique (capacité à convertir les photons en signal) et du bruit de lecture des capteurs. Des CMOS modernes peuvent améliorer le rapport signal/bruit, ce qui aide à détecter des objets plus faibles ou à réduire le temps de pose pour une même qualité d’image. En UV, où le flux de photons peut être faible et où les contraintes instrumentales sont fortes, gagner en efficacité se traduit directement par une meilleure profondeur de cartographie et des mesures plus précises. L’autre atout est la lecture rapide et flexible, utile pour surveiller de larges champs et suivre des phénomènes variables.

articles.title: I’ve already found 17 early Black Friday TV deals worth nabbing: save big on LG, Samsung, Sony and more

Plus, some superb deals on soundbars not to be missed
- Black Friday officially begins November 27
- Some Black Friday TV deals have gone live early
- Prices can fluctuate regularly, and could improve closer to Black Friday
- Soundbars also receive big discounts
If you've been eyeing up a new TV, then the next few weeks could well be your favourite of the year. Yes, it's Black Friday sales time in Australia, and that means many of the best TVs will be seeing their prices slashed at a variety of retailers.
Whether you're after a big-screen OLED TV or a smaller mini-LED model for a bedroom or gaming setup, the Black Friday TV sales often deliver some of the lowest prices of the entire year. I'll be keeping this page updated throughout the shopping period, and will continue tracking prices beyond Cyber Monday to catch any deals that stick around.
Highlights so far include AU$1,464 off the Sony Bravia 8 II; AU$1,864 off the Samsung S95H; and even AU$251 off the Sonos Beam (Gen 2).
I should point out that TV prices can fluctuate throughout the Black Friday sales period, and in previous years I've seen certain sizes discounted one day, and others the next. In short, if you see a price you like on a TV you love, it can pay to take the plunge right away.
And it's not just huge price cuts you should be looking out for. Some Australian retailers also offer bundle deals, allowing you to save even more when you pair a new TV with a soundbar.
Speaking of soundbars, they also receive their fair share of discounts during Black Friday, and you'll find my top recommendations towards the bottom of this page.

Black Friday TV deals 2026 FAQ
When will the best Black Friday TV deals start in 2026?
Black Friday has been officially penned in for Friday November 27 2026. However, as we saw in November 2025, the discounts started to crop up earlier. This varies from retailer to retailer as they try to outdo each other with earlier and earlier sales, but the best deals typically happen between Black Friday and Cyber Monday.
Where are the best places to find Black Friday TV deals?
In Australia, you'll find the best Black Friday TV deals from many of the usual brick and mortar retailers including JB Hi-Fi and The Good Guys, along with several reliable online stores. Discounts will usually consist of hundreds of dollars off the usual RRP, while some models (most often clearance stock from last year) will even get slashed by thousands.
Should I wait until Black Friday for TV deals?
In general, yes. However, there will be other major sales events during the year, including the EOFY sales and Afterpay Day. Both of these can often be good times to look out for TV deals, but from our experience, Black Friday is when we usually see the biggest discounts.
Then there's also Cyber Monday to consider. However, we'd recommend going for the best Black Friday TV deals rather than waiting for Cyber Monday, but if you don't find what you're looking for, it's a great second chance to find a discounted TV.
Essentially, any online store is worth keeping an eye on over Black Friday weekend; after all, it's a sales event dedicated to online shopping.

articles.title: Qui est Colette Kress, qui remplace Jensen Huang à la tête de Nvidia ?
articles.text:
C’est un séisme dans la tech. Le conseil d’administration de Nvidia a annoncé ce jeudi la démission de Jensen Huang de ses postes de président, de PDG et de membre du conseil, avec effet immédiat.
Le cofondateur a donc été poussé vers la sortie après des révélations sur deux liaisons présumées, dont l’une avec une femme soupçonnée d’espionnage pour le compte de la Chine.
Pour le remplacer, le conseil a choisi Colette Kress, la femme qui tient les finances de Nvidia depuis treize ans. Une gestionnaire plutôt qu’une ingénieure, qui a accompagné toute l’explosion de l’entreprise portée par l’IA. Sa mission est toutefois temporaire : selon le communiqué, le conseil a lancé le recrutement d’un PDG permanent et étudiera des candidatures internes comme externes.
Une première en 33 ans
Depuis sa création en 1993, Nvidia n’avait connu qu’un seul patron. Jensen Huang occupait les fonctions de président et de PDG depuis la fondation de l’entreprise. Colette Kress devient donc la première personne après lui à diriger Nvidia, et la première femme, donc.
Dans le même communiqué, le conseil a aussi nommé Harvey C. Jones à un poste qui n’existait pas jusqu’ici : président du conseil d’administration. Selon Harvey Jones, cité dans le communiqué, Colette Kress a contribué à mener Nvidia « à travers une période de croissance extraordinaire ».
Colette Kress n’est pas ingénieure : elle a fait toute sa carrière dans la finance des grands noms de la tech. Selon le document officiel publié lors de son recrutement, elle a d’abord passé huit ans chez Texas Instruments, à divers postes financiers.
Elle rejoint ensuite Microsoft, où elle reste de 1997 à 2010. À partir de 2006, elle y est directrice financière de la division Serveurs et Outils, responsable de la stratégie financière, de la planification et du reporting. En 2010, elle part chez Cisco, comme vice-présidente et directrice financière d’une de ses branches. Côté formation, elle est diplômée en finance de l’université de l’Arizona et titulaire d’un MBA de la Southern Methodist University, au Texas.
La gardienne des comptes du boom de l’IA
Colette Kress arrive chez Nvidia en septembre 2013, à 46 ans, comme vice-présidente exécutive et directrice financière. Son recrutement met fin à plus de deux ans de recherche : le poste était occupé par intérim depuis le départ de son prédécesseur en 2011. À l’époque, Nvidia vend surtout des cartes graphiques pour PC.
En treize ans, elle a tenu les finances pendant toute la mue de l’entreprise en géant des puces pour l’IA. Sur l’exercice 2025 (février 2024 à janvier 2025), le chiffre d’affaires de Nvidia a bondi de 114 %, à 130,5 milliards de dollars, selon les résultats officiels publiés par l’entreprise.
Cette ascension l’a aussi enrichie. Sa participation dans Nvidia valait 977 millions de dollars au 31 octobre 2026, selon Zonebourse.
Un intérim, pas (encore) une succession
Colette Kress ne remplace pas tout à fait Jensen Huang. Le communiqué la présente comme PDG par intérim et directrice financière : elle cumule les deux casquettes. Elle y promet de bâtir sur « les fondations extraordinaires » posées par Jensen Huang en 33 ans. « Nous continuerons à développer les technologies qui ont fait de NVIDIA un leader du calcul accéléré et de l’IA, et à saisir les opportunités qui s’offrent à nous. Notre priorité demeure le service à nos clients, partenaires, développeurs et actionnaires. », a-t-elle également assuré.
« Colette a contribué à guider NVIDIA à travers une période de croissance exceptionnelle et possède une connaissance approfondie de notre activité, de nos clients, de nos opérations et de notre situation financière », a déclaré Harvey Jones, président du conseil d’administration de NVIDIA.
La recherche d’un patron permanent a déjà commencé. Nvidia travaille avec un cabinet de recrutement extérieur, selon Bloomberg. Un défi de taille : avant cette crise, le conseil d’administration n’avait pas de plan de succession clair. Reste à savoir si Colette Kress sera candidate au poste.

articles.title: Jensen Huang dimite como CEO y Nvidia anuncia su plan de transición para frenar la sangría en bolsa
articles.text:
Tras los escándalos extramatrimoniales y sospechas de espionaje, Jensen Huang ha dimitido como presidente, director ejecutivo y miembro del consejo de Nvidia, con efecto inmediato, según anunciado Nvidia en un comunicado.
Colette Kress, actual directora financiera de la compañía, pasará a ocupar el puesto de CEO interina y mantendrá sus tareas de finanzas hasta que haya un relevo definitivo para Huang. El consejo busca candidatos de dentro y de fuera de la empresa.
Dos relaciones bajo la lupa. El inicio de la caída Huang al frente de Nvidia comenzó tras la exclusiva de The New York Times en la que se contaba que los servicios de inteligencia de EEUU habían detectado un vínculo estrecho entre Huang y Alice Huang, compradora de los chips que fabrica Nvidia y ciudadana china.
Alice Huang llegó a ser directiva de Megaspeed, una empresa de centros de datos con sede en Singapur que ha comprado más de 4.800 millones de dólares en chips desde junio de 2024, y de la que se sospecha que podría haber tenido acceso a información sensible de Nvidia y haber espiado para China. El gobierno de Xi Jimping niega las acusaciones de espionaje.
El domingo, el consejo abrió una investigación y Huang admitió una infidelidad a su esposa, con quien lleva casado 41 años. El problema se complicó cuando salió a la luz una segunda relación, con Kimberly Powell, de 48 años, vicepresidenta que depende directamente de él. Tras esa noticia, el consejo empezó a debatir su futuro.
El desplome en bolsa. En solo cuatro días, la cotización de las acciones de Nvidia han caído casi un 8%. Después de las nuevas informaciones, se produjo otro descalabro en el que se dejaron otro 8% fuera del horario normal de Wall Street. Tras conocerse su dimisión, las acciones han vuelto a caer.
El viernes cerró en algo más de 188 dólares. Cuando abran los mercados en Wall Street podría abrir por debajo de los 158 dólares. En ese caso, la empresa pasaría de valer 4,5 billones de dólares a 3,8 billones, provocando un serio quebranto en las cuentas de los inversores.
Según recogía la BBC, Baird y Bernstein Research rebajaron sus recomendaciones sobre las acciones de Nvidia, y Morgan Stanley lo sacó de su lista Top Pick. Es un gesto poco habitual, porque Wall Street llevaba más de cuatro años casi unida en su apoyo. Aun así, la mayoría de las casas de inversión sigue recomendando comprar.
Un lío político y sin relevo para Huang. Según recogía Reuters, el senador republicano Kevin Cramer pidió públicamente que Huang dejara su cargo al frente de Nvidia. En el Congreso también apareció la amenaza de una citación judicial para obligarle a dar explicaciones por saltarse las restricciones comerciales sobre la venta de chips a China.
Huang posee cerca del 3,6% de las acciones y la empresa no tenía un sucesor evidente. En el comunicado publicado por Nvidia, Kress ha intentado transmitir calma a sus inversores: "La fortaleza de Nvidia siempre ha residido en su gente, y junto con nuestro equipo directivo, me comprometo a seguir construyendo sobre la extraordinaria base que Jensen creó durante los últimos 33 años", escribió la ya nueva CEO de Nvidia.
Como colofón a todo el sainete protagonizado por Huang, Nvidia presentará sus resultados del tercer trimestre el 17 de noviembre, como estaba previsto. Sin duda será una presentación en la que deberán darse muchas explicaciones.

articles.title: Police dismantle Gootloader, CastleRAT, StealC malware infrastructure
articles.text:
Europol and law enforcement partners from nine countries have seized hundreds of servers and domains used by the Gootloader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware operations.
Gootloader is a malware loader active since 2020, StealC is an infostealer that helps exfiltrate credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, and other sensitive information from victims' devices, and CastleRAT is a remote access trojan that surfaced last year. All three malware families have been used by various cybercriminal operations, including ransomware gangs.
The joint action is part of Operation Endgame, an international law enforcement effort targeting cybercrime and "cybercrime-as-a-service" networks. This stage of Operation Endgame included law enforcement agencies from Bulgaria, Canada, Denmark, Germany, Moldova, the Netherlands, Poland, the United Kingdom, and the United States, with Europol and Eurojust coordinating the effort.
Together with private partners who helped identify, take down, seize, and block infrastructure tied to the three malware operations, the authorities seized 257 domains and 235 servers.
They also identified 6.4 million victim datasets on the targeted criminal infrastructure, stolen from malware-infected systems for use in other cyberattacks, including ransomware breaches.
"During the action, over 6 million victim credentials were identified in the criminal infrastructure owned by the cybercriminals and seized by the authorities during this week. The suspects were using these credentials, stolen from the victims after they infected them, to sell them and later be used for other cyber-attacks such as ransomware," Europol said.
"Victim data will be made available via platforms HaveIBeenPwned, DIVD, CheckjeHack, NoMoreLeaks, Sekoia, The Shadowserver Foundation, and NL-NCSC, alerting victims of stolen credentials caused by the CastleRAT malware. WordPress users are urged to update credentials, enable multi-factor authentication, and patch vulnerabilities."
Previous Operation Endgame actions
In June, as part of the same operation, law enforcement agencies also cleaned nearly 15,000 malware-infected WordPress websites and seized 106 servers used by the SocGholish botnet and the Evil Corp Russian cybercrime group.
Later that month, Operation Endgame disrupted malicious infrastructure used by the Amadey and StealC malware operations, taking down 326 servers and 142 domains and recovering around 27 million credentials stolen from more than 385,000 compromised systems.
One year ago, the same joint law enforcement action also took down over 1,000 servers used by the Rhadamanthys, VenomRAT, and Elysium botnet malware operations.
Previously, Operation Endgame targeted Smokeloader botnet customers and servers, ransomware infrastructure, the AVCheck site, and various other major malware operations, including DanaBot, IcedID, Pikabot, Trickbot, Smokeloader, Bumblebee, and SystemBC.

articles.title: Global by default, local by design: What Indian founders learned about scaling across borders
articles.text:
Stripe
View Brand Publisher
Global by default, local by design: What Indian founders learned about scaling across borders
At a Stripe roundtable at TechSparks 2026, leaders from edtech, commerce, fintech, and consumer hardware shared how to pick markets, localize smartly, and build the payments and compliance spine that makes expansion repeatable
For many Indian businesses, going global does not begin with a grand strategy. It begins with a signup from a shopper in Texas, a lead from Dubai that lands at 2 a.m., or a customer in London who wants to pay in pounds. The first sale feels like proof. The harder question is whether the next market will follow the same path or demand starting from scratch. That question anchored a roundtable by Stripe on building a repeatable global growth playbook at TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s flagship event.
The table brought together leaders from organisations like Xoxoday, upGrad, Dodo Payments, Bhanzu, Borderless Access, Cuemath, FreshtoHome, Codingal, Codeyoung and Ultrahuman.
Representing the host was Manish Maheshwari, Managing Director, India, Stripe. The conversation was moderated by Madanmohan Rao, Research Director, YourStory.
Prove demand before crossing borders
The discussion opened with a shared instinct: start small and start by listening. Companies weigh customer acquisition cost, lifetime value, and operational scalability, along with whether reliable payment rails and local talent exist. One approach was to collect leads and call them before a product even existed, since online research rarely surfaces micro-level insight. A market that keeps asking for the same thing earns a place on the roadmap, while a single large client in one location is better treated as a customization. The first paying customer proves little, while repeat purchases and low dispute rates tell the real story.
Localize the edges, standardize the core
Anything that touches the end user, such as catalogs, curriculum and preferred payment modes like ACH in the United States or direct debit in the United Kingdom, can flex by market. Anything that moves money, including core fraud rules, stays standard. Legal and regulatory needs come first, followed by customer-specific requests, whether that means a bright red palette in China or tax-inclusive pricing in India. Pricing deserves equal care, as carrying Indian price points into the US took one team a long time to correct. Partnerships help too. In the UAE, a government tie-up won acceptance for credentials, while local payment partners improved affordability and brought in new customers.
Treat payments as a growth lever
Maheshwari offered a caution that resonated across the table: “Your payment failure or your checkout failure can be mistaken as a demand failure.”
Pricing in local currency is a big part of the fix, with Stripe’s data showing that 76% of customers prefer to pay in their own currency. Local payment methods and installments for large purchases help, as does a stack that is standard at the core but adaptable by country. Fraud control is a balancing act, because tightening rules too far turns away genuine buyers. Tracking chargebacks, refunds and failure rates by country also helps teams find leaks, such as overseas customers whose one-time passwords never arrived under Indian authentication rules.
Make compliance part of the product
Revenue brings obligations. US states set their own tax thresholds, Europe and India have data rules, and even text messaging follows different regulations in each country. Notices and penalties tend to arrive just as growth does, and one founder recalled how an India-only business shrank overnight after a regulatory shock. Stripe’s view was that a global stack chosen on day one costs less, since “going back and fixing it is far more expensive”.
Tools such as Stripe Atlas, helps businesses create a US entity,, set up local banking, accept payments and raise funds early in their journey, before international growth makes those decisions harder to revisit.
Let AI speed things up, with guardrails
AI is already compressing timelines. Content localization has become nearly 4X faster, with human verification and evaluation layers still in place, and engineers increasingly act as reviewers of AI-written code. Sales bots handle lead qualification and reminders across time zones, lifting funnel performance by an estimated 20-25%. Speed, however, raises questions of stability, safety and security, and cybersecurity was flagged as the topic most missing from the conversation.
Plant the flag where the pull is
Being global by default does not mean opening offices everywhere. One team that localized its curriculum and hired instructors and sales staff in Japan saw momentum fade within three months, because the effort amounted to a separate business. The lesson was to scale where strengths already exist, go deep, and then widen.
Audiences beyond the Indian diaspora need a different approach altogether, with local hiring, community events and even offline centers in the US to feel like a native brand.
A playbook still taking shape
Taken together, the repeatable playbook is clear: validate repeat demand, keep the money-moving core standard, localize what customers see, build finance and compliance muscle early, and enter markets where pull already exists.
Gaps remain. Paying individuals abroad, such as teachers, from an Indian entity is still expensive, and the infrastructure for it is thin.
As the evening closed, the shared belief was that the best learning comes from peers who work in the field. For Indian businesses, going global market by market is less a leap than a discipline, built one repeatable decision at a time.

articles.title: Una comunidad exige a un propietario que quite el cañizo del muro de separación con el vecino: la justicia dice que se deja porque no afecta a los elementos comunes ni a la estética de la fachada
articles.text:
Instalar un cañizo para separar tu casa de la del vecino se puede convertir en un problema con la comunidad de propietarios. Justo eso es lo que vivió un vecino de Las Palmas de Gran Canaria al que la junta exigió retirar el cañizo que había colocado en el muro de separación porque, a su juicio, afectaba a la estética del edificio. Sin embargo, el propietario decidió acudir a la justicia y terminó saliéndose con la suya al lograr que se anulara el acuerdo.
Como recoge NoticiasTrabajo en su información sobre el conflicto vecinal, la comunidad había aprobado un requerimiento para que el hombre retirara la instalación en un plazo de 2 meses. Tras advertirle que podrían tomar medidas judiciales si no lo hacía, el vecino impugnó la decisión al considerar que le causaba un perjuicio injustificado. ¿Lo mejor para él? El Juzgado de Primera Instancia número 16 de Las Palmas de Gran Canaria le dio la razón y el acuerdo se declaró nulo.
Cuando la comunidad recurrió la decisión, la Audiencia Provincial de Las Palmas confirmó la decisión del juzgado. El cañizo estaba instalado en un muro interior de separación entre viviendas y, como no afectaba a la fachada del edificio, nunca alteró la configuración ni entraba en conflicto con los elementos comunes. Así, el argumento de que perjudicaba la estética no fue suficiente para obligar al propietario a retirarlo.
En este punto entra en juego el artículo 7 de la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal, que permite realizar modificaciones dentro de una propiedad privada siempre que no se altere la seguridad, la estructura general o el estado exterior del edificio, ni se perjudiquen los derechos de otros propietarios. Por eso, no todas las instalaciones que desagradan a la comunidad pueden prohibirse, ya que también hay que comprobar dónde se encuentran y si realmente incumplen alguna de estas limitaciones.
A todo esto debemos sumar que el artículo 18 de la misma ley permite impugnar determinados acuerdos comunitarios ante los tribunales. En este caso, la Audiencia desestimó el recurso de la comunidad y mantuvo la nulidad del requerimiento, por lo que el propietario pudo conservar el cañizo. Eso sí, la sentencia no era firme cuando se publicó la noticia y todavía cabía recurrir ante el Tribunal Supremo si se cumplían los requisitos legales.

articles.title: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia — who is Colette Kress, his interim replacement? | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The Nvidia Board of Directors announced on Thursday morning that the company’s co-founder and CEO of 33 years, Jensen Huang, has resigned as president, CEO, and member of the board, effective immediately.
This is a shocking twist for one of the most valuable companies in the world, which designs the chips that make the AI boom possible. Few people would have predicted this turn of events even just a week ago, as Huang has been so central to Nvidia throughout the company’s existence that he never even established a succession plan. But Huang has now been ousted after reports that he had affairs with both an alleged Chinese spy and one of his direct reports at Nvidia.
While the company conducts a more thorough search for Huang’s successor, Nvidia CFO and Executive Vice President Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO. But beyond her name and job title, what do we know about the person who will now lead a company worth about $3.8 trillion?
According to Nvidia’s website, Kress has worked at the company since September 2013. Before that, she spent three years as an SVP and CFO of Cisco’s Business Technology Operations Finance organization. She also worked at Microsoft for 13 years, where she spent four years as CFO of the Server and Tools division. She holds a finance degree from the University of Arizona and an MBA from Southern Methodist University.
The California-based 59-year-old has a very limited social media presence — on Linkedin, she has commented some well wishes on former colleagues’ posts about their retirement. But as CFO, she’s been a regular presence on Nvidia’s earnings calls, making her a familiar figure for analysts covering the company.
According to Forbes’ list of America’s Richest Self-Made Women, Kress’ net worth is estimated to be about $1.2 billion. Her Forbes profile adds that she initially joined Nvidia in part because her two sons endorsed the company for its role in the video game industry, which it was best known for at the time.
“Nvidias strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” Kress said in a statement. “We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”
Nvidia is slated to report its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, when we will likely hear more from Kress about her plans for the company’s immediate future.

articles.title: Microsoft veut vous laisser désactiver les réponses IA dans Bing
articles.text:
Microsoft est sur le point de donner une véritable leçon à Google. La firme de Redmond vient en effet d’annoncer dans un billet de blog qu’elle allait permettre aux utilisateurs de son moteur de recherche Bing de désactiver les réponses générées par l’intelligence artificielle.
Microsoft propose une extension pour donner le choix aux utilisateurs
Avec cette annonce, la firme de Redmond va à contre-courant de ce qui se fait actuellement, notamment du côté de Google qui a activé ses AI Overview dans les résultats de recherche, sans offrir d’option pour les désactiver.
« En matière d’IA, nous pensons que les utilisateurs de Bing devraient avoir le choix dans la manière dont ils effectuent leurs recherches. C’est pourquoi Bing propose des expériences de recherche à la fois basées sur l’IA et traditionnelles, y compris une extension de navigateur qui permet aux utilisateurs de désactiver facilement les fonctionnalités d’IA dans Bing » a ainsi expliqué Microsoft.
Microsoft, qui explique ainsi que ses recherches ont montré que les utilisateurs veulent avoir la possibilité de choisir si l’IA doit être impliquée dans chacune de leurs sessions de recherche, a ainsi développé une extension de navigateur permettant de désactiver à la volée les réponses générées par l’IA.
Proposée gratuitement sur Google Chrome et Microsoft Edge, l’extension Microsoft Bing AI Search Choice, c’est son nom, donne accès à un simple bouton qui permet de basculer d’une recherche avec des réponses IA à une recherche classique « à l’ancienne », dans son moteur de recherche Bing. Attention toutefois, l’installation de l’extension sur votre navigateur définit Bing en tant que moteur de recherche par défaut. Si l’initiative est à saluer, on peut se demander pourquoi la firme de Redmond n’a pas intégré directement l’option dans son navigateur Microsoft Edge.
Les utilisateurs pourront donc choisir d’activer les réponses IA s’ils cherchent à obtenir des résumés rapides, ou de les désactiver s’ils préfèrent privilégier des résultats de recherche classiques.
Des opérateurs de recherche pour s’affranchir de l’IA
Une bonne nouvelle n’arrivant jamais seule, Microsoft a par ailleurs indiqué que vous pouvez à présent utiliser un opérateur à ajouter dans vos requêtes pour esquiver les réponses générées par l’IA sans avoir à installer la moindre extension.
En rajoutant simplement « -ai » après une requête lancée dans Bing, le moteur de recherche n’affichera aucune réponse générée par l’intelligence artificielle. À noter que l’astuce n’est pas réservée qu’à Bing. Si vous utilisez le moteur de recherche de Google, l’ajout de la mention -ai après une requête vous permettra également de vous affranchir des résultats AI Overviews de la firme de Mountain View.

Black Friday 2026 - La batterie externe Anker Zolo 20 000 mAh est à 29,99 € (-35 %)
Deux câbles USB-C intégrés, 45 W de puissance et 20 000 mAh : la batterie externe Anker Zolo passe à 29,99 € chez Amazon, soit 16 € sous son prix conseillé.
Vendue par AnkerDirect FR et expédiée par Amazon, cette batterie noire affiche 29,99 € contre 45,99 € pour le prix conseillé, soit une remise de 35 % dans le cadre des offres pré-Black Friday d'Amazon. C'est aussi 6 € de moins que son plus bas prix des 30 derniers jours (35,99 €).
Deux câbles intégrés et 45 W
Cette batterie de 20 000 mAh intègre deux câbles USB-C, testés pour résister à plus de 10 000 torsions, et ajoute un port USB-C et un port USB-A : elle peut recharger quatre appareils à la fois.
Elle délivre jusqu'à 45 W et prend en charge la charge Super Fast de Samsung ainsi que la charge à 40 W des iPhone 17.

C'est un modèle très populaire : il est noté 4,5/5 par plus de 17 000 acheteurs, et Amazon indique plus de 300 achats le mois dernier.

articles.title: EU's proposed Digital Fairness Act takes aim at Duolingo streaks, autoplay, and manipulative apps
articles.text:
In brief: Plenty of apps work hard to retain users, whether it's a pop-up claiming only two items are left or even something like a Duolingo streak you're scared to break. On Wednesday, the European Commission proposed a Digital Fairness Act that would outlaw many of those manipulative "dark patterns." Surprisingly, it doesn't stop at protecting kids. Adults would get to switch off addictive features like autoplay and streaks, too.
That off switch could reach well beyond social media. As WIRED notes, it would cover the daily streaks in apps like Strava and Duolingo. That could sting, since streaks are how those apps keep people coming back. Duolingo once wrote that a new streak animation alone made brand-new learners 1.7% more likely to stick around for a week.
Until now, Brussels could only really chase these designs on online platforms through the Digital Services Act. Last Friday, it accused TikTok of trapping users in "rabbit holes" through its For You feed, months after flagging the app's infinite scroll and autoplay. Its proposed Kids Act targets addictive design too, but only for children.
Beyond addictive features, the new act also names specific dark patterns. Fake claims that a product is almost sold out would be banned, along with opt-out buttons worded to make you feel bad for declining.
Subscriptions get a cleanup as well. Free trials couldn't roll into a paid plan without your active approval. Canceling one would have to be easy, too. If something still goes wrong, you'd have the right to speak to an actual human customer service representative.
Ticketmaster users won't get nearly as much relief. Despite years of fury over surge-priced concert tickets, the act doesn't ban dynamic pricing outright. Instead, officials settled on transparency, as The Irish Times reports. So people waiting in a virtual queue would see the current price and the highest it could climb, in real time.
To make all this stick, the Commission wants the power to investigate large cross-border cases itself. In those instances, fines could reach 6% of global annual turnover. None of it is law yet, though. The European Parliament and member states still have to agree on the text, and the rules would only apply a year after the law enters into force.
Meanwhile, Google, Meta, and TikTok sued last week to block a California law will ban addictive feeds, endless scrolling, and autoplay starting in January. That one only covers kids under 16. Europe's version would hand the same off switch to adults as well.

articles.title: Chrome, Firefox Updates Patch Over 180 Vulnerabilities
articles.text:
Google and Mozilla have released fresh Chrome and Firefox security updates that resolve more than 180 vulnerabilities.
The Chrome refresh fixes 83 security defects, including five critical-severity use-after-free issues in ServiceWorker, CSS, Layout, Skia, and Accessibility.
All the remaining 78 bugs are high-severity weaknesses, mostly use-after-free (24), out-of-bounds read/write (10), type confusion (9), uninitialized resource (9), and incorrect/missing authorization (8).
Google discovered 52 of the vulnerabilities internally, and Anthropic and OpenAI researchers reported 18 more. No monetary reward will be handed out for any of these flaws.
The internet giant has paid a $4,000 bug bounty reward for a high-severity use-after-free in V8, but has not determined the amounts to be handed out for the remaining 12 externally reported flaws.
The latest Chrome iteration is now rolling out as versions 157.0.8103.78/.79 for Windows and macOS, and as version 157.0.8103.78 for Linux.
Firefox 160 arrived this week with patches for 99 vulnerabilities, including 57 high-severity security weaknesses.
Most of the flaws are use-after-free, incorrect boundary, and sandbox escape issues. The browser refresh also resolved invalid pointer, privilege escalation, information disclosure, and same-origin policy bypass bugs.
Mozilla included patches for most of these security defects in Thunderbird 160, which landed this week with 103 fixes. Thunderbird 153.7, Firefox ESR 153.7, and Firefox ESR 115.45 also rolled out with dozens of vulnerability patches.
Google and Mozilla make no mention of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild.

articles.title: LinkedIn Replaces Argo CD with a Custom GitOps Engine for Kubernetes Deployments
articles.text:
In a recent post, LinkedIn revealed it has replaced Argo CD with its own GitOps engine. This new system deploys applications across over 250 Kubernetes clusters. It supports more than 4,000 services and manages over 100,000 deployments each week. According to a post, deployment infrastructure failures fell from 925 to 63 despite a 3.7x increase in deployment volume. The median time to detect and conclude a failed deployment dropped from 16.1 to 2.45 minutes.
LinkedIn started with one Argo CD instance per cluster, a topology it chose because Argo CD already managed its cluster add-ons that way. Clusters run up to 5,000 nodes each. A central deployment orchestrator spawned an ephemeral pod per deployment, with Argo CD hidden behind it. The team lists seven problems that emerged at scale. Argo CD doesn't have an observedGeneration, so you can't link sync and health status to a specific deployment. LinkedIn created a Lua health check that uses a tracking annotation to address this. A Synced and Healthy application could also resolve to an unintended revision when stale repo-server cache entries were used.
Two of the issues were architectural. Argo CD maintains one watch per group-version-resource across Applications. LinkedIn’s clusters have low resource-type diversity. This means etcd churn from one app can slow syncs for all apps. In one test, sync took under 3 minutes on a cluster with 60,000 pods and over 10 minutes with more than 80,000. The second was server-side-apply PATCH. Kubernetes truncates managedFields once an object has had more than 10 distinct field managers, and the API server then forgets who owns a field. In LinkedIn's AI workloads, which run multiple containers per Pod, a container removed from a manifest could therefore survive on the live Pod. The team had pruning disabled because destructive operations in production require approval. The remaining problems were CRD schema changes that required controller restarts across the fleet. Some OutOfSync states did not reflect real drift. Error messages were buried in boilerplate.
LinkedIn evaluated Flux but found it shared the same controller paradigm, so it built the engine as a library. Each deployment runs in its pod, with no shared controller state. Updates use PUT for full replacements, not PATCH. They retry on resourceVersion conflicts with exponential backoff. A 3-way diff across the live object, the previously deployed manifest, and the newly rendered manifest detects drift, and genuine drift fails the deployment. The same pod then watches the object's status until it converges or times out, and the API server unwraps errors for the user. Objects missing from the rendered manifest become deletion candidates, subject to delete protection, and convergence logic for LinkedIn's CRDs is built in.
The comparison uses the same calendar month a year apart. The migration ran from July 2025 to April 2026, which makes May 2026 the first clean post-migration month. The infra failure count covers only failures caused by the deployment system and excludes drift errors, since the two systems define drift differently. LinkedIn states that the improvement isn't solely due to the new engine. The orchestrator's error classification and reliability also got better during this time. The median duration for successful deployments is similar for both systems. However, the mean and tail have improved. The team attributes this to a namespace-scoped informer cache.
The engine is internal, and no open-source release is mentioned. Argo CD remains in use at LinkedIn for cluster add-ons and system services. The team had also found that maintaining 200+ Argo CD instances made each upgrade a multi-week project.
Teams running Argo CD at scale can check two things without a rewrite. Count the field managers on long-lived objects, since managedFields truncation can leave orphaned containers that produce no error. Then check whether sync latency tracks total pod count on shared clusters, which points to watch contention. LinkedIn concludes that the build-or-extend decision relies on the operational model. They say that per-deployment isolation, not controller tuning, allows the system to scale with compute.
LinkedIn is not the only large operator to build deployment logic around Kubernetes rather than adopt a general-purpose GitOps controller. Uber’s Up platform assigns each deployment to a dedicated controller. This is the Uber Deployment Controller. It translates the intent into Kubernetes primitives and sends status updates. This helps the workflow move forward. Uber keeps a long-running controller, while LinkedIn runs one ephemeral pod per deployment with no shared controller state.
Airbnb went further back and built its own tooling years earlier. In a talk at QCon London 2019 on InfoQ, infrastructure engineer Melanie Cebula introduced kube-gen. This internal framework creates Kubernetes configuration from one versioned project file. It also includes a deploy tool that applies or replaces objects and restarts pods, so changes take effect right away. Airbnb's deploy tool also returns an atomic success or failure, and a container that restarts for 30 seconds at the start of a rollout counts as a failed deploy. Airbnb was then at roughly 125,000 production deploys a year.

articles.title: Microsoft Outlook is down
articles.text:
Over the last hour or so, reports have come in from around the world that people can’t access their Outlook email, either through the web or apps. Microsoft has acknowledged the issue from its Microsoft 365 Status account, saying that “We’ve determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors.”
Microsoft Outlook is down
Microsoft 365 issues are cutting people off from their email right now.
There were also some reports of problems with Teams, but some of the people reporting issues say Teams is still working now.
Now, as of 3:30PM ET, Microsoft says:
While we haven’t identified any recent changes that correlate with the start of impact, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component on the affected servers that’s responsible for processing them.
We’re deploying a targeted change to bypass this component on a subset of servers to validate whether this restores availability, and we’ve taken steps to prevent additional servers from being removed from service while we work to return the affected servers to service. We’re also investigating why affected servers are experiencing elevated processor usage while handling requests.
But it’s still unclear how long it will take before access is restored, or if that will fix all of the issues people are seeing. On DownDetector, reports of issues with Outlook started to spike just before 1PM ET, and they have not completely gone away yet. It’s also probably not the best sign that we’re struggling to consistently load Microsoft’s own status pages to check on progress. If there are any more details, we will update this article.
Update, 3:42PM ET: Added latest status update from Microsoft.

articles.title: Designing Edge AI SoCs At Near-Threshold: Why Foundation IP Can Help You Break Down The Power Wall
articles.text:
Traditional voltage scaling is no longer sufficient to deliver real-time performance within tight energy and thermal limits.
Lowering operating voltage is a key to SoC power optimization. In advanced FinFET processes at ~0.4–0.5V, it can also start to become a design risk. As edge AI pushes inference closer to endpoints, edge-AI SoCs must deliver real-time performance within tight energy and thermal limits. Traditional voltage scaling is no longer sufficient.
SoC designs are shifting towards much more extensive use of near-threshold operation to achieve step-function improvements in performance per watt. But this shift fundamentally changes how chips behave: delays increase non-linearly, variability grows significantly, and underpinning predictable operation becomes a critical enabler to minimizing power.
Design success in this operating regime depends heavily on the underlying quality, modeling accuracy, and integration of Foundation IP with EDA flows and silicon validation. Embedded memories, logic libraries, and I/Os must be selected carefully and any targeted optimization carried out and fully validated at an early stage—not treated as a possible downstream option.
Every SoC designer understands that lowering supply voltage reduces energy—but at near threshold voltages, it changes transistor behavior and challenges traditional design assumptions.
Fig. 1: Energy efficiency improves at lower voltage, but delay and variability increase sharply near threshold.
As shown in Figure 1, reducing voltage lowers energy per operation, but comes with significant trade-offs: delay grows rapidly, variability increases, and noise margins shrink.
In this regime:
Voltage scaling is no longer an isolated optimization—it introduces tightly coupled challenges across the entire design stack.
Meeting power targets at ultra-low voltage is not sufficient; designs must achieve this predictably and without introducing additional silicon risk. This can be where Foundation IP moves from an incidental enabler to a significant part of the design success. The quality of logic libraries, memory compilers, and I/Os can directly determine the robustness of design closure and silicon outcomes.
A unified, silicon-proven Foundation IP platform—tightly coupled with EDA flows, built with the most accurate modelling and characterization methodologies and meticulously validated on silicon —provides the accuracy and consistency needed to enable PPA winning designs at ultra-low voltages, with reliable behavior from early design through signoff.
Memory is a dominant contributor to area and power—and often determines the system’s minimum operating voltage (Vmin) if not architecturally decoupled. This is addressed through flexible architectures:
Fig. 2: Dual-rail memory architecture decouples logic and memory VDD, validated at ISSCC 2025 with a 38 Mb/mm² SRAM at 380/540 mV in 3nm FinFET.
Different AI subsystems require different memory strategies: MAC tiles benefit from small, distributed SRAM blocks; activation units from ULP RFs with wide data-paths; and shared system buffers from high-bandwidth AXI interfaces.
Logic libraries must be engineered specifically with low-voltage operation in mind:
This modeling accuracy is essential to avoid unexpected surprises during low voltage signoff or timing failures on silicon.
In many designs, I/O domains define system-level Vmin. If I/O cannot operate reliably at reduced voltages, it blocks near-threshold logic benefits regardless of how well the core is optimized.
The portfolio spans control interfaces (GPIO, I3C/I2C, SWI3S), high-speed data links (LVDS, RGMII), clock and reference inputs, storage interfaces (SD/eMMC), test I/O, and 2.5D/3D integration I/O for chiplet-based systems—each validated for consistent operation across varying supply levels.
Achieving predictable, optimized operation at ~0.4–0.5V requires tight alignment across Foundation IP, EDA tools, modeling, and silicon validation.
Fig. 3: A closed-loop methodology aligns Foundation IP, tools, and silicon feedback to ensure optimized low-voltage design.
As shown in Figure 3, optimal low-voltage design depends on an iterative, closed-loop enablement process:
Synopsys Application Engineers bridge the gap between IP/EDA R&D experts and SoC designers during the customer design engagement, ensuring that the features are fully exploited and technologies are optimally deployed. The co-optimization of tools and IP keeps device physics, modeling assumptions, and silicon outcomes tightly coupled—transforming near-threshold design into a low risk, production-ready solution.
A power-sensitive AI networking SoC targeting high volumes in an advanced technology node, using near-threshold design, needed expert enablement. Supporting extremely low operating voltages for a design executed under a very compressed schedule. The Foundation IP solution included specially tuned low-voltage logic cells, custom level shifters and a custom dual-rail memory compiler, with specifically targeted PVT corner set all specifically selected to achieve the optimum design trade-offs for the best power efficiency through near-threshold signoff.
The results:
The key outcome: predictable execution without schedule or silicon risk.
Synopsys provides comprehensive documentation, design reviews, PPA tuning sessions, and direct application engineering engagement. DTCO and PPA exploration help customers select optimal IP configurations, while custom characterization services extend the platform for specialized requirements.
As edge AI workloads proliferate, supporting near-threshold operation is becoming a central requirement to enable power-optimized SoC design. Synopsys Foundation IP solutions—logic, memory, and I/O—deliver the architectural rigor, modeling accuracy, and rigorous silicon validation this regime demands. A broad portfolio, with extensive IP sets implemented with design consistency and supporting wide voltage ranges, simplifies IP reuse, enabling easier product migration across process generations and foundries.
Engage Synopsys early to define optimal voltage targets, select the right Foundation IP configurations, and establish a low-voltage-ready methodology tailored to your product goals. The power wall is real—but it’s not insurmountable.
