articles.title: Plus besoin de chercher vos clés : Google Wallet ouvre votre porte d'entrée tout seul
articles.text:
Google Wallet pourra bientôt stocker la clé numérique de votre porte d’entrée, grâce au standard Aliro.
Google ne manque pas d'idées pour perfectionner son portefeuille numérique. Le géant a récemment développé une couche de sécurité supplémentaire pour les paiements sans contact. Un historique des paiements unifié est aussi en préparation. Désormais, Google s’intéresse aussi à vos serrures.
Google Wallet se substitue à vos clés de maison
Jusqu’ici la clé virtuelle de votre serrure connectée était gérée par Google Home. Mais cela va changer puisqu’il sera bientôt possible d’y avoir accès avec Google Wallet : « configurez votre serrure connectée et gérez l’accès à votre domicile dans l’application Google Home, puis ajoutez d’un simple geste une clé numérique à Google Wallet, au même endroit que vos cartes de paiement et vos titres de transport », explique notamment Google dans un article explicatif.
Pour déverrouiller une porte, il suffira d’approcher le téléphone de la serrure, même si l’écran est verrouillé (il faut toutefois avoir déverrouillé l’appareil dans les heures précédentes). Les plus prudents pourront activer une option qui exigera une authentification par code ou biométrie à chaque passage
À noter, la clé est liée au logement et non à une serrure : un seul badge pourra donc ouvrir toutes les portes compatibles. Tous les membres du foyer pourront également ajouter la clé à leur Wallet et les invités devront se contenter de codes temporaires. Une désactivation automatique est notamment prévue lorsqu’on quitte le foyer dans Google Home.
Google rattrape enfin son retard sur Apple et Samsung
Tout cela est possible grâce à la prise en charge par Google Wallet du standard Aliro. Mais Google a un peu de retard par rapport à la concurrence : la possibilité de déverrouiller des portes avec Apple Wallet existe depuis 2021 et Samsung a lancé sa propre clé numérique pour serrures connectées en mars 2026. Google ayant activement participé au développement d’Aliro, l’ironie est on ne peut plus mordante.
- Un logiciel compatible avec de nombreux appareils connectés Google
- Des outils complets associés à des commandes simples
- Une interface intuitive adaptée à tous les publics
Qu’à cela ne tienne, l’ouverture par contact fonctionne désormais sur tous les smartphones Android dotés du NFC, sous système Android 9 ou supérieur. Le déverrouillage automatique ne sera, lui, proposé que sur les Pixel 10 Pro et suivants : les modèles Fold et XL ne sont malheureusement pas encore inclus. Wear OS ne fait pas non plus partie du lot.
Le catalogue de serrures compatibles est, pour l’instant, assez limité : Google indique, en effet, que seuls les modèles Aqara u400, Schlage Sense Pro et Nuki Keypad 2 NFC sont pris en charge. En plus d’une serrure certifiée Matter et Aliro, un Google Hub compatible avec Thread Border Router est également indispensable.
Le déploiement de cette nouveauté démarre avec le programme Public Preview de Google Home et sera généralisé dans les semaines à venir.

articles.title: World of Warcraft: Forever a un problème avec son économie
articles.text:
World of Warcraft: Forever, sorti le 4 novembre et inclus dans l’abonnement à World of Warcraft, est en train de réconcilier une bonne partie des fans avec le MMORPG culte de Blizzard Entertainment.
Le retour aux sources, motivé par une envie de nostalgie, fonctionne, et Blizzard revendique déjà le plus gros lancement de l’histoire de World of Warcraft, avec un pic de joueurs connectés jamais vu pour un lancement du jeu (sans toutefois publier le moindre chiffre). Néanmoins, cela ne veut pas dire que WoW: Forever est une expérience parfaite. Son économie, notamment, est perfectible.
Contrairement àWorld of Warcraft et World of Warcraft: Classic, World of Warcraft: Forever ne convertit pas les points d’expérience en pièces d’or une fois le niveau maximum atteint. Cette fonctionnalité avait été introduite en 2006, quelques semaines avant la sortie de Burning Crusade (janvier 2007), pour permettre aux joueuses et aux joueurs de remplir leur compte en banque en prévision de la sortie de la première extension.
Cette absence est assumée par Blizzard, qui a quand même déployé un correctif ce mercredi 11 novembre pour répondre aux plaintes.
Pourquoi WoW: Forever ne permet pas de gagner facilement de l’or
Blizzard a fait ce choix pour éviter un phénomène simple : voir des joueuses et des joueurs enchaîner les quêtes et ne les valider qu’une fois atteint le niveau maximum, fixé à 60, pour s’enrichir d’un coup.
« Dans ces conditions, la façon optimale pour les joueurs de monter jusqu’au niveau 60 consistait simplement à tuer des créatures en boucle pour gagner de l’EXP sans jamais rendre de quêtes, ce qui n’est pas une mécanique de jeu que nous souhaitons conserver dans WoW: Forever », justifie ce mardi 10 novembre Kaivax, community manager de Blizzard, sur les forums officiels.
Il reconnaît toutefois que seulement 25 % environ des quêtes du WoW d’origine rapportent directement de l’or. Supprimer la conversion a donc un peu plus pénalisé les revenus des joueurs à l’approche du niveau 60 que ne l’avait prévu le studio.
Seulement, tout a tendance à être très cher dans World of Warcraft: Forever, à commencer par la réinitialisation des talents.
Nova_TANK s’en plaint sur Reddit, dans un sujet publié ce jeudi 12 novembre : « Je suis un nouveau joueur et, à ce titre, je commence tout juste à prendre mes marques avec tout ce qu’il y a dans ce jeu. Je suis niveau 15 et je suis paralysé à l’idée de choisir des points de talent par peur de me tromper. Blizzard a permis aux joueurs de réinitialiser leurs talents (respec) à bas prix pendant la bêta, ce qui était logique, mais pourquoi le coût dans la version finale est-il si élevé avant même d’avoir terminé sa montée en niveau ? Et aussi, 50 pièces d’or pour la double spécialisation au niveau 40 ?! C’est quoi cette histoire ?! »
Blizzard ne s’en cache pas : ces tarifs sont voulus. « Nous ne voulons pas de réinitialisations bon marché », expliquait l’équipe de WoW: Forever à TechRadar en octobre. Elle prévenait que le prix grimperait vite après le lancement et ne baisserait qu’une fois par semaine, pour que les choix de talents aient du poids.
Autrement dit, on a, d’un côté, un jeu dans lequel il est plus difficile d’amasser de l’or et, de l’autre, le sentiment que tout est un peu trop cher. En résulte une économie à la dure, qui soulève quelques critiques. Pour pallier ces soucis, Blizzard a ajouté des récompenses en or supplémentaires pour la plupart des quêtes de niveau 48 et plus, « y compris l’ajout d’or aux quêtes supérieures au niveau 48 qui n’en rapportaient jamais auparavant », avait annoncé Kaivax sur les forums. De quoi rééquilibrer un peu l’économie de World of Warcraft: Forever.
Toutes les quêtes ne sont pas concernées. Les notes de correctif de Blizzard laissent de côté les quêtes qui offrent déjà un objet de valeur, les quêtes que l’on peut répéter et celles qui se bouclent en quelques instants. Quant à la conversion de l’expérience en or au niveau 60, elle ne revient pas : rendre une quête une fois le niveau maximum atteint ne rapporte que l’or qu’elle prévoit déjà.

articles.title: Your Endpoint Management Platform Could Be Your Biggest Security Risk
articles.text:
Author: Gene Moody, Field CTO at Action1
Endpoint management platforms have become essential in modern IT operations and enterprise security. They allow administrators to deploy patches, install software, execute scripts, enforce configurations, and remotely manage thousands of devices from a centralized system.
Without these types of systems, maintaining consistent security across large environments would be extremely difficult and labor-intensive.
However, the administrative authority that makes these platforms valuable also makes them very attractive targets for attackers. An endpoint management platform already has established and approved communication channels, elevated permissions, and trusted relationships with the devices it manages.
Any attacker who gains control of that infrastructure will be able to use those existing capabilities to distribute malware, execute malicious commands, disable security controls, or disrupt operations across an entire organization. All with the same level of authority as the real admin.
The same capabilities that allow an administrator to secure thousands of endpoints can allow an attacker to compromise them.
When trusted management infrastructure is compromised
Recent incidents demonstrate how compromised remote management infrastructure can extend attacks across compromised environments.
In 2026, Huntress documented attackers abusing compromised BeyondTrust Bomgar remote support infrastructure to deploy ransomware and access downstream organizations. In 2025, ransomware operators compromised an MSP's SimpleHelp platform, using its existing management capabilities to access protected systems, steal information, and deploy ransomware.
Similarly, in 2024, attackers exploited ConnectWise ScreenConnect vulnerabilities, with investigators documenting Play ransomware deployment through a compromised MSP instance. And who will forget the 2024 incident abusing Microsoft Intune to remotely wipe hundreds of thousands of corporate devices at Stryker!
In each of these cases, attackers exploited the administrative reach of infrastructure already trusted by the organization. The incidents warn us why protecting systems against the management platforms’ misuse is essential, and why independently verifying sensitive endpoint operations can help limit the consequences of a successful compromise.
These attacks against centralized management and software distribution systems often lead to compromise well beyond the initially compromised infrastructure.
For cloud-hosted platforms, the security of the provider's hosting environment, management services, and software delivery mechanisms becomes particularly important. A compromise there may affect multiple environments simultaneously.
Why traditional security controls have limitations
Multi-factor authentication, role-based access controls, privileged access management, and activity monitoring are bare minimum safeguards. They help restrict administrative access, limit permissions, and identify suspicious behavior.
However, these protections primarily operate within the management platform's security boundaries.
An attacker exploiting a vulnerability in the underlying system, compromising a privileged service, or hijacking an authenticated administrative session may be granted the ability to issue commands that endpoints recognize as legitimate. Because they are impersonating a user, and the restriction is BY user.
Even with strong authentication and carefully configured permissions, the endpoint may have no independent way to determine whether a sensitive instruction was explicitly approved by a legitimate administrator.
This security implication is: high-risk endpoint operations should have authorization that remains verifiable independently of the management platform delivering them!
Adding owner-controlled authorization
Cryptographically verified authorization, independent of anything the platform stores or directly handles, provides the platform a way to establish that independent security boundary.
Under this approach, sensitive endpoint operations require authorization signed using a private cryptographic key controlled only by the legitimate admin. The endpoint independently verifies the signature before executing the protected instruction.
The management platform can continue coordinating and delivering administrative operations, while the authority to approve protected actions remains separately controlled.
An attacker who compromises the management infrastructure cannot simply create valid authorizations without obtaining the owner’s signing key or compromising the verification process.
Action1 implements this approach through Endpoint Takeover Prevention (ETP).
ETP uses customer-controlled cryptographic authorization to protect high-risk operations, including script execution, software deployment, automations, and remote sessions.
Because the private authorization key is maintained independently of Action1's cloud infrastructure, a compromise of the management platform alone does not provide the ability to authorize these protected actions.
Keep Attackers from Taking Over Your Endpoints
Action1's Endpoint Takeover Prevention (ETP) protects high-risk endpoint actions with customer-controlled cryptographic authorization, even if the management platform is compromised.
Take control of endpoint security with Action1. Your first 200 endpoints are free forever.
Start Now
Of course, the effectiveness of this protection depends on secure key management, endpoint integrity, and appropriate configuration of protected operations, but that becomes customer responsibility by becoming customer privilege. It is protected by a key they, and only they control.
Securing an essential part of enterprise IT
Endpoint management platforms will continue to be essential parts of modern infrastructure by maintaining secure and operationally manageable environments. But they now demand particularly strong safeguards against compromise and abuse. We have new threat metrics, we need new defense metrics,
Organizations should re-evaluate how these platforms are secured, how suspicious activity is monitored, and which protections remain effective if management infrastructure is compromised. Practice failure, so when it happens you can understand it, and contain it more effectively.
Customer-controlled cryptographic authorization adds a crucial layer by ensuring that sensitive endpoint operations require independently verifiable approval.

The goal is to preserve the administrative power organizations depend on while keeping the authority to approve its most sensitive uses under the owner’s control.

articles.title: Nvidia s'apprêterait à licencier son PDG Jensen Huang suite à une nouvelle révélation
articles.text:
Le patron de Nvidia Jensen Huang est vraiment dans la tourmente. Depuis quelques jours, le scandale a éclaté : il a eu une liaison extra-conjugale avec une femme d’affaires qui pourrait bien être une espionne chinoise. Nvidia avait ouvert une enquête dans la foulée pour faire la lumière sur cette affaire. Mais l’entreprise semble avoir découvert une deuxième liaison, avec une autre salariée de Nvidia : et pour le conseil d’administration, ça ne passe pas.
Une seconde liaison… avec une autre salariée de Nvidia
C’est le New York Times qui a révélé cette deuxième relation ce 11 novembre, selon les informations de sources anonymes. Jensen Huang aurait entretenu une relation amoureuse avec Kimberly Powell, vice-présidente de Nvidia en charge des soins de santé. Il s’agit donc d’une salariée subordonnée à Jensen Huang. Une source de CNBC ajoute même que cette relation ne serait pas nouvelle : les rumeurs circuleraient depuis longtemps chez Nvidia.
Selon deux employés de Nvidia, Huang et Powell auraient été filmés « en train de se montrer affectueux dans un hôtel de San Jose, en Californie, lors d’une conférence de l’entreprise en mars », écrit le journal. Le service de sécurité du dirigeant aurait aperçu le passant filmant la scène et l’aurait interpellé : un accord de confidentialité lui aurait été proposé.
Cependant, le code de conduite de Nvidia stipule que les employés doivent éviter les situations de conflits entre eux. Le conseil d’administration, mis au courant de cette relation, pourrait s’appuyer sur ce code (qui comprend une lettre de Jensen Huang !) pour licencier Jensen Huang. Contacté, le dirigeant de Nvidia s’est refusé à tout commentaire, comme son entreprise.
Des relations extraconjugales qui coûtent cher à Nvidia
Ces deux polémiques autour de relations extra-conjugales pourraient bien coûter sa place à Jensen Huang. D’autres dirigeants de grandes entreprises se sont déjà fait licencier pour des relations avec des salariés subordonnés par le passé aux États-Unis. Une situation qui pourrait paraître ubuesque pour certains : Huang serait remercié pour sa relation avec Powell, mais pas pour celle avec une femme qui pourrait être une espionne chinoise. Jensen Huang pourrait aussi décider lui-même de démissionner de son poste.
Depuis les révélations autour de la relation de Jensen Huang avec une potentielle espionne, Pékin a totalement démenti ces accusations. Quant au président Donald Trump, il continue de soutenir l’homme d’affaires, ce qui est loin d’être étonnant. Il serait même au courant de cette histoire depuis plusieurs mois. Après la clôture de la bourse de Wall Street ce mercredi 11 novembre, l’action de Nvidia avait chuté de plus de 7 %. Une baisse qui n’est pas la première depuis ces dernières semaines : il y avait déjà eu une baisse de 10% en quelques jours. Et avec une valorisation à plusieurs milliards de dollars, chaque baisse coûte des dizaines, voire des centaines de milliards de dollars à Nvidia.

articles.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 12, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 12, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Thursday, November 12, 2026.
From Jensen Huang's position as the CEO of Nvidia, to why Vikas Malpani thought he would feel like he had won when Quikr bought CommonFloor in 2016, here are the latest developments across sectors.
Featured Stories
Nvidia board to meet to decide CEO Jensen Huang's future at the company
Jensen Huang's position as the CEO of Nvidia looks increasingly uncertain with new details of extra-marital affairs emerging. The board is meeting soon to decide whether to oust him from the company he co-founded in 1993, according to reports.
Reports say Jensen had another extramarital affair with a senior executive of Nvidia. This is in addition to the relationship he had with a Chinese national Alice Huang, who was allegedly recruited as an intelligence asset by the Chinese government.
Latest News
Why CommonFloor’s $200M exit felt like a loss to co-founder Vikas Malpani
Vikas Malpani founded CommonFloor in 2007 with Sumit Jain and Lalit Mangal. In January 2016, Quikr announced it was merging the portal with QuikrHomes, its real estate business. The companies did not disclose the financial terms. Business Standard reported the deal was worth $200 million, while Malpani put the figure at more than $200 million in his LinkedIn post. All three co-founders left CommonFloor about a year after the acquisition.
The acquisition came as investors were growing wary of startups burning through cash and Indian tech companies were buying smaller rivals to expand their businesses. Quikr struck two deals in 2015 and seven in 2016, according to VCCEdge data. CommonFloor gave it a bigger presence in online property listings, while another purchase that year, Grabhouse, helped it expand into managed rentals. Quikr also bought recruitment portal Hiree and folded it into QuikrJobs.
Funding News
ValueQuest commits Rs 775 Cr to advance India’s defence, manufacturing push
ValueQuest Investment Advisors, a Mumbai-based investment manager, has made a total commitment of Rs 775 crore to three Indian businesses in defence technology, precision engineering, and power infrastructure.
The investment firm announced new investments in Sagar Defence Engineering and Rational Engineers and also added to its earlier investment in TASE Global. The Rs 775 crore is a portfolio commitment, not a single company’s fundraise.
Other News
IIT Madras unveils SEANAV, a real-time digital twin for autonomous ship navigation
Researchers at IIT Madras’s Department of Ocean Engineering have developed SEANAV, a Unity3D-based digital twin that lets autonomous maritime navigation systems be tested and trained in a realistic virtual ocean. It fuses LiDAR, radar and stereo-camera data while modelling noise, delays and poor visibility, and supports multi-agent AI that follows COLREGs in crowded waterways. A Meta Quest interface gives trainees a ship’s-bridge view.
Calibrated on a 320-metre tanker, the platform could cut costly sea trials, improve port safety and lower emissions. Published in an ASME journal, future work targets digital twins of major Indian ports and certified VR pilot training."
Ultraviolette appoints ex-Royal Enfield marketer Abhijit Singh Brar as head of marketing
Ultraviolette has appointed Abhijit Singh Brar as Head of Marketing, tasking him with brand positioning, product launch strategy and demand generation as it widens its portfolio across India and overseas. Brar brings over two decades of experience, including more than eight years at Royal Enfield, where he built the marketing function from scratch and later led international marketing across Europe, the Americas, Australia and Southeast Asia.
He most recently held senior roles at Lodha, and earlier worked at Bacardi and Diageo. CEO Narayan Subramaniam said Brar's ability to build brands at scale will help the company reach new rider segments.
(This article will be updated with the latest news throughout the day.)

articles.title: Allée, portail ou jardin : quelle caméra Reolink en promotion choisir pendant le Black Friday ? — Frandroid
articles.text:
Une allée plongée dans le noir à la nuit tombée. Un garage sans éclairage extérieur. Pourquoi ne pas installer une caméra équipée d’un projecteur ? Pour surveiller un portail un peu éloigné ou un bout de jardin exposé, les besoins changent. L’alimentation, le champ de vision de la caméra ou la connectivité sont autant de facteurs qui entrent en ligne de compte au moment de choisir son équipement.
Pour son Black Friday, organisé de ce jeudi 12 novembre au mercredi 2 décembre, Reolink propose cinq caméras d’extérieur en promotion, du modèle solaire avec projecteur à la caméra panoramique capable de suivre un mouvement dans son champ de vision. Autre bon point pour le budget, les caméras Reolink enregistrent les images en local, sur carte microSD, sans abonnement. Pour choisir le modèle qui vous correspond le mieux, le plus simple reste encore de partir de l’endroit où vous comptez installer une caméra.
Les offres du Black Friday de Reolink :
- la caméra de sécurité Solar Floodlight Cam à 83,99 € au lieu de 119,99 € ;
- la caméra de sécurité OMVI 2i Ultra à 169,99 € au lieu de 229,99 € ;
- la caméra de sécurité TrackMix WiFi Grey à 149,99 € au lieu de 199,99 € ;
- la caméra de sécurité TrackMix PoE à 139,99 € au lieu de 199,99 € ;
- la caméra de sécurité OMVI 3i WiFi à 223,99 € au lieu de 319,99 €.
Pas de prise à proximité ? Deux caméras solaires pour l’allée ou le portail
Selon l’endroit choisi, installer une caméra de surveillance à l’extérieur de chez soi peut vite se transformer en casse-tête logistique. Le plus gros problème ? L’alimentation. Pour pallier l’absence de prise ou de source électrique proche, Reolink a conçu une gamme de caméras de surveillance qui fonctionnent à l’énergie solaire, comme la Solar Floodlight Cam et l’OMVI 2i Ultra. Il faut juste veiller à installer la caméra dans un endroit suffisamment ensoleillé pour ne plus avoir à s’inquiéter de ses besoins en énergie.
La Solar Floodlight Cam se démarque grâce à un double projecteur qui monte jusqu’à 1 000 lumens et s’allume dès qu’il détecte un mouvement. Idéal pour retrouver ses clefs devant la porte ou éclairer une entrée de garage, mais aussi identifier ou faire détaler les indésirables.
La caméra, de son côté, filme en 2K (4 mégapixels) avec un champ de vision de 150° pour une couverture étendue des lieux à surveiller. Un panneau solaire de 3 watts recharge sa batterie de 7 800 mAh. Côté prix, la Solar Floodlight Cam bénéficie d’une réduction de 30 % qui permet de faire baisser son prix de 119,99 € à 83,99 €.
Si vous voulez surtout suivre ce qui se passe chez vous, l’OMVI 2i Ultra est plus indiquée grâce à ses deux caméras. D’un côté, un objectif grand-angle en 4K permet de garder une zone précise dans le cadre. De l’autre, un objectif motorisé 3K pivote pour suivre un éventuel intrus.
Avec son panneau solaire de 6 watts et sa batterie amovible de 10 000 mAh, cette caméra s’installe à peu près partout, sans tirer de câble ni ajouter de prise électrique. Reolink annonce qu’une demi-heure de soleil par jour suffit à la faire fonctionner. Vérifiez simplement que le signal Wi-Fi est suffisant à cet endroit si vous comptez consulter le flux vidéo en direct ou recevoir des alertes sur votre téléphone. Quant au prix ? Pendant le Black Friday, Reolink vous propose une réduction de 26 % qui permet d’obtenir cette caméra à 169,99 € au lieu de 229,99 €, chez Amazon ou sur le site de Reolink.
Suivre un mouvement en gros plan ou garder toute la cour dans le cadre : quelle solution choisir en fonction de vos besoins ?
Au-delà de l’alimentation, une autre question permet de définir quel modèle de caméra choisir pour assurer la surveillance de votre extérieur. Demandez-vous ce que vous voulez voir à l’écran lorsque quelqu’un ou quelque chose entre dans le champ de la caméra. 
Avec la gamme TrackMix (WiFi Grey ou PoE), vous gardez la scène dans le cadre tout en suivant les mouvements en gros plan. Ces caméras embarquent deux objectifs : un grand-angle 4K pour la vue d’ensemble et un téléobjectif avec zoom hybride x6 pour le gros plan. La caméra pivote d’elle-même pour suivre ce qui bouge. La principale différence entre les deux modèles de la série TrackMix actuellement en promotion réside dans la manière de les alimenter et d’accéder à leurs données. 
La TrackMix WiFi Grey se branche directement sur le secteur et se connecte en Wi-Fi 6, sur les bandes 2,4 et 5 GHz. La TrackMix PoE gère son alimentation et la transmission des données par un seul câble Ethernet. Le modèle qu’il vous faut dépend donc de la configuration de votre installation et de l’accès au courant ou à internet.

articles.title: El país sin mar que más se acerca a tener una costa: hizo el negocio del siglo al ceder un tramo de carretera a Ucrania antes de que llegara Rusia
articles.text:
Cuando la Unión Soviética se desintegró en 1991, Moldavia se convirtió en un país independiente con un pequeño problema geográfico: tenía el mar Negro prácticamente a las puertas, pero carecía de litoral. Ocho años después, sus dirigentes encontraron una solución que pasaba por un insólito intercambio territorial con Ucrania. Moldavia cedió un trozo de carretera y recibió a cambio unos cientos de metros de ribera. Aquella operación terminaría convirtiéndose en uno de los negocios más importantes de su historia.
A las puertas del mar. Encajada entre Rumanía y Ucrania, Moldavia ocupa una superficie de 33.846 kilómetros cuadrados y carece de costa marítima. Su extremo meridional, sin embargo, alcanza uno de los grandes corredores comerciales de Europa: el Danubio, el segundo río más largo del continente, que desemboca en el mar Negro.
Durante sus primeros años de independencia, Moldavia dependía de sus vecinos para buena parte de sus importaciones y exportaciones. Para un país cuya economía estaba estrechamente vinculada a la agricultura y que necesitaba importar petróleo y gas, disponer de una vía comercial propia hacia aguas internacionales podía cambiarlo todo.
El negocio del siglo. En 1995, el Gobierno moldavo decidió construir una terminal petrolera en Giurgiulești, una localidad situada en la confluencia de los ríos Prut y Danubio. El proyecto inicial, desarrollado con inversores griegos, pronto atravesó dificultades financieras.
La gran oportunidad llegó en 1999, cuando Moldavia y Ucrania alcanzaron un acuerdo territorial largamente negociado. Moldavia cedió a su vecino un tramo de 7,77 kilómetros de la carretera que conecta Odesa con Reni y obtuvo aproximadamente 450 metros de ribera del Danubio. Aquella diminuta franja de terreno permitió ampliar el proyecto original y construir un puerto capaz de recibir buques marítimos.
Un puerto marítimo sin tener mar. El 26 de octubre de 2006 comenzó a funcionar la terminal petrolera del Puerto Internacional Libre de Giurgiulești. En marzo de 2009 abrió una terminal de pasajeros y cuatro meses después se inauguraron las instalaciones para el transporte de cereales.
En 2011 se añadió una terminal de mercancías. Situado a 133,8 kilómetros de navegación del mar Negro y con una profundidad máxima de siete metros, el puerto puede recibir tanto embarcaciones fluviales como marítimas. Moldavia había conseguido algo extraordinario: disponer de acceso comercial a aguas internacionales sin tener un solo kilómetro de costa marítima.
450 metros que valen millones. Con el paso de los años, Giurgiulești se convirtió en una de las infraestructuras más importantes de Moldavia. Su terminal petrolera tiene capacidad para almacenar 63.000 toneladas de combustible, dispone de dos terminales de cereales y cuenta con conexiones ferroviarias que facilitan el transporte internacional de mercancías. Las inversiones de las empresas instaladas en el puerto superaban los 100 millones de dólares en 2022.
Actualmente, según los datos recogidos por Interfax, concentra más del 70% de las importaciones y exportaciones moldavas transportadas por vía acuática. El pequeño terreno que Ucrania había cedido a Moldavia se había convertido en una puerta comercial al resto del mundo.
El favor que Ucrania recuperó 23 años después. Cuando Rusia invadió Ucrania en febrero de 2022 y bloqueó sus puertos del mar Negro, Giurgiulești adquirió una importancia que nadie podía imaginar en 1999. El puerto comenzó a facilitar la exportación de cereales ucranianos y la entrada de combustible en el país.
En mayo de 2022, el volumen mensual de productos petrolíferos gestionados por sus instalaciones había pasado de una media de 34.000 toneladas a 65.000, más de la mitad destinadas previsiblemente a Ucrania. Aquel año, Giurgiulești alcanzó un récord de 1,8 millones de toneladas de mercancías. El país que había ayudado a Moldavia a conseguir una salida comercial al mar encontraba ahora en ella una alternativa para sortear el bloqueo ruso.
El puerto que todos quieren. La importancia estratégica de Giurgiulești terminó despertando el interés de varios países. En 2024, Rumanía inició negociaciones para adquirir la empresa que gestiona el Puerto Internacional Libre, propiedad del Banco Europeo para la Reconstrucción y el Desarrollo desde 2021. Entre los interesados también figuraban los multimillonarios búlgaros Kiril y Georgi Domuschiev, propietarios de un importante conglomerado marítimo.
Bucarest considera que Giurgiulești puede desempeñar un papel fundamental en la reconstrucción de Ucrania y complementar las operaciones del puerto rumano de Constanza, con el que ya mantiene conexiones ferroviarias para el transporte de contenedores.
El negocio continúa. Las autoridades moldavas han autorizado la adquisición de Danube Logistics, la empresa operadora del puerto, por parte de la compañía estatal rumana que administra Constanza. La operación contempla inversiones superiores a los 24 millones de euros para construir una terminal de contenedores, modernizar el ferrocarril y ampliar las instalaciones de almacenamiento.
Lo importante es que Moldavia conserva la propiedad del terreno: lo que cambia de manos es la empresa que dispone de una concesión de 99 años para explotar el puerto. Así, más de un cuarto de siglo después, aquel intercambio territorial sigue demostrando su extraordinario valor. Moldavia no pudo cambiar su geografía del todo, por supuesto, pero consiguió que dejara de ser un obstáculo. Y para ello le bastó con cambiar unos kilómetros de asfalto por 450 metros de río.

articles.title: Un comando de Windows para liberar 10 GB de espacio en el disco duro
articles.text:
Cuando el disco duro principal empieza a quedarse sin espacio, solemos buscar qué carpetas del sistema están devorando nuestros gigas. Y es que, si revisamos a fondo la partición del sistema, no es raro encontrarse con que la carpeta WinSxS ha ido creciendo con el paso de las semanas hasta ocupar 10 GB, 12 GB o incluso más de 20 GB sin que nos hayamos dado cuenta.
El almacén del sistema. WinSxS funciona como un repositorio interno de componentes de Microsoft. Su función principal es la de conservar versiones paralelas de diferentes archivos esenciales y librerías DLL para evitar conflictos de compatibilidad, y permitir recuperar versiones anteriores tras cada actualización. El sistema una tarea automática para hacer limpieza llamada StartComponentCleanup, pero no se activa hasta que pasan 30 días enteros tras una actualización, pero si necesitas espacio urgentemente puedes lanzarlo manualmente.
Comprobar el peso real. Muchos de los archivos que residen dentro de WinSxS están vinculados con la carpeta System32, lo que provoca que las propiedades convencionales de Windows Explorer muestren un cálculo distorsionado del espacio. Para salir de dudas y comprobar exactamente cuánto almacenamiento puedes recuperar, basta con abrir PowerShell o el Símbolo del sistema con permisos de administrador y ejecutar el siguiente comando:
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /AnalyzeComponentStore
Windows se pondrá a analizar el almacén de componentes, y te dirá el tamaño real que ocupa en el disco, diciéndote de paso si se recomienda hacer limpieza.
Limpiar con seguridad. Si la herramienta te confirma que hay paquetes prescindibles y puedes eliminarlos, ahora tendrás que escribir lo siguiente:
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup
Con este comando, la herramienta borra las versiones obsoletas previas conservando únicamente los archivos de la actualización más reciente, garantizando así un respaldo seguro si hiciera falta revertir cambios.
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup /ResetBase
También puedes añadir el parámetro /ResetBase al final del comando para hacer una limpieza más profunda de todo el historial de actualizaciones, aunque no es recomendable porque elimina la posibilidad de desinstalar los parches acumulativos aplicados hasta la fecha.
Para quienes sigan necesitando arañar espacio extra en discos SSD ajustados, existen otros ajustes tradicionales en el sistema que pueden ayudar, como desactivar la hibernación o recortar los puntos de restauración del sistema.

articles.title: Comment obtenir les plus fidèles sur vos écrans ? Les explications des professionnels d’Hollywood
articles.text:
Comment obtenir les plus fidèles sur vos écrans ? Les explications des professionnels d’Hollywood
Comment s'assurer que les couleurs d'un film sont bien celles voulues par son réalisateur ? Le cinquième épisode de Color Matters réunit trois experts hollywoodiens pour expliquer pourquoi la calibration des écrans est essentielle, du studio de cinéma jusqu'à votre salon.
La troisième saison de Color Matters – Masters of Color se poursuit avec un cinquième épisode qui réunit Jill Bogdanowicz, Stephen Nakamura et John Quartel, trois spécialistes de l'image chez Company 3, un des plus grands studios hollywoodiens. Après avoir exploré les choix artistiques des coloristes et les coulisses techniques des grandes productions hollywoodiennes, cette nouvelle vidéo s'intéresse à une étape essentielle du processus : la calibration des écrans.
Des couleurs fidèles du tournage jusqu'à nos salons
La couleur joue un rôle essentiel dans la manière dont nous percevons un film. Elle permet de transmettre des émotions, de créer une atmosphère ou encore de transporter le spectateur dans une autre époque. Autant de choix artistiques minutieusement travaillés par les réalisateurs, directeurs de la photographie et coloristes, qui peuvent toutefois être altérés si les écrans utilisés ne reproduisent pas correctement les images.
John Quartel résume d'ailleurs cette problématique avec une phrase que redoutent tous les coloristes : « Ce n'est pas mon film ». Car après des semaines de travail sur l'étalonnage, rien de plus frustrant pour un réalisateur que de découvrir son œuvre avec des couleurs différentes de celles qu'il avait imaginées.
Pour éviter cela, Company 3 doit garantir une parfaite cohérence tout au long de la chaîne de production, depuis les premiers moniteurs utilisés sur les tournages jusqu'aux écrans de référence servant à finaliser les films. Un travail qui nécessite de maîtriser les caractéristiques des caméras, les transformations colorimétriques et, bien sûr, la calibration des diffuseurs.
LG 55G6
Des outils de précisions essentiels pour les studios
Pour maintenir cette précision, les équipes de Company 3 utilisent notamment des sondes de mesure, des spectroradiomètres haute résolution et le logiciel de calibration Calman. Chez Les Numériques, nous avons la chance d’être équipé de ce même matériel de pointe, notamment depuis l’arrivée de notre spectroradiomètre au labo.
Chez Company 3, dont les équipes collaborent régulièrement à distance entre plusieurs studios répartis dans le monde, elles peuvent ainsi s'assurer que les différents écrans respectent bien les mêmes standards, même lorsque les artistes travaillent à des milliers de kilomètres les uns des autres.
Cette recherche de précision ne concerne pas uniquement les professionnels. Les trois intervenants rappellent que les efforts réalisés tout au long de la production peuvent être en partie perdus si le téléviseur du spectateur affiche des couleurs trop saturées, une température de couleur incorrecte ou des traitements d'image excessifs.
C’est aussi pour ça que nous testons TV, moniteurs et vidéoprojecteurs sous toutes les coutures dans nos labos, afin de nous assurer du rendu de ces derniers pour vos salons.

articles.title: Anthropic's Dario Amodei uses IPO pitch to promise AI will eliminate cancer and Alzheimer's within a decade
articles.text:
Facepalm: AI still hasn't cured cancer, or any disease, for that matter. Don't worry, though, because Anthropic boss Dario Amodei has assured us that the technology will not only eliminate this disease but also Alzheimer's, heart disease, and mental illness in a decade. The fact that this bold and heavily mocked statement came as part of his IPO pitch is absolutely unrelated, because who among us wouldn't want to invest in a company that is going to "create an age of miracles?"
Amodei made his latest wild prediction during an IPO roadshow video the company released yesterday. It's around 42 minutes long, but the part receiving the most attention is his ambitious plan for the future of medicine.
"You know, if today we look at things like cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease, mental illness, these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade."
If that wasn't enough to emphasize the godlike power of AI, Amodei added that the technology, presumably Anthropic's, will catapult us into a utopia where illness vanishes.
"I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," he gushed.
 – NIK (@ns123abc) November 10, 2026
The CEO obviously had to include something about where his own AI giant fits into all this. "And I believe that the company which gets the risks right will also be the company that has the license to operate that society trusts and society believes can build the benefits in the right way," he said. Given the number of rogue AI incidents and Amodei's many prophecies of AI-related destruction, society probably wouldn't trust Anthropic even if it did cure cancer.
Needless to say, Amodei is being pulled apart by the medical community over his claims. While some experts have acknowledged that AI could play an important role in the fight against cancer and Alzheimer's, they say there is no chance a complete cure will be available within 10 years, given the long-term trials involved. That will likely come as a disappointment to the AI researchers who, according to Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar, have taken up smoking because they're so confident AI will cure cancer.
 – Melinda B. Chu (@MelindaBChu1) November 10, 2026
There's also been criticism over Amodei using such comments in an IPO pitch. Biotech executive Rami Elghandour said it reeks "of desperation."
 – Rami Elghandour (@RamiElghandour) November 11, 2026
In fairness to Amodei, he's not the only one framing AI as a future magical cure-all/fountain of youth. Last week, OpenAI president Greg Brockman said AI will make significant strides in biology and health, including the treatment of diseases, over the next 12 to 18 months. He said that eventually, it could even make death a choice. At the moment, most people would be happy if AI just stopped hacking other companies and worrying everyone.

articles.title: Man's secret use of synthetic testosterone for cows nearly destroyed his heart
articles.text:
For 11 years, a Massachusetts man had an alarming array of health problems, most notably that his heart kept failing. He landed in the hospital over and over again, needed life support at one point, spent years going to specialists, and underwent a barrage of tests along the way.
But through it all, he never revealed a key detail behind his ailments: He was taking powerful, illicit synthetic testosterone derivatives (aka anabolic-androgenic steroids, or AAS). One of the drugs he took was approved only for use in animals; it’s primarily used to beef up cows.
Left in the dark, his doctors had to puzzle this out on their own. In a case report in this week’s issue of the New England Journal of Medicine, they explain how they did it. They also offer a warning: These cases will only become more common, and clinicians need to know what they look like.
“Use of AAS has now become a major international substance use disorder,” they wrote. In the US, it’s estimated that between 2.9 and 4 million people, mostly male athletes, use AAS. To put this in a public health perspective, this is more than the number of people in the US with an HIV infection.
“Clinicians should be prepared to encounter increasing numbers of patients presenting with the long-term effects of AAS exposure, including cardiomyopathy, atherosclerotic disease, and anabolic steroid–induced hypogonadism.”
Patients also need to be prepared for what recovery looks like, which they described as being “lengthy and varied.” The man’s case offers a stark example.
Troubling tale
The problems started when he was 39. He fell ill after returning from a trip to the Caribbean and went to Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston with a fever, chills, and trouble breathing. Tests suggested he had an acute kidney injury, liver damage, and an injured heart. Testing of his heart showed that the left chamber was pumping out just 21 percent of its blood in a beat (a normal amount is above 50 percent). His heart only got worse from there, and within hours, he ended up on a type of life support called ECMO (venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation), a machine that does the work of both the heart and lungs in dire circumstances. He luckily recovered—and quickly. But doctors were baffled by the cause.

articles.title: Las empresas chinas buscan reservar chips de Nvidia fuera del país ante posibles controles de Washington
articles.text:
Empresas chinas de inteligencia artificial intentan alquilar capacidad de cómputo con chips de Nvidia en centros de datos fuera de China. Temen que el escándalo de Jensen Huang, director ejecutivo de la fabricante, lleve a Washington a restringir el uso remoto de esos procesadores, según tres personas citadas por la agencia Reuters.
Washington prohíbe exportar a China los chips más avanzados de Nvidia. Pero las compañías del país asiático pueden usarlos a distancia si alquilan potencia de cálculo en servidores situados en otros países. Ese resquicio es el que temen que se cierre.
Una proveedora china de servicios en la nube discutió internamente si debía asegurar capacidad de chips de la empresa en el exterior, dijeron las fuentes. Algunas empresas ya contactaron a operadores de centros de datos para reservarla.
Los laboratorios de IA más pequeños evalúan pasos parecidos, entre ellos acercarse a grandes proveedores de potencia de cálculo en alquiler del sudeste asiático. Estos chips sirven para entrenar y hacer funcionar los modelos que hay detrás de los chatbots.
Una ley que regularía el acceso a distancia
El temor se concentra en la Ley de Seguridad de Acceso Remoto (RASA, por sus siglas en inglés). El proyecto daría al Departamento de Comercio de Estados Unidos autoridad para regular el acceso remoto, por la nube, a tecnología restringida. La Cámara de Representantes lo aprobó en enero por 369 votos contra 22 y espera la decisión del Senado.
Huang confesó el domingo que había sido infiel a su esposa. The New York Times informó que la mujer era Alice Huang, exejecutiva de la empresa de computación en la nube Megaspeed, con sede en Singapur, y que las autoridades estadounidenses concluyeron que era una agente de inteligencia china. Reuters no pudo verificar esa acusación, que China negó.
Según dos fuentes de Reuters, Alice Huang tuvo negocios e inversiones con varias grandes tecnológicas chinas, entre ellas Tencent y Alibaba. Registros comerciales de Singapur muestran que Apex Enterprise Solutions, filial de Alibaba, financió a Speedmatrix, una empresa de Malasia vinculada a Megaspeed. La compañía enfrenta sospechas de haber ayudado a clientes chinos a acceder a chips sujetos a controles de exportación. La compañía negó haberlos desviado ilegalmente a China.
El mercado gris también acumula chips
La perspectiva de un control más estricto también aumentó la demanda de chips restringidos en el mercado gris chino, el circuito informal de compraventa. Comerciantes e intermediarios empezaron a acumularlos. Los compradores temen una ofensiva más amplia de Washington contra el contrabando de chips y servidores de IA hacia China.
El Congreso ya mueve fichas. Según Reuters, tres medidas sobre chips pueden incluirse en la ley anual de defensa: la que daría al Congreso poder sobre las exportaciones de chips avanzados, la que exigiría rastrear los chips para combatir el contrabando y la que presionaría a los aliados de Estados Unidos a restringir más equipos de fabricación de chips.
La senadora demócrata Elizabeth Warren y el senador republicano Jim Banks afirmaron en un comunicado conjunto que la relación de Huang con una sospechosa de espiar para China vuelve estas preocupaciones “aún más urgentes”. Nvidia es considerada la mayor opositora de dos de las medidas, según un exasesor del Congreso citado por Reuters.
Los controles ya tenían grietas. La agencia informó el 5 de noviembre de que unos 600.000 chips H200 de Nvidia esperaban en Hong Kong un permiso de importación de Beijing, y que varias grandes empresas chinas de internet habían obtenido unos 10.000 cada una. Una universidad ligada al Ejército Popular de Liberación compró H200 el mes pasado pese a figurar en una lista negra estadounidense.
En marzo, fiscales de Estados Unidos acusaron a Yih-Shyan Liaw, cofundador de Super Micro Computer, y a otras dos personas de desviar a China servidores con chips de Nvidia. Según la fiscalía, una empresa del sudeste asiático compró unos USD 2.500 millones en servidores a Super Micro entre 2024 y 2025, y una parte sustancial terminó en China. Los acusados no fueron condenados.

articles.title: Attacker Targets 60,000 GitHub Repositories in Credential Theft Campaign
articles.text:
An attacker has tested stolen access to more than 60,000 GitHub repositories and inserted credential-stealing code in thousands of them, several security firms report.
Aikido Security said the operation, which it calls wfx-loot, began on November 10. It identified roughly 4,800 compromised accounts behind probe pull requests submitted to 61,764 repositories.
The requests were used to establish whether the stolen access permitted changes to a repository. “The pull request does nothing by itself,” StepSecurity explained, noting that malware was subsequently deployed in repositories where the permissions and configuration allowed it.
Aikido found signs that the stealer ran in more than 1,800 repositories. SafeDep separately counted 8,093 public repositories that received malicious commits, a figure that does not necessarily indicate successful execution.
“The attacker does not exploit a bug in GitHub Actions,” StepSecurity noted. The intruder instead relies on valid tokens belonging to developer and bot accounts.
The attacker placed the malware in existing or new GitHub Actions workflows, shell scripts run by CI systems, and npm installation hooks. The npm method also poses a risk to developers who install dependencies while the malicious changes are present.
The script looks for GitHub tokens, repository secrets, cloud credentials and AI service keys. It also reads GitHub Actions runner process memory and has functionality designed to expand access and establish persistence in AWS and Azure.
The attacker usually reversed the code changes and deleted workflow runs to conceal the activity.
StepSecurity traced 173 probe pull requests to tokens issued to the Fly.io GitHub app. The firm said it could not determine how the tokens were obtained and had no evidence that Fly.io’s infrastructure had been breached.
Affected software releases include a Packagist package and versions of two Go modules.
Aikido identified similarities with October’s GhostAction campaign but assessed that the two operations probably involved different actors.
The security firm warned that organizations should assume all accessible secrets were compromised if the malware executed. Organizations have been advised to revoke compromised tokens, rotate exposed secrets, and check for unauthorized cloud changes.

articles.title: Qvyon Technologies emerges from stealth with $8 million USD to prepare physical AI for dangerous edge cases | BetaKit
articles.text:
The former CEO of automotive tech company LeddarTech has launched a physical AI startup to help autonomous vehicle and other robot makers deal with one of the big obstacles to real-world deployment: unpredictable, dangerous edge cases.
Montréal-based Qvyon Technologies, led by co-founder and CEO Frantz Saintellemy, publicly launched on Thursday with $8 million USD ($11.4 million CAD) in seed financing. The round, which closed in April, consists of $6 million USD in equity from Mac Venture Capital, BDC Capital’s Black Entrepreneurs Fund, BKR Capital, and Spotlight VP, as well as $2 million in venture debt from RBCx.
“We see an opportunity for us to scale very rapidly and to create a foundational company here in Canada.”
Frantz Saintellemy, Qvyon
Qvyon’s goal is to allow companies to test and validate AI-enabled robots and self-driving vehicles before putting them to work. As generative AI capabilities have ramped up interest in deploying smart robots in factories and on roads, the unpredictability of the physical world (and random human behaviours) has created challenges for companies hoping to earn public trust and drive adoption.
Saintellemy told BetaKit that when he was working on autonomous vehicle software at LeddarTech, the biggest challenges were finding enough real-world data to reliably test and validate the systems.
Founded in 2007 as a spin-off of Québec’s National Optics Institute, it developed environmental-sensing solutions for autonomous vehicles and driver-assistance systems. After going public on the Nasdaq in 2023, the company faced challenges repaying its debts, eventually cutting nearly all its staff and filing for bankruptcy last year. Some of Qvyon’s other founding members are from LeddarTech as well.
Now, Saintellemy and the team are taking the lessons learned beyond the automotive sector to help companies validate their robots across all kinds of hazardous situations.
“These situations were difficult to anticipate, expensive to capture, sometimes dangerous to reproduce, and sometimes statistically impossible to recreate in nature,” Saintellemy said in an interview. “But these are the types of scenarios any autonomous system must learn to handle.”
Simulation and synthetic data alone couldn’t solve the problem, he said, so Qvyon took a different approach. Its software product, MIMIC Core, blends real-world data—which a company can input from its own cameras or sensors—with an AI system that can then generate tons of variations from one recording, allowing a company’s engineers to learn where their systems are making mistakes.
Jason Baibokas, managing director at BDC Capital who leads the Black Entrepreneurship Fund, said in a statement to BetaKit that every industry putting AI into physical action will have to prove it’s safe before deployment. “Qvyon is building the answer,” he said.
RELATED: LeddarTech cuts 95 percent of staff in bid to rescue its business
“Edge cases” with unfortunate outcomes have hurt public perception for companies like self-driving giant Waymo, which has had cars accidentally drive over an exploding firework or be unable to navigate out of gridlock.
Some self-driving companies have developed validation tech in-house. Toronto-based Waabi has its Waabi World AI system to train and improve the performance of its autonomous vehicles on synthetic data, which it says is a cheaper, safer, and more scalable method than traditional road testing-first strategies.
Qvyon says its tech can be a complement to existing AI simulators, like a “reality infrastructure” layer on top that uses real-world data—which Saintellemy is hoping to sell to similar companies in the driving and industrial sectors. One of its first customers is the autonomous trucking company NuPort Robotics, based in Markham, Ont., which partnered with Canadian Tire and says it is testing trucks with customers in multiple provinces.
Beyond the self-driving sector, it has landed another customer in US manufacturer Voltava, which Qvyon says will use its tech to validate inspection systems in factories.
Qvyon’s roughly 20-person team plans to use the funding to deploy the MIMIC platform and land customers in the US, Europe, and Japan, with a roadmap to launching new products in 2027: a system to measure and document test results, and one to improve the AI system using information from machines already in use.
“We see an opportunity for us to scale very rapidly and to create a foundational company here in Canada,” Saintellemy said.

articles.title: Norwest pushes deeper into AI with new $4B fund | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Norwest, a firm backed solely by Wells Fargo, has raised a $4 billion fund as it sets out to invest more in AI. This is the eighteenth fund for the 65-year-old multi-stage investment firm, and its largest to date.
The fund will be invested across various sectors and multiple countries, notably the United States, India, and Israel. But the big story here is AI, and Norwest’s plans to expand its investment in this area.
Norwest said Thursday it aims to capitalize on AI startups developing products and services across core industries such as consumer, healthcare, and technology. The investment firm, which has backed Plaid, Spotify, Uber, and Vuori, said it will continue to expand its investments in physical AI, voice AI, agentic cybersecurity, and aerospace.
If that sounds like a broad approach, it is intended to be, Jeff Crowe, a senior managing partner at Norwest, told TechCrunch.
“We’re taking a broad approach to AI because its impact is broad,” Crowe added, as AI is not limited by industry, geography, or application. “Just as digital transformation did, AI transformation has the potential to touch most layers of enterprise, consumer, and healthcare solutions: networking, enterprise IT and applications. Adapting to an agentic environment means applying AI broadly across products and services that solve problems.”
Crowe added that the firm is particularly excited about early-stage companies building AI-native application and infrastructure, physical AI, domain-specific models, and cybersecurity solutions.
Some of the firm’s recent investments reflect this strategy. For instance, the firm invested in Coval, which builds tools to test and evaluate AI agents, and Generalist AI, a startup that has developed AI foundation models for robots.
Since the launch of its seventeenth fund, a $3 billion raise that closed in 2024, the firm has made more than 87 investments.

articles.title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
articles.text:
Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
The Chip Security Act is getting renewed attention following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that the tracking requirements of his Chip Security Act meant to combat smuggling were technically possible, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while its industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”
Representative Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, co-sponsored the Chip Security Act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify locations of advanced AI chips to prevent their smuggling to China, in 2025. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
When the Chip Security Act was introduced in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it exists, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.”
But privately, representatives from Nvidia working with Foster on the technical possibility of such safeguards told the lawmaker that the company could implement them.
“They never put anything in writing, but when I had technical discussions,” Foster said, the reaction was, “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgement to Foster goes farther than anything Nvidia has previously stated.
Other technology built by Nvidia for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, Nvidia announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow its customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling.
Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.
MIT Technology Review asked Nvidia in early October if its Fleet Intelligence tool could be used to prevent smuggling, which lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in. The company declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled U.S. products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”
The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.
The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option.
Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.
But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.
In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

articles.title: Meet the people who want peptides to be made in America
articles.text:
This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. We’ll be taking a break next week and will be back on November 25th. Opt in for Optimizer here.
Meet the people who want peptides to be made in America
For some, the answer to a dodgy gray market is to bring the pharmaceutical supply chain back to American soil.
The SS Jeremiah O’Brien is a World War II Liberty ship. The hulking vessel was built in 56 days. It made 11 trips to Normandy, France, to supply the Allied powers in the fight against German U-boats. Last week, it was the site of a black-tie peptide party thrown by a trio of Gen Z venture capitalists.
Roughly 150 people attended the event, where four types of peptide samples were provided to guests — no injections. One was a topical cream with GHK-Cu, while the other three were dissolvable sublingual strips from peptide startup Afterglow. GHK-Cu is a popular skincare ingredient, but it’s unclear how well sublingual peptide strips work. The topic of the night wasn’t just the state of peptides. The venue was a deliberate reference to American industrial prowess — and why the pharmaceutical supply chain ought to be centered in the United States.
The timing couldn’t have been more pointed.
Sourcing is one of the biggest question marks with gray-market peptides — something the US Department of Health and Human Services is trying to address with its recent interim policy decision allowing certain unapproved peptides for compounding.
The decision is a controversial one. FDA career scientists haven’t endorsed it, though to the average person it might seem like they have. In fact, at a public hearing in July, FDA scientists categorically stated that there wasn’t enough evidence proving safety or efficacy for the experimental peptides in question. Some industry experts have cautioned that the HHS’s decision threatens the current clinical trial framework. By circumventing gold-standard clinical trials, it arguably allows telehealth providers and compounding pharmacies to bypass the approval process and create a parallel, dubiously regulated market.
But for the party’s organizers Roxana Grunenwald, Yuva Krishnapillai, and Elia Ahmadi — all three are from Haus Fund, a biotech accelerator — this was an opportunity to make the case for American peptides. Hence the party on a wartime cargo ship, where guests left with stickers and hats emblazoned with “My Peptides Are Made in America.”
Listening to the three speak, they wouldn’t strike you as typical hooah patriots or MAHA activists — though there’s some overlap in their talking points. They’re venture capitalists promoting a certain viewpoint that’s trending in Silicon Valley right now. But it’s not just them making this argument. Hims & Hers — one of the most recognizable telehealth brands right now — is also hopping on the American peptide bandwagon.
The push for American manufacturing is a thorny one. Last year, President Donald Trump’s tariff policies also reignited the American manufacturing argument, though the reality is it’s difficult to return to “made in America” after decades spent shaping the country into a services-based economy.
Pharmaceuticals have also globalized. According to the US Pharmacopeia, 51 percent of all US prescription active pharmaceutical ingredients (API) comes from India and the European Union. China accounts for 10 percent. But when it comes to gray-market peptides, there’s a reason they’re commonly referred to as “Chinese peptides.” The vast majority of these research chemicals sold online come from Chinese manufacturers.
“Right now, Americans are buying consumer peptides from gray-market sellers in China. And that concerns me because American consumers have little recourse if something goes wrong,” Ahmadi said in response to a panel question. “This is not a blanket criticism of China. This is not a criticism of Chinese people. America needs to be able to make its own medicines.”
“I think this is a really good first step in solving the gray market problem,” Krishnapillai tells me, referring to the HHS’s interim decision. While building industrial infrastructure is a lengthy, complicated, and expensive process, he argues that this decision opens the door for compounding pharmacies to build a supply chain that adheres to US consumer safety laws. That in turn could give the FDA more insight into how to more effectively regulate the market. “The FDA [will be] able to see from a bird’s-eye view a lot more clarity, which will allow for structure to be built out and eventually a new path to API classification,” he adds.
“We’re taking the stance that if people will be purchasing these peptides and taking them, sometimes even injecting, we want them to be American peptides,” adds Grunenwald. “We want them to be both compounded, produced, and verified on American soil.”
“The hardware industry — semiconductors, the compute industry, electronics — have all recognized that the reliance on China for critical minerals is a huge issue. That’s very clear. The bio industry has not yet had that same pushback and the same epiphany about our reliance on Chinese APIs. We aim to bring this onshore. It’ll take a lot of money and a lot of time, but it’s not impossible,” says Grunenwald.
For Ahmadi, onshoring peptides back to America is also a matter of regulatory consistency.
“That made-in-America stamp is really only the beginning,” he says. “If we don’t have our own domestic production, we won’t be able to enforce our own regulations. Our markets are always going to be flooded by foreign imports and we won’t be able to have accountability to American consumers. So, we see this as the first step in a larger conversation to have America set the global standard for quality and safety in this new space.”
Broadly speaking, these points have some merit. Several gray-market peptide users I’ve spoken with for an upcoming story stated that the mere act of importing “research drugs” and worrying about customs was a significant source of anxiety. That said, cost is another major reason why my sources tell me they opted to seek Chinese suppliers. It’s too soon to tell, but American-made peptides will likely be more expensive. That’s because an end-to-end US supply chain for these drugs is no easy feat.
Even so, for some, that extra expense is worth it if it means signaling a higher-quality product.
“We purchased an API manufacturing facility in California recently … Our intention is to leverage that capability to provide US-made API, and as a result, US-made product through the whole supply chain,” says Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, chief medical officer at Hims & Hers. The company purchased the facility last year, though it does partner with other companies globally to deliver compounded medications outside the US.
But in this particular case, Vinjamoori is also specifically referring to Peptides Plus, a forthcoming service from Hims & Hers announced in the wake of the HHS interim policy. In a blog announcing Peptides Plus, Hims & Hers CEO Andrew Dudum writes that the company “spent years building the infrastructure we need in our very own U.S.-based peptide manufacturing facility.” At launch, the company plans to provide access to “Sermorelin, Glutathione, B12, NAD+, and L-carnitine, with BPC-157 and TB-500 to follow when allowable.” Notably, some of these substances, like vitamin B12 and NAD+, aren’t peptides at all. Meanwhile, sermorelin and glutathione are already legal. All of these, with the exception of BPC-157 and TB-500, are currently available through legal pathways.
“I think it’s important not just to be able to say, ‘Oh, this is US made,’ but because it gives us direct oversight into the whole process,” says Vinjamoori, who says that he had prescribed peptides to patients in the past before the Biden administration moved certain research peptides to the no-compounding list.
“Even then, there was inconsistency between compounding pharmacies. Everyone knew this,” he says, noting that doctors would individually recommend pharmacies based on what they were prescribing. “That to me, is still not ideal. That’s why we really felt it was worth making this investment — and to be clear, this is not easy.”
When asked about how this might affect Peptide Plus pricing, Vinjamoori demurred, stating that the company would have more to share in “due time.”
There are yet many unknowns with regard to the HHS decision and how it’ll impact the peptide economy at large. The decision is most notably an interim policy. It’s not necessarily a permanent or lasting change. It was also made before the midterm elections, so who can say how the policy winds will shift concerning tariffs and whether the zeal for “made in America” will fizzle as a result.
But for now, it’s more than likely that you’ll start seeing some vendors touting that their peptides are proudly made in America. It’s entirely possible that they might imply that makes their product “safer.” That might be true with regard to sourcing and, to a degree, accountability. But it’s not the whole story. After all, in peptide America, sourcing is only part of the problem.

articles.title: Pese a las acusaciones de abuso de menores y la petición del Gobierno, TikTok no será prohibido en España
articles.text:
Así lo ha confirmado la propia Agencia Española de Protección de Datos, al que el Gobierno solicitó el bloqueo de la red social. Finalmente, el organismo público no bloqueará TikTok por los contenidos de pederastia y abuso de menores que ha expuesto la investigación de Maldita y, de momento, se limitará a que se eliminen los “contenidos concretos y determinados que supongan un tratamiento ilícito de datos de menores”.
No obstante, la polémica está lejos de terminar. Tras una investigación de Maldia, que expuso contenido de abuso de menores y pederastia en la red social, el Gobierno solicitó el bloqueo de la red social en España a la vez que la Fiscalía de Criminalidad Informática investiga “los posibles delitos relacionados con la elaboración y difusión de contenidos de abuso sexual infantil”.
Ahora la Agencia Española de Protección de Datos ha decidido que, de momento, no se bloqueará el acceo a TikTok en España, pese a que reconoce que "los delitos que atentan contra niñas y niños son especialmente graves y exigen una respuesta inmediata". Aunque no bloquerará la red social tras la petición del Ministerio de infancia, sí que ha uesto en marcha una serie de medidas, como ha confirmado la propia Agencia.
No habrá bloqueo de TikTok, de momento
De momento, el organismo público ha solicitado a Maldita.es la relación de los enlaces con el contenido de abuso para requerir a TikTok información concreta sobre sus actuaciones para la retirada de los contenidos denunciados y, posteriormente, ordenar el bloqueo que impida el acceso a los enlaces y contenidos concretos y determinados que supongan un tratamiento ilícito de datos de menores, pero de forma quirúrgica y no a la totalidad de la red social. Para la AEPD, se tratará de una medida concreta, proporcionada y adecuada, de acuerdo a la ley.
La investigación de Maldita ha sacado a la luz un submundo de contenidos de abuso de menores en TikTok, y aunque todavía sigue en marcha, puede ser el primer paso para una investigación más profunda. en el seno de la Unión Europea que puede traer enormes problemas a TikTok por la supuesta falta de moderación de contenidos, sobre todos los relacionados con menores.

articles.title: Black Friday has come early for the Apple Watch Series 12, with a massive 20% saving
articles.text:
Black Friday has come early for the Apple Watch Series 12, with a massive 20% saving
Grab the newest mainline Apple wearable for just AU$517
Apple launched the newest iteration of its mainline wearable, the Apple Watch Series 12, in September, alongside the Apple Watch Ultra 4, iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and the much-anticipated iPhone Duo foldable.
Knowing Apple, we anticipated that these devices would be unlikely to see any discounts until much later in their lifecycles, so it was a pleasant surprise seeing the Apple Watch Series 12 already getting a 20% discount on Amazon Australia — and its Black Friday event hasn’t even kicked off yet!
In fact, it seems Amazon is in a particularly giving mood when it comes to Apple, as the AirPods Pro 3 and Max 2 models are also discounted right now.
Our Apple Watch Series 12 review called it the best mainline version of the wearable in years, and is a compelling upgrade option for anyone using a Series 9 or older. It features a new S11 chip, providing smooth, responsive performance, and our reviewer also praised the Readiness Score and the newly refreshed Health Sensing System, as well as the all-day battery life. This price is available for both the 42mm (S/M) and 46mm (M/L) sizes, but only for select colours.
The main hardware upgrade from the Series 11 to the 12 is the new S11 chip, but Apple has also doubled RAM from 2GB to 4GB, and also added a Ceramic Shield 2 glass cover for extra durability.
The heart rate monitor is swapped for a new Health Sensing System with a new optical and electrical sensors that track heart rate every 5 seconds (compared to periodic tracking) and measure heart rate variability (HRV) more often.
Our reviewer found the Series 12 to be a comfortable everyday smartwatch, and also slim and compact enough for wearing it overnight for sleep tracking and to get a more accurate Readiness Score.
Not quite the Apple wearable you want? While the more rugged Apple Watch Ultra 4 isn’t discounted on Amazon yet, the Apple Watch SE 3 from last year is also discounted at 21% off or AU$317.
