articles.title: El botón HD no basta: así se envían fotos en calidad real por WhatsApp
articles.text:
Enviar una fotografía marcada como HD en WhatsApp mejora la nitidez frente al modo estándar, pero no garantiza el archivo original. La aplicación sigue aplicando compresión, reduce el peso del archivo y elimina los metadatos EXIF, esos datos que registran la fecha, la ubicación y los ajustes de cámara con los que se tomó la imagen.
Para fotógrafos y diseñadores que necesitan preservar esa información, existe una única alternativa: enviar la imagen como documento, el único método que conserva la resolución nativa, el perfil de color y todos los metadatos sin ningún tipo de reprocesamiento.
Qué diferencia hay entre el envío estándar, HD y como documento
Los tres modos de envío de WhatsApp producen resultados distintos en cuanto a calidad final. El envío estándar aplica una compresión alta que reduce la resolución hasta unos 1600 píxeles y elimina por completo los metadatos EXIF.
El modo HD, aunque reprocesa la imagen con una compresión media o baja y permite alcanzar hasta 4000 píxeles de resolución, también descarta esos datos técnicos y sigue sin entregar el archivo tal como fue capturado.
El envío como documento es el único que no aplica compresión. La imagen mantiene el 100% de su resolución original, conserva intactos los metadatos EXIF y respeta el perfil de color. La contrapartida es que no se muestra como una vista previa grande dentro del chat, sino como un archivo descargable que el receptor debe abrir para visualizar.
Esta distinción resulta especialmente relevante para quienes trabajan con material audiovisual de manera profesional. Un fotógrafo que necesita acreditar la fecha y el lugar exacto de una toma, o un diseñador que depende del perfil de color original para un proyecto, no pueden permitirse que esos datos se pierdan en el trayecto de un chat.
Pasos para enviar fotos sin compresión desde Android
En los dispositivos con sistema Android, el proceso para enviar una imagen en calidad original comienza dentro del chat de WhatsApp, donde debe pulsarse el icono del clip ubicado en la barra inferior. Esta acción despliega un menú con distintas opciones, entre ellas Documento, Cámara, Galería y Audio.
El siguiente paso es tocar la opción Documento, identificada con un icono morado, que abre el explorador de archivos del sistema o la lista de documentos recientes.
Desde allí, hay que pulsar en Seleccionar de la galería o bien en Buscar otros documentos, y utilizar el menú lateral para ingresar a la carpeta de Imágenes o Fotos, donde es posible navegar por las carpetas de la cámara, las descargas o las capturas de pantalla.
Una vez localizadas las imágenes, se seleccionan manteniendo pulsada la primera y tocando las siguientes, para luego confirmar con Seleccionar o Enviar. En el chat aparecerá el nombre exacto del archivo, por ejemplo IMG_20261111.jpg, junto con su peso real en megabytes, una confirmación de que el envío se realizó sin reducción de calidad.
Cómo lograr el mismo resultado en un iPhone
En los dispositivos con iOS, WhatsApp accede a la aplicación Archivos cuando se envían documentos, y no directamente al carrete de Fotos, salvo que se utilice una opción integrada más reciente.
El primer paso consiste en abrir el chat y pulsar el ícono “+” situado en la esquina inferior izquierda, lo que despliega una lista con alternativas como Fotos, Cámara, Ubicación y Documento.
Al seleccionar Documento, aparece un menú emergente donde conviene elegir Seleccionar foto o video, disponible en las versiones recientes de la aplicación, o bien Seleccionar archivo si la imagen ya está guardada en iCloud Drive o en el propio dispositivo. La primera alternativa abre de forma directa el carrete de la app Fotos.
El último paso es marcar las imágenes deseadas y pulsar el botón azul Enviar, o Abrir si el acceso se hizo desde la app Archivos. El mensaje se envía conservando el formato original, ya sea JPG, HEIC, PNG o RAW, junto con el tamaño exacto del archivo, sin ningún tipo de reducción.
Para quienes utilizan versiones de WhatsApp que no muestran la opción “Seleccionar foto o video” dentro de Documento, existe una alternativa: abrir primero la app Fotos, tocar el botón de compartir sobre la imagen elegida, guardarla en Archivos y luego seleccionarla desde WhatsApp mediante Documento y Seleccionar archivo.
Límites de peso y ajustes para el envío diario
WhatsApp permite enviar documentos de hasta 2 GB, un margen que habilita el envío de archivos pesados en formato RAW o de lotes grandes de fotografías sin inconvenientes. Esta capacidad convierte al envío como documento en una opción viable incluso para quienes manejan bancos de imágenes extensos o material de alta resolución generado por cámaras profesionales.
Para quienes no necesitan preservar los metadatos en cada envío y consideran suficiente la calidad que ofrece el modo HD en el uso cotidiano, existe la posibilidad de fijar esa opción como configuración permanente.
Esto se logra ingresando en Ajustes de WhatsApp, luego en Almacenamiento y datos, y finalmente en Calidad de carga de los archivos multimedia, donde puede marcarse la opción Calidad HD para que se aplique de manera automática en todos los envíos posteriores.

articles.title: Gemini in action: How voice, agents, and coding tools are changing the way businesses use AI
articles.text:
Gemini in action: How voice, agents, and coding tools are changing the way businesses use AI
At TechSparks 2026, Google Cloud’s Rajesh Shewani walked through how businesses are using Gemini for voice, agents, and coding, and why the systems built around a model now matter as much as the model itself.
Generative AI, in the form most people know it, is only about three years old. In that short time, Rajesh Shewani believes it has already moved through three distinct eras.
First came retrieval: chatbots that answer a question and wait for the next one. Then came agents that take action on a user’s behalf. Now, he said, the industry is entering what he calls the harness era, where orchestration, memory, and guardrails around a model let it carry out work from start to finish.
“An agent is nothing now but a model plus a harness,” said Shewani, Head of AI Customer Engineering for Digital Natives, Startups and ITeS at Google Cloud, at TechSparks 2026.
In a masterclass titled ‘Gemini in action’, Shewani promised a look at what is happening rather than a sales pitch. He covered where businesses are putting AI to work, how voice is becoming an interface, the tools Google uses to build its own software, and the questions organisations need to answer as agents become everyday users of their systems.
Shewani said organizations are no longer just discussing AI but executing in five broad areas.
- Agents, which are changing how companies work and how startups build for other businesses.
- Creative work, from image and video generation to marketing and branding, was one of the earliest areas to take off.
- Multimodal AI, which lets models work with images, video, and voice, not just text.
- Physical AI, including robotics and self-driving cars, which he expects to grow fast as the “brain” of large language models gains a body.
- AI fluency, a priority for traditional organizations in banking, insurance, retail, and telecom.
For those traditional businesses, the worry is less about building models and more about whether employees can use AI in their daily jobs. They don’t need to be experts or developers, he said, but they do need to be fluent.
What every agent needs
The three eras are cumulative, Shewani explained. Agents build on retrieval, and harnesses build on agents. AI is no longer an assistant that appears and disappears, but something closer to an autonomous colleague.
“It’s no longer just about the model,” he said. “It’s the model plus everything that you build around it”, from memory and context management to sandboxing.
He described four things every agent needs:
- A goal: booking a ticket, making an entry in an SAP system, or negotiating a price by voice.
- Instructions: guidance that goes beyond a single prompt and can be stored for reuse, much as new employees learn how an organization works.
- Knowledge: a company’s own data, since models are trained on public information, not internal records.
- Tools: the means to act, such as updating a CRM or placing an outbound call.
Knowledge is where much of the effort is going. Many teams had begun building their own “LLM wikis” for agents, and Google is now trying to standardize the approach with the Open Knowledge Format (OKF). OKF v0.1 represents knowledge as a directory of markdown files with YAML frontmatter, which agents can read directly. Shewani compared its role to what Model Context Protocol (MCP) did for backend integration.
A shared knowledge layer, combining a knowledge graph with plain text, also keeps costs down, he said. Rather than querying everything for every prompt, agents are pointed to structured context, which uses fewer tokens.
Voice becomes the interface
“Voice is becoming the new user interface,” Shewani said, whether for customers, employees, or users who prefer to speak in local languages. He noted that Google DeepMind’s team in Bengaluru is doing extensive work on Indic languages. Gemini Live now supports more than 90 Indian languages and dialects, including Sanskrit, Bhojpuri, and Maithili.
He showed a live translation demo built for Grab, the Southeast Asian ride-hailing platform, in which a passenger and driver who do not share a language coordinate a pickup.
Grab says travellers and driver-partners make more than 10 million voice calls a month, and it has been testing Gemini 3.5 Live Translate, which offers two-way translation in more than 70 languages.
Shewani said Gemini 3.8 Live, launched in September, improves further on noise cancellation and conversations between multiple speakers.
Another demo, built in India, dubbed a news video into Marathi and Malayalam from a single prompt while matching lip movements and facial expressions. Dubbing once required complex pipelines with many steps, he said, but live models have cut those down significantly, making it easier to create training videos and marketing content across languages.
He also showed Citi Sky, Citi’s AI-powered wealth assistant, which uses a virtual avatar to walk clients through options for a maturing certificate of deposit and complete the renewal. For such experiences, latency is critical. “If a flow breaks even for a second or a millisecond, it doesn’t work,” he said.
The stack under the hood
Shewani then walked through the tools that sit beneath these experiences.
Gemini agent is a single agent that can carry out tasks end to end. Google Cloud introduced it on October 8, 2026, and it can keep working in the cloud for hours or days, even when a user’s device is offline.
Shewani gave the example of a procurement team asking it to research options, write a request for proposal, send it to vendors, evaluate responses, and produce a shortlist. According to Google, the agent routes each task to the most suitable model, currently choosing between Gemini and Anthropic’s Claude models.
Gemini Enterprise adds guardrails and quotas for businesses, which Shewani said helps keep costs from running away, a key concern in tokenomics. Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian has said nearly 90% of Fortune 100 companies use Gemini Enterprise.
Antigravity is Google’s harness for building software, available as a command-line tool and as extensions for code editors. Shewani said most of Google’s own code is now written using the same harness, known internally as Jetski. Google CEO Sundar Pichai has said 75% of new code at Google is now generated by AI and reviewed by engineers, up from 25% in October 2024.
CodeMender scans code for vulnerabilities, creates patches, tests them in a sandbox, and can integrate with a GitHub repository. When Google DeepMind first announced it in October 2025, it had already contributed 72 security fixes to open-source projects.
Google is also giving every agent its own identity, which Shewani likened to an LDAP directory for agents, so organisations can track which agent took which action.
Choosing the right model for the job
No model can be cheapest, fastest, and most capable at once, Shewani said, so businesses need a range of models and should match each task to the right one. Google’s Flash models are its workhorses for everyday tasks that do not need complex reasoning.
“If I need to get to office every day, I don’t need to have a Ferrari,” he said. For the hardest work, there is Gemini 4 Argon.
Google made Gemini 4 Argon, its latest frontier model, generally available on October 13, 2026, at an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens 95% cheaper. Google says it ranks first on the Vals Index, and Shewani pointed to software engineering, cybersecurity, and knowledge work in finance, legal, HR, and procurement as its main use cases.
He showed two examples. In one, Argon processed more than 80,000 raw files from NASA’s open archive, including CSVs, images, PDFs, logs, and videos, and turned the analysis into a presentation that followed a custom slide template. In another, it wrote more than 5,000 lines of Python to render a photorealistic 3D library interior from scratch, with no graphics libraries or rendering engine.
Argon can also generate up to one million output tokens, not just accept one million as input. Shewani said this helps with tasks such as mathematical proofs and multi-file code generation, where producing one large output instead of many small ones uses fewer tokens and runs faster.
Questions every organization should ask
Shewani closed with the questions businesses need to start answering now that agents are here. Will agents become the primary users of their systems? Are their databases ready for swarms of agents firing queries that no person wrote? How will they manage agents that do things they are not allowed to do?
Roles will change too. “Developers are essentially going to become managers of agents,” he said. Organizations will also need to manage budgets, route tasks across a mix of models, track telemetry and memory, and prepare for agents that generate their own user interfaces.
Asked about education, he said agents are already being used to create content in multiple languages, build AI tutors, generate quizzes, and grade students. Google offers such tools through Google for Education, he noted, and many edtech companies are building their own. In education, he added, avoiding hallucination is critical, which is why grounding agents in a trusted knowledge repository matters.
For Shewani, the shift is clear. The competition between models will continue, but the advantage increasingly lies in what businesses build around them: the knowledge they give agents, the guardrails they set, and the systems ready to work alongside them.

articles.title: La France pourrait accueillir les données climatiques que Donald Trump menace d’effacer
articles.text:
Alors que des données climatiques américaines risquent de disparaître, le CNRS estime que l'infrastructure française Data Terra pourrait les accueillir. Au Sénat, une proposition de loi veut ériger la conservation des données sur le climat en mission de service public.
Une proposition de loi déposée au Sénat le 26 février ressort du bois aujourd'hui, en ce qu'elle entend confier à la recherche publique française la collecte, la diffusion et la conservation des données scientifiques sur le climat, la Terre et l'environnement. Le texte arrive alors que plusieurs bases de données climatiques américaines, riches de décennies d'observations, sont menacées de fermeture. Pour les héberger, la France pourrait s'appuyer sur l'infrastructure Data Terra, à condition de multiplier par six sa capacité de stockage. Le CNRS a chiffré l'accueil des archives menacées.
Data Terra, l’arche française des données climatiques comme potentiel refuge aux archives du climat
Aux États-Unis, plusieurs bases qui compilent des décennies de mesures climatiques et environnementales sont menacées de fermeture. L'administration américaine a en effet décidé de réduire, voire d'arrêter, certains programmes de collecte. C'est un signal d'alarme pour les réseaux internationaux d'observation, dont la France est un rouage essentiel. Car ces archives ne se rattrapent pas. La concentration de CO2 dans l'atmosphère, suivie depuis les années 1950, ne se remesure pas après coup. On observe ce qu'on ne peut pas mettre en éprouvette, des objets « trop grands comme l'océan ou l'espace » ou qui évoluent trop lentement, résume Jean-François Doussin, ancien directeur de CNRS Terre & Univers. Et le moment est plutôt mal choisi pour baisser la garde. « Nous entrons dans une ère climatique inconnue », prévient-il.
Pour mettre ces trésors à l'abri, la France ne part pas de zéro. Elle dispose de Data Terra, une infrastructure de recherche numérique nationale, reconnue à l'échelle européenne et dotée d'un budget annuel de 42 millions d'euros. Elle range déjà une immense quantité d'informations dans cinq grandes parties, dédiées aux océans, à l'atmosphère, à la biodiversité, à la terre solide et aux surfaces continentales. Elle abrite les données nationales, mais pourrait aussi recevoir, « si cela devenait indispensable, des données venant de pays étrangers », avance Jean-François Doussin.
Encore faudrait-il pousser les murs. Multiplier par six la capacité de stockage de Data Terra, de 100 à 600 pétaoctets, permettrait notamment d'accueillir les données américaines menacées d'effacement. Pour donner une idée de l'échelle, un pétaoctet équivaut à un million de gigaoctets. CNRS Terre & Univers estime le coût de l'opération à environ 17 millions d'euros. Gilles Gesquière, chercheur dans un laboratoire d'informatique lyonnais, invite toutefois à ne pas se focaliser que sur l'urgence. Pour lui, il faut aussi savoir stocker et rendre accessibles des informations « qui pourront être utiles dans trente ans ».
Une loi pour sortir les données climatiques de la précarité
Un texte a ains été déposé au Sénat le 26 février par Pierre Ouzoulias, sénateur et chercheur au CNRS, et Laurent Lafon, président de la commission de la culture, avec des collègues issus de tous les groupes parlementaires. Pierre Ouzoulias considère de façon assez paradoxale que la France a « une très grande richesse de données », mais qu'hélas aucun organisme n'a pour mission de service public de les conserver et de les valoriser. Le pays contribue pourtant à de grands programmes internationaux comme Copernicus, le Groupe sur l'observation de la Terre (GEO) ou l'Organisation météorologique mondiale. Les auteurs du texte demandent donc d'assurer la continuité de ses propres séries et de les conserver de façon souveraine. « Rester souverain sur les données permet de s'assurer qu'on ne puisse jamais en être privé », insiste Jean-François Doussin. C'est aussi ce qui permet de rester libre de les partager.
Le point faible derrière la volonté française, c'est probablement le financement. Sur le terrain, l'observation s'appuie notamment sur des services nationaux labellisés et gérés par CNRS Terre & Univers. L'un suit l'évolution des glaciers, comme la Mer de Glace. Un autre étudie la dynamique du littoral et du trait de côte, un troisième les gaz à effet de serre des tourbières.
Mais la collecte et la conservation des données passent encore très souvent par des appels à projets qui « s'étendent sur trois ans, parfois cinq », rappelle Jean-François Doussin. C'est trop court pour suivre sur des décennies la montée des mers, les glissements de terrain ou le retrait des sols argileux, qui se contractent en s'asséchant. Pierre Ouzoulias craint de son côté que les aléas budgétaires et les réorganisations de l'enseignement supérieur et de la recherche ne fragilisent cette mission. Que ce soit pour les navires océanographiques, les stations d'altitude ou les postes en Arctique et en Antarctique, l'effort budgétaire doit durer. « Et le risque serait de penser que d'autres pays feront ces observations à notre place », avertit Jean-François Doussin.
Ces relevés ne profitent pas qu'aux laboratoires, car assureurs, professionnels du bâtiment et agriculteurs y puisent aussi des informations précieuses. Elles aideront même à « adapter nos villes au climat de demain », selon Gilles Gesquière, qui codirige un programme national de recherche sur la ville durable et les bâtiments innovants. Pour étudier les îlots de chaleur urbains et la pollution, il faut des relevés ininterrompus, explique-t-il, et le vent et la pluie pèsent lourd dans la gestion de la pollution. Encore faut-il que ces données restent faciles à trouver, accessibles, interopérables et réutilisables, selon le principe FAIR qu'il défend. Cécile Callou, déléguée scientifique à la gestion des données à CNRS Écologie & Environnement, évoque des téraoctets qui dorment sur des ordinateurs et des disques durs, sans compter les données restées dans des carnets de terrain, qui sont de « véritables mines d'or ». Mais on ne pourra pas tout garder, prévient-elle, faute de moyens et à cause de l'empreinte écologique des centres de données. Il faudra trier, avec l'aide de comités scientifiques.

articles.title: Blue quiere que dejes el iPhone por un Android con un agente de IA dentro. La gran duda es cómo pagarlo
articles.text:
El ecosistema de smartphones está suficientemente consolidado, es muy difícil que una nueva marca logre hacerse hueco. Pero eso no implica que los recién llegados dejen de intentarlo, sobre todo si se presentan con algo único: Blue, una startup respaldada por Y Combinator, quiere anticiparse a los grandes fabricantes con un móvil orquestado por un agente IA. Ya se puede comprar en Estados Unidos, aunque con matices.
El Blue Phone. Este es un teléfono Android que admite aplicaciones del sistema operativo desde Google Play. El uso es el habitual en un smartphone, lo que cambia es el alcance de la IA: mientras Siri y Gemini tienen limitado el acceso al hardware y resto de apps, el agente del Blue Phone puede controlar por completo su entorno. Es justo lo que lo hace diferencial.
Blue es la capa inteligente que funciona en segundo plano y que orquesta todo lo que sucede en el móvil. Prioriza notificaciones, añade contexto para que sean fáciles de entender y de responder, organiza las citas pendientes, controla el flujo diario y puede interactuar con el resto de apps para ejecutar tareas de manera autónoma. La empresa plantea un agente IA móvil en toda la extensión del concepto.
Primero en un Google Pixel. Blue OS, el sistema del Blue Phone, es una capa sobre Android que podría funcionar en otros teléfonos. La empresa no permite descargar dicha capa ni la ofrece aún como servicio, sí dispone de un primer Blue Phone que es un Google Pixel 10 Pro. ¿Quieres probar ya mismo la experiencia? Si entregas tu iPhone, Blue te da a cambio uno de sus Pixel modificados con el sistema agéntico.
La empresa ofrece la beta sobre los citados Google Pixel 10 Pro: acceder a ellos cuesta 1.299 dólares (o también se puede cambiar el iPhone, como comentaba). Este precio supone un sobrecoste de 300 dólares sobre lo que ya vale el móvil de Google que sirve como base. Es solo el principio de lo que hay que pagar por un agente IA 100 %.
¿Cuánto va a costar realmente? El Blue Phone con hardware propio es un móvil que la empresa venderá en 2027 y que ya se puede reservar (por 100 dólares, reembolsables). Actualmente, el sistema funciona sobre hardware conocido. Y en ninguno de los dos viene incluido el uso del agente más allá de un periodo inicial: mientras la beta del Pixel trae tres meses gratuitos, la del futuro Blue Phone solo incluirá uno.
La empresa prevé que el coste de la IA empiece en los 20 dólares mensuales. Con distintos niveles de uso y límites aún no especificados. Dado que un agente IA, operativo todo el tiempo en el móvil, consume una altísima capacidad de los modelos, esos 20 dólares podrían quedarse cortos demasiado pronto.
Todo apunta a que el Blue Phone funciona (y funcionará) con modelos de IA en la nube. El futuro teléfono vendrá con modelos locales en los que apoyarse, pero el servicio principal seguirá orientado a LLMs fuera del teléfono. Blue no detalla qué funciona offline: el móvil podrá usarse sin conexión a Internet como cualquier Android, aunque seguramente se reduzcan las capacidades del agente si no está conectado.
La privacidad, el otro peaje. En el móvil tenemos la vida al completo. Datos personales, fotos privadas, agenda... Darle a una IA control total supone confiarle, literalmente, nuestra vida. En este punto, Blue asegura que guarda las contraseñas y datos sensibles en una bóveda cifrada (AES-256-GCM): el asistente puede usarla sin ver su contenido. El resto de datos sincronizados con su nube sí quedan en parte accesibles para el agente, con el riesgo de privacidad que ello supone.
Detrás de Blue hay exingenieros de Google Assistant y Gemini Live, no son precisamente ajenos al mundo de la IA. Mientras Google y Apple terminan por liberar un agente propio y capaz para sus sistemas, empresas como Blue tienen una oportunidad única para aprovechar ese espacio sin cubrir. Lo que está por ver es si la solución agéntica termina convenciendo a los usuarios.

articles.title: Energiesparen: Aufklärung oder Nudging – was wirkt wirklich?
articles.text:
Energiesparen: Was Aufklärung und Nudging wirklich bringen
Energiesparen ist eine Frage der Motivation. Doch wie genau motiviert man Menschen am besten? Eine deutsch-schwedische Studie hat zwei Ansätze empirisch miteinander verglichen: Erstens das sogenannte „Nudging“ – also das mentale „Hinschubsen“ in Richtung energiersparender Verhaltensweisen. Zweitens den „Kompetenz-Boost“ – also die Aufklärung darüber, auf welche Weise sich Energie sparen lässt.
Für einen 24 Wochen langen Versuch rekrutierte das Forschungsteam 140 Studierende in einem Stockholmer Wohnheim und teilte sie in drei Gruppen auf. Die Mitglieder der Nudging-Gruppe bekamen über ein personalisiertes Dashboards wöchentlich mitgeteilt, wieviel Strom sie im Vergleich zum Durchschnitt der Teilnehmenden verbraucht haben – und wieviel im Vergleich zu den sparsamsten 15 Prozent. Das ganze wurde durch fröhliche oder stirnrunzelnde Emojis garniert.
Ein Sechstel eingespart
Die „Booster“ bekamen Aufkleber mit QR-Codes ausgehändigt, die sie auf ihre elektrischen Geräte kleben sollten. Über diese Codes konnten sie regelmäßig neue Spartipps aufrufen – etwa Rezepte zum Kochen mit der Mikrowelle, Hinweise zum Abtauen des Kühlschranks oder zur Reinigung des Radiators. Daneben gab es noch eine unbeeinflusste Kontrollgruppe.
Das zentrale Ergebnis: Beide Versuchsgruppen konnten ihren Stromverbrauch gegenüber der Kontrollgruppe um ungefähr ein Sechstel senken. Der Unterschied zwischen Nudging und Aufklärung war minimal.
Wenig dazugelernt
Allerdings ließen die Einsparungen bei beiden Gruppen gegen Ende des Versuchs wieder nach. Das ist besonders erstaunlich bei der Aufklärungsgruppe. Eigentlich hatten die Forschenden erwartet, dass die regelmäßigen Tipps zu einer höheren Kompetenz in Sachen Energiesparen führen, und damit zu wachsenden Einsparungen. Doch in abschließenden Wissenstests schnitten beide Versuchsgruppen kaum besser ab als die Kontrollgruppe.
Den größten Einfluss auf die erzielte Senkung hatte das Verbrauchsniveau vor dem Versuch. Logisch: Wer viel verbraucht, kann auch viel sparen. Ein weiterer Einflussfaktor war die generelle Kompetenz und Motivation zum Energiesparen. Da die Teilnahme am Versuch freiwillig war, haben sich möglicherweise viele ohnehin schon motivierte Menschen angemeldet. Die Forschenden räumen selbst ein, dass diese Vorselektion die Ergebnisse verfälscht haben könnte. Das bedeutet: In der breiten Bevölkerung sind die Effekte möglicherweise geringer.
Trotzdem gibt es auch eine positive Erkenntnis aus der Studie: Offenbar bringt es schon etwas, überhaupt die Aufmerksamkeit auf das Thema Energiesparen zu lenken – egal, auf welche Weise.

articles.title: 25 years later, Xbox is trying to reinvent itself again
articles.text:
Microsoft has spent the past 25 years trying to shake up the game console market. The original Xbox, which launched on November 15th in 2001, took on an industry dominated by Sony and Nintendo. Twenty-five years later, Xbox finds itself in a similar position. It’s not starting from scratch this time around, but to reach another 25-year milestone, it needs to do something radically different.
25 years later, Xbox is trying to reinvent itself again
Xbox has always been about trying something new, so what does Microsoft do next?
The original Xbox was radically different. Born out of a fear of Sony putting a PC in the living room, Microsoft built its first game console around familiar PC technology. A custom Intel Pentium III processor powered the original Xbox, alongside an Nvidia GPU and 64MB of unified RAM. It was different from the fully custom architectures that Sony and Nintendo used at the time, allowing Microsoft to entice developers to its platform with tools that were more familiar to PC game makers.
Microsoft also included two hardware features that were unusual for a console at the time: a built-in hard drive and Ethernet port. The hard drive let game developers cache content without having to rely fully on optical discs, and Xbox players could also use it for game saves without having to purchase a separate memory card. You could even rip CDs to an Xbox and listen to custom soundtracks while playing games.
Xbox wasn’t the first to bring online gaming to consoles, but Microsoft took a different approach. Instead of relying on a built-in modem like Sega’s Dreamcast, Microsoft included an Ethernet port, anticipating a shift toward broadband internet connections. Xbox Live, which launched in November 2002, really nailed the entire online experience. There were friends lists, unique gamertags, voice chat through a bundled headset, and integrated multiplayer services. Microsoft created an entire platform for online gaming, making it easier for developers to support and fundamentally changing how people played games together.
The Xbox 360 took these ideas a step further, with swappable hard drives, digital game downloads, wireless controllers, and backward compatibility. It also turned Microsoft’s game console into an entertainment hub for the living room, complete with streaming video apps. Kinect was perhaps its most radical addition. Launched in 2010, the motion-sensing device used cameras and microphones to let players control games with their bodies and voices. It quickly became the fastest-selling consumer electronics device in early 2011.
But the success of Kinect and Microsoft’s ambition to turn Xbox into a home entertainment device helped lead to its first major strategic misstep with the Xbox One. Microsoft positioned the successor to the Xbox 360 around TV, entertainment, and an always-online future, instead of focusing on the games that had made Xbox successful. Its plans for online DRM and restrictions on used games sparked a huge backlash, while bundling Kinect pushed the console’s price $100 above Sony’s PlayStation 4. Six months after launch, Microsoft was forced to drop Kinect from the Xbox One console bundle to close that price gap.
The Xbox One showed what happens when Microsoft loses sight of what gamers want. The company spent most of that generation playing catch-up to Sony’s impressive PlayStation 4 sales. But its weakened position also forced Microsoft to once again try something radically different with Xbox Game Pass.
Introduced in 2017, Game Pass shook up the very economics of how people play games. The subscription service lets you access hundreds of games instead of buying them individually. Microsoft went on an acquisition spree to power its Game Pass ambitions, buying up smaller studios, Bethesda, and eventually Activision Blizzard.
Game Pass has become one of Xbox’s most compelling features, but it has also raised difficult questions about the economics of putting all of Microsoft’s first-party games into a subscription service on day one. It has pleased Xbox fans, but Microsoft hasn’t demonstrated that it can turn the service into the mass-market success it once envisioned. Microsoft has also stopped regularly disclosing subscriber numbers, making it harder to judge if the service is growing or not.
These days, Microsoft is spinning many Xbox plates. The Xbox Series X and S consoles that launched in 2020 are way behind Sony’s PS5 sales numbers, and Xbox Cloud Gaming hasn’t yet been able to reach the millions more players that Microsoft has always wanted for its ecosystem.
Xbox Cloud Gaming promised to make games accessible on phones and tablets without needing a dedicated console, and combined with Microsoft’s messy project to bring Xbox games to PS5 and Nintendo consoles, the efforts have raised questions about what the Xbox brand actually represents these days. Microsoft hasn’t quite decided whether it wants to be a full third-party publisher, an ecosystem owner, or an unusual combination of both.
Some of Microsoft’s recent radically different Xbox bets haven’t paid off, so it’s now turning its attention to a much smaller Xbox division, with a restructuring that will see overall Xbox headcount reduced by 20 percent by the end of Microsoft’s fiscal year in June 2027. “I believe the future of gaming will look more like its beginning, when a small team with a big idea could change how the world plays,” Xbox CEO Asha Sharma wrote in a message to Xbox employees today.
Microsoft is celebrating 25 years of Xbox today with an event in Seattle for fans, where it’s launching Xbox Playback, a personalized look back at players’ 25-year Xbox history. There will be more fan-focused announcements throughout the day, but I’m not expecting any news on the next Xbox console. The celebration is awkwardly timed, because rumors have suggested that Microsoft is also preparing for more Xbox layoffs in November, during the same month it’s celebrating a milestone.
The reset also comes as Microsoft is preparing for a next-generation Xbox console, codenamed Project Helix, which will play both Xbox games and PC titles. It sounds like an effort to combine Windows and Xbox like never before. The next Xbox could also play every Xbox game ever made, thanks to Microsoft’s impressive bets on backward compatibility over the years.
It’s an interesting full-circle moment. The original Xbox was essentially a PC built for the living room. Project Helix appears to be taking a similar approach, but this time around bringing the flexibility of PC gaming into a console experience. If Microsoft gets it right, it could open Xbox up to a much bigger library of games, and entice people trying to decide between a console or a gaming PC.
The problem for Xbox is getting consumers to care about this next console, especially when its games are available on PC and sometimes on Sony’s and Nintendo’s platforms. “Xbox has the best console ecosystem around, packed with consumer-friendly features like free cloud saves, Game Pass, and my preferred controller,” says Jon Clarke, cofounder and editor-in-chief of DayOne. “None of these things are particularly sexy or flashy. They’re simply features that work, and that can make them difficult to get customers excited about.”
Rebuilding the Xbox brand and launching a new console gives Microsoft an unusual opportunity to make another bold bet on the future, just like it did 25 years ago. But the risks this time around are greater, after more than a decade of trying and failing to catch up to the competition.
“Up against competitors that have firmly established their place in the market, Xbox finds itself in a difficult position,” says Clarke. “Rebuilding the brand will be an expensive endeavor, and the bold ambition of combining the best of console gaming with the openness and flexibility of PC is easier said than done.”
Xbox also needs good games, and after years of studio acquisitions it now has plenty of IP to play with. “Many of those franchises have lost their luster owing to years of mismanagement and potentially a generalized lack of vision,” says Jez Corden, executive editor at Windows Central. “Microsoft from the top will need to be willing to invest here to ensure Xbox’s franchises can not only find new audiences, but simply maintain what they already have.”
Xbox also faces the challenge of RAMageddon’s impact on the hardware industry right now, pushing the prices of components beyond levels that consumers can comfortably afford. “If Xbox is to reclaim any of its former glory, innovating on the costs of the traditional video game ‘console’ will be absolutely paramount, otherwise it’s hard to imagine that it will continue to exist in its current form,” says Corden.
A console projected to cost between $1,200 and $1,800 won’t grow the Xbox ecosystem. It could make more sense to let PC makers build their own Xbox hardware, opening up the platform to a wider range of prices and devices rather than relying on expensive flagship consoles.
Twenty-five years ago, Microsoft built a PC and called it an Xbox. Now it’s preparing to build something that looks increasingly like a PC again, only this time it needs to convince people that it should still be called an Xbox. Microsoft has another opportunity to shake up the console industry, but its biggest challenge might be convincing players that Xbox needs to exist as a console at all.
The pad
- Protesters break into Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam. Protesters broke into the construction site of a new Microsoft data center in Amsterdam earlier this week. Around 100 people made it into the site, with some scaling a crane to place a “fuck AI” banner. Protesters also unfurled a “Microsoft powers genocide” banner on the construction site, and chanted “Microsoft has got to go” and “free Palestine.” There has been intense opposition to new data centers in Amsterdam, after the city banned new projects until 2030. Microsoft will be the sole tenant of this new data center, and the project is proceeding as it was planned as far back as 2016, before a ban was put in place.
- Microsoft is reportedly “winding down” a cloud AI deal with Oracle. Bloomberg reports that Microsoft has been turning off rented capacity from Oracle, after declining to renew a 2023 deal. Oracle has been using older-generation Nvidia chips, reportedly making the renting deal less useful to the software maker. Microsoft is also reportedly reconsidering deals to rent server capacity from so-called “neoclouds” to power its AI efforts.
- GTA VI will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming for Xbox One consoles. Microsoft and Rockstar Games have officially confirmed that Grand Theft Auto VI will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming next week, but there’s a pretty big catch. You’ll only be able to access the game using an Xbox Series S / X or Xbox One console. That’s unusual as you can normally stream Xbox Cloud Gaming titles to phones, PCs, TVs, tablets, and even web browsers. Microsoft also effectively has an exclusive on streaming Grand Theft Auto VI from the cloud for launch, albeit only to Xbox consoles.
- Microsoft’s DLSS competitor is out for the Xbox Ally X and works in handheld mode. Microsoft is now rolling out Automatic Super Resolution (Auto SR), an upscaling technology that competes with Nvidia’s DLSS, for the Xbox Ally X, Xbox Ally X20, and select Windows Copilot Plus PCs. The full release of Auto SR now works while you’re playing handheld and running on battery, and it also supports games running at 1080p. Previously, Auto SR was also limited to frame rates of “around” 60 to 75fps, but support for a new Auto SR Performance mode will allow you to hit frame rates of up to 120fps. The new performance mode and compatibility with Auto HDR is rolling out through Windows updates.
- Hackers are already exploiting an Outlook spoofing vulnerability. Microsoft is urging IT admins to install its latest Outlook patch this week, after it discovered a flaw that is being actively exploited. Hackers can send a specially crafted message to Outlook users that would force them to connect to an attacker-controlled network where authentication hashes could be stolen to impersonate users. Microsoft has marked this as moderate, but security researchers say a stolen hash can open the door to many other parts of a network, beyond just a mailbox.
- Anthropic has its own AI-powered office suite now. Microsoft has ruled the productivity software world for decades with its own Office suite, but Anthropic unveiled new tools this week that are targeted at knowledge workers. Claude Meetings, Claude Sheets, and Claude Whiteboards are all what they sound like, equivalents to Microsoft’s Office apps that join Claude Docs, Slides, and others. The tools are some of the company’s first native products for non-technical workers and are the latest AI-shaped warning shot against Microsoft’s Office empire.
- Microsoft is bringing two popular Sysinternals tools to Linux and macOS. Linux users are getting a native version of Autoruns, the popular utility for managing what apps run at startup in Windows. Process Explorer, which is essentially a more powerful Task Manager, is also arriving on macOS. These are the latest Sysinternals tools to arrive on non-Windows platforms, as Neowin notes Sysmon, Procmon, and ProcDump are all available for Linux, and ZoomIt for macOS.
- Microsoft’s Project Zenith devices are now available. At IFA earlier this year Microsoft and AMD both announced Project Zenith, a new “distraction-free Windows experience” for developers. This tweaked version of Windows 11 is now launching first on new AMD Ryzen AI Halo devices. You don’t need a whole new device to take advantage of the config tweaks of Project Zenith, as developers can use Microsoft’s Windows Developer Config from GitHub.
I’m always keen to hear from readers, so please drop a comment here, or you can reach me at notepad@theverge.com if you want to discuss anything else. If you’ve heard about any of Microsoft’s secret projects, you can reach me via email at notepad@theverge.com or speak to me confidentially on the Signal messaging app, where I’m tomwarren.01. I’m also tomwarren on Telegram, if you’d prefer to chat there.
Thanks for subscribing to Notepad.

articles.title: NVIDIA CEO and Co-Founder Jensen Huang Resigns, Effective Immediately
articles.text:
We pulled today’s planned review because, well, there is huge news in the world of technology. Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of NVIDIA, marking the end of an era.
In a brief press release published by NVIDIA a bit before 6:00am PT, the company announced that Jensen Huang, the co-founder and CEO of NVIDIA, has resigned from the company effective immediately. He will be replaced on an interim basis by Colette Kress, NVIDIA’s current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, while the company undertakes a search for a permanent CEO.
Jensen Huang’s Resignation
Officially, NVIDIA and its board have not commented on why Huang is resigning. However, the NVIDIA leader and his reputation have been very publicly impaired in recent weeks by the allegations of multiple extramarital affairs with significant geopolitical considerations. The first of which involved a Chinese citizen, and attracted the attention of the US government due to concerns over Huang being the target of a foreign intelligence effort. That affair was confirmed by Huang and the company on Sunday, when Huang sent out an email to the company apologizing for his actions.
The events behind that letter had already spurred NVIDIA’s Board of Directors to initiate an independent investigation, with the company hiring Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz and former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim to lead the investigation.
More recently, yesterday the New York Times reported on a second affair. This one involved an NVIDIA employee, Kimberly Powell, who is NVIDIA’s Vice President of Health Care. Following that news story, media reports indicated that NVIDIA’s Board of Directors held a same-day meeting to discuss the fate of Huang and the company.
But whatever the underpinning reasons, the situation has escalated to the point where Huang is resigning from NVIDIA, effective immediately. And with it, NVIDIA’s Board is taking a number of steps to ensure the continuity and stability of the company.
For the time being, NVIDIA’s CFO Colette Kress will be stepping up to lead the company on an interim basis. Kress has been a steady hand at NVIDIA for over a decade, though with a primary focus on financial matters for the rapidly growing company. NVIDIA is due to report its Q3’2027 earnings next week on Tuesday, November 17th, a call that Kress will now lead.
Meanwhile, the NVIDIA Board is initiating a search for a permanent CEO to replace Huang. With Huang having no clearly-defined successor within NVIDIA, the Board has stated that they will be looking at candidates from both inside and outside of the company.
Huang’s resignation has also triggered the Board to appoint a chairperson for the first time in its history. Harvey C. Jones, a Managing Partner at Square Wave Ventures and formerly the CEO of Synopsys, will serve as the Chair of the Board.
Replacing a Singular Leader
Jensen Huang’s resignation leaves NVIDIA in the position of trying to replace a CEO who has been a singular leader for NVIDIA since its inception. As one of NVIDIA’s co-founders (and the only still involved in the business), Huang has been with the company since its beginning and been at the center of defining the company’s vision. Huang well-known for his hands-on management style, which saw him operate with over 60 direct reports and a very centralized management structure with him at the top. This has allowed Huang to take the company in the direction he wants to go – and make risky bets on things like CUDA and automotive – but it means that his unplanned resignation leaves a large hole in NVIDIA’s managerial structure.
Looking to ensure the stability of the company, the NVIDIA Board has already stated that it has “full confidence in Colette and the leadership team,” and that they “expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.” Meanwhile in her first comment as NVIDIA’s CEO, Peters has stated that under her watch, NVIDIA “will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader.”
And whatever the circumstances are behind Huang’s resignation, publicly the company is parting with Huang on friendly terms. The announcement from the company included a brief comment thanking Jensen “for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.”
With that said, it is difficult to imagine who will – or even could – take the reins from Jensen to serve as the company’s new leader. While Patrick is out on assignment this week, I pinged him for his thoughts on the matter, which he summed up rather succinctly: “Jensen is a singular leader in the industry who made a big bet on, and then inspired the industry to develop the current advancements in AI. These will not be easy shoes for NVIDIA to fill.”
Similarly, I have covered NVIDIA’s wares for 21 years and periodically met with Huang for almost as long. NVIDIA has always been Jensen’s company, for both the good and the bad that come with a having a strong-but-demanding leader at the top. A Steve Jobs comparison might be apt here, but even as a co-founder himself, Jobs was never quite so heavily integrated into Apple like Huang is at NVIDIA. Though both were visionaries for their respective industries, which means that recent events have not just cost NVIDIA their leader, but the AI and graphics industries are similarly losing one of their biggest driving forces.
Final Words
The sheer speed of the events surrounding Jensen Huang’s resignation mean that even with today’s announcement, a lot of questions remain. More than just who will replace Huang as the permanent CEO, what kind of changes will they enact at NVIDIA as they eventually make their own mark on the company? Will Huang’s departure eventually bring about a change to NVIDIA’s dual focus on hardware and software, which has come in large part due to having a both a business-savvy and highly-capable engineer at the top? And how will this impact the AI industry, which NVIDIA’s modern fortune is built from, and which NVIDIA is currently the de facto leader of?
Answers will undoubtedly be slower to arrive than the turmoil that surrounds Huang’s departure. But as the company’s investigations move forward and the Board winnows down the field to find a new CEO, those answers will arrive. Replacing Jensen Huang will be an incredibly difficult task, but in the wide field of talent in Silicon Valley, there is someone out there who will be up to the challenge.
What a POS

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
- November 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Regensburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Regensburg. Original written by Karoline Stürmer. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- S. Maier, R. Spachtholz, K. Glöckl, C. M. Bustamante, S. Lingl, M. Maczejka, J. Schön, A. Riedel, K. Richter, F. J. Giessibl, F. P. Bonafé, M. A. Huber, A. Rubio, J. Repp, R. Huber. Tracking electrons at the space-time limit. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (8): 961 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01932-0

articles.title: Hackers Target N-central Zero-Days as N-able Rushes Patches
articles.text:
N-able has rolled out patches for several of the zero-days a researcher dropped over the weekend and warned of in-the-wild activity targeting them.
Security researcher Sean Bales published details and proof-of-concept (PoC) on more than 30 N-central vulnerabilities he calls Able2Shell, saying he did not responsibly disclose them because he was unhappy with N-able not patching two flaws he previously reported in another product.
On Monday, the company took hosted N-central environments offline to investigate the security defects and develop fixes, urging customers to disconnect their on-premises deployments as well.
Although patches have been developed only for the more important bugs, N-able has brought the hosted environments back online, saying the risk is largely mitigated.
According to the company, all the vulnerabilities that could be exploited without authentication have been resolved, with fixes prioritized based on severity and exploitability.
“The remaining vulnerabilities require an authenticated N-central account often with elevated privileges, or additional conditions that limit exploitability, and will be addressed through subsequent hotfixes as we continue to prioritize the security and protection of our customers,” N-able says.
The resolved vulnerabilities include CVE-2026-125883 (multiple XXE issues, CVSS score of 9.3), CVE-2026-125878 (XSS flaws, CVSS score of 8.7), CVE-2026-125879 (privilege escalation, CVSS score of 8.6), CVE-2026-125880 (XSS, CVSS score of 8.3), CVE-2026-125881 (SSRF, CVSS score of 9.3), and CVE-2026-91000 (missing authentication, leading to privilege escalation, CVSS score of 8.4).
Additionally, the update resolves CVE-2026-125882 (path traversal to remote code execution, CVSS score of 8.6), which was reported by Nate Fair of Sprocket Security.
N-central 2026.4 HF2 includes the necessary patches, and all on-premises N-central deployments should be updated as soon as possible, as attackers are already probing exposed instances, the company notes.
“We are observing scanning activity associated with the publicly released proof-of-concept code, but we have seen no indications of compromise within N-central hosted servers,” N-able says.
Cybersecurity firm Defused says initial scanning started on Monday: “We have seen opening of anonymous agent sessions, pulling appliance config and hitting the remote-control endpoint without auth. These pathways are part of the 0-day exploit surface.”
N-able also refuted Bales’s claim that it ignored responsible disclosure, noting that the researcher did not contact it through its established reporting channels regarding the dropped vulnerabilities. However, it made no mention of previous vulnerability reports submitted by the researcher.
“Publishing exploit code before customers have had the chance to act doesn’t make anyone safer. It hands attackers a head start. This is a moment for our industry to recommit to putting customers first and honoring that duty to protect: being diligent, being transparent, and being measured in how we act,” N-able president and CEO John Pagliuca said.

articles.title: Nine Korean startups vie for a spot in Disrupt 2027's Startup Battlefield 200 competition | TechCrunch
articles.text:
TechCrunch’s yearly Startup Battlefield 200 competition sees hundreds of companies from across the world trying every year to get a chance to pitch in front of VCs and the international tech community at the TechCrunch Disrupt conference.
This week, nine early-stage South Korean startups pitched at DETO 2026, a technology conference in Seoul, to earn a spot in next year’s Startup Battlefield 200.
The startups work across the deep tech sector, including healthcare, fintech, energy, semiconductors, and AI. All nine startups are looking to enter the U.S. market as part of the broader international expansion plans.
Voinosis, which develops AI to detect changes in brain health through voice analysis, won the competition. The other eight startups are listed below in alphabetical order.
Voinosis
Voinosis is developing an AI tool that analyzes speech patterns such as pitch, pauses, rhythm, and response times to detect changes linked to brain health. Each voice check takes less than five minutes.
The company says its technology has been tested in Greek, Japanese, and English, and its product doesn’t require separate training for each language. In a clinical study involving 146 participants, the startup claims its tech achieved 88% accuracy in screening for potential cognitive issues.
Voinosis targets hospitals, senior living facilities, insurers, and individual consumers. It also plans to link voice checks with cognitive training, assessments, and treatment provided by healthcare professionals.
The startup was founded by Grace Shin, who spent more than 25 years as an otologic surgeon. The startup is currently raising a Series A round and has already secured a South Korean pharmaceutical company as a strategic investor.
Awesome Lab
Awesome Lab, based in Seoul, makes ThermoFlux, a heating system that uses water electrolysis and ionization to generate heat. The system can manage heat production for buildings, water supply, and industrial processes. The company says its technology can reduce energy consumption and carbon emissions.
For its international expansion, Awesome Lab is taking a different approach in each market. In the U.S., it plans to supply core OEM modules and work with boiler, water heater, and HVAC companies on product development.
Crosshub
Crosshub helps travelers and international visitors verify their identities and set up payment methods abroad. Its platform, IDBlock, combines identity verification and payment services using self-sovereign identity (SSI) and zero-knowledge proof.
The company says its platform helps users prove their identity across borders without sharing unnecessary personal information. Crosshub is also integrating this technology with payment systems to improve access to financial services for travelers.
DeepFusion AI
DeepFusion AI has developed a 4D radar-based imaging system with additional sensors for autonomous mobility, robotaxi, maritime surveillance, and defense applications. The system combines RF sensors with radar and lidar to detect objects, movement, or distance without a direct line of sight. All sensors are supposedly packed into a single, customizable unit.
EFLOW
EFLOW develops special motors that can produce more torque, or rotational force, while taking up less space for use in robots, drones, satellites, and other mobility applications. The startup also develops actuators that control how robotic joints move.
Otiton Medical
Otiton Medical makes two medical devices: One specializes in measuring body temperature, while another can capture ear canal images and analyze the eardrum. The company says its AI was trained on about 55,000 images of eardrums, and the device has received medical certification in South Korea.
Riibotics
Riibotics says it can deploy robots into warehouses within a day. Riibotics wants to reduce deployment costs for warehouses by streamlining setup, which includes infrastructure setup, warehouse mapping, system integration through custom middleware, task programming, and safety checks.
Ternell
Ternell, a semiconductor startup based in Ulsan, is developing a new type of memory to help AI chips use less power.
Unlike conventional two-state memory, Ternell’s T-SRAM system adds a third state for more efficient data storage. Founded in 2019 by KyungRok Kim, a former Samsung Electronics engineer, Ternell reports that tests with 28-nanometer chips showed a 33% to 102% increase in memory capacity per area, and a 55% to 71% reduction in energy needed to access data, compared with conventional SRAM.
Testbank
Testbank is a Korean edtech startup developing Solve, an app that converts printed study materials, such as workbooks and test-prep books, into interactive digital versions.
The startup uses AI to identify question and answer spaces in publishers’ PDF files while preserving the original layout. Solve lets you write answers directly on the page and be graded automatically.

articles.title: Nvidia tenta acalmar funcionários após saída de Jensen Huang
articles.text:
A saída repentina de Jensen Huang do comando da Nvidia levou os novos líderes da companhia a enviar mensagens aos funcionários nesta quinta-feira (12). Em comunicados internos obtidos pelo Business Insider, a CEO interina, Colette Kress, e o novo presidente do conselho, Harvey Jones, buscaram transmitir confiança na continuidade dos negócios e explicaram como será conduzida a transição.
Kress agradeceu à equipe pela dedicação durante o período de turbulência e afirmou que a empresa realizará reunião geral com os funcionários em 18 de novembro, às 14h (horário de Brasília). O encontro deverá abordar o futuro da companhia.
“Esta empresa conquistou tanto por causa do trabalho que todos vocês realizam todos os dias”, escreveu a executiva. Ela também destacou a importância dos funcionários, clientes e parceiros para as atividades da Nvidia.
A CEO interina afirmou ainda que a companhia tem um papel importante na construção das tecnologias que impulsionam a revolução da inteligência artificial (IA) e que há muito trabalho pela frente.
Nvidia procura substituto definitivo para Jensen Huang
- Em outro comunicado, Harvey Jones confirmou que o conselho de administração iniciou a busca por um substituto permanente para Huang. Segundo ele, a seleção considerará candidatos internos e externos à companhia;
- Jones também explicou que Kress foi escolhida para assumir o comando interinamente enquanto o processo acontece. A executiva ocupa o cargo de diretora financeira da Nvidia há mais de 13 anos e, segundo o presidente do conselho, teve papel importante no crescimento da empresa e em sua estratégia de capital;
- “O conselho tem plena confiança na capacidade de Colette de cumprir nossos compromissos com acionistas, clientes, parceiros e com cada um de vocês”, escreveu Jones;
- O executivo também destacou a contribuição de Huang para a trajetória da Nvidia, que ajudou a desenvolver a computação acelerada, consolidou o mercado moderno de unidades de processamento gráfico (GPUs, na sigla em inglês) e construiu plataforma utilizada no desenvolvimento da IA;
- Jones assumiu a presidência do conselho de administração, tornando-se o primeiro a ocupar essa função na história da companhia.
Leia mais:
- Entenda a sequência de fatos que levou à saída de Jensen Huang
- Trump quer ex-CEO da Apple no comando da Nvidia após renúncia de Huang
- Saída de Jensen Huang abala Nvidia e pode redefinir o futuro da inteligência
Liderança tenta garantir continuidade dos negócios
As mensagens foram enviadas após Huang deixar os cargos de CEO e integrante do conselho de administração da Nvidia, empresa que cofundou há mais de três décadas.
Nos comunicados, os novos líderes enfatizaram a experiência da equipe e a estrutura da companhia como elementos importantes para atravessar o período de transição.
Jones afirmou estar confiante de que, sob a liderança de Kress e com o apoio do conselho, a Nvidia continuará expandindo seus negócios e liderando o setor.
A empresa ainda não anunciou quem ocupará definitivamente o lugar de Huang.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Un ‘USB’ universal de creación europea para dar una segunda vida a los satélites y reducir la basura espacial
articles.text: Imagen del proyecto Space USB, destacado en la plataforma CORDIS de la Comisión Europea. ¿No resulta molesto tener que viajar con varios adaptadores durante las vacaciones? Pues lo mismo ocurre en el espacio , donde las naves espaciales y los satélites suelen utilizar diferentes conectores para transmitir energía, datos y otros servicios. Un equipo internacional de investigadores ha estado estudiando si una interfaz común puede facilitar estas conexiones. Su idea, desarrollada en el marco del proyecto Space USB, financiado por la UE, se parece un poco a los puertos USB tan extendidos en el ámbito informático: una conexión normalizada admite diferentes funciones en diversos diseños de satélites. articles.title: Foundation IP For The AI Era: Why Execution Shapes SoC Cost ─ eBook
articles.text:
How an integrated foundation IP strategy can reduce execution risk, enable faster tape-out, and lower TCO.
As AI workloads push power, performance, voltage, and process variation to new limits, the economics of advanced-node SoCs are changing. In addition to the cost of the IP itself, hidden costs often arrive later in the design cycle: integration delays, schedule slips, re-spins, and missed market windows. As design complexity rises, predictable execution is becoming a critical factor in total cost of ownership (TCO) alongside power, performance, and area (PPA).
Sourcing Foundation IP piece by piece can add another layer of complexity. Logic libraries, embedded memories, I/Os, and OTP NVM IP from multiple suppliers bring different deliverables, roadmaps, support models, and integration requirements. An integrated Foundation IP platform can reduce these seams by bringing the core building blocks together as one silicon-proven, verified stack, with sign-off-ready characterization and IP + EDA co-optimization to improve PPA and accelerate implementation. This tighter alignment helps design teams move toward tape-out with greater predictability.
The impact extends beyond integration. Across HPC and Edge AI designs, improvements in PPA can translate into meaningful economic value through smaller die area, lower operating power, and increased performance, while avoiding a re-spin or major tape-out delay can protect even more value. The Synopsys eBook “Foundation IP for the AI Era” explores these tradeoffs through 3nm data center and Edge AI SoC examples, combining silicon-proven Synopsys Foundation IP PPA benchmarks with modeled cost estimates based on public market data to illustrate how execution decisions can affect TCO.
Download the eBook to see how an integrated Foundation IP strategy can help reduce execution risk, enable faster tape-out, and lower TCO for HPC and Edge AI SoCs.
